The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional, null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Cursor skill
skill.desc: Skill defined by a SKILL.md file that packages task instructions for the assistant. The allowedTools list bounds which tools the skill may invoke, argumentHint documents its expected arguments, and content holds the full definition. Use sha256 to detect tampering.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Installed skills

cursor.title: Cursor editor (AI-powered) instance
cursor.desc: Cursor AI code editor installed on the host. Queryable through it are the configured MCP servers, the global and project rules that steer the assistant, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. Useful for auditing what tools and instructions govern the AI assistant. URL: https://www.cursor.com/

cursor.mcpServer.name: cursor.mcpServer

args.name: args
args.title: Command-line arguments passed to the server command

command.name: command
command.title: Local command launched for stdio-type servers

hasEnv.name: hasEnv
hasEnv.title: Whether environment variables (for example API keys) are configured

running.name: running
running.title: Discovered MCP server asset
running.desc: Points at the asset discovered for this MCP server, anchored on this resource. The reference is typed to the `mcp` root: the resource that roots the MCP server's own tree. See ADR 030 and ADR 031.

type.name: type
type.title: Server transport type, for example "stdio" or "http"

url.name: url
url.title: Endpoint URL for sse or streamable-http servers

cursor.mcpServer.title: Cursor MCP server configuration
cursor.mcpServer.desc: Model Context Protocol server Cursor is configured to use. Stdio servers run a local command; sse and streamable-http servers connect to a url. `type` reports the transport and the hasEnv flag reports whether environment variables (often holding API keys or tokens) are configured for the server.

cursor.repo.name: cursor.repo

branch.name: branch
branch.title: Currently checked-out branch
branch.desc: The branch referenced by HEAD, for example main. Empty when HEAD is detached or cannot be read.

host.name: host
host.title: Remote host parsed from the origin URL
host.desc: For example github.com or gitlab.com. Empty when there is no remote or the URL cannot be parsed.

name.name: name
name.title: Repository slug parsed from the origin URL
name.desc: The owner-and-name path, for example mondoohq/mql. Empty when there is no remote or the URL cannot be parsed.

remotes.name: remotes
remotes.title: All configured remotes, keyed by remote name

url.name: url
url.title: Origin remote URL
url.desc: The fetch URL of the remote named origin, or the first remote found when there is no origin. Empty for a repository with no remotes.

cursor.repo.title: Cursor workspace repository
cursor.repo.desc: Git repository backing a workspace folder opened in Cursor, derived from the editor's opened-folder history and resolved through its `.git/config`. Exposes the origin remote `url`, the parsed `host` (for example github.com) and `name` (org/repo slug), the checked-out `branch`, all configured `remotes`, and the working-tree root `path`. Repositories are deduplicated by their working-tree root. Opened folders that are not git working trees are omitted.

cursor.rule.name: cursor.rule

content.name: content
content.title: Full content of the rule file

source.name: source
source.title: Path to the rule file

cursor.rule.title: Cursor rule file
cursor.rule.desc: Rule file that injects standing instructions into the Cursor assistant's context, either globally or scoped to a project. The content field holds the full rule text, which shapes how the AI behaves and is worth reviewing for injected or unexpected directives.

cursor.skill.name: cursor.skill

allowedTools.name: allowedTools
allowedTools.title: Tools the skill is allowed to use

argumentHint.name: argumentHint
argumentHint.title: Hint describing the skill's expected arguments

content.name: content
content.title: Full markdown content of the skill definition

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL identifying the skill's git origin

sha256.name: sha256
sha256.title: SHA-256 hash of the skill content, for integrity checks

source.name: source
source.title: Path to the SKILL.md file that defines the skill

cursor.skill.title: Cursor skill
cursor.skill.desc: Skill defined by a SKILL.md file that packages task instructions for the assistant. The allowedTools list bounds which tools the skill may invoke, argumentHint documents its expected arguments, and content holds the full definition. Use sha256 to detect tampering.

package.name: package
package.title: Dart/Flutter package dependency
package.desc: Single Dart or Flutter package in the software inventory, exposing its unique `id`, `name`, `version`, `purl` identifier, CPE identifiers for vulnerability matching, and the lock files that declared it.

packages.name: packages
packages.title: Dart/Flutter package inventory
packages.desc: Dart and Flutter packages resolved from a project's pubspec.lock, covering the root project, its direct dependencies, and the full transitive dependency tree. Set `path` to the directory holding the pubspec.lock.

dart.package.name: dart.package

cpes.name: cpes
cpes.title: Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) identifiers for matching against vulnerability advisories

files.name: files
files.title: Lock files that contributed this package to the inventory

id.name: id
id.title: Unique identifier for the package within the inventory

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL (purl), a standardized identifier for the package

dart.package.title: Dart/Flutter package dependency
dart.package.desc: Single Dart or Flutter package in the software inventory, exposing its unique `id`, `name`, `version`, `purl` identifier, CPE identifiers for vulnerability matching, and the lock files that declared it.

dart.packages.name: dart.packages

files.name: files
files.title: Files used to determine the packages

dart.packages.title: Dart/Flutter package inventory
dart.packages.desc: Dart and Flutter packages resolved from a project's pubspec.lock, covering the root project, its direct dependencies, and the full transitive dependency tree. Set `path` to the directory holding the pubspec.lock.

docker.name: docker

container.name: container
container.title: Single Docker container on the host
container.desc: A container on the Docker host, running or stopped, with its `state`, `status`, source `image`, startup `command`, and `labels`. The confinement settings describe what the container can reach on the host: `privileged` disables nearly every confinement at once, `capAdd` and `capDrop` adjust the capability set, `seccompProfile`, `apparmorProfile`, and `noNewPrivileges` report the process restrictions, and the namespace modes (`networkMode`, `pidMode`, `ipcMode`, `utsMode`, `usernsMode`, `cgroupnsMode`) report which host namespaces it shares. `mounts`, `devices`, and `ports` list what of the host is exposed inside it, for example `docker.containers.none(mounts.any(hostPath == "/var/run/docker.sock"))` finds containers that control the Docker daemon. Filter by state, for example `docker.containers.where(state == "running")`.

containers.name: containers
containers.title: All Docker containers on the host, running and stopped

daemon.name: daemon
daemon.title: Configuration of the Docker Engine daemon on the host

file.name: file
file.title: Dockerfile parser
file.desc: Parsed contents of a Dockerfile, giving structured access to every build instruction rather than the raw text. The `stages` field breaks a multi-stage build into its `FROM`/`RUN`/`COPY`/`ENV`/`EXPOSE`/`USER`/ `HEALTHCHECK` instructions, `instructions` returns them in file order, and `finalStage` points at the stage that produces the image. Select a file with `docker.file(path: "/path/to/Dockerfile")` and audit it, for example `docker.file("Dockerfile").stages.all(runsAsRoot == false)`.

image.name: image
image.title: Single Docker image on the host
image.desc: An image stored on the Docker host, with its content-addressable `id`, the `tags` and `repoDigests` it is known by, its `size`, and its `labels`. The image configuration reports what a container started from it runs: `user` and `runsAsRoot`, `entrypoint` and `cmd`, `exposedPorts`, the health check, and the platform (`os`, `architecture`, `variant`) and build time (`createdAt`). `containers` lists the containers created from it. Use it to inventory images and check provenance, for example `docker.images.where(tags.none(_ == /latest/))` to find images not pinned to a floating tag, or `docker.images.where(runsAsRoot)` to find images whose containers run as root unless told otherwise.

images.name: images
images.title: All Docker images stored on the host

network.name: network
network.title: Docker network
network.desc: A network defined on the Docker host, selected by `name`, for example `docker.network(name: "bridge")`. `internal` marks a network with no route to the outside, `subnets` holds the address ranges containers on it receive, and for the bridge driver `icc`, `ipMasquerade`, and `hostBindingIpv4` report whether containers on the network can reach each other, whether their traffic leaves through the host's address, and the address published ports bind to. `containers` lists the containers connected to it, for example `docker.networks.where(internal == false) { name containers.length }`.

networks.name: networks
networks.title: All networks defined on the Docker host, including the predefined bridge, host, and none

volume.name: volume
volume.title: Docker volume
volume.desc: A volume stored on the Docker host, selected by `name`, for example `docker.volume(name: "pgdata")`. `mountpoint` is the host path backing the volume, which is what a container writing to the volume ultimately writes to, and `containers` lists the containers that mount it, for example `docker.volumes.where(containers.length == 0)` for volumes nothing uses.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: All volumes stored on the Docker host, named and anonymous

docker.title: Docker host
docker.desc: Images and containers managed by the local Docker daemon. The `images` field lists every image stored on the host with its ID, tags, digests, size, and labels; `containers` lists running and stopped containers with their state, image, command, and labels. Use it to audit what is deployed on a Docker host, for example `docker.containers.where(status == /Up/)` for currently running workloads. `daemon` reports the configuration the Docker daemon runs with.

docker.container.name: docker.container

apparmorProfile.name: apparmorProfile
apparmorProfile.title: AppArmor profile the container runs with
apparmorProfile.desc: For example `docker-default` or `unconfined`. Empty when the host does not use AppArmor.

capAdd.name: capAdd
capAdd.title: Capabilities requested in addition to the engine default (e.g., CAP_NET_ADMIN)
capAdd.desc: In upper case with the CAP_ prefix, however the request spelled them.

capDrop.name: capDrop
capDrop.title: Capabilities requested to be removed from the engine default (e.g., ALL)
capDrop.desc: In upper case with the CAP_ prefix, however the request spelled them.

command.name: command
command.title: Command the container runs as its main process

cpuShares.name: cpuShares
cpuShares.title: CPU shares relative to other containers, null when left at the engine default (1024)

device.name: device
device.title: Host device exposed inside a Docker container

devices.name: devices
devices.title: Host devices exposed inside the container

hasHealthcheck.name: hasHealthcheck
hasHealthcheck.title: Whether the container has a health check
hasHealthcheck.desc: False when neither the container nor its image defines one, or when it was disabled with `--no-healthcheck`.

healthStatus.name: healthStatus
healthStatus.title: Health status (e.g., starting, healthy, unhealthy), null when the container has no health check or is not running

healthcheckInterval.name: healthcheckInterval
healthcheckInterval.title: Seconds between health checks, null when the container has no health check
healthcheckInterval.desc: Reports the engine default of 30 when the health check does not set one.

healthcheckTest.name: healthcheckTest
healthcheckTest.title: Health check command, for example ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost/"]
healthcheckTest.desc: The first entry is `CMD` or `CMD-SHELL`, or `NONE` when the image's health check is disabled. Empty when there is none.

hostConfig.name: hostConfig
hostConfig.title: Host-dependent runtime configuration
hostConfig.desc: The daemon-side `HostConfig` from container inspection, covering privilege (`Privileged`), added/dropped Linux capabilities, `NetworkMode`, port bindings, bind mounts, and restart policy. Central to container-hardening audits, for example checking `hostConfig["Privileged"] == false`.

image.name: image
image.title: Image reference the container was created from (`repo:tag`)

imageid.name: imageid
imageid.title: ID of the image the container was created from

ipcMode.name: ipcMode
ipcMode.title: IPC namespace mode (e.g., private, shareable, host, container:<id>)

memoryLimit.name: memoryLimit
memoryLimit.title: Memory limit in bytes, null when the container's memory is unlimited

mount.name: mount
mount.title: Mount in a Docker container
mount.desc: One volume, bind mount, or tmpfs mount. `hostPath` is the host side of a bind mount or the storage location of a volume, so `mounts.where(type == "bind" && hostPath == "/var/run/docker.sock")` finds a container that can control the Docker daemon.

mounts.name: mounts
mounts.title: Volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts in the container

names.name: names
names.title: Names assigned to the container (leading `/` stripped)

nanoCpus.name: nanoCpus
nanoCpus.title: CPU quota in billionths of a CPU (e.g., 500000000 for half a CPU), null when unlimited

networkMode.name: networkMode
networkMode.title: Network mode (e.g., bridge, host, none, container:<id>)

networks.name: networks
networks.title: Networks the container is connected to

noNewPrivileges.name: noNewPrivileges
noNewPrivileges.title: Whether the container's processes are prevented from gaining privileges
noNewPrivileges.desc: True when the container was started with the `no-new-privileges` security option, which stops setuid binaries and file capabilities from raising the privileges of a process. Reports the container's own option only: false when the option is absent, even if the daemon applies it to every container by default, which `docker.daemon.noNewPrivileges` reports.

pidMode.name: pidMode
pidMode.title: PID namespace mode, `host` when it shares the host's processes, empty when private

pidsLimit.name: pidsLimit
pidsLimit.title: Maximum number of processes in the container, null when unlimited

port.name: port
port.title: Port a Docker container publishes on the host

ports.name: ports
ports.title: Ports published on the host
ports.desc: The bindings the container was created with, also reported when it is stopped. `ports.where(allInterfaces)` lists the ports reachable on every host interface rather than on one address such as 127.0.0.1.

privileged.name: privileged
privileged.title: Whether the container runs privileged
privileged.desc: A privileged container keeps every capability, drops the seccomp and device restrictions, and can reach host devices directly, so it is close to running as root on the host.

readOnlyRootfs.name: readOnlyRootfs
readOnlyRootfs.title: Whether the container's root filesystem is read-only

restartMaxRetries.name: restartMaxRetries
restartMaxRetries.title: Number of restart attempts the on-failure restart policy makes, 0 when unlimited or unused

restartPolicy.name: restartPolicy
restartPolicy.title: Restart policy name (e.g., no, always, on-failure, unless-stopped)

running.name: running
running.title: The running container as its own asset
running.desc:
A container is a separate asset, not a part of this host, so its operating system is reached by resolving into it rather than by reading a field here. `docker.containers { running.packages }` connects to the container and reports the container's packages. Null when the container is not running, since there is nothing to connect to. See ADR 031.

This replaces an embedded `os` which reported the *host* for every container: an Alpine container answered with the Arch host's 1359 packages and the host's hostname. Every member of that embed was wrong in the same way, so it was removed rather than deprecated.

seccompProfile.name: seccompProfile
seccompProfile.title: Seccomp profile the container runs with
seccompProfile.desc: One of `default` (the engine's built-in profile), `unconfined` (no system call is filtered), or `custom` (another profile). A container that names no profile runs with the daemon's, which is `unconfined` when the daemon is started with `--seccomp-profile=unconfined` or the kernel lacks seccomp. A privileged container, and one whose profile allows every system call, also reports `unconfined`.

securityOptions.name: securityOptions
securityOptions.title: Security options applied to the container
securityOptions.desc: Entries such as `seccomp=unconfined`, `apparmor=unconfined`, `label=disable`, or `no-new-privileges`, as passed to the engine. A custom seccomp profile appears as `seccomp=` followed by the profile's JSON.

sourceImage.name: sourceImage
sourceImage.title: Image the container was created from
sourceImage.desc: Null when the image is no longer stored on the host.

state.name: state
state.title: Container lifecycle state (e.g., created, running, paused, restarting, exited, dead)

status.name: status
status.title: Human-readable status message (e.g., "Up 3 hours", "Exited (0) 2 days ago")

ulimit.name: ulimit
ulimit.title: Resource limit set for a Docker container

ulimits.name: ulimits
ulimits.title: Resource limits set for the container's processes
ulimits.desc: Only the limits set on the container itself; the rest come from the daemon's defaults.

user.name: user
user.title: Account the main process runs as, empty when it runs as root
user.desc: Set by the container or, when it sets none, by the image's `USER`, for example `1000:1000` or `nginx`.

usernsMode.name: usernsMode
usernsMode.title: User namespace mode, empty when the container uses the daemon's setting
usernsMode.desc: `host` turns off user namespace remapping for this container when the daemon enables it.

utsMode.name: utsMode
utsMode.title: UTS namespace mode, `host` when it shares the host's hostname, empty when private

docker.container.title: Single Docker container on the host
docker.container.desc: A container on the Docker host, running or stopped, with its `state`, `status`, source `image`, startup `command`, and `labels`. The confinement settings describe what the container can reach on the host: `privileged` disables nearly every confinement at once, `capAdd` and `capDrop` adjust the capability set, `seccompProfile`, `apparmorProfile`, and `noNewPrivileges` report the process restrictions, and the namespace modes (`networkMode`, `pidMode`, `ipcMode`, `utsMode`, `usernsMode`, `cgroupnsMode`) report which host namespaces it shares. `mounts`, `devices`, and `ports` list what of the host is exposed inside it, for example `docker.containers.none(mounts.any(hostPath == "/var/run/docker.sock"))` finds containers that control the Docker daemon. Filter by state, for example `docker.containers.where(state == "running")`.

docker.container.device.name: docker.container.device

permissions.name: permissions
permissions.title: Device cgroup permissions, a combination of r (read), w (write), and m (mknod)

docker.container.device.title: Host device exposed inside a Docker container

docker.container.mount.name: docker.container.mount

driver.name: driver
driver.title: Volume driver (e.g., local), empty for other mount types

hostPath.name: hostPath
hostPath.title: Path on the host that is mounted, empty for a tmpfs mount

mode.name: mode
mode.title: Mode options supplied with the mount (e.g., ro, z, Z)

name.name: name
name.title: Volume name, empty for other mount types

propagation.name: propagation
propagation.title: Mount propagation (e.g., rprivate, rshared, rslave), empty when not applicable

type.name: type
type.title: Mount type: bind, volume, tmpfs, image, npipe, or cluster

docker.container.mount.title: Mount in a Docker container
docker.container.mount.desc: One volume, bind mount, or tmpfs mount. `hostPath` is the host side of a bind mount or the storage location of a volume, so `mounts.where(type == "bind" && hostPath == "/var/run/docker.sock")` finds a container that can control the Docker daemon.

docker.container.port.name: docker.container.port

allInterfaces.name: allInterfaces
allInterfaces.title: Whether the port is reachable on every host interface

hostIp.name: hostIp
hostIp.title: Host address the port is bound to, empty when bound to every interface

hostPort.name: hostPort
hostPort.title: Host port, 0 when the engine picks a free port when the container starts

docker.container.port.title: Port a Docker container publishes on the host

docker.container.ulimit.name: docker.container.ulimit
docker.container.ulimit.title: Resource limit set for a Docker container

docker.daemon.name: docker.daemon

authorizationPlugins.name: authorizationPlugins
authorizationPlugins.title: Authorization plugins every Engine API request is checked against

cgroupParent.name: cgroupParent
cgroupParent.title: Parent cgroup of all containers; empty when dockerd uses its default for the cgroup driver

configFile.name: configFile
configFile.title: Daemon configuration file
configFile.desc: The file the running dockerd's `--config-file` flag names, otherwise /etc/docker/daemon.json. Reported even when it does not exist, since dockerd runs without one.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: Settings from the configuration file and the process flags
configuration.desc: Keyed by the configuration file's keys. Flags appear under the key their setting has in the file (`--host` as `hosts`, `--log-opt` as `log-opts`). dockerd refuses to start when a setting is in both, so a flag only fills in what the file leaves out, except for `runtimes`, which dockerd takes from both. Holds only what is set, no defaults.

dataRoot.name: dataRoot
dataRoot.title: Root directory of the daemon's persistent state; dockerd's default is "/var/lib/docker"

defaultRuntime.name: defaultRuntime
defaultRuntime.title: Runtime containers use unless they ask for another; dockerd's default is "runc"

experimental.name: experimental
experimental.title: Whether experimental daemon features are on; dockerd's default is false

features.name: features
features.title: Daemon features turned on (true) or off (false), for example "containerd-snapshotter"

hosts.name: hosts
hosts.title: Addresses the Engine API listens on
hosts.desc: As configured, for example "unix:///var/run/docker.sock", "fd://" (the socket systemd passes in) or "tcp://0.0.0.0:2376". When none is configured dockerd listens on "unix:///var/run/docker.sock" alone, which is what this reports then.

icc.name: icc
icc.title: Whether containers on the default bridge network can talk to each other; dockerd's default is true

insecureRegistries.name: insecureRegistries
insecureRegistries.title: Registries the daemon reaches over plain HTTP or without verifying their TLS certificate

ipForward.name: ipForward
ipForward.title: Whether dockerd turns on IP forwarding in the kernel; dockerd's default is true

iptables.name: iptables
iptables.title: Whether dockerd manages iptables rules for container networking; dockerd's default is true

liveRestore.name: liveRestore
liveRestore.title: Whether containers keep running while dockerd is down or restarting; dockerd's default is false

logDriver.name: logDriver
logDriver.title: Default logging driver for containers; dockerd's default is "json-file"

logLevel.name: logLevel
logLevel.title: Logging level of the daemon itself; dockerd's default is "info"

logOpts.name: logOpts
logOpts.title: Default options of the logging driver (for example "max-size": "10m")

noNewPrivileges.name: noNewPrivileges
noNewPrivileges.title: Whether containers run with no-new-privileges unless they opt out; dockerd's default is false

process.name: process
process.title: Running dockerd process; null when dockerd is not running or the process list cannot be read

registryMirrors.name: registryMirrors
registryMirrors.title: Registry mirrors the daemon pulls Docker Hub images through

runtimes.name: runtimes
runtimes.title: Runtimes registered besides the built-in ones
runtimes.desc: The runtime's name mapped to its binary (`path`) or, for a runtime with its own containerd shim, its `runtimeType`, from daemon.json and the --add-runtime flags together.

seccompProfile.name: seccompProfile
seccompProfile.title: Seccomp profile containers get unless they set one
seccompProfile.desc: "builtin" is Docker's default profile, which dockerd uses when none is configured. "unconfined" turns seccomp off; any other value is the path of a profile file.

selinuxEnabled.name: selinuxEnabled
selinuxEnabled.title: Whether dockerd applies SELinux labels to containers; dockerd's default is false

storageDriver.name: storageDriver
storageDriver.title: Storage driver for images and containers; empty when dockerd picks one itself

tls.name: tls
tls.title: Whether the Engine API serves TLS on its TCP listeners
tls.desc: Set by `tls`, and turned on by any `tlsverify` setting, true or false.

tlsCaCert.name: tlsCaCert
tlsCaCert.title: CA certificate file client certificates are verified against (`tlscacert`); null when not configured

tlsCert.name: tlsCert
tlsCert.title: Server certificate file the Engine API presents (`tlscert`); null when not configured

tlsKey.name: tlsKey
tlsKey.title: Private key file of the server certificate (`tlskey`); null when not configured

tlsVerify.name: tlsVerify
tlsVerify.title: Whether the Engine API requires and verifies client certificates
tlsVerify.desc: From `tlsverify`, otherwise from `tls`: `tls` alone also verifies client certificates. False when TLS is off, so a TCP listener in `hosts` with this false accepts unauthenticated clients.

ulimit.name: ulimit
ulimit.title: Default resource limit of the Docker daemon

userlandProxy.name: userlandProxy
userlandProxy.title: Whether published ports are forwarded through the userland proxy process; dockerd's default is true

usernsRemap.name: usernsRemap
usernsRemap.title: User and group that container root is remapped to (`userns-remap`); empty when user namespace remapping is off

docker.daemon.title: Docker Engine daemon configuration
docker.daemon.desc: The settings dockerd runs with, read from its configuration file (`configFile`, /etc/docker/daemon.json unless the running dockerd names another with `--config-file`) and the command-line flags of the running `process`. It reads files and the process list, not the Docker API, so it works over SSH and on images and mounted filesystems where nothing is running. Settings neither source sets report the value dockerd uses by default, as each field says. The headline audit is a TCP listener in `hosts` without `tlsVerify`, for example `docker.daemon { hosts.where(_ == /^tcp:/).length == 0 || tlsVerify }`.

docker.daemon.ulimit.name: docker.daemon.ulimit
docker.daemon.ulimit.title: Default resource limit of the Docker daemon

docker.file.name: docker.file

add.name: add
add.title: Dockerfile ADD instruction
add.desc: Files brought into the image with `ADD`, which unlike `COPY` can fetch remote URLs and auto-extract archives. The `checksum` and `excludes` flags, plus the remote-fetch capability, make `ADD` a frequent audit target.

arg.name: arg
arg.title: Dockerfile ARG instruction
arg.desc: A build argument declared with `ARG`, giving its `name` and optional `default` value. Build arguments are commonly misused to pass secrets, so their names are worth auditing.

copy.name: copy
copy.title: Dockerfile COPY instruction
copy.desc: Files copied into the image with `COPY`, including cross-stage and cross-image copies via `--from`. Auditing `from` reveals which build stages or external images contribute files to the final image.

directives.name: directives
directives.title: Parser directives declared at the top of the Dockerfile
directives.desc: Keys include `syntax` (frontend image pin, e.g. `docker/dockerfile:1.7`), `escape` (line-continuation token, default `\`), and `check` (Buildkit build-check toggles).

env.name: env
env.title: Dockerfile ENV instruction
env.desc: An environment variable declared with `ENV`, as a `name`/`value` pair. Because `ENV` values persist into the running container and image history, they are a frequent place for accidentally baked-in secrets.

expose.name: expose
expose.title: Dockerfile EXPOSE instruction
expose.desc: A network port advertised by `EXPOSE`, with its `port` number and `protocol`. A port range such as `8000-8010` has one entry per port. This documents intended listening ports, useful for reconciling against what a container actually binds.

file.name: file
file.title: File information about this Dockerfile

finalStage.name: finalStage
finalStage.title: Final stage in this Dockerfile
finalStage.desc: Shortcut to the last `docker.file.stage`, which is the one that produces the image when the build runs without `--target`. Null for an empty file.

from.name: from
from.title: Dockerfile FROM instruction
from.desc: The base image a stage is built from, parsed into its `image`, `tag`, `digest`, and optional `platform`, plus the stage `name` when written as `FROM ... AS <name>`. Pinning by `digest` rather than a floating `tag` is a common supply-chain requirement.

hasSyntaxDirective.name: hasSyntaxDirective
hasSyntaxDirective.title: Whether the Dockerfile pins a frontend via the `syntax` parser directive
hasSyntaxDirective.desc: Set when the file begins with `# syntax=<image>` (e.g. `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7`). The directive selects a specific BuildKit frontend version. Note that BuildKit-only features such as `RUN --mount=type=secret` work without this directive too, so `false` does not mean BuildKit is unused.

healthcheck.name: healthcheck
healthcheck.title: Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK instruction
healthcheck.desc: The container health probe declared with `HEALTHCHECK`: the `test` command and its timing parameters (`interval`, `timeout`, `startPeriod`, `retries`). `none` is true for `HEALTHCHECK NONE`, which disables any inherited check.

instructions.name: instructions
instructions.title: All instructions in the order they appear in the file

multiStage.name: multiStage
multiStage.title: Whether the Dockerfile defines more than one stage

oci.name: oci
oci.title: OpenContainer image annotations declared in a build stage
oci.desc: The `org.opencontainers.image.*` labels set via `LABEL` instructions in a single build stage. The standard annotations defined by the OpenContainer image specification are surfaced as named fields so you can read provenance and metadata without remembering the full annotation keys, for example the upstream repository (`source`), the commit it was built from (`revision`), the release (`version`), and the SPDX license expression (`licenses`). The `all` field holds every `org.opencontainers.*` label found on the stage, including vendor-specific annotations that have no named field. A field is empty when its annotation is not declared in the stage. Surrounding quotes are removed from values, so a quoted `LABEL` reads back unquoted; the verbatim form remains available in the stage `labels` map.

onbuild.name: onbuild
onbuild.title: Dockerfile ONBUILD instruction
onbuild.desc: A trigger instruction registered with `ONBUILD` that runs later, when an image built from this Dockerfile is used as the base of a downstream build.

run.name: run
run.title: Dockerfile RUN instruction
run.desc: A command executed at build time via `RUN`, with the raw `script`, its BuildKit flags (`mounts`, `network`, `security`), the shell-versus-exec form, and a parsed `commands` breakdown. Use `commands` to audit the programs invoked and their options, and `mountsSecret`/`mountsSsh` to spot build-time credential handling.

shell.name: shell
shell.title: Dockerfile SHELL instruction
shell.desc: The default shell used for shell-form `RUN`, `CMD`, and `ENTRYPOINT` instructions, as set by `SHELL`. Adding `-o pipefail` here is a common hardening step.

stage.name: stage
stage.title: Build stage in a Dockerfile
stage.desc: One `FROM`-rooted stage of a Dockerfile, with every instruction it contains exposed as a field: base image (`from`), environment (`env`), build arguments (`arg`), labels, commands (`run`, `cmd`, `entrypoint`), file operations (`add`, `copy`), exposed ports, health checks, volumes, and the effective user. The `runsAsRoot`, `hasHealthcheck`, and `final` predicates support common hardening audits such as checking that no stage runs as root.

stages.name: stages
stages.title: Build stages defined in this Dockerfile

stopsignal.name: stopsignal
stopsignal.title: Dockerfile STOPSIGNAL instruction
stopsignal.desc: The signal Docker sends to the container's main process on stop, as declared by `STOPSIGNAL`.

user.name: user
user.title: Dockerfile USER instruction
user.desc: The identity a stage switches to via `USER`, split into `user` and optional `group`, with `isRoot` flagging containers that would run privileged.

volume.name: volume
volume.title: Dockerfile VOLUME instruction
volume.desc: A mount point declared with `VOLUME`, whose contents are excluded from image layers and persist outside the container.

workdir.name: workdir
workdir.title: Dockerfile WORKDIR instruction
workdir.desc: The working directory set by `WORKDIR` for subsequent instructions and the container's default directory at runtime.

docker.file.title: Dockerfile parser
docker.file.desc: Parsed contents of a Dockerfile, giving structured access to every build instruction rather than the raw text. The `stages` field breaks a multi-stage build into its `FROM`/`RUN`/`COPY`/`ENV`/`EXPOSE`/`USER`/ `HEALTHCHECK` instructions, `instructions` returns them in file order, and `finalStage` points at the stage that produces the image. Select a file with `docker.file(path: "/path/to/Dockerfile")` and audit it, for example `docker.file("Dockerfile").stages.all(runsAsRoot == false)`.

docker.file.add.name: docker.file.add

checksum.name: checksum
checksum.title: SHA256 digest the remote download must match (`--checksum=sha256:...`)
checksum.desc: Empty when the flag is not set. Frequently required by audit policies to prevent unverified remote tarballs from entering the image.

chmod.name: chmod
chmod.title: Permissions applied to the copied files (`--chmod=<octal>`)

chown.name: chown
chown.title: Ownership applied to the copied files (`--chown=<user>:<group>`)

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

link.name: link
link.title: Whether `--link` was set, enabling cache-friendly layered copies

src.name: src
src.title: Source paths, URLs, or archives to add

docker.file.add.title: Dockerfile ADD instruction
docker.file.add.desc: Files brought into the image with `ADD`, which unlike `COPY` can fetch remote URLs and auto-extract archives. The `checksum` and `excludes` flags, plus the remote-fetch capability, make `ADD` a frequent audit target.

docker.file.arg.name: docker.file.arg

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

default.name: default
default.title: (optional) Default value of the variable
default.desc: The value the build uses: shell quotes are removed and variables set earlier in the Dockerfile are substituted. A reference to a variable without a value in the Dockerfile stays as written, for example `$PATH`.

docker.file.arg.title: Dockerfile ARG instruction
docker.file.arg.desc: A build argument declared with `ARG`, giving its `name` and optional `default` value. Build arguments are commonly misused to pass secrets, so their names are worth auditing.

docker.file.copy.name: docker.file.copy

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

dst.name: dst
dst.title: The destination in the image for the file(s)

from.name: from
from.title: Stage or image to copy from (`--from=<name>`)
from.desc: Set when `COPY --from=<stage>` references the output of an earlier multi-stage build or an external image such as `nginx:1.27`.

link.name: link
link.title: Whether `--link` was set, enabling cache-friendly layered copies

parents.name: parents
parents.title: Whether `--parents` was set to preserve source directory structure

src.name: src
src.title: Optional source to copy file(s) from when not using the default build context

docker.file.copy.title: Dockerfile COPY instruction
docker.file.copy.desc: Files copied into the image with `COPY`, including cross-stage and cross-image copies via `--from`. Auditing `from` reveals which build stages or external images contribute files to the final image.

docker.file.env.name: docker.file.env

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

value.name: value
value.title: Value of the variable
value.desc: The value the build sets: shell quotes are removed and variables set earlier in the Dockerfile are substituted. A reference to a variable without a value in the Dockerfile stays as written, for example `$PATH`.

docker.file.env.title: Dockerfile ENV instruction
docker.file.env.desc: An environment variable declared with `ENV`, as a `name`/`value` pair. Because `ENV` values persist into the running container and image history, they are a frequent place for accidentally baked-in secrets.

docker.file.expose.name: docker.file.expose

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

port.name: port
port.title: Port that is exposed

protocol.name: protocol
protocol.title: Protocol that is exposed (evaluates to `tcp` if not specified)

docker.file.expose.title: Dockerfile EXPOSE instruction
docker.file.expose.desc: A network port advertised by `EXPOSE`, with its `port` number and `protocol`. A port range such as `8000-8010` has one entry per port. This documents intended listening ports, useful for reconciling against what a container actually binds.

docker.file.from.name: docker.file.from

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

digest.name: digest
digest.title: Image digest, e.g. `sha256:...`; empty when referenced by tag

image.name: image
image.title: Base image repository, e.g. `alpine` or `docker.io/library/nginx`
image.desc: Global `ARG` values declared before the first `FROM` are substituted, as the build does.

name.name: name
name.title: Stage name from `FROM ... AS <name>`, empty for an unnamed stage

platform.name: platform
platform.title: Target platform for the base image (`--platform=<os>/<arch>`), empty when not set

tag.name: tag
tag.title: Image tag, e.g. `3.19`; empty when the image is pinned by digest only

docker.file.from.title: Dockerfile FROM instruction
docker.file.from.desc: The base image a stage is built from, parsed into its `image`, `tag`, `digest`, and optional `platform`, plus the stage `name` when written as `FROM ... AS <name>`. Pinning by `digest` rather than a floating `tag` is a common supply-chain requirement.

docker.file.healthcheck.name: docker.file.healthcheck

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

interval.name: interval
interval.title: Time between running the check in nanoseconds
interval.desc: 0 when `--interval` is not set, in which case Docker uses 30 seconds.

none.name: none
none.title: Whether HEALTHCHECK is set to NONE (disables any inherited healthcheck)

retries.name: retries
retries.title: Number of consecutive failures needed to report unhealthy
retries.desc: 0 when `--retries` is not set, in which case Docker uses 3.

startInterval.name: startInterval
startInterval.title: Interval between checks during start period in nanoseconds
startInterval.desc: 0 when `--start-interval` is not set, in which case Docker uses 5 seconds.

startPeriod.name: startPeriod
startPeriod.title: Start period for the container to initialize before counting retries in nanoseconds
startPeriod.desc: 0 when `--start-period` is not set, which is also Docker's default.

test.name: test
test.title: The health check test command (e.g., ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1"])

timeout.name: timeout
timeout.title: Time to wait before considering the check hung in nanoseconds
timeout.desc: 0 when `--timeout` is not set, in which case Docker uses 30 seconds.

docker.file.healthcheck.title: Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK instruction
docker.file.healthcheck.desc: The container health probe declared with `HEALTHCHECK`: the `test` command and its timing parameters (`interval`, `timeout`, `startPeriod`, `retries`). `none` is true for `HEALTHCHECK NONE`, which disables any inherited check.

docker.file.oci.name: docker.file.oci

all.name: all
all.title: Every `org.opencontainers.*` label on the stage, keyed by full annotation name
all.desc: Includes the standard annotations surfaced as named fields as well as any vendor-specific or non-standard annotations under the `org.opencontainers` namespace.

authors.name: authors
authors.title: Contact details of the people or organization responsible for the image (`org.opencontainers.image.authors`)

baseDigest.name: baseDigest
baseDigest.title: Digest of the base image this image was built on (`org.opencontainers.image.base.digest`)

baseName.name: baseName
baseName.title: Image reference of the base image this image was built on (`org.opencontainers.image.base.name`)

created.name: created
created.title: Date and time the image was built, as an RFC 3339 string (`org.opencontainers.image.created`)

description.name: description
description.title: Human-readable description of the software packaged in the image (`org.opencontainers.image.description`)

documentation.name: documentation
documentation.title: URL to get documentation about the image (`org.opencontainers.image.documentation`)

licenses.name: licenses
licenses.title: License(s) under which the contained software is distributed (`org.opencontainers.image.licenses`)
licenses.desc: An SPDX license expression, for example `Apache-2.0` or `MIT OR GPL-2.0-only`.

refName.name: refName
refName.title: Name of the reference for the image's target (`org.opencontainers.image.ref.name`)

revision.name: revision
revision.title: Source control revision the image was built from (`org.opencontainers.image.revision`)

source.name: source
source.title: URL to the source code that built the image (`org.opencontainers.image.source`)

url.name: url
url.title: URL to find more information about the image (`org.opencontainers.image.url`)

vendor.name: vendor
vendor.title: Name of the distributing entity, organization, or individual (`org.opencontainers.image.vendor`)

docker.file.oci.title: OpenContainer image annotations declared in a build stage
docker.file.oci.desc: The `org.opencontainers.image.*` labels set via `LABEL` instructions in a single build stage. The standard annotations defined by the OpenContainer image specification are surfaced as named fields so you can read provenance and metadata without remembering the full annotation keys, for example the upstream repository (`source`), the commit it was built from (`revision`), the release (`version`), and the SPDX license expression (`licenses`). The `all` field holds every `org.opencontainers.*` label found on the stage, including vendor-specific annotations that have no named field. A field is empty when its annotation is not declared in the stage. Surrounding quotes are removed from values, so a quoted `LABEL` reads back unquoted; the verbatim form remains available in the stage `labels` map.

docker.file.onbuild.name: docker.file.onbuild

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

expression.name: expression
expression.title: The triggered instruction, exactly as written after `ONBUILD`

docker.file.onbuild.title: Dockerfile ONBUILD instruction
docker.file.onbuild.desc: A trigger instruction registered with `ONBUILD` that runs later, when an image built from this Dockerfile is used as the base of a downstream build.

docker.file.run.name: docker.file.run

command.name: command
command.title: Single command parsed from a Dockerfile RUN, CMD, or ENTRYPOINT
command.desc: One entry per command in the instruction's shell pipeline. Select the program with `binary` and, for tools with subcommands, `subcommand`, for example `binary == "apt-get"` and `subcommand == "install"`, then inspect `flags` for required options such as `--no-install-recommends`.

commands.name: commands
commands.title: Individual commands parsed from the instruction
commands.desc: The script split on the shell operators `&&`, `||`, `;`, and `|` (and newlines) into separate commands, each tokenized into its executable and arguments with leading `VAR=value` assignments removed. Exec-form instructions yield a single command from the argv. Use this to audit the program invoked and its options instead of substring-matching the raw `script`. Parsing is best-effort: it does not descend into subshells or command substitutions, and redirections (`>`, `>>`, `<`, `2>&1`) appear as ordinary tokens in the following command's `args`.

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

isExecForm.name: isExecForm
isExecForm.title: Whether the instruction is written in exec form
isExecForm.desc: Exec form (`RUN ["echo", "hi"]`) executes the program directly without a shell, so pipes, redirects, and `${VAR}` expansion are not interpreted.

isShellForm.name: isShellForm
isShellForm.title: Whether the instruction is written in shell form
isShellForm.desc: Shell form (`RUN echo hi`) wraps the command in the stage `SHELL` (default `/bin/sh -c`), allowing shell expansion, pipes, and variable substitution.

mount.name: mount
mount.title: Dockerfile RUN --mount flag
mount.desc: One entry per `--mount=...` flag on a `RUN` instruction.

mounts.name: mounts
mounts.title: `--mount=...` flags applied to this RUN
mounts.desc: Each mount exposes a build-time secret, ssh agent socket, cache directory, tmpfs, or bind-mounted source.

network.name: network
network.title: `--network=...` value
network.desc: One of `default`, `none`, or `host`. Empty when the flag is not set (BuildKit treats that as `default`).

script.name: script
script.title: Raw command text of the RUN instruction

security.name: security
security.title: `--security=...` value
security.desc: One of `sandbox` or `insecure`. Empty when the flag is not set. `insecure` runs the step with elevated privileges and is commonly flagged by security policies.

docker.file.run.title: Dockerfile RUN instruction
docker.file.run.desc: A command executed at build time via `RUN`, with the raw `script`, its BuildKit flags (`mounts`, `network`, `security`), the shell-versus-exec form, and a parsed `commands` breakdown. Use `commands` to audit the programs invoked and their options, and `mountsSecret`/`mountsSsh` to spot build-time credential handling.

docker.file.run.command.name: docker.file.run.command

args.name: args
args.title: All arguments after the executable, in the order they appear

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Dash-prefixed options, e.g. ["--no-install-recommends", "-y"]
flags.desc: A flag that carries an `=`-joined value is kept as one token, so `--mount=type=bind` matches `flags.contains("--mount=type=bind")` or `flags.any(_.contains("--mount"))`, not `flags.contains("--mount")`.

subcommand.name: subcommand
subcommand.title: First non-flag argument, e.g. "install" or "add"
subcommand.desc: Empty when the command takes no subcommand. Resolved independently of flag position, so `apt-get -y install` and `apt-get install -y` both report `install`.

docker.file.run.command.title: Single command parsed from a Dockerfile RUN, CMD, or ENTRYPOINT
docker.file.run.command.desc: One entry per command in the instruction's shell pipeline. Select the program with `binary` and, for tools with subcommands, `subcommand`, for example `binary == "apt-get"` and `subcommand == "install"`, then inspect `flags` for required options such as `--no-install-recommends`.

docker.file.run.mount.name: docker.file.run.mount

env.name: env
env.title: Environment variable that exposes the secret to the RUN command

from.name: from
from.title: Stage or image to bind-mount from (`--from=<name>`)

gid.name: gid
gid.title: Owner GID for secret / ssh mounts

id.name: id
id.title: Identifier
id.desc: For `cache` mounts this is the cache id; for `secret` and `ssh` mounts this is the secret/ssh id supplied via `id=...`.

mode.name: mode
mode.title: File mode for secret / ssh mounts (octal)

required.name: required
required.title: Whether the secret or ssh mount is required to exist at build time

sharing.name: sharing
sharing.title: Cache sharing mode
sharing.desc: For `cache` mounts: `shared`, `private`, or `locked`. Empty for other types.

source.name: source
source.title: Source path or context for `bind` and `cache` mounts

target.name: target
target.title: Mount destination inside the build container

type.name: type
type.title: Mount type

uid.name: uid
uid.title: Owner UID for secret / ssh mounts

docker.file.run.mount.title: Dockerfile RUN --mount flag
docker.file.run.mount.desc: One entry per `--mount=...` flag on a `RUN` instruction.

docker.file.shell.name: docker.file.shell

command.name: command
command.title: Shell executable and flags (e.g., ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"])

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

docker.file.shell.title: Dockerfile SHELL instruction
docker.file.shell.desc: The default shell used for shell-form `RUN`, `CMD`, and `ENTRYPOINT` instructions, as set by `SHELL`. Adding `-o pipefail` here is a common hardening step.

docker.file.stage.name: docker.file.stage

file.name: file
file.title: Dockerfile this stage belongs to

final.name: final
final.title: Whether this stage is the final stage in the Dockerfile
final.desc: Only the final stage produces the image when the Dockerfile is built without `--target`.

from.name: from
from.title: Base image this stage builds on, from its `FROM` instruction

hasHealthcheck.name: hasHealthcheck
hasHealthcheck.title: Whether this stage defines a HEALTHCHECK
hasHealthcheck.desc: True when the stage's last `HEALTHCHECK` instruction defines a check. False when there is none or when it is `HEALTHCHECK NONE`, which disables any check inherited from the base image. The `healthcheck` field still returns the `NONE` instruction, with `none` set.

labels.name: labels
labels.title: LABEL instructions in this stage, as key/value pairs
labels.desc: Keys are unquoted the way the build reads them, so `LABEL "a"=b` is `labels["a"]`. Values are kept as written, including their quotes.

oci.name: oci
oci.title: OpenContainer image annotations parsed from this stage's labels

onbuild.name: onbuild
onbuild.title: ONBUILD instructions in this stage
onbuild.desc: ONBUILD instructions are deferred and run when an image built from this Dockerfile is itself used as the base image of a downstream build.

runsAsRoot.name: runsAsRoot
runsAsRoot.title: Whether this stage runs as root
runsAsRoot.desc: True when the stage's last `USER` instruction resolves to UID 0 (`root`, or a number equal to 0 such as `0` or `00`), or is set from a variable that has no value in the Dockerfile, such as an `ARG` without a default. A stage without `USER` has the user of the stage it is built from (`FROM <stage>`). A stage built from an image and without `USER` counts as root, because the image's user is not visible from the Dockerfile alone.

docker.file.stage.title: Build stage in a Dockerfile
docker.file.stage.desc: One `FROM`-rooted stage of a Dockerfile, with every instruction it contains exposed as a field: base image (`from`), environment (`env`), build arguments (`arg`), labels, commands (`run`, `cmd`, `entrypoint`), file operations (`add`, `copy`), exposed ports, health checks, volumes, and the effective user. The `runsAsRoot`, `hasHealthcheck`, and `final` predicates support common hardening audits such as checking that no stage runs as root.

docker.file.stopsignal.name: docker.file.stopsignal

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

signal.name: signal
signal.title: Signal name or number sent to the container on stop (e.g., `SIGTERM`, `9`)

docker.file.stopsignal.title: Dockerfile STOPSIGNAL instruction
docker.file.stopsignal.desc: The signal Docker sends to the container's main process on stop, as declared by `STOPSIGNAL`.

docker.file.user.name: docker.file.user

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

group.name: group
group.title: Group name or GID the stage switches to (optional)

isRoot.name: isRoot
isRoot.title: Whether the declared user is root
isRoot.desc: True when `user` is `root` or a number equal to 0 (such as `0` or `00`), or is set from a variable that has no value in the Dockerfile. The group is not considered.

user.name: user
user.title: User name or UID the stage switches to
user.desc: Variables are substituted with their values in the Dockerfile. A variable without a value stays as written, for example `$UID`.

docker.file.user.title: Dockerfile USER instruction
docker.file.user.desc: The identity a stage switches to via `USER`, split into `user` and optional `group`, with `isRoot` flagging containers that would run privileged.

docker.file.volume.name: docker.file.volume

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

docker.file.volume.title: Dockerfile VOLUME instruction
docker.file.volume.desc: A mount point declared with `VOLUME`, whose contents are excluded from image layers and persist outside the container.

docker.file.workdir.name: docker.file.workdir

context.name: context
context.title: Contextual info, where this resource is located and defined

docker.file.workdir.title: Dockerfile WORKDIR instruction
docker.file.workdir.desc: The working directory set by `WORKDIR` for subsequent instructions and the container's default directory at runtime.

docker.image.name: docker.image

architecture.name: architecture
architecture.title: Processor architecture the image targets (e.g., amd64, arm64)

author.name: author
author.title: Author recorded in the image, for example by `MAINTAINER`

cmd.name: cmd
cmd.title: Default arguments to `entrypoint`, or the command when there is no entrypoint

containers.name: containers
containers.title: Containers created from the image, running or stopped

createdAt.name: createdAt
createdAt.title: Time the image was built, null when the image does not record it

entrypoint.name: entrypoint
entrypoint.title: Command the image runs, prefixed to `cmd` (e.g., ["/docker-entrypoint.sh"])

exposedPorts.name: exposedPorts
exposedPorts.title: Ports the image declares with `EXPOSE`, as `port/protocol` (e.g., 80/tcp)
exposedPorts.desc: Exposing a port documents it, it does not publish it on the host; see `docker.container.ports` for what is published.

hasHealthcheck.name: hasHealthcheck
hasHealthcheck.title: Whether the image defines a health check
hasHealthcheck.desc: False when it defines none, or when it disables the one of its base image with `HEALTHCHECK NONE`.

healthcheckInterval.name: healthcheckInterval
healthcheckInterval.title: Seconds between health checks, null when the image has no health check
healthcheckInterval.desc: Reports the engine default of 30 when the health check does not set one.

healthcheckTest.name: healthcheckTest
healthcheckTest.title: Health check command, for example ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost/"]
healthcheckTest.desc: The first entry is `CMD` or `CMD-SHELL`, or `NONE` when the image disables its base image's health check. Empty when there is none.

id.name: id
id.title: Image ID, the content-addressable digest of the image config

layers.name: layers
layers.title: Digests of the image's filesystem layers, base layer first
layers.desc: The digests of the uncompressed layer contents (diff IDs), which stay the same whichever registry or compression the image came from, so a layer of a known base image can be found in images built from it.

os.name: os
os.title: Operating system the image targets (e.g., linux, windows)

repoDigests.name: repoDigests
repoDigests.title: Repository digests (`repo@sha256:...`) the image is published under

runsAsRoot.name: runsAsRoot
runsAsRoot.title: Whether a container started from the image runs as root
runsAsRoot.desc: True when `user` is empty, or its user part is `root` or a number equal to 0 (such as `0` or `00`). A name other than `root` counts as not root, even when the image's /etc/passwd gives it UID 0.

size.name: size
size.title: Image size in bytes, including all layers

user.name: user
user.title: Account a container started from the image runs as, empty when it runs as root
user.desc: The image's `USER`, for example `1000:1000` or `nginx`. A container can override it, which `docker.container.user` reports.

variant.name: variant
variant.title: Processor architecture variant (e.g., v7, v8), empty when the image sets none

workingDir.name: workingDir
workingDir.title: Working directory of the image's command, empty when the image sets none

docker.image.title: Single Docker image on the host
docker.image.desc: An image stored on the Docker host, with its content-addressable `id`, the `tags` and `repoDigests` it is known by, its `size`, and its `labels`. The image configuration reports what a container started from it runs: `user` and `runsAsRoot`, `entrypoint` and `cmd`, `exposedPorts`, the health check, and the platform (`os`, `architecture`, `variant`) and build time (`createdAt`). `containers` lists the containers created from it. Use it to inventory images and check provenance, for example `docker.images.where(tags.none(_ == /latest/))` to find images not pinned to a floating tag, or `docker.images.where(runsAsRoot)` to find images whose containers run as root unless told otherwise.

docker.network.name: docker.network

attachable.name: attachable
attachable.title: Whether standalone containers can connect to this swarm network

containers.name: containers
containers.title: Containers connected to the network, running or stopped

driver.name: driver
driver.title: Network driver (e.g., bridge, host, null, overlay, macvlan, ipvlan)

hostBindingIpv4.name: hostBindingIpv4
hostBindingIpv4.title: Default host address ports published on the network bind to
hostBindingIpv4.desc: The `com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4` option, for example `127.0.0.1`. Null when the network does not set it, in which case a published port binds to the daemon's default address, every interface (`0.0.0.0`) unless dockerd is started with `--ip`. Null for a network whose driver is not bridge.

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the active Exim configuration file
configPath.desc: On Debian-family systems this is `/etc/exim4/exim4.conf` when that hand-written config exists, otherwise `/etc/exim4/update-exim4.conf.conf`.

localInterfaces.name: localInterfaces
localInterfaces.title: Local interfaces parsed and normalized into a list
localInterfaces.desc: An unset or empty setting means Exim listens on every interface, reported as Exim's own default `::0` and `0.0.0.0`. Macro references such as `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` are resolved. On Debian-family systems the list comes from the generated `/var/lib/exim4/config.autogenerated` that Exim loads, so a `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` in `exim4.conf.localmacros` wins over `dc_local_interfaces`. For the installed Exim's own config, a daemon started with `-oX` reports the interfaces given there (with their `.port` suffix), taken from the running daemons or, when none runs, from `/etc/default/exim4`. Several daemons report every interface they listen on. Empty when no Exim configuration exists.

params.title: Parsed macros and main-section options
params.desc: `.ifdef` and `.ifndef` blocks are evaluated like Exim does, including tests of Exim's built-in feature macros such as `_HAVE_OPENSSL`, which are read from the installed `exim` binary.

exim.title: Exim mail transfer agent configuration
exim.desc: Exim configuration. `params` holds the macros and main-section options parsed from the active config file, covering both the Debian `update-exim4.conf.conf` key/value form and the monolithic `exim.conf` main section (options before the first `begin` block). `localInterfaces` normalizes the local interface list, handling the Debian `dc_local_interfaces` `' ; '`-separated form and the Exim `local_interfaces` list, so policies can compare it directly. By default the per-distribution config location is used; select an alternate file with `exim("/path/to/exim.conf")`.

find.title: File search results

Narrow the walk with `type` (file, directory, device, and so on), `regex` (path/name pattern), `permissions` (octal mode floor), `name` (filename glob), `depth` (maximum traversal depth), and `xdev` (whether to cross into other mounted filesystems). firefox.name: firefox

addon.name: addon
addon.title: Firefox browser addon
addon.desc: Single addon installed in a Firefox-family profile, parsed from the profile's extensions.json. Beyond `name`, `version`, and `type`, the record exposes enablement state (`active`, `userDisabled`, `disabled`), where it came from (`sourceUri`, `location`), whether auto-update is on (`autoupdate`), and the combined API `permissions` and host origins it was granted, so you can audit addon trust and overreach per user.

addons.name: addons
addons.title: All installed Firefox addons across all profiles and users

policies.name: policies
policies.title: Firefox enterprise policy configuration
policies.desc:
Effective enterprise policy configuration for a managed Firefox installation — the settings an administrator deploys to lock the browser down (TLS floor, telemetry, private browsing, sanitize-on-shutdown, locked preferences, and so on). Firefox shows this state at `about:policies`; this resource resolves it off-host from the policy file and, on Windows, additionally from the Mozilla policy keys in the registry.

`params` holds the normalized policy set — the contents of the top-level "policies" object — in the same shape regardless of which platform or source it came from, so one check works everywhere. `inputs` exposes the unmerged sources for hosts where an operator needs to see what each one contributed on its own.

Precedence follows Firefox. On Windows the registry and the policy file are combined with the registry winning per top-level policy key, and the merge is shallow: if the registry sets a policy at all, the file's entire object for that policy is discarded rather than merged into. On Linux and macOS Firefox reads exactly one policy file — on Linux the administrator-owned `/etc/firefox/policies/policies.json` outranks the install prefix, and the files are never merged with each other. Flathub's Firefox ignores both and reads `policies/policies.json` in its `org.mozilla.firefox.systemconfig` extension (`/var/lib/flatpak/extension/...`, or a user's own `~/.local/share/flatpak/extension/...`, which replaces the system one for that user). Those locations are used when the flatpak is the only Firefox on the host; when a distribution Firefox is installed too, the resource reports the distribution Firefox.

A host with no enterprise policy anywhere is the normal unmanaged state, not an error: `configured` is false, `source` is empty, and `params` is null.

unreadableAddons.name: unreadableAddons
unreadableAddons.title: Number of addon records that could not be read
unreadableAddons.desc: Counts the entries skipped while decoding every profile's extensions.json, for example an entry holding a value of a type the record does not describe, plus one for each extensions.json and each user's home the scan was not permitted to read (another user's home on a non-root scan). Those are left out of addons rather than failing the whole list, so any value above zero means addons is an incomplete view of what is installed.

firefox.title: Firefox-family browsers
firefox.desc: Installed browser addons discovered across every user account and profile for Firefox and its derivatives (Firefox Developer Edition, Nightly, LibreWolf, Waterfox, Floorp, Zen, Tor Browser, and Mullvad Browser). Iterate `addons` to inventory extensions and themes, spot disabled or side-loaded addons, and review the API permissions and host origins each addon requests. Mozilla-shipped system addons, locales, and dictionaries are filtered out.

configured.name: configured
configured.title: Whether any enterprise policy configuration was found on this host

file.name: file
file.title: Policy file that contributed to the effective configuration
file.desc: Null when the configuration came from the registry alone, or when the host is unmanaged. Compose permission and ownership checks onto it to confirm the file an administrator deployed is not writable by others.

input.name: input
input.title: Firefox enterprise policy input
input.desc: One input that contributed to the effective policy configuration, before merging: which kind of `source` it is, the `path` it was read from, and the `params` that source alone declared. Use it to see what a single source contributes when several disagree.

inputs.name: inputs
inputs.title: Unmerged configuration from each source that contributed
inputs.desc:
In increasing order of precedence, so the last entry is the one that wins a conflicting key. Empty on an unmanaged host.

Named `inputs` rather than `sources` because a resource named `firefox.policies.source` would shadow the `source` field above: `firefox.policies.source` resolves to the resource, not the field, which would put the effective-source string out of reach.

params.name: params
params.title: Normalized enterprise policy configuration
params.desc: The merged, precedence-resolved policy set, keyed by Mozilla policy name (e.g. `params["SSLVersionMin"]`, `params["SanitizeOnShutdown"]["Cookies"]`, `params["Preferences"]["security.default_personal_cert"]["Status"]`). Null on an unmanaged host, so a check against it evaluates to false rather than passing vacuously.

source.name: source
source.title: Where the effective configuration came from
source.desc: One of `file`, `registry`, or `file+registry`, and empty when the host carries no enterprise policy configuration at all.

firefox.policies.title: Firefox enterprise policy configuration
firefox.policies.desc:
Effective enterprise policy configuration for a managed Firefox installation — the settings an administrator deploys to lock the browser down (TLS floor, telemetry, private browsing, sanitize-on-shutdown, locked preferences, and so on). Firefox shows this state at `about:policies`; this resource resolves it off-host from the policy file and, on Windows, additionally from the Mozilla policy keys in the registry.

`params` holds the normalized policy set — the contents of the top-level "policies" object — in the same shape regardless of which platform or source it came from, so one check works everywhere. `inputs` exposes the unmerged sources for hosts where an operator needs to see what each one contributed on its own.

Precedence follows Firefox. On Windows the registry and the policy file are combined with the registry winning per top-level policy key, and the merge is shallow: if the registry sets a policy at all, the file's entire object for that policy is discarded rather than merged into. On Linux and macOS Firefox reads exactly one policy file — on Linux the administrator-owned `/etc/firefox/policies/policies.json` outranks the install prefix, and the files are never merged with each other. Flathub's Firefox ignores both and reads `policies/policies.json` in its `org.mozilla.firefox.systemconfig` extension (`/var/lib/flatpak/extension/...`, or a user's own `~/.local/share/flatpak/extension/...`, which replaces the system one for that user). Those locations are used when the flatpak is the only Firefox on the host; when a distribution Firefox is installed too, the resource reports the distribution Firefox.

A host with no enterprise policy anywhere is the normal unmanaged state, not an error: `configured` is false, `source` is empty, and `params` is null.

richrule.desc: Single firewalld rich rule parsed into its parts: the address family, the source and destination it matches (each with a negation flag for `NOT` address forms), and the action it takes. zone.name: zone

Audit `services`, `ports`, and `protocols` for what the zone permits, `richRules` for expressive per-source rules, and `masquerade` / `forwardPorts` for NAT behavior. Select a zone by name with `firewalld.zone(name: "public")`.

config.title: GRUB bootloader configuration
config.desc: GRUB bootloader settings drawn from /etc/default/grub and the generated grub.cfg, or from the single menu file of a GRUB legacy host. The `params` map holds the key-value defaults (for example GRUB_TIMEOUT and GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX), `entries` lists the boot entries with their kernel command lines, and `passwordProtected` reports whether superuser plus password_pbkdf2 protection is configured, a common boot-security check. Override the file locations with `grub.config(defaultsPath: "...", grubPath: "...")`.

grub.config.name: grub.config

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Boot entries the bootloader offers on the next boot
entries.desc: Read from the Boot Loader Specification files under /boot/loader/entries when grub.cfg delegates to them, which is what Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and later, CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, and Amazon Linux 2023 do, or under loader/entries on the EFI system partition, where SUSE Linux Enterprise 16 and openSUSE Leap 16 keep them, from the menu entries in grub.cfg otherwise, and from the title blocks of the menu file on a GRUB legacy host. Null when no source yields an entry, since a host whose boot entries cannot be read has none to report rather than an empty list of them, which would satisfy every assertion made over the entries.

entry.name: entry
entry.title: GRUB boot entry
entry.desc: Single boot entry, from a menu entry in grub.cfg, a Boot Loader Specification file under /boot/loader/entries or the EFI system partition's loader/entries, or a title block in the menu file of a GRUB legacy host. `parameters` and `flags` hold the kernel command line split into key-value directives and bare tokens, so a check can assert on a parameter such as audit without matching text. `cmdline` keeps the command line as it appears in the file and `kernel` names the kernel image the entry boots. `kind` separates a normal entry from a recovery, memory test, or submenu entry, and `bootable` reduces that to the distinction a control over boot parameters rests on, since only an entry that boots an operating system carries parameters to audit. `source` is the file the entry was read from.

grubPath.name: grubPath

grubPath.desc: The generated grub.cfg, or the menu file of a GRUB legacy host, which is menu.lst on Debian and Ubuntu and grub.conf on the Red Hat family and Amazon Linux 1.

params.name: params
params.title: Configuration parameters from /etc/default/grub (e.g., GRUB_TIMEOUT, GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX)
params.desc: The values grub-mkconfig uses: the defaults file, then on Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives each *.cfg file in /etc/default/grub.d in name order, where a later file overrides an earlier one. The grub2-mkconfig of SUSE, Fedora and the Red Hat family reads the defaults file alone.

passwordProtected.name: passwordProtected
passwordProtected.title: Whether GRUB password protection is enabled
passwordProtected.desc: True when grub.cfg names a superuser and carries a matching password or password_pbkdf2 credential, including a credential kept in the user.cfg file beside grub.cfg. A credential that is still an unexpanded shell variable, such as the templated block many distributions emit unconditionally, does not count. On a GRUB legacy host it is the menu-level password directive, which is what gates the interactive command line and the editing of an entry there. Null when no GRUB configuration exists, since a host that does not use GRUB is neither protected nor unprotected.

The `params` map holds the key-value defaults (for example GRUB_TIMEOUT and GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX), `entries` lists the boot entries with their kernel command lines, and `passwordProtected` reports whether superuser plus password_pbkdf2 protection is configured, a common boot-security check.
