bootable.name: bootable
bootable.title: Whether the entry boots an operating system
bootable.desc: True for a normal or recovery entry, which are the entries a control over kernel parameters applies to. False for a submenu, a memory test, and an entry that boots no kernel at all, such as one that opens the firmware settings.

cmdline.name: cmdline
cmdline.title: Kernel command line
cmdline.desc: The linux, linux16, or linuxefi line of a menu entry, the options line of a Boot Loader Specification entry, or the kernel line of a GRUB legacy entry.

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Bare kernel command line tokens, such as ro, quiet, or single

initrd.name: initrd
initrd.title: Initrd path
initrd.desc: The initrd, initrd16, or initrdefi line, with the variables GRUB expands resolved. A variable with no value expands to nothing, as it does when GRUB boots the entry, so the `$tuned_initrd` the Red Hat family appends leaves only the image paths.

kind.name: kind
kind.title: Entry role
kind.desc: One of `normal`, `recovery`, `memtest`, `submenu`, or `other`. `other` covers an entry that boots no kernel, such as one that opens the firmware settings.

parameterValues.name: parameterValues
parameterValues.title: Every value of each kernel command line parameter
parameterValues.desc: Values of each key-value token in command-line order, for a parameter the kernel reads once per occurrence. The Red Hat family's cloud images boot with `console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200n8`, which is `parameterValues["console"] == ["tty0", "ttyS0,115200n8"]`.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Kernel command line parameters
parameters.desc: Key-value tokens from the kernel command line, with a variable that the bootloader expands resolved first. When a parameter appears more than once the last occurrence wins, which is how the kernel reads most of them. `parameterValues` keeps every occurrence.

source.name: source
source.title: Path of the file the entry was read from

grub.config.entry.title: GRUB boot entry
grub.config.entry.desc: Single boot entry, from a menu entry in grub.cfg, a Boot Loader Specification file under /boot/loader/entries or the EFI system partition's loader/entries, or a title block in the menu file of a GRUB legacy host. `parameters` and `flags` hold the kernel command line split into key-value directives and bare tokens, so a check can assert on a parameter such as audit without matching text. `cmdline` keeps the command line as it appears in the file and `kernel` names the kernel image the entry boots. `kind` separates a normal entry from a recovery, memory test, or submenu entry, and `bootable` reduces that to the distinction a control over boot parameters rests on, since only an entry that boots an operating system carries parameters to audit. `source` is the file the entry was read from.

haproxy.name: haproxy

config.name: config
config.title: HAProxy configuration
config.desc: Parsed haproxy.cfg, every other file haproxy loads with `-f` (read from the running haproxy process or the haproxy systemd service and its environment files; a directory loads its `*.cfg` files), and every file pulled in by `!include` / `!includeglob` directives (HAProxy 2.4+). Exposes each section as a dedicated resource, plus a raw view over every section for types that are not modeled. Pass `init(path: "...")` to point at a non-default config file.

version.name: version
version.title: HAProxy version string extracted from the haproxy binary (e.g., "2.8.4-1")

haproxy.title: HAProxy load balancer
haproxy.desc: HAProxy daemon version and configuration. The configuration covers the global section, defaults blocks, frontends, backends, listens, the servers behind each backend, and supporting sections (resolvers, userlists, peers).

haproxy.config.name: haproxy.config

backend.name: backend
backend.title: HAProxy backend section
backend.desc: Backend server pool. Exposes the load-balancing algorithm, the servers behind it, their TLS posture (ssl/verify/ca-file) and health-check configuration (`option httpchk`/`http-check`), `default-server` defaults, stick-table/cookie persistence, request mutators, and timeouts. Useful for verifying that backend connections are encrypted and health-checked.

bind.name: bind
bind.title: HAProxy bind listener
bind.desc: Single listener address produced by a `bind` directive. A `bind a:1,b:2 ssl crt foo` directive expands into one of these per address form; the shared parameters (ssl, crt, alpn, verify, etc.) are copied onto each entry. Fields expose the listen address/port and the full TLS posture, so you can assert that exposed listeners require modern TLS and client verification.

defaults.name: defaults
defaults.title: Defaults sections: one unnamed block in classic configs, possibly several named blocks in HAProxy 2.4+

defaultsSection.name: defaultsSection
defaultsSection.title: HAProxy defaults section
defaultsSection.desc: Inherited defaults applied to every frontend, backend, and listen that doesn't override a setting locally. HAProxy 2.4+ supports multiple named defaults blocks; `name` selects which one.

file.name: file
file.title: Primary configuration file (the first file haproxy loads, defaults to /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg)

files.name: files
files.title: All configuration files visited (primary file, other `-f` files, and !included files)

frontend.name: frontend
frontend.title: HAProxy frontend section
frontend.desc: Inbound traffic acceptor. Exposes its `bind` listeners (with TLS settings), ACL definitions, request routing rules, the default backend, and the timeout/log/option set applied to client traffic. Useful for auditing which addresses and ports are exposed and whether TLS is enforced on them.

listen.name: listen
listen.title: HAProxy listen section
listen.desc: Combined frontend and backend section. Exposes the same audit surface as a backend (servers, balance, health checks) plus the frontend's `bind` listeners and ACL/routing surface, for the shorthand where a single section both accepts client traffic and defines its server pool.

peersSection.name: peersSection
peersSection.title: HAProxy peers section
peersSection.desc: Peers section used for stick-table replication between HAProxy instances. Exposes the peer servers and the replicated stick-table definitions.

resolversSection.name: resolversSection
resolversSection.title: HAProxy resolvers section
resolversSection.desc: DNS resolver pool used by `server` directives that resolve hostnames at runtime via `resolvers <name>`. Exposes the configured nameservers, retry/timeout tuning, and caching (`hold`) policy.

section.name: section
section.title: HAProxy configuration section (raw view)
section.desc: Arbitrary section addressed by type and name. Useful for sections not modeled as their own resources (mailers, cache, program, ring, http-errors, fcgi-app, crt-store) and for low-level audits that need every directive in source order.

sections.name: sections
sections.title: Every parsed section in source order, including types not exposed as dedicated resources

server.name: server
server.title: HAProxy backend server
server.desc: Single member of a backend server pool. Captures the server identity (name/address/port), TLS posture toward the backend (ssl, verify, ca-file, sni, alpn), the health check tuning (inter/rise/fall/observe), connection limits, and persistence hooks. Useful for confirming that upstream connections are encrypted, verified, and actively health-checked.

userlist.name: userlist
userlist.title: HAProxy userlist section
userlist.desc: HTTP-auth userlist consumed by `http-request auth` / `http-request deny unless { http_auth(<list>) }`. Captures users (with a flag indicating whether the password is hashed) and groups, so you can audit for cleartext (`insecure-password`) credentials.

joined.desc: True when the device belongs to at least one. False when every identity provider looked for on the platform was read and none has the device as a member. Null where no identity provider is read, and where Active Directory membership is looked for but cannot be read, such as a Linux scan without root, which cannot read sssd.conf, or a scan of a Windows disk image: no complete lookup happened there, so the device may well be a member.

idp.title: Identity provider this device belongs to
idp.desc: The identity providers the device is joined to, bound to, or registered with, alongside mdm for its management and edr for its endpoint protection. A device can belong to several at once (for example a hybrid join to Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID), so each one is its own field and is null when the device does not belong to it. Independent of MDM enrollment: a device can belong to an identity provider without being enrolled in an MDM service, and the other way round. Microsoft Entra ID is detected on Windows client editions, and Active Directory on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Others (for example FreeIPA, LDAP/Kerberos realms, or JumpCloud) can be added as fields later. This is the device's own identity, not the user-facing federation an `idp` resource describes in the SaaS providers.

idp.activeDirectory.name: idp.activeDirectory

domain.name: domain
domain.title: DNS name of the Active Directory domain, in lower case
domain.desc: For example `corp.example.com`. On Windows, a domain without a DNS name reports its NetBIOS name.

forest.name: forest
forest.title: DNS name of the Active Directory forest the domain belongs to, in lower case
forest.desc: Read on Windows and macOS. Null on Linux, where neither SSSD nor Samba keeps the forest in its configuration.

idp.activeDirectory.title: Active Directory domain membership
idp.activeDirectory.desc: The Active Directory domain the device is joined to, read from the device's own configuration without contacting a domain controller. On Windows, the machine's domain role, domain, and forest from the local security authority; on macOS, the binding of the opendirectoryd Active Directory plugin (dsconfigad); on Linux, an enabled SSSD domain with the ad identity provider (as realmd and adcli join a domain), or Samba as a member (security = ads, as winbind joins) or as an Active Directory domain controller. The resource is only returned for a member, so idp.activeDirectory not being null means the device is joined to a domain.

idp.entra.name: idp.entra

deviceId.name: deviceId
deviceId.title: ID of the device object in Microsoft Entra ID

joinType.name: joinType
joinType.title: How the device is attached to Microsoft Entra ID
joinType.desc: `joined` for a device joined to Microsoft Entra ID only, and `hybrid` for a Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device, which is also joined to an on-premises Active Directory domain. These are the device states `dsregcmd /status` reports from AzureAdJoined and DomainJoined, derived from the machine's Entra join record and its domain membership. Null when the join state cannot be read, such as on scans of a disk image, where domain membership is not available. An Entra registration (workplace join) belongs to a user profile rather than the machine, so a device that is only registered is not reported here.

tenantId.name: tenantId
tenantId.title: Entra tenant the device belongs to

idp.entra.title: Microsoft Entra ID membership
idp.entra.desc: The device's identity in Microsoft Entra ID, read on Windows from the device's Entra device certificate. The resource is only returned for a member, so idp.entra not being null means the device has an Entra device identity. `joinType` tells an Entra join from a hybrid join.

iis.name: iis

appPool.name: appPool
appPool.title: IIS application pool
appPool.desc: The worker process configuration a site or application runs under: the identity it runs as, when it recycles, and how it reacts to repeated failures. The `name` field selects a pool, for example the "DefaultAppPool" that a stock installation ships.

appPools.name: appPools
appPools.title: Application pools defined on this server
appPools.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed.

application.name: application
application.title: Application mounted under an IIS site
application.desc: An application is a configuration boundary: it runs in its own application pool and its web.config overrides what the site and the server declare. The `path` field is the virtual path it is mounted at, "/" for the site root.

applicationHost.name: applicationHost
applicationHost.title: applicationHost.config, for ownership and permission checks
applicationHost.desc:
The shared configuration file as a file, so its permissions and owner can be audited and its raw text read. Its contents are what IIS starts from, not what it ends up with: a setting overridden by a site or an application still reads here with the server-level value. Use `config`, `iis.site.config` and `iis.application.config` for the values in force.

The typed fields leave credentials behind, but this file does not: it can hold encrypted application pool passwords and machine keys, so reading its content returns whatever it holds. Null when IIS is not installed.

binding.name: binding
binding.title: Address, port and protocol an IIS site answers on

config.name: config
config.title: Configuration in force at server scope
config.desc: The defaults every site inherits unless it overrides them, equivalent to the MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST configuration path. This includes the ASP.NET sections: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, but the server-scope configuration resolves the whole inheritance chain, so they read here with the values a site inherits. Null when IIS is not installed.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: IIS configuration in force at one scope
configuration.desc:
The configuration IIS applies at a single point in its hierarchy, after the whole machine.config, root web.config, applicationHost.config, location, site and application chain has been resolved. This is what the server acts on, which is not what any one configuration file says: reading applicationHost.config directly reports a value a site or application may override, and a check written against that file passes on exactly the override it exists to catch.

The `path` field is the IIS configuration path the values were resolved at, for example "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST" for the server or "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST/Default Web Site" for a site.

A field is null when its section is not declared at this scope. The ASP.NET sections are not such a case: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, and every scope here (the server's included) resolves the inheritance chain, so they carry the effective value at each one.

Each field names the section and attribute it resolves. A setting with no field of its own is reachable at the same place through `sections`, which carries every section this scope declares under its full path.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the web server is present on this host
installed.desc: True when the shared configuration file and the IIS management assembly are both present under %windir%\system32\inetsrv. The assembly ships with the web server itself, so this stays true on an installation that omits the optional management scripting tools.

site.name: site
site.title: Website hosted by IIS
site.desc: A single site: its bindings, the application pool it runs under, the applications mounted beneath it, its log settings, and the configuration in force at the site root. The `name` field is the site name as IIS knows it, which is also what identifies the site in its configuration path.

sites.name: sites
sites.title: Websites hosted by this server
sites.desc: Every site defined on the server, running or stopped. Empty when IIS is not installed, which makes `all()` over this list vacuously true; guard on `length` or on `installed`.

version.name: version
version.title: Version reported by the installation, for example "10.0"
version.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed or the version cannot be read.

virtualDirectory.name: virtualDirectory
virtualDirectory.title: Virtual directory of an IIS application

iis.title: Internet Information Services web server
iis.desc:
IIS installation on a Windows host: the websites it serves, the application pools that run them, and the configuration in force at each level. Values are reported as IIS resolves them, after machine.config, the root web.config, applicationHost.config, location sections, a site's own web.config and a nested application's web.config have all been applied in order. A setting a site or application overrides therefore reads with the overriding value, not the one applicationHost.config declares.

On a host that does not run IIS, `installed` is false, `config` and `applicationHost` are null, and `sites` and `appPools` are empty. An empty list satisfies `all()`, so a check that iterates sites needs a `iis.sites.length > 0` guard or an `iis.installed` filter to avoid passing on a host that serves nothing.

iis.appPool.name: iis.appPool

autoStart.name: autoStart
autoStart.title: Whether the pool starts automatically with the server

disallowRotationOnConfigChange.name: disallowRotationOnConfigChange
disallowRotationOnConfigChange.title: Whether a configuration change is prevented from triggering a recycle

enable32BitAppOnWin64.name: enable32BitAppOnWin64
enable32BitAppOnWin64.title: Whether 32-bit applications are enabled on a 64-bit host

identityType.name: identityType
identityType.title: Account the worker process runs as
identityType.desc: One of "ApplicationPoolIdentity", "LocalSystem", "LocalService", "NetworkService" or "SpecificUser". ApplicationPoolIdentity gives the pool a distinct virtual account, which is what keeps one site's worker process out of another's files.

idleTimeout.name: idleTimeout
idleTimeout.title: Seconds of inactivity after which the worker process is shut down
idleTimeout.desc: 0 disables the idle timeout, which leaves a worker process resident indefinitely.

loadUserProfile.name: loadUserProfile
loadUserProfile.title: Whether the worker process loads the user profile of its identity

logEventOnRecycle.name: logEventOnRecycle
logEventOnRecycle.title: Recycle causes written to the event log
logEventOnRecycle.desc: Joined with a comma and a space, the way .NET renders a flags enum, for example "Time, Requests, Schedule, Memory". A recycle trigger that is not listed here recycles the pool without leaving a record of why, so match on the individual cause names rather than comparing the whole string.

managedRuntimeVersion.name: managedRuntimeVersion
managedRuntimeVersion.title: Managed .NET runtime version, for example "v4.0"
managedRuntimeVersion.desc: Empty for a pool that hosts no managed code.

maxProcesses.name: maxProcesses
maxProcesses.title: Worker processes the pool runs, greater than 1 for a web garden

periodicRestartMemory.name: periodicRestartMemory
periodicRestartMemory.title: Virtual memory in kilobytes that triggers a recycle, 0 when off

periodicRestartPrivateMemory.name: periodicRestartPrivateMemory
periodicRestartPrivateMemory.title: Private memory in kilobytes that triggers a recycle, 0 when off

periodicRestartRequests.name: periodicRestartRequests
periodicRestartRequests.title: Requests served before the pool recycles, 0 when recycling on requests is off

periodicRestartSchedule.name: periodicRestartSchedule
periodicRestartSchedule.title: Times of day the pool recycles at, as seconds past midnight
periodicRestartSchedule.desc: Empty when the pool does not recycle on a schedule.

periodicRestartTime.name: periodicRestartTime
periodicRestartTime.title: Seconds between scheduled recycles, 0 when recycling on an interval is off

pingingEnabled.name: pingingEnabled
pingingEnabled.title: Whether the pool health-checks its worker processes

queueLength.name: queueLength
queueLength.title: Requests queued before the pool starts rejecting them

rapidFailProtection.name: rapidFailProtection
rapidFailProtection.title: Whether the pool is disabled after repeated worker process failures

rapidFailProtectionInterval.name: rapidFailProtectionInterval
rapidFailProtectionInterval.title: Seconds over which failures are counted toward rapid fail protection

rapidFailProtectionMaxCrashes.name: rapidFailProtectionMaxCrashes
rapidFailProtectionMaxCrashes.title: Failures within the interval that disable the pool

state.name: state
state.title: Runtime state
state.desc: One of "Started", "Stopped", "Starting", "Stopping" or "Unknown", the members of the IIS object-state enumeration. Empty when the state cannot be read at all; "Unknown" is IIS itself reporting that it cannot tell.

userName.name: userName
userName.title: Account name used when identityType is "SpecificUser", empty otherwise
userName.desc: The account name only. The password configured alongside it is not reported.

iis.appPool.title: IIS application pool
iis.appPool.desc: The worker process configuration a site or application runs under: the identity it runs as, when it recycles, and how it reacts to repeated failures. The `name` field selects a pool, for example the "DefaultAppPool" that a stock installation ships.

iis.application.name: iis.application

appPool.name: appPool
appPool.title: Application pool this application runs under
appPool.desc: Null when the application names a pool the server does not define.

config.name: config
config.title: Configuration in force for this application
config.desc: Resolved at the application's own configuration path, so it reflects the application's web.config on top of everything the site and the server declare. For the root application this is the same configuration the site reports.

enabledProtocols.name: enabledProtocols
enabledProtocols.title: Protocols the application is enabled for, as a comma-separated list

path.name: path
path.title: Virtual path the application is mounted at, "/" for the site root

physicalPath.name: physicalPath
physicalPath.title: Filesystem path the application root maps to

virtualDirectories.name: virtualDirectories
virtualDirectories.title: Virtual directories declared under this application

iis.application.title: Application mounted under an IIS site
iis.application.desc: An application is a configuration boundary: it runs in its own application pool and its web.config overrides what the site and the server declare. The `path` field is the virtual path it is mounted at, "/" for the site root.

iis.binding.name: iis.binding

bindingInformation.name: bindingInformation
bindingInformation.title: Raw binding string as IIS stores it
bindingInformation.desc: For an HTTP binding this is address:port:hostname, for example "*:443:www.example.com". A binding with an empty hostname answers for every name that resolves to the address.

certificateHash.name: certificateHash
certificateHash.title: Thumbprint of the certificate bound to an HTTPS binding
certificateHash.desc: The SHA-1 hash as uppercase hex, empty for a binding with no certificate. This is a public identifier, not key material.

certificateStoreName.name: certificateStoreName
certificateStoreName.title: Certificate store the bound certificate is held in, for example "My"

hostName.name: hostName
hostName.title: Host header the binding answers for, empty when it answers for any

ipAddress.name: ipAddress
ipAddress.title: Address the binding listens on, "0.0.0.0" for every address

port.name: port
port.title: Port the binding listens on, 0 for a binding with no endpoint

sslFlags.name: sslFlags
sslFlags.title: SSL binding flags
sslFlags.desc: A bit field. 1 selects the certificate by hostname (SNI) and 2 uses the central certificate store. IIS 10 1809 and later add bits that disable transport features rather than select a certificate: 4 disables HTTP/2, 8 disables OCSP stapling, 16 disables QUIC, 32 disables TLS 1.3 over TCP and 64 disables legacy TLS. 0 means none of them are set, so test the individual bits rather than comparing the whole value.

iis.binding.title: Address, port and protocol an IIS site answers on

iis.configuration.name: iis.configuration

allowDoubleEscaping.name: allowDoubleEscaping
allowDoubleEscaping.title: Whether a doubly-escaped request is accepted
allowDoubleEscaping.desc: From requestFiltering/allowDoubleEscaping. Double escaping is how a request smuggles a path separator past a filter that only inspects the URL once.

allowHighBitCharacters.name: allowHighBitCharacters
allowHighBitCharacters.title: Whether non-ASCII characters are accepted in a URL

allowUnlistedFileExtensions.name: allowUnlistedFileExtensions
allowUnlistedFileExtensions.title: Whether unlisted file extensions are served (fileExtensions/allowUnlisted)
allowUnlistedFileExtensions.desc: Serving unlisted extensions means a file type nobody considered, dropped into the content directory, is served on request. The matching setting for verbs sits under requestFiltering/verbs/allowUnlisted in `sections`, where the two cannot be mistaken for each other.

anonymousAuthenticationUser.name: anonymousAuthenticationUser
anonymousAuthenticationUser.title: Account anonymous requests are served as (anonymousAuthentication/userName)
anonymousAuthenticationUser.desc: Empty when anonymous requests run as the application pool identity, which keeps one site's anonymous requests out of another site's files.

aspKeepSessionIdSecure.name: aspKeepSessionIdSecure
aspKeepSessionIdSecure.title: Whether classic ASP keeps the session id secure over HTTPS

authenticationMode.name: authenticationMode
authenticationMode.title: ASP.NET authentication mode (system.web/authentication/mode)
authenticationMode.desc: One of "None", "Windows", "Passport", "Forms" or "Federated". The forms fields below apply when this is "Forms".

basicAuthenticationEnabled.name: basicAuthenticationEnabled
basicAuthenticationEnabled.title: Whether basic authentication is accepted (basicAuthentication/enabled)
basicAuthenticationEnabled.desc: Basic authentication sends the password base64-encoded, which is plaintext to anything on the path unless the binding is HTTPS.

clientCertificateMappingAuthenticationEn.name: clientCertificateMappingAuthenticationEnabled
clientCertificateMappingAuthenticationEn.title: Whether client certificates are mapped to Active Directory accounts
clientCertificateMappingAuthenticationEn.desc: From clientCertificateMappingAuthentication/enabled, which resolves the certificate against the directory rather than against IIS configuration.

compilationDebug.name: compilationDebug
compilationDebug.title: Whether ASP.NET compiles debug binaries (compilation/debug)
compilationDebug.desc: Debug compilation slows every request, disables timeouts, and puts source paths into error output.

customErrorsMode.name: customErrorsMode
customErrorsMode.title: Who receives detailed ASP.NET error pages (customErrors/mode)
customErrorsMode.desc: One of "On", "Off" or "RemoteOnly". "Off" sends the exception, its message and its stack trace to every client.

customHeaders.name: customHeaders
customHeaders.title: Custom response headers, by header name (httpProtocol/customHeaders)
customHeaders.desc: The section's collection flattened to a map, so both a header that should be present ("Strict-Transport-Security") and one that should not ("X-Powered-By", which advertises the framework version) are one lookup. Empty when the section declares no headers.

deploymentRetail.name: deploymentRetail
deploymentRetail.title: Whether the application is deployed in retail mode (deployment/retail)
deploymentRetail.desc: Retail mode overrides debug, trace and detailed errors across the whole machine, whatever an individual application asks for.

directoryBrowsingEnabled.name: directoryBrowsingEnabled
directoryBrowsingEnabled.title: Whether a directory request returns a listing (directoryBrowse/enabled)
directoryBrowsingEnabled.desc: A listing hands out the names of every file in the directory, including ones no page links to.

formsCookieless.name: formsCookieless
formsCookieless.title: How forms authentication carries its ticket (forms/cookieless)
formsCookieless.desc: One of "UseCookies", "UseUri", "AutoDetect" or "UseDeviceProfile". "UseUri" puts the ticket in the URL, where it reaches proxy logs and referer headers.

formsCredentialsDeclared.name: formsCredentialsDeclared
formsCredentialsDeclared.title: Whether inline forms credentials are declared at this scope
formsCredentialsDeclared.desc: True when forms/credentials holds at least one user, which is the thing to check rather than the format it stores them in.

formsCredentialsPasswordFormat.name: formsCredentialsPasswordFormat
formsCredentialsPasswordFormat.title: Storage format of inline credentials (forms/credentials/passwordFormat)
formsCredentialsPasswordFormat.desc: One of "Clear", "SHA1" or "MD5". Null when no inline credentials are declared, which is the state to prefer: inline credentials put account material in a configuration file whatever the format.

formsProtection.name: formsProtection
formsProtection.title: Protection applied to the forms ticket (forms/protection)
formsProtection.desc: One of "All", "None", "Encryption" or "Validation". "All" both encrypts the ticket and validates it against tampering.

formsRequireSsl.name: formsRequireSsl
formsRequireSsl.title: Whether the forms ticket is only sent over HTTPS (forms/requireSSL)
formsRequireSsl.desc: A forms cookie sent in the clear is a replayable credential.

formsTimeout.name: formsTimeout
formsTimeout.title: Seconds before a forms ticket expires (forms/timeout)

handlerAccessPolicy.name: handlerAccessPolicy
handlerAccessPolicy.title: Level of access handlers are allowed (handlers/accessPolicy)
handlerAccessPolicy.desc: This is a **flags** attribute: it holds several names at once, joined with a comma and a space in the order IIS declares them. "Read, Script" is the stock value. The names are "None", "Read", "Write", "Execute", "Source", "Script", "NoRemoteWrite", "NoRemoteRead", "NoRemoteExecute" and "NoRemoteScript"; "None" appears alone when nothing is set. "Write" combined with "Script" or "Execute" lets an upload be run, so match on the names present rather than comparing the whole string.

httpCookiesHttpOnly.name: httpCookiesHttpOnly
httpCookiesHttpOnly.title: Whether cookies are marked HttpOnly (httpCookies/httpOnlyCookies)
httpCookiesHttpOnly.desc: An HttpOnly cookie is not readable from script, which is what stops a cross-site scripting flaw from becoming a stolen session.

httpCookiesRequireSsl.name: httpCookiesRequireSsl
httpCookiesRequireSsl.title: Whether cookies are only sent over HTTPS (httpCookies/requireSSL)

httpErrorsMode.name: httpErrorsMode
httpErrorsMode.title: Who receives detailed IIS error pages (httpErrors/errorMode)
httpErrorsMode.desc: One of "DetailedLocalOnly", "Custom" or "Detailed". "Detailed" sends physical paths and error details to remote clients.

iisClientCertificateMappingAuthenticatio.name: iisClientCertificateMappingAuthenticationEnabled
iisClientCertificateMappingAuthenticatio.title: Whether client certificates are mapped to local accounts
iisClientCertificateMappingAuthenticatio.desc: From iisClientCertificateMappingAuthentication/enabled. The mapping lives in IIS configuration and needs no directory to resolve.

machineKeyValidation.name: machineKeyValidation
machineKeyValidation.title: Algorithm validating view state and forms tickets (machineKey/validation)
machineKeyValidation.desc: One of "MD5", "SHA1", "3DES", "AES", "HMACSHA256", "HMACSHA384" or "HMACSHA512". "SHA1" is the value a stock installation reports and is the weakest of them. The keys on this section are dropped during collection and reach neither this field nor `sections`.

maxAllowedContentLength.name: maxAllowedContentLength
maxAllowedContentLength.title: Largest request body accepted, in bytes (requestLimits/maxAllowedContentLength)

maxQueryString.name: maxQueryString
maxQueryString.title: Longest query string accepted, in characters (requestLimits/maxQueryString)

maxUrl.name: maxUrl
maxUrl.title: Longest request URL accepted, in characters (requestLimits/maxUrl)

notListedCgisAllowed.name: notListedCgisAllowed
notListedCgisAllowed.title: Whether unlisted CGI programs may run
notListedCgisAllowed.desc: From isapiCgiRestriction/notListedCgisAllowed, which sits on the same element as the ISAPI setting above and differs only in name.

notListedIsapisAllowed.name: notListedIsapisAllowed
notListedIsapisAllowed.title: Whether unlisted ISAPI extensions may run

path.name: path
path.title: IIS configuration path these values were resolved at

removeServerHeader.name: removeServerHeader
removeServerHeader.title: Whether the Server response header is suppressed

sections.name: sections
sections.title: Every resolved configuration section, keyed by section path
sections.desc: The full result of the resolution, for reaching a setting that has no field of its own, for example `sections["system.webServer/security/dynamicIpSecurity"]["enableLoggingOnlyMode"]`. Each entry holds the section's attributes and its child elements; sections whose members carry the setting also hold a "collection" list of those members. Durations are in seconds throughout, and machineKey's validationKey and decryptionKey are dropped before the section is reported. A section that is not declared at this scope has no key here, and reading through a key that is absent yields null rather than an error.

sessionStateCookieless.name: sessionStateCookieless
sessionStateCookieless.title: How the session id is carried (sessionState/cookieless)
sessionStateCookieless.desc: One of "UseCookies", "UseUri", "AutoDetect" or "UseDeviceProfile". "UseUri" puts the session id in the URL, where it is shared by every copy of the link.

sessionStateMode.name: sessionStateMode
sessionStateMode.title: Where ASP.NET session state is kept (sessionState/mode)

sessionStateTimeout.name: sessionStateTimeout
sessionStateTimeout.title: Seconds an idle session is kept before it is abandoned (sessionState/timeout)

sslFlags.name: sslFlags
sslFlags.title: Transport requirements for requests (security/access/sslFlags)
sslFlags.desc: The names of the bits the attribute sets, drawn from "Ssl", "SslNegotiateCert", "SslRequireCert", "SslMapCert" and "Ssl128". IIS reports the attribute as a number on some installations and as names on others; both resolve here to names, and a bit with no name of its own is kept as its own number, one entry per bit, so it is not silently dropped. An empty list means requests are accepted over plain HTTP.

traceEnabled.name: traceEnabled
traceEnabled.title: Whether ASP.NET request tracing is enabled (system.web/trace/enabled)
traceEnabled.desc: Tracing exposes request contents, cookies and server variables through trace.axd.

trustLevel.name: trustLevel
trustLevel.title: Code access security level for ASP.NET applications (trust/level)
trustLevel.desc: One of "Full", "High", "Medium", "Low" or "Minimal". "Full" places no restriction on what application code may do.

windowsAuthenticationEnabled.name: windowsAuthenticationEnabled
windowsAuthenticationEnabled.title: Whether integrated Windows authentication is accepted

iis.configuration.title: IIS configuration in force at one scope
iis.configuration.desc:
The configuration IIS applies at a single point in its hierarchy, after the whole machine.config, root web.config, applicationHost.config, location, site and application chain has been resolved. This is what the server acts on, which is not what any one configuration file says: reading applicationHost.config directly reports a value a site or application may override, and a check written against that file passes on exactly the override it exists to catch.

The `path` field is the IIS configuration path the values were resolved at, for example "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST" for the server or "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST/Default Web Site" for a site.

A field is null when its section is not declared at this scope. The ASP.NET sections are not such a case: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, and every scope here (the server's included) resolves the inheritance chain, so they carry the effective value at each one.

Each field names the section and attribute it resolves. A setting with no field of its own is reachable at the same place through `sections`, which carries every section this scope declares under its full path.

iis.site.name: iis.site

appPool.name: appPool
appPool.title: Application pool the site root runs under
appPool.desc: Null when the site names a pool the server does not define, so a dangling reference is visible instead of reading as a pool with default settings.

applications.name: applications
applications.title: Applications mounted under this site, including the root application "/"

bindings.name: bindings
bindings.title: Addresses, ports and protocols the site answers on

config.name: config
config.title: Configuration in force at the site root

hsts.name: hsts
hsts.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security settings for this site
hsts.desc: The attributes of the site's hsts element, carrying "enabled", "max-age", "includeSubDomains", "preload" and "redirectHttpToHttps". Null on an IIS version that has no built-in HSTS support, where the header is set through a custom response header instead and shows up in `config.customHeaders`.

id.name: id
id.title: Numeric site id, which also keys the site's log file directory

logDirectory.name: logDirectory
logDirectory.title: Directory log files are written to, with environment variables unexpanded
logDirectory.desc: For example "%SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs\LogFiles". Each site writes into a W3SVC<id> subdirectory of this path.

logEnabled.name: logEnabled
logEnabled.title: Whether request logging is enabled for this site

logFields.name: logFields
logFields.title: Fields recorded in W3C format
logFields.desc: Joined with a comma and a space, the way .NET renders a flags enum, for example "Date, Time, ClientIP, UserName, Method, UriStem, HttpStatus". IIS keeps the selection even while another log format is active, so this is populated regardless of logFormat. Match on the individual field names rather than comparing the whole string.

logFormat.name: logFormat
logFormat.title: Log file format
logFormat.desc: One of "W3C", "IIS", "NCSA" or "Custom". Only the W3C format supports selecting which fields are recorded.

logLocalTimeRollover.name: logLocalTimeRollover
logLocalTimeRollover.title: Whether log rollover follows local time rather than UTC

logPeriod.name: logPeriod
logPeriod.title: How often a new log file is started
logPeriod.desc: One of "MaxSize", "Daily", "Weekly", "Monthly" or "Hourly". "MaxSize" rolls over on logTruncateSize instead of on a schedule.

logTarget.name: logTarget
logTarget.title: Where W3C log entries are sent
logTarget.desc: "File", "ETW", or both as "File, ETW", joined with a comma and a space the way .NET renders a flags enum. Empty on an installation that predates the setting, in which case entries go to a file.

logTruncateSize.name: logTruncateSize
logTruncateSize.title: Size in bytes at which a log file is rolled over, when logPeriod is "MaxSize"

physicalPath.name: physicalPath
physicalPath.title: Filesystem path the site root maps to
physicalPath.desc: The physical path of the root virtual directory. Empty when the site declares no root application.

serverAutoStart.name: serverAutoStart
serverAutoStart.title: Whether the site starts automatically with the server

state.name: state
state.title: Runtime state
state.desc: One of "Started", "Stopped", "Starting", "Stopping" or "Unknown", the members of the IIS object-state enumeration. Empty when the state cannot be read at all, which happens when the world wide web publishing service is not running; "Unknown" is IIS itself reporting that it cannot tell.

iis.site.title: Website hosted by IIS
iis.site.desc: A single site: its bindings, the application pool it runs under, the applications mounted beneath it, its log settings, and the configuration in force at the site root. The `name` field is the site name as IIS knows it, which is also what identifies the site in its configuration path.

iis.virtualDirectory.name: iis.virtualDirectory

path.name: path
path.title: Virtual path, "/" for the application root

config.name: config
config.title: inetd super-server configuration
config.desc: Services the inetd (or compatible) super-server is configured to launch on demand. Each active entry pairs a service with its socket type, protocol, wait mode, run-as user, and server program. The configuration is assembled from /etc/inetd.conf together with any drop-in files under /etc/inetd.d. An xinetd configuration, such as inetd.config("/etc/xinetd.conf"), is read with the files it includes, and its entries are the service blocks xinetd runs: blocks with disable = yes, or disabled by the enabled and disabled lists of the defaults block, are left out. A missing configuration yields no entries, so audits such as serviceNames.none("ftp") hold trivially on systems that don't run inetd.

Entries that are commented out with a leading # are disabled and excluded.

keystore.name: keystore
keystore.title: Java keystore or trust store
keystore.desc:
The certificates a JVM trusts, and the ones it presents. Select a store with `java.keystore("/opt/java/lib/security/cacerts")`, or reach every trust store the asset has with `java.truststores`.

The store is read straight from the file. A JKS store keeps its certificates unencrypted — only private keys are protected, and the store password guards an integrity digest rather than the contents — so no credential is needed and the store is readable on a container image or a mounted filesystem, where nothing can be executed.

jboss.title: JBoss EAP / WildFly application server
jboss.desc:
Locates a JBoss installation through JBOSS_HOME and exposes the server configuration it holds: the management section (management interfaces, security realms, the audit log and access control), the network interfaces and socket bindings, the password vault, and the subsystems declared in each profile. Nothing here needs a running JVM or the management CLI, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Both operating modes are covered. In standalone mode `config` is the profile the server is actually started with — which is not always standalone.xml, since `--server-config` selects one of the four shipped profiles. In domain mode `config` is domain.xml and `host` is the host controller's host.xml, which is where a domain keeps its management interfaces and security realms.

Every nested collection (profiles, subsystems, interfaces, socket bindings, security realms, management interfaces, audit handlers, connectors, log handlers) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-realm server keeps working when a second realm is added.

Pass `init(home: "...")` to point at an installation the discovery does not find, and `init(configFile: "...")` to read a profile other than the active one.

config.name: config
config.title: systemd journald configuration
config.desc: Configuration for the systemd journal daemon parsed from journald.conf. Exposes the [Journal] and other sections, letting you audit settings such as log Storage, Compress, retention limits, and forwarding. Access the parsed content through `sections`, or the effective values journald applies after drop-ins and defaults through `storage`, `compress`, and `forwardToSyslog`. Without an argument, the main file and drop-ins are read from /etc/systemd, /run/systemd, /usr/local/lib/systemd, and /usr/lib/systemd. With a path, for example `journald.config("/srv/journald.conf")`, that file and its `.d` drop-in directory are read instead.

compress.title: Whether journald compresses large journal entries
compress.desc: The last valid Compress assignment in the [Journal] section across journald.conf and its drop-ins. Accepts the boolean spellings journald accepts (yes, no, true, false, on, off, 1, 0, in any case); a size threshold such as `512K` also enables compression, and an empty assignment restores the default. `true` when no file sets Compress. Null when the system has no systemd-journald binary.

forwardToSyslog.name: forwardToSyslog
forwardToSyslog.title: Whether journald forwards messages to a syslog daemon
forwardToSyslog.desc: The last valid ForwardToSyslog assignment in the [Journal] section across journald.conf and its drop-ins, including vendor drop-ins such as Debian's /usr/lib/systemd/journald.conf.d/syslog.conf. Accepts the boolean spellings journald accepts, in any case. When no file sets ForwardToSyslog, the default journald was built with, as documented by the commented-out `#ForwardToSyslog=` line in the main journald.conf (`yes` on Debian and on Ubuntu up to 22.04), or `false`, the upstream default since systemd 216, when the file does not document one. The `systemd.journald.forward_to_syslog` kernel command line option, which overrides the files at boot, is not considered. Null when the system has no systemd-journald binary.

module.name: module
module.title: System kernel module information
module.desc: Single kernel module: its `name`, in-memory `size`, and whether it is currently `loaded`. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.module(name: "nf_conntrack")`) to check a specific module, or iterate from `kernel.modules` to audit the full loaded-module list. Module names are normalized the way modprobe normalizes them, so `firewire-core` and `firewire_core` select the same module and match a rule written with either spelling. Use `blacklisted`, `installBypass`, and `disabled` to express CIS-style "module must not load" controls without falling back to raw modprobe.d file parsing. Use `onDisk` to tell whether a loadable module file is available for the running kernel even when it isn't currently loaded, and `builtIn` to detect functionality compiled directly into the kernel (which is always active and cannot be blacklisted or unloaded). On FreeBSD, modules carry the names `kldstat -v` lists, such as `msdosfs` or `pci/ena`, including the modules compiled into the kernel; a loaded file name such as `zfs.ko` also selects its module.

parameter.name: parameter
parameter.title: Kernel parameter (sysctl), live and configured
parameter.desc:
One kernel parameter with the value the running kernel uses (`value`) and the value the configuration files will apply at the next boot (`configured`), kept apart so a check can require both. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.parameter("fs.protected_hardlinks")`) or iterate `kernel.sysctls`. Names use the dotted form `sysctl -a` prints; a name written with slashes is accepted too.

Configuration is read from the sysctl.d directories (/etc, /run, /usr/local/lib, /usr/lib, /lib) with the precedence systemd-sysctl applies at boot: a file hides a same-named file in a lower-priority directory, the files are applied in file name order, and the last assignment wins. An explicit assignment beats a glob, and `-name` excludes a parameter from globs. Without systemd-sysctl, /etc/sysctl.conf is applied after the sysctl.d files, as `sysctl --system` does. On BSD and macOS it is /etc/sysctl.conf (and /etc/sysctl.conf.local on FreeBSD).

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Kernel parameters map (sysctl key-value pairs)
parameters.desc: Live values only, as the kernel prints them. Use `sysctls` or `kernel.parameter` for the value the configuration files set as well. Those collapse whitespace in values (the tab in `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` becomes a space), so the same parameter can read differently here.

sysctls.name: sysctls
sysctls.title: Every kernel parameter that is live, configured, or both
sysctls.desc: A parameter set in a configuration file but not exposed by the running kernel, such as one of an unloaded module, is listed with `active` false. A glob assignment is expanded against the live parameters; one that matches none is listed under its pattern.

kernel.title: Running kernel and its modules
kernel.desc: Running kernel and its configuration surface. Exposes kernel version info, sysctl `parameters` and `sysctls`, `modules`, installed kernel versions, ASLR state (`aslr`, Linux and FreeBSD), and, on Linux, hardening state (`cmdline`, `taint`, `lockdown`) and the live patches applied in memory (`livepatch`).

kernel.aslr.name: kernel.aslr

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether ASLR is enabled (`mode > 0`)

level.name: level
level.title: Human-readable level
level.desc: On Linux one of `disabled`, `conservative`, `full`, or `unknown`. On FreeBSD one of `disabled`, `enabled`, or `unknown`.

mode.name: mode
mode.title: Raw ASLR mode value
mode.desc: On Linux, the value of /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space: `0` disabled, `1` conservative (stack, libraries, vdso), `2` full (also heap/brk). On FreeBSD, the value of kern.elf64.aslr.enable: `0` disabled, `1` enabled. `-1` when the setting is unavailable.

kernel.aslr.title: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) state
kernel.aslr.desc: Kernel userspace ASLR setting. ASLR randomizes memory layout to make memory-corruption exploits harder. On Linux the setting comes from /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space, where `mode` 2 is full randomization. On FreeBSD 13 and later it comes from kern.elf64.aslr.enable (kern.elf32.aslr.enable on 32-bit platforms), a switch that is either on or off.

kernel.cmdline.name: kernel.cmdline

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Bare flags on the kernel command line (tokens without `=`)

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Parameters parsed from `key=value` tokens
parameters.desc: When a parameter appears multiple times on the command line (e.g. `console=tty0 console=ttyS0`), the last occurrence wins. Use `raw` for full-fidelity inspection.

kernel.cmdline.title: Linux kernel boot command line
kernel.cmdline.desc: Kernel command line passed by the bootloader at boot time (the contents of /proc/cmdline). Use `parameters` for `key=value` directives and `flags` for bare tokens such as `ro`, `quiet`, or `nosmt`. The `raw` string is preserved for direct inspection or for callers that need to recover duplicate tokens.

kernel.livepatch.name: kernel.livepatch

active.name: active
active.title: Whether a live patch is applied to the running kernel
active.desc: True when a patch in /sys/kernel/livepatch is enabled. Unlike the "kernel was live-patched" reason in `kernel.taint`, which stays set once any patch was ever loaded, this reflects the patches applied now. Null when the running kernel's state cannot be read, such as in an image scan.

cves.name: cves
cves.title: CVEs the live patch client reports as fixed in the running kernel
cves.desc: Upper-case CVE IDs such as `CVE-2026-31431`. Empty when the client reports no fixes, and null when no client reports on the running kernel.

patch.name: patch
patch.title: Kernel live patch
patch.desc: A single live patch loaded into the running kernel, from /sys/kernel/livepatch/<name>.

patches.name: patches
patches.title: Live patches loaded into the running kernel
patches.desc: Null when the running kernel's state cannot be read.

provider.name: provider
provider.title: Tool that applied the live patches
provider.desc: `canonical-livepatch` when the Canonical Livepatch client is installed or one of its patches is loaded, `klp` for patches from another source, and empty when neither a client nor a patch is present. Null when the running kernel's state cannot be read.

state.name: state
state.title: Patch state reported by the live patch client
state.desc: For Canonical Livepatch, for example `applied` or `nothing-to-apply`. Null when no client reports on the running kernel.

version.name: version
version.title: Patch version reported by the live patch client, such as `121.4`
version.desc: Null when no client reports on the running kernel, including a Canonical Livepatch client that is installed but not enabled.

kernel.livepatch.title: Kernel live patching
kernel.livepatch.desc: Live patches applied to the running kernel in memory. A live patch fixes the kernel without a reboot, so it changes neither `kernel.info` nor `kernel.installed`. `active`, `provider`, and `patches` come from the kernel's livepatch interface in /sys/kernel/livepatch, whichever tool loaded the patch. `version`, `state`, and `cves` come from the Canonical Livepatch client on Ubuntu, so an audit can ask whether the running kernel carries a fix, for example `kernel.livepatch.cves.contains("CVE-2026-31431")`. Patches applied by KernelCare or Oracle Ksplice are not reported.

kernel.livepatch.patch.name: kernel.livepatch.patch

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether the patch is enabled

name.name: name
name.title: Patch name, which is also the name of the kernel module that carries it

objects.name: objects
objects.title: Kernel objects the patch changes: `vmlinux` for the core kernel, or a module name

transition.name: transition
transition.title: Whether tasks are still moving to or from the patched code

kernel.livepatch.patch.title: Kernel live patch
kernel.livepatch.patch.desc: A single live patch loaded into the running kernel, from /sys/kernel/livepatch/<name>.

kernel.lockdown.name: kernel.lockdown

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether lockdown is enforced (mode is `integrity` or `confidentiality`)

kernel.lockdown.title: Linux kernel lockdown mode
kernel.lockdown.desc: Kernel lockdown LSM state from /sys/kernel/security/lockdown. Lockdown restricts modifications to a running kernel even from root: `integrity` blocks features that could let userspace modify the kernel (kexec, /dev/mem, etc.) and `confidentiality` additionally blocks features that expose kernel memory contents. `mode` is `unavailable` when the kernel was built without lockdown support.

kernel.module.name: kernel.module

blacklisted.name: blacklisted
blacklisted.title: Whether the module is blacklisted in modprobe configuration
blacklisted.desc: True when any modprobe configuration file declares `blacklist <name>`. Blacklisted modules will not auto-load (e.g., from udev or hotplug events) but root can still force-load them with `modprobe --force` or by writing to `/sys/module/...`. CIS macOS/Linux benchmarks check for this to ensure unused filesystems/protocols stay off. On FreeBSD, true when `module_blacklist` in the loader configuration (/boot/defaults/loader.conf, /boot/loader.conf, /boot/loader.conf.d, /boot/loader.conf.local) names the module: the loader skips its `<name>_load="YES"`, but kldload, rc.conf `kld_list` and devd still load it.

builtIn.name: builtIn
builtIn.title: Whether the module is compiled into the kernel image
builtIn.desc: True when the functionality is built directly into the kernel (configured `=y`) rather than shipped as a loadable file, as listed in the running kernel's `modules.builtin` index. Built-in modules are always active: they never appear in `loaded`, have no file on disk (`onDisk` is false), and cannot be blacklisted or unloaded. On FreeBSD, true when `kldstat -v` lists the module under the kernel; such a module is also `loaded`.

disabled.name: disabled
disabled.title: Whether the module is effectively disabled
disabled.desc: True when the module is either blacklisted or has an install short-circuit rule. Use this as the canonical "module will not load without explicit override" predicate. On FreeBSD it equals `blacklisted`; only a module with no .ko file (`onDisk` false) cannot be loaded at all.

installBypass.name: installBypass
installBypass.title: Whether the module's load is short-circuited to /bin/true or /bin/false
installBypass.desc: True when any modprobe configuration file declares `install <name> /bin/false` (or `/bin/true`). This is stronger than blacklisting: even an explicit `modprobe <name>` is replaced with the no-op binary, so the module cannot be loaded without overriding the install rule. Always false on FreeBSD, which has no such rule.

loaded.name: loaded
loaded.title: Whether the module is loaded
loaded.desc: On FreeBSD, true for every module `kldstat -v` lists, which includes the modules compiled into the kernel (as `kldstat -m <name>` reports them).

onDisk.name: onDisk
onDisk.title: Whether a loadable module file is installed on disk for the running kernel
onDisk.desc: True when a `.ko` (or compressed `.ko.xz` / `.ko.zst` / `.ko.gz`) file for this module exists under `/lib/modules/<version>/`, as listed in that kernel's `modules.dep` index. This reports presence independently of `loaded`, so it answers "the module is available to load but isn't loaded right now." Modules compiled into the kernel have no file on disk and report false here (see `builtIn`). On FreeBSD, true when `<name>.ko` exists in a directory of `kern.module_path`, so kldload can load it.

size.name: size
size.title: Size of the kernel module
size.desc: On FreeBSD, the size of the .ko file the module is in, and empty for a module compiled into the kernel.

kernel.module.title: System kernel module information
kernel.module.desc: Single kernel module: its `name`, in-memory `size`, and whether it is currently `loaded`. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.module(name: "nf_conntrack")`) to check a specific module, or iterate from `kernel.modules` to audit the full loaded-module list. Module names are normalized the way modprobe normalizes them, so `firewire-core` and `firewire_core` select the same module and match a rule written with either spelling. Use `blacklisted`, `installBypass`, and `disabled` to express CIS-style "module must not load" controls without falling back to raw modprobe.d file parsing. Use `onDisk` to tell whether a loadable module file is available for the running kernel even when it isn't currently loaded, and `builtIn` to detect functionality compiled directly into the kernel (which is always active and cannot be blacklisted or unloaded). On FreeBSD, modules carry the names `kldstat -v` lists, such as `msdosfs` or `pci/ena`, including the modules compiled into the kernel; a loaded file name such as `zfs.ko` also selects its module.

kernel.parameter.name: kernel.parameter

active.name: active
active.title: Whether the running kernel exposes this parameter
active.desc: False for a configured parameter the kernel does not have, such as one of an unloaded module, a disabled feature or an absent interface. Null when no running kernel can be read, such as in an image scan.

configured.name: configured
configured.title: Value the configuration files set
configured.desc: The value of the assignment that takes effect. Null when no configuration file sets the parameter, or when every glob that matches it is excluded.

setting.name: setting
setting.title: Kernel parameter assignment
setting.desc: One `name = value` line in a sysctl configuration file.

settings.name: settings
settings.title: Every assignment that names this parameter, in the order applied
settings.desc: Includes assignments that do not take effect, such as an earlier one overridden by a later file or a glob overridden by an explicit assignment. Exactly one has `effective` set when `configured` is set.

value.name: value
value.title: Value the running kernel uses
value.desc: Whitespace runs are collapsed to one space, so a value with several parts compares equal to the same value in a configuration file: `32768 60999`, where `kernel.parameters` has `32768\t60999`. Null when the parameter is not active.

kernel.parameter.title: Kernel parameter (sysctl), live and configured
kernel.parameter.desc:
One kernel parameter with the value the running kernel uses (`value`) and the value the configuration files will apply at the next boot (`configured`), kept apart so a check can require both. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.parameter("fs.protected_hardlinks")`) or iterate `kernel.sysctls`. Names use the dotted form `sysctl -a` prints; a name written with slashes is accepted too.

Configuration is read from the sysctl.d directories (/etc, /run, /usr/local/lib, /usr/lib, /lib) with the precedence systemd-sysctl applies at boot: a file hides a same-named file in a lower-priority directory, the files are applied in file name order, and the last assignment wins. An explicit assignment beats a glob, and `-name` excludes a parameter from globs. Without systemd-sysctl, /etc/sysctl.conf is applied after the sysctl.d files, as `sysctl --system` does. On BSD and macOS it is /etc/sysctl.conf (and /etc/sysctl.conf.local on FreeBSD).

kernel.parameter.setting.name: kernel.parameter.setting

effective.name: effective
effective.title: Whether this assignment sets the parameter's configured value

file.name: file
file.title: Configuration file containing the assignment

ignoreErrors.name: ignoreErrors
ignoreErrors.title: Whether a leading `-` tells the tool to ignore a failure to apply it

key.name: key
key.title: Key as written, without a leading `-`; may be a glob

kernel.parameter.setting.title: Kernel parameter assignment
kernel.parameter.setting.desc: One `name = value` line in a sysctl configuration file.

kernel.taint.name: kernel.taint

reasons.name: reasons
reasons.title: Human-readable taint reasons in bit order
reasons.desc: See the kernel.org "Tainted kernels" documentation for the full list of bit meanings (proprietary module, out-of-tree module, unsigned module, oops, soft lockup, live-patched, etc.).

tainted.name: tainted
tainted.title: Whether any taint bit is set

kernel.taint.title: Linux kernel taint status
kernel.taint.desc: Kernel taint flags as reported by /proc/sys/kernel/tainted. A non-zero bitmask indicates that the kernel has loaded proprietary or out-of-tree modules, hit a hardware error, oopsed, or otherwise entered a state that diverges from a clean reference kernel. Use `tainted` for a boolean check and `reasons` for the human-readable list of contributing bits.

description.name: description

name.name: name

source.name: source

allowedUnsafeSysctls.name: allowedUnsafeSysctls
allowedUnsafeSysctls.title: Unsafe sysctls pods on this node may set (for example "net.ipv4.ip_forward")

anonymousAuthEnabled.name: anonymousAuthEnabled

clientCAFile.name: clientCAFile

clientCAs.name: clientCAs
clientCAs.title: Certificate authorities the kubelet server trusts for client certificates, from `clientCAFile`

configDir.name: configDir
configDir.title: Directory of kubelet drop-in configuration files
configDir.desc: The `--config-dir` directory, whose `*.conf` files override the config file in name order. K3s and RKE2 write most of the kubelet's configuration here. Empty when the kubelet uses no drop-in directory.

configDropIns.name: configDropIns
configDropIns.title: Drop-in configuration files the kubelet applies, in the order it applies them

configuration.name: configuration

enableDebuggingHandlers.name: enableDebuggingHandlers

enableSystemLogQuery.title: Whether the kubelet server answers node log queries on /logs/query

eventRecordQPS.name: eventRecordQPS

featureGates.name: featureGates

imagePullCredentialsVerificationPolicy.name: imagePullCredentialsVerificationPolicy

class.name: class

class.desc: One login class record. `capabilities` holds what the record itself writes, `effective` what applies after `tc=` inheritance, and `inherits` the classes it includes. Values keep their text as written (for example `90d` or `022`); boolean capabilities read as true. Select a class with `loginconf.class("default")`, which also matches an alias.

file.name: file
file.title: login.conf file that the classes are read from

loginconf.title: BSD login class capability database (/etc/login.conf)
loginconf.desc: Login classes parsed from /etc/login.conf on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `loginconf.class` per class. Login classes hold the password policy (password format, expiry, warning period), umask, resource limits, and environment for the accounts assigned to them in /etc/master.passwd. The file uses the getcap(3) format, and the system reads the compiled login.conf.db that `cap_mkdb` builds from it, so an edit takes effect only after `cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf`. Read another file with `loginconf("/path/to/login.conf")`.

loginconf.class.name: loginconf.class

aliases.name: aliases
aliases.title: Other names from the record header (`name|alias|...`)
aliases.desc: On FreeBSD the last one is often a description, such as `Russian Users Accounts`.

capabilities.name: capabilities
capabilities.title: Capabilities written in this class
capabilities.desc: The first occurrence of each capability, before `tc=` inheritance. A capability cancelled with `cap@` is left out, and `tc=` references are listed in `inherits` instead.

effective.name: effective
effective.title: Capabilities after `tc=` inheritance
effective.desc: The capabilities login_getclass(3) returns for this class: each `tc=` is replaced by the referenced class's capabilities, the first occurrence of a capability wins, and one cancelled with `cap@` stays absent. A class does not inherit from `default` unless it says `tc=default`; for an unset capability the system uses its built-in default. A `tc=` that does not resolve, or a reference loop, is an error, as login refuses such a class.

inherits.name: inherits
inherits.title: Classes this class includes with `tc=`, in order

name.name: name
name.title: Class name, the first name in the record header

loginconf.class.title: Login class from /etc/login.conf
loginconf.class.desc: One login class record. `capabilities` holds what the record itself writes, `effective` what applies after `tc=` inheritance, and `inherits` the classes it includes. Values keep their text as written (for example `90d` or `022`); boolean capabilities read as true. Select a class with `loginconf.class("default")`, which also matches an alias.

logindefs.name: logindefs

content.name: content
content.title: Content of the configuration file

file.name: file
file.title: Current configuration file for resource

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed login.defs parameters as a name/value map (e.g. PASS_MAX_DAYS, UMASK, ENCRYPT_METHOD)

logindefs.title: Shadow password suite (login.defs) configuration
logindefs.desc: Password aging, UID/GID ranges, and login policy parameters parsed from /etc/login.defs. The params map exposes settings such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, UMASK, and ENCRYPT_METHOD, which drive account and password-policy audits. Point at an alternate file with the `path` argument.

logrotate.name: logrotate

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Per-file/glob rotation entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Logrotate configuration entry for a specific log path
entry.desc: Rotation rule for one log path or glob. `path` is the log the block applies to and `config` holds every directive inside the block as key-value pairs (e.g. "rotate", "daily", "compress", "maxage"). `file` and `lineNumber` locate the block in its source configuration file.

files.name: files
files.title: List of configuration files (main + logrotate.d fragments)

logrotate.title: logrotate configuration
logrotate.desc: Log rotation configuration parsed from the main logrotate.conf and the fragments under logrotate.d. `globalConfig` holds the directives that apply outside any log block, `entries` holds the per-log-path rotation rules, and `files` lists the configuration files read. Audit rotation frequency, retention counts, and compression to confirm logs are kept long enough and pruned safely.

logrotate.entry.name: logrotate.entry

config.name: config
config.title: All directives in this block as key-value pairs

file.name: file
file.title: Configuration file where this entry is defined

lineNumber.name: lineNumber
lineNumber.title: Line number in the configuration file

path.name: path
path.title: Log file path or glob pattern
