logrotate.entry.desc: Rotation rule for one log path or glob. `path` is the log the block applies to and `config` holds every directive inside the block as key-value pairs (e.g. "rotate", "daily", "compress", "maxage"). `file` and `lineNumber` locate the block in its source configuration file.

lsblk.name: lsblk

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Unix block device
entry.desc: Single block device reported by `lsblk`: its device `name`, filesystem type (`fstype`), `label`, UUID, `mountpoints` list, and device `type`. `parents` and `children` walk the device stack (disk, partition, dm-crypt mapping, LVM volume), and `encrypted` reports whether the data on the device passes through a dm-crypt mapping. Filter to audit disk layout and mount configuration, e.g. `lsblk.where(mountpoints.contains("/"))`, or reach the device behind a mount with `mount.point(path: "/").blockDevice`.

lsblk.title: Unix block devices (lsblk)
lsblk.desc: Block devices reported by `lsblk`, each carrying its device name, filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount points. Iterate to audit disk layout, filesystem labels, and mount configuration.

lsblk.entry.name: lsblk.entry

children.name: children
children.title: Devices built on this device
children.desc: For example, the partitions of a disk, or the dm-crypt mapping opened on a LUKS partition.

encrypted.name: encrypted
encrypted.title: Whether the data on this device is encrypted by dm-crypt
encrypted.desc: True when this device is a dm-crypt mapping, or when every device it is built on is encrypted, so an LVM volume on a LUKS mapping is encrypted and an LVM volume that spans an encrypted and an unencrypted physical volume is not. A LUKS partition itself holds ciphertext and reports false, the mapping opened on it reports true. Null when the device type is unknown.

parents.name: parents
parents.title: Devices this device is built on
parents.desc: For example, the partition that holds a dm-crypt mapping, or every physical volume under an LVM logical volume. Empty for a whole disk.

type.name: type
type.title: Device type
type.desc: Device type as the kernel reports it, for example disk, part, crypt, lvm, raid1, loop, or rom.

lsblk.entry.title: Unix block device
lsblk.entry.desc: Single block device reported by `lsblk`: its device `name`, filesystem type (`fstype`), `label`, UUID, `mountpoints` list, and device `type`. `parents` and `children` walk the device stack (disk, partition, dm-crypt mapping, LVM volume), and `encrypted` reports whether the data on the device passes through a dm-crypt mapping. Filter to audit disk layout and mount configuration, e.g. `lsblk.where(mountpoints.contains("/"))`, or reach the device behind a mount with `mount.point(path: "/").blockDevice`.

package.name: package
package.title: Lua package
package.desc: Single installed LuaRocks rock with its `name`, `version`, and a `purl` (Package URL) for SBOM and vulnerability matching, plus the `files` that declared it.

packages.name: packages
packages.title: Lua/LuaRocks package inventory
packages.desc: Installed LuaRocks rocks with their versions, for every Lua version, gathered from `luarocks list` and the system rock trees (`/usr/local/lib/luarocks` and `/usr/lib/luarocks`, each `rocks` and `rocks-*` directory), plus every user's `~/.luarocks` tree. Pass `path` to search a specific rock tree, such as `/usr/local` or a rocks directory. Each entry carries a `purl` for SBOM and vulnerability matching.

lua.package.name: lua.package

files.name: files
files.title: Files that declared the package

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL (purl) identifying the package for SBOM and vulnerability matching

lua.package.title: Lua package
lua.package.desc: Single installed LuaRocks rock with its `name`, `version`, and a `purl` (Package URL) for SBOM and vulnerability matching, plus the `files` that declared it.

lua.packages.name: lua.packages

files.name: files
files.title: Files used to build the package list

path.name: path
path.title: Filesystem path searched for installed LuaRocks rocks (empty scans the default rock trees)

lua.packages.title: Lua/LuaRocks package inventory
lua.packages.desc: Installed LuaRocks rocks with their versions, for every Lua version, gathered from `luarocks list` and the system rock trees (`/usr/local/lib/luarocks` and `/usr/lib/luarocks`, each `rocks` and `rocks-*` directory), plus every user's `~/.luarocks` tree. Pass `path` to search a specific rock tree, such as `/usr/local` or a rocks directory. Each entry carries a `purl` for SBOM and vulnerability matching.

luks.name: luks

keyslot.name: keyslot
keyslot.title: LUKS keyslot
keyslot.desc: One keyslot in a LUKS header: its index, state, and the key-derivation parameters used to wrap the master key. Audit for weak KDFs, low iteration or memory costs, and unexpectedly large numbers of active slots (each active slot is a passphrase that can unlock the volume).

volume.name: volume
volume.title: LUKS-encrypted block device
volume.desc: Single LUKS-formatted block device: its header version, label, master-key size and offset, cipher, and keyslots. Select a volume by its `uuid` (e.g., `luks.volumes.where(uuid == "fd44f17a-...")`) or by the underlying block device's `name`.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: LUKS-formatted block devices on the host

luks.title: LUKS-encrypted volumes on the host
luks.desc: Block devices that carry a LUKS header, exposing each volume's on-disk format version, cipher, key-derivation parameters, and every keyslot. Both LUKS1 and LUKS2 headers are reported through the same schema; the `version` field on each volume distinguishes them and version-specific fields (label, subsystem, and tokens for LUKS2; AF-splitter stripes for LUKS1) are populated only where they apply.

luks.keyslot.name: luks.keyslot

hash.name: hash
hash.title: Hash used by the KDF (pbkdf2 only; e.g., sha256, sha512)

index.name: index
index.title: Slot index (0–7 on LUKS1, 0–31 on LUKS2)

kdf.name: kdf
kdf.title: KDF used for this slot
kdf.desc: One of pbkdf2, argon2i, or argon2id.

memory.name: memory
memory.title: argon2 memory cost in KiB (argon2* only)

state.name: state
state.title: Slot state
state.desc: ENABLED or DISABLED on LUKS1; active or inactive on LUKS2.

luks.keyslot.title: LUKS keyslot
luks.keyslot.desc: One keyslot in a LUKS header: its index, state, and the key-derivation parameters used to wrap the master key. Audit for weak KDFs, low iteration or memory costs, and unexpectedly large numbers of active slots (each active slot is a passphrase that can unlock the volume).

luks.volume.name: luks.volume

label.name: label
label.title: Label assigned in the LUKS2 header (empty on LUKS1)

name.name: name
name.title: Path of the underlying block device (e.g., /dev/sda3)

subsystem.name: subsystem
subsystem.title: Subsystem string from the LUKS2 header (empty on LUKS1)

tokens.name: tokens
tokens.title: LUKS2 tokens attached to the header (empty on LUKS1)
tokens.desc: Each entry carries the token id, type (e.g., luks2-keyring, systemd-tpm2, systemd-fido2, systemd-pkcs11), the keyslot indices the token unlocks, and any token-type-specific metadata.

luks.volume.title: LUKS-encrypted block device
luks.volume.desc: Single LUKS-formatted block device: its header version, label, master-key size and offset, cipher, and keyslots. Select a volume by its `uuid` (e.g., `luks.volumes.where(uuid == "fd44f17a-...")`) or by the underlying block device's `name`.

luks.volume.cipher.name: luks.volume.cipher

hash.name: hash
hash.title: Hash used by the AF splitter (LUKS1) or sector integrity (LUKS2)

spec.name: spec
spec.title: Combined cipher spec as cryptsetup reports it

luks.volume.cipher.title: LUKS cipher specification
luks.volume.cipher.desc: Symmetric cipher protecting a LUKS volume's master key. `name` is the cipher family, `mode` is the chaining mode, and `spec` is the combined cryptsetup string (e.g., `aes-xts-plain64`). On LUKS1, `hash` carries the AF-splitter hash; on LUKS2 it is the integrity hash when sector integrity is configured.

lvm.name: lvm

logicalVolume.name: logicalVolume
logicalVolume.title: LVM logical volume
logicalVolume.desc: Single LVM logical volume: `name`, full device `path`, `uuid`, parent volume group (`volumeGroupName`), attribute flags, size in bytes, snapshot `origin`, and thin-pool data usage. For thin volumes, `poolName` is set; for snapshots, `origin` is the source LV name.

logicalVolumes.name: logicalVolumes
logicalVolumes.title: Logical volumes across all volume groups

physicalVolume.name: physicalVolume
physicalVolume.title: LVM physical volume
physicalVolume.desc: Single block device initialized as an LVM physical volume: device path (`name`), `uuid`, the volume group it belongs to (`volumeGroupName`, empty if unassigned), on-disk `format`, attribute flags, and total/free byte counts.

volumeGroup.name: volumeGroup
volumeGroup.title: LVM volume group
volumeGroup.desc: Single LVM volume group: `name`, `uuid`, attribute flags, total and free byte counts, and the counts of physical volumes, logical volumes, and snapshots it contains. Useful for auditing capacity headroom and group-level policy.

lvm.title: Linux Logical Volume Manager
lvm.desc: LVM block-device storage on Linux: physical volumes initialized for LVM, volume groups that aggregate them, and the logical volumes carved out of those groups. Iterate `physicalVolumes`, `volumeGroups`, and `logicalVolumes` to audit LVM layout, free capacity, thin-pool usage, and snapshot relationships.

lvm.logicalVolume.name: lvm.logicalVolume

attributes.name: attributes
attributes.title: LV attribute flags
attributes.desc: Ten-character status string covering volume type, permissions, allocation policy, fixed minor, state, open device, target type, zeroing, and skipped activation. See lvm(8) `lv_attr` for the full set.

dataPercent.name: dataPercent
dataPercent.title: Data percentage used (for thin pools, thin volumes, snapshots, mirrors); null if not applicable

origin.name: origin
origin.title: Origin LV name for snapshots, empty if not a snapshot

poolName.name: poolName
poolName.title: Pool name for thin volumes, empty if not a thin volume

volumeGroupName.name: volumeGroupName
volumeGroupName.title: Name of the volume group this LV belongs to

lvm.logicalVolume.title: LVM logical volume
lvm.logicalVolume.desc: Single LVM logical volume: `name`, full device `path`, `uuid`, parent volume group (`volumeGroupName`), attribute flags, size in bytes, snapshot `origin`, and thin-pool data usage. For thin volumes, `poolName` is set; for snapshots, `origin` is the source LV name.

lvm.physicalVolume.name: lvm.physicalVolume

attributes.name: attributes
attributes.title: PV attribute flags
attributes.desc: Three-character status string. Common values include `a` (allocatable), `x` (exported), and `m` (missing). See lvm(8) `pv_attr` for the full set.

volumeGroupName.name: volumeGroupName
volumeGroupName.title: Name of the volume group this PV belongs to (empty if unassigned)

lvm.physicalVolume.title: LVM physical volume
lvm.physicalVolume.desc: Single block device initialized as an LVM physical volume: device path (`name`), `uuid`, the volume group it belongs to (`volumeGroupName`, empty if unassigned), on-disk `format`, attribute flags, and total/free byte counts.

lvm.volumeGroup.name: lvm.volumeGroup

attributes.name: attributes
attributes.title: VG attribute flags
attributes.desc: Six-character status string covering permissions, resizability, export state, partial state, allocation policy, and clustering. See lvm(8) `vg_attr` for the full set.

logicalVolumeCount.name: logicalVolumeCount
logicalVolumeCount.title: Number of logical volumes in this group

physicalVolumeCount.name: physicalVolumeCount
physicalVolumeCount.title: Number of physical volumes in this group

snapshotCount.name: snapshotCount
snapshotCount.title: Number of snapshots in this group

lvm.volumeGroup.title: LVM volume group
lvm.volumeGroup.desc: Single LVM volume group: `name`, `uuid`, attribute flags, total and free byte counts, and the counts of physical volumes, logical volumes, and snapshots it contains. Useful for auditing capacity headroom and group-level policy.

machine.name: machine

baseboard.name: baseboard
baseboard.title: SMBIOS baseboard (or module) information
baseboard.desc: Baseboard manufacturer, product name, version, serial number, and asset tag as reported in SMBIOS Type 2 tables. Used for hardware inventory and to correlate physical boards with asset-tracking systems.

bios.name: bios
bios.title: SMBIOS BIOS information
bios.desc: Firmware vendor, version string, and release date as reported by SMBIOS Type 0 tables. Used to inventory BIOS versions across a fleet and to flag hosts that have not applied vendor firmware updates.

chassis.name: chassis
chassis.title: SMBIOS system enclosure or chassis
chassis.desc: Chassis manufacturer, version, serial number, and asset tag as reported in SMBIOS Type 3 tables. Useful for physical-hardware audits and correlating enclosures with asset-tracking records.

cpu.name: cpu
cpu.title: CPU information
cpu.desc: CPU manufacturer, model name, number of physical processor packages (sockets), and total physical core count as reported by the system. Used for capacity planning, licensing audits, and hardware-baseline policies.

secureboot.name: secureboot
secureboot.title: Secure Boot status
secureboot.desc: EFI Secure Boot posture: whether the system booted in EFI/UEFI mode (`efi`), whether Secure Boot is currently enabled (`enabled`), and whether it is in setup mode (`setupMode`, meaning keys can be modified without authentication). Read from EFI variables on Linux and from the UEFI firmware on Windows; legacy-BIOS systems resolve to `efi` and `enabled` false rather than erroring. Used to assert that Secure Boot is enforced and that setup mode is not active.

system.name: system
system.title: SMBIOS system information
system.desc: Manufacturer, product name, version, serial number, UUID, SKU number, and family string as reported in SMBIOS Type 1 tables. Useful for asset inventory, warranty lookups, and supply-chain reviews.

machine.title: Hardware identity from SMBIOS / DMI
machine.desc: Namespace for low-level hardware identity exposed by the firmware. The sub-resources below (`machine.bios`, `machine.system`, `machine.baseboard`, `machine.chassis`, `machine.cpu`, and `machine.secureboot`) surface the SMBIOS / DMI tables (vendor, version, and release date for the BIOS; manufacturer, product, SKU, UUID, and serial for the system; baseboard and chassis identifiers; CPU socket and core counts) plus the EFI Secure Boot posture read from EFI variables on Linux. Used for inventory, warranty and supply-chain reviews, and platform-firmware compliance.

machine.baseboard.name: machine.baseboard
machine.baseboard.title: SMBIOS baseboard (or module) information
machine.baseboard.desc: Baseboard manufacturer, product name, version, serial number, and asset tag as reported in SMBIOS Type 2 tables. Used for hardware inventory and to correlate physical boards with asset-tracking systems.

machine.bios.name: machine.bios
machine.bios.title: SMBIOS BIOS information
machine.bios.desc: Firmware vendor, version string, and release date as reported by SMBIOS Type 0 tables. Used to inventory BIOS versions across a fleet and to flag hosts that have not applied vendor firmware updates.

machine.chassis.name: machine.chassis
machine.chassis.title: SMBIOS system enclosure or chassis
machine.chassis.desc: Chassis manufacturer, version, serial number, and asset tag as reported in SMBIOS Type 3 tables. Useful for physical-hardware audits and correlating enclosures with asset-tracking records.

machine.cpu.name: machine.cpu

coreCount.name: coreCount
coreCount.title: Total number of physical CPU cores

maxClockSpeed.name: maxClockSpeed
maxClockSpeed.title: Maximum rated clock speed in MHz, null where the platform does not report it

machine.cpu.title: CPU information
machine.cpu.desc: CPU manufacturer, model name, number of physical processor packages (sockets), and total physical core count as reported by the system. Used for capacity planning, licensing audits, and hardware-baseline policies.

machine.secureboot.name: machine.secureboot

efi.name: efi
efi.title: Whether the system is booted in EFI/UEFI mode

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether Secure Boot is enabled

setupMode.name: setupMode
setupMode.title: Whether Secure Boot is in setup mode (keys can be modified without authentication)

machine.secureboot.title: Secure Boot status
machine.secureboot.desc: EFI Secure Boot posture: whether the system booted in EFI/UEFI mode (`efi`), whether Secure Boot is currently enabled (`enabled`), and whether it is in setup mode (`setupMode`, meaning keys can be modified without authentication). Read from EFI variables on Linux and from the UEFI firmware on Windows; legacy-BIOS systems resolve to `efi` and `enabled` false rather than erroring. Used to assert that Secure Boot is enforced and that setup mode is not active.

machine.system.name: machine.system
machine.system.title: SMBIOS system information
machine.system.desc: Manufacturer, product name, version, serial number, UUID, SKU number, and family string as reported in SMBIOS Type 1 tables. Useful for asset inventory, warranty lookups, and supply-chain reviews.

macos.name: macos

alf.name: alf
alf.title: macOS application layer firewall (raw ALF preference values)
alf.desc: Raw integer flags read from the Application Layer Firewall plist (`/Library/Preferences/com.apple.alf.plist`). Prefer `macos.firewall`, which decodes these into boolean fields; use this resource only when you need the underlying preference values.

filevault.name: filevault
filevault.title: macOS FileVault full-disk encryption
filevault.desc: FileVault full-disk encryption state: whether it is `enabled`, the current `status`, whether personal and institutional recovery keys exist, and the `users` permitted to unlock the encrypted volume at boot. CIS macOS benchmarks require FileVault enabled.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: macOS application layer firewall
firewall.desc: Decoded Application Layer Firewall configuration: whether the firewall is `enabled`, whether it blocks all incoming connections, stealth mode, logging, the signed-app auto-allow policy, and per-application rules. CIS macOS benchmarks expect the firewall enabled with stealth mode on. See `macos.alf` for the raw preference values.

gatekeeper.name: gatekeeper
gatekeeper.title: macOS Gatekeeper application execution policy
gatekeeper.desc: Gatekeeper policy that controls whether downloaded applications may run: whether assessments are `enabled` and the human-readable `status`. Disabling Gatekeeper lets unsigned or unnotarized software launch without a warning, so benchmarks expect it enabled.

globalAccountPolicies.name: globalAccountPolicies
globalAccountPolicies.title: Global account (password) policy directives applied to all local users

hardware.name: hardware
hardware.title: macOS hardware overview
hardware.desc: Hardware and firmware details reported by `system_profiler`: chip type, model identifiers, installed memory, serial number, and Activation Lock status. Useful for asset inventory and for distinguishing Apple Silicon from Intel Macs in conditional audits.

mdm.name: mdm
mdm.title: macOS MDM (Mobile Device Management) enrollment state
mdm.desc: MDM enrollment state for this Mac: whether it is enrolled, the enrollment server, and whether enrollment was performed via Automated Device Enrollment (formerly DEP) or user-approved. Use `macos.profiles` to enumerate the configuration profiles delivered to the device. Backed by `profiles status -type enrollment`.

profile.name: profile
profile.title: macOS Configuration Profile
profile.desc: Single Configuration Profile: its `identifier`, `uuid`, human-readable `displayName`, `description`, `organization`, `type`, whether it is install-locked (`removalDisallowed`), the scope it applies to (`scope`: `system` or `user`), and the individual `payloads` that carry the actual policy directives.

profiles.name: profiles
profiles.title: macOS configuration profiles installed on the system
profiles.desc: Every Configuration Profile delivered to the device, both MDM-delivered and manually installed `.mobileconfig` payloads, so you can audit what policies are actually in force. Backed by `profiles list -all -output stdout-xml`; requires root to see system-level (`_computerlevel`) profiles, otherwise only the current user's profiles are returned.

sharing.name: sharing
sharing.title: macOS Sharing service state
sharing.desc:
State of each toggle in the unified Sharing panel (System Settings > Sharing on macOS Ventura+, System Preferences > Sharing on older versions). CIS macOS benchmarks require most of these off unless the device explicitly needs the service. Backed by `system_profiler SPSharingDataType`, so the values match exactly what the System Settings UI displays.

`system_profiler SPSharingDataType` also reports `Remote Login` and `Remote Apple Events`; those are intentionally not exposed here because `macos.systemsetup.remoteLogin` and `macos.systemsetup.remoteAppleEvents` already cover them via the `systemsetup` CLI. This resource covers the rest of the panel.

sip.name: sip
sip.title: macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP)
sip.desc: System Integrity Protection state, the kernel-level protection that restricts modification of protected system files and processes even by root. Exposes whether SIP is `enabled` and the raw `status` message from `csrutil status`. Disabling SIP is a significant hardening regression.

softwareupdate.name: softwareupdate
softwareupdate.title: macOS Software Update configuration and pending updates
softwareupdate.desc: Automatic-update policy and the list of updates currently available to install. Policy fields read from `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.SoftwareUpdate.plist` (with `/Library/Managed Preferences/` taking precedence when an MDM configuration profile has been delivered). The `updates` list is produced from `softwareupdate -l --no-scan` so it does not initiate a network check.

systemExtension.name: systemExtension
systemExtension.title: macOS system extension
systemExtension.desc: Installed system extension read from /Library/SystemExtensions/db.plist: its `identifier`, `uuid`, `version`, `teamID` of the signing developer, declared `categories` (such as network or endpoint-security extensions), and `bundlePath`. The `state` string reports the extension's lifecycle, with `enabled` and `active` derived from it. `mdmManaged` is true when the extension or its team is allowlisted by an MDM system-extension policy, which distinguishes centrally approved extensions from user-installed ones.

systemExtensions.name: systemExtensions
systemExtensions.title: Installed system extensions (network, endpoint security, and driver extensions)

systemsetup.name: systemsetup
systemsetup.title: macOS machine settings via the systemsetup CLI
systemsetup.desc: Date/time, sleep and wake, remote login, power, and network-time settings surfaced by the `systemsetup` CLI, with each field mapping to one `systemsetup -get*` query. Requires at least admin privileges to run.

timemachine.name: timemachine
timemachine.title: macOS Time Machine backup configuration
timemachine.desc: Time Machine backup configuration read from its preferences: configured backup destinations, the automatic backup schedule, and the paths excluded from backups, exposed as the raw `preferences` dict.

userHostPreferences.name: userHostPreferences
userHostPreferences.title: Per-user, per-host macOS defaults (ByHost preferences), keyed by preference domain

userPreferences.name: userPreferences
userPreferences.title: Per-user macOS defaults (preferences), keyed by preference domain

xprotect.name: xprotect
xprotect.title: macOS XProtect anti-malware bundle
xprotect.desc:
Version and last-modified timestamp of the XProtect signature bundle (and, when present, the legacy Malware Removal Tool). CIS macOS benchmarks expect XProtect signatures to be current; checking `modified` against the auditor's freshness threshold catches devices that have stopped receiving updates.

XProtect.bundle lives at `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` on modern macOS (with `/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` as the legacy fallback). `mrtVersion` and `mrtModified` are empty or null on macOS 13+ where MRT has been retired in favor of XProtectRemediator.

macos.title: macOS-specific operating system surfaces
macos.desc: macOS host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: the machine's `computerName`, per-user and per-host defaults (preferences), the global account/password policy, and installed `systemExtensions`. A starting point for macOS-specific audits alongside the dedicated resources such as firewall, filevault, gatekeeper, and sip.

macos.alf.name: macos.alf

allowDownloadSignedEnabled.name: allowDownloadSignedEnabled
allowDownloadSignedEnabled.title: Whether the firewall service allows downloaded software to receive incoming connections

allowSignedEnabled.name: allowSignedEnabled
allowSignedEnabled.title: Whether the firewall service allows built-in software to receive incoming connections for signed software

explicitAuths.name: explicitAuths
explicitAuths.title: Services explicitly allowed to perform networking

globalState.name: globalState
globalState.title: Global firewall state (0=off, 1=on for specific services, 2=block all incoming connections)

stealthEnabled.name: stealthEnabled

mariadb.name: mariadb

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MariaDB option files
conf.desc:
Options from the MariaDB server option file chain on disk, useful for auditing settings as they are written to the file before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the on-disk configuration and a running server. The `!include` and `!includedir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in contribute to `sections`, and option names are normalized so `-` and `_` are interchangeable, matching how the server treats them.

Options stay grouped as the server reads them. `sections` holds every option group and `serverOptions` merges the groups mariadbd reads: `[mysqld]`, `[server]`, `[mariadb]`, `[mariadbd]` (from 10.4), `[client-server]`, `[galera]` on a server built with wsrep (from 10.1, whether or not wsrep is on), and the version-suffixed groups for the installed server version, such as `[mariadb-11.4]` on 11.4, or `[mariadb-11]` from 11.8.7 and 12.3.2 on. That set is not an extension of MySQL's, because packaged fragments since 11.0 configure the server under `[mariadbd]` and ship no `[mysqld]` group at all. `galeraOptions` also breaks out `[galera]` on its own so cluster transport settings stay separable, and `clientOptions` merges the client groups, where a `password` option means credentials are stored in the file.

By default the option files are the ones the server reads: those named with `--defaults-file` or `--defaults-extra-file` on the command line of the running server or of its systemd unit, or else every default option file the installed server binary lists, in its order, including the server account's `~/.my.cnf`. Where the binary cannot be run, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. The resource returns nothing when the host runs MySQL rather than MariaDB, or runs no database server at all. The installed server binary decides, so option files that a client library ships (such as `[client-mariadb]` on a RHEL host running MySQL) do not. Pass an explicit path with `mariadb.conf("/etc/mysql/mariadb.cnf")` to parse a file regardless of which product it belongs to.

`serverOptions` applies the options on that command line over the files. A setting made at runtime with `SET GLOBAL` is not visible here, and an option nothing sets reads null rather than zero.

The `!include` and `!includedir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in contribute to `sections`, and option names are normalized so `-` and `_` are interchangeable, matching how the server treats them.

Options stay grouped as the server reads them. `sections` holds every option group and `serverOptions` merges the groups mariadbd reads: `[mysqld]`, `[server]`, `[mariadb]`, `[mariadbd]` (from 10.4), `[client-server]`, `[galera]` on a server built with wsrep (from 10.1, whether or not wsrep is on), and the version-suffixed groups for the installed server version, such as `[mariadb-11.4]` on 11.4, or `[mariadb-11]` from 11.8.7 and 12.3.2 on. That set is not an extension of MySQL's, because packaged fragments since 11.0 configure the server under `[mariadbd]` and ship no `[mysqld]` group at all. `galeraOptions` also breaks out `[galera]` on its own so cluster transport settings stay separable, and `clientOptions` merges the client groups, where a `password` option means credentials are stored in the file.

By default the option files are the ones the server reads: those named with `--defaults-file` or `--defaults-extra-file` on the command line of the running server or of its systemd unit, or else every default option file the installed server binary lists, in its order, including the server account's `~/.my.cnf`. Where the binary cannot be run, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. The resource returns nothing when the host runs MySQL rather than MariaDB, or runs no database server at all. The installed server binary decides, so option files that a client library ships (such as `[client-mariadb]` on a RHEL host running MySQL) do not. Pass an explicit path with `mariadb.conf("/etc/mysql/mariadb.cnf")` to parse a file regardless of which product it belongs to.

`serverOptions` applies the options on that command line over the files. A setting made at runtime with `SET GLOBAL` is not visible here, and an option nothing sets reads null rather than zero.

mongodb.name: mongodb

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MongoDB configuration file
conf.desc:
Settings from mongod.conf as written on disk, useful for auditing the configuration before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the file and a running server. The file is a nested YAML document and has no include mechanism, so a parse reads exactly one file and `params` holds the whole tree as written. A file in the legacy `name = value` format the server also reads (`bind_ip`, `auth`, `sslMode`), as shipped in /etc/mongodb.conf by older Debian and Ubuntu packages, is translated into the same tree, and options with no YAML counterpart stay at the top level under their legacy names.

Convenience fields flatten the branches that carry security posture: network binding, TLS material, authentication and authorization, the setParameter block, the audit log, the system log, storage, process management, replication and sharding, and query profiling. Each reports the value the server would use, so an option left out of the file reads as the server default rather than as empty. That matters most where the default is permissive: javascriptEnabled and enableLocalhostAuthBypass are both on unless the file turns them off.

Options written under the pre-4.2 `net.ssl` tree are reported through the `tls` fields, since the server still accepts them as aliases. By default the file is located by probing the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu, RPM, and Homebrew installations; pass an explicit path with `mongodb.conf("/path/to/mongod.conf")`.

version.name: version
version.title: MongoDB version (e.g., "7.0.14")
version.desc: Read by running the server binary, so it reports nothing over a transport that cannot run commands. The configuration file mongodb.conf reads is unaffected, since it comes off the filesystem.

mongodb.title: MongoDB Server
mongodb.desc: MongoDB server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use mongodb.conf for the parsed configuration file, covering network binding, TLS material, authentication and authorization, auditing, encryption at rest, replication, and query profiling.

mongodb.conf.name: mongodb.conf

It is null when the option is unset and the server version cannot be read or predates 3.0.

authorization.title: security.authorization option (enabled, disabled)
authorization.desc: Reported as written, and empty when unset. This stays a string rather than becoming a boolean because it is not the only thing that turns authorization on: setting keyFile enables client authorization by itself, so an empty value here does not on its own mean access control is off. When neither option is set it reports the server default for the installed version: 127.0.0.1 from 3.6 on, and 0.0.0.0 (plus :: with ipv6) before 3.6, when the server listened on every interface. It is null when neither option is set and the server version cannot be read. Both spellings the server reads are accepted: a comma-delimited string and a YAML sequence.

mongodb.conf.title: MongoDB configuration file
mongodb.conf.desc:
Settings from mongod.conf as written on disk, useful for auditing the configuration before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the file and a running server. The file is a nested YAML document and has no include mechanism, so a parse reads exactly one file and `params` holds the whole tree as written. A file in the legacy `name = value` format the server also reads (`bind_ip`, `auth`, `sslMode`), as shipped in /etc/mongodb.conf by older Debian and Ubuntu packages, is translated into the same tree, and options with no YAML counterpart stay at the top level under their legacy names.

On Windows the path matches without regard to case or a trailing backslash, so `mount.point(path: "C:")`, `mount.point(path: "c:\\")` and `mount.point(path: os.base.env["SystemDrive"])` all select the `C:\` volume.

mysql.name: mysql

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MySQL option files
conf.desc:
Options from the MySQL server option file chain on disk, useful for auditing settings as they are written to the file before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the on-disk configuration and a running server. The `!include` and `!includedir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in contribute to `sections`, and option names are normalized so `-` and `_` are interchangeable, matching how the server treats them.

Options stay grouped as the server reads them. `sections` holds every option group, `serverOptions` merges the groups mysqld itself reads (`[mysqld]`, `[server]`, the version-suffixed group for the installed server version, such as `[mysqld-8.0]` on 8.0, and `[mysql_cluster]` where the build reads it), and `clientOptions` merges `[client]`, `[mysql]`, and `[client-server]`, where a `password` option means credentials are stored in the file. Convenience views cover networking, TLS, authentication and password policy, filesystem privileges, logging, binary logging and replication, and encryption at rest. `userFiles` reports the per-user option files under home directories.

By default the option files are the ones the server reads: those named with `--defaults-file` or `--defaults-extra-file` on the command line of the running server or of its systemd unit, or else every default option file the installed server binary lists, in its order, including the server account's `~/.my.cnf`. Where the binary cannot be run, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. The resource returns nothing when the host runs MariaDB rather than MySQL, or runs no database server at all. The installed server binary decides, so option files that a client library ships (such as `[client-mariadb]` on a RHEL host running MySQL) do not. Pass an explicit path with `mysql.conf("/etc/mysql/my.cnf")` to parse a file regardless of which product it belongs to.

`serverOptions` applies the options on that command line over the files, and then the settings `SET PERSIST` wrote to `mysqld-auto.cnf` in the data directory, which the server applies last. A setting made at runtime with `SET GLOBAL` is not visible here, and an option nothing sets reads null rather than zero. An option belonging to a plugin or component the server does not load (`validate_password.*` without the component, `audit_log_*` on a server without the audit plugin, a `loose-` option the version does not know) is reported as written but has no effect on the server.

flavor.name: flavor

mysql.title: MySQL Server

Use mysql.conf for the parsed option files, including option groups, server and client scope options, TLS material, and the per-user option files under home directories. MariaDB installations are covered by the mariadb resource.

nftables.name: nftables

chain.name: chain
chain.title: nftables chain
chain.desc: Ordered list of rules within a table. A base chain attaches to a kernel hook and carries a type, hook, priority, and default policy, so it decides the fate of packets that fall through all its rules. A regular (non-base) chain is only reached by an explicit jump or goto and leaves those fields empty. Check `isBaseChain` to distinguish the two, and `policy` (accept or drop) to see the default action for a base chain, which is the key setting for a default-deny firewall.

rule.name: rule
rule.title: nftables rule
rule.desc: Single rule within a chain, identified by its handle number. The matching criteria and the action (accept, drop, jump, log, and so on) are parsed into `expr` as structured expression data, and `comment` carries any inline rule comment. Use `chainRef` and `tableRef` to walk back to the chain and table that contain the rule.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: All rules across all tables and chains

set.name: set
set.title: nftables named set or map
set.desc: Named collection of elements referenced by rules in a table, keyed by family, table, and name. A plain set holds a group of values (addresses, ports, MAC addresses) that rules match against, while a map (`isMap` true, `valueType` non-empty) associates each key with a value for verdict or NAT lookups. The `keyType` gives the element data type (for example ipv4_addr, inet_service, ether_addr), `flags` reports set attributes (constant, interval, timeout, dynamic), and `elements` lists the current members as strings.

sets.name: sets
sets.title: All named sets across all tables

table.name: table
table.title: nftables table
table.desc: Top-level container in the nftables ruleset, keyed by address family and name. A table holds the chains, rules, and named sets that make up a firewall configuration. The `family` field selects which protocol the table governs (ip for IPv4, ip6 for IPv6, inet for both, arp, bridge, or netdev), and `flags` reports table attributes such as dormant (rules present but not evaluated), owner, or persist. Traverse `chains`, `rules`, and `sets` to audit the packet-filtering policy defined here.

nftables.title: nftables firewall
nftables.desc: The host's nftables ruleset across all address families (ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge, netdev). Flattened accessors return everything at once: `tables`, `chains` (across all tables), `rules` (across all chains), and named `sets`. nftables is the modern replacement for iptables, so audit it on current distributions to confirm chains have restrictive policies and expected rules.

conf.name: conf
conf.title: Nginx HTTP Server configuration
conf.desc: Parsed Nginx configuration covering flat directives, per-server blocks, upstream backend pools, and listen addresses, merged across the main config and every include fragment. Surfaces TLS settings and response headers per server block for hardening audits. TCP and UDP proxying declared in the stream block is covered by streamParams, streamServers, and streamUpstreams. Pass `init(path: "...")` to point at a non-default config file.

modules.name: modules
modules.title: Modules nginx runs with, named as in its configure arguments
modules.desc: Every module compiled into the binary (for example `http_ssl_module`), plus each dynamic module (`--with-<name>=dynamic`) that the configuration loads with `load_module`. `--with-stream` and `--with-mail` are listed as `stream_module` and `mail_module`; when they are dynamic, their `stream_*` and `mail_*` submodules are listed only while that module is loaded.

nginx.title: Nginx HTTP Server
nginx.desc: Nginx daemon version and the modules compiled into the binary. Use nginx.conf for the parsed configuration, including server blocks, upstream pools, and listen addresses.

file.title: Primary configuration file
file.desc: The file the running nginx master loads: its `-c` argument, or else the `--conf-path` its binary was built with, with a relative path resolved against the `-p` prefix. params.desc: A directive that may repeat, such as `listen`, `include`, `load_module`, `error_log`, or `env`, keeps every value, comma-separated. Directives the running nginx master was given with `-g` count as main context directives of the file it loads.

streamServers.name: streamServers
streamServers.title: Server blocks inside the stream block
streamServers.desc: TCP and UDP proxy listeners. Each carries its own listen address and TLS settings, so protocol and cipher checks reach mail, database, and other non-HTTP traffic that Nginx terminates.

streamUpstreams.name: streamUpstreams

config.name: config
config.title: Ollama server configuration on the host
config.desc:
Configuration the Ollama server on this host runs with. Ollama keeps no configuration file: every setting is an environment variable read when the daemon starts, so the settings are reconstructed from the systemd unit that starts the server, the drop-ins and environment files that override it, and server.json in the server account's Ollama directory. Each field reports the value the server would actually use, so a setting nothing declares reads as Ollama's own default rather than as empty. That matters most where the default is the safe one: an undeclared bind address is the loopback interface, not nothing.

bindAddress, listensOnAllInterfaces, origins, and authEnabled describe who can reach the API. Ollama requires no authentication and serves plain HTTP out of the box, so a server that binds a routable address is readable and writable by anyone who can reach the port. cloudEnabled, remotes, and the proxy settings describe where prompts may travel; debugLogRequests and historyEnabled describe what is written to disk.

integrations lists the coding tools on the host that were pointed at this server, and models the model store it serves. The settings resolved from the environment are null when Ollama is not installed, so a check that reads them fails on a host without a server rather than passing against a default.

authEnabled.name: authEnabled
authEnabled.title: Whether the server requires authentication
authEnabled.desc: Reports OLLAMA_AUTH. False is the default, meaning any client that can reach the port can list models, run inference, and pull or delete models.

binaryPath.name: binaryPath
binaryPath.title: Path to the server binary, empty when it was not found

cloudDisabledSource.name: cloudDisabledSource
cloudDisabledSource.title: What turned the cloud features off
cloudDisabledSource.desc: One of "none", "env", "config", or "both", naming whether the decision came from OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD, from server.json, or from both. "none" means the features are on.

cloudEnabled.desc: False when cloud inference and web search are turned off. While true, prompts for cloud-hosted models leave the host and are processed by Ollama Cloud.

contextLength.name: contextLength

contextLength.desc: 0 means Ollama picks a length from the available VRAM rather than being told one.

debugLogRequests.desc: Reports OLLAMA_DEBUG_LOG_REQUESTS, which writes the body of every inference request, prompts included, to a temporary directory along with a command to replay it. Intended for debugging and false by default.

installed.desc: True when the server binary or a unit that starts it was found. Every setting resolved from the environment is null when this is false.

The `name` field is the key Ollama files the tool under, for example "claude", "codex", "opencode", "cline", "copilot", or "qwen". Reading these answers which assistants on the host send their prompts to a local model rather than to a vendor API, and, through `models`, whether the model each one asks for is actually present in the store.

modelsPath.desc: The resolved OLLAMA_MODELS, defaulting to the Ollama directory under the server account's home. Packaged installations routinely move this, so it is rarely the default on a server.

noProxy.name: noProxy
noProxy.title: Hosts excluded from the configured proxies, empty when unset

noPrune.name: noPrune
noPrune.title: Whether unused model blobs are kept rather than pruned at startup

numParallel.name: numParallel
numParallel.title: Maximum number of requests served in parallel

origins.name: origins
origins.title: Browser origins the API accepts cross-origin requests from
origins.desc: The entries of OLLAMA_ORIGINS, empty when it is unset. Ollama always additionally accepts localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 on any port, and the app, file, tauri, vscode-webview and vscode-file schemes, whatever this is set to. Those additions are not listed here, which reports only what the host was configured with.

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed the server
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the server when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the server's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version.

port.name: port
port.title: Port the API binds to

remotes.name: remotes
remotes.title: Hosts remote models may be served from
remotes.desc: The entries of OLLAMA_REMOTES, defaulting to ollama.com. A model served from one of these hosts runs there, so prompts for it leave this machine.

schedSpread.name: schedSpread
schedSpread.title: Whether a model is spread across every GPU rather than fitted onto one

service.name: service
service.title: Service that runs the server
service.desc: Reports whether the server is enabled and running. Null on a host with no unit for it, including one where the server is started by hand.

tls.name: tls
tls.title: Whether the API is addressed over TLS
tls.desc: False when the server is served over plain HTTP, in which case prompts, completions, and any API token sent to it travel in the clear.

user.name: user
user.title: Account the server runs as
user.desc: From the unit's User= setting. Empty when the unit names none, in which case a system service runs as root.

variableSources.name: variableSources
variableSources.title: File each declared variable was read from
variableSources.desc: Keyed the same as variables, so a setting can be traced to the unit, a drop-in, or an environment file. For a server that runs, or is started by a scanned container image, the environment is the server's own: `/proc/<pid>/environ` or `image configuration`.

variables.name: variables
variables.title: Ollama settings as declared, before defaults are applied
variables.desc: A variable absent here is one nothing gave the daemon. Read this to tell a setting that was chosen from one that merely matches the default. Only the variables Ollama reads are reported: a unit's environment is a common place to keep credentials for unrelated purposes, so anything outside Ollama's own settings is left out, and so is anything whose name is credential-shaped.

version.name: version
version.title: Version of the installed server
version.desc: Matches the host against published Ollama advisories. Empty when no version can be determined without running the binary.

ollama.config.title: Ollama server configuration on the host
ollama.config.desc:
Configuration the Ollama server on this host runs with. Ollama keeps no configuration file: every setting is an environment variable read when the daemon starts, so the settings are reconstructed from the systemd unit that starts the server, the drop-ins and environment files that override it, and server.json in the server account's Ollama directory. Each field reports the value the server would actually use, so a setting nothing declares reads as Ollama's own default rather than as empty. That matters most where the default is the safe one: an undeclared bind address is the loopback interface, not nothing.

bindAddress, listensOnAllInterfaces, origins, and authEnabled describe who can reach the API. Ollama requires no authentication and serves plain HTTP out of the box, so a server that binds a routable address is readable and writable by anyone who can reach the port. cloudEnabled, remotes, and the proxy settings describe where prompts may travel; debugLogRequests and historyEnabled describe what is written to disk.

integrations lists the coding tools on the host that were pointed at this server, and models the model store it serves. The settings resolved from the environment are null when Ollama is not installed, so a check that reads them fails on a host without a server rather than passing against a default.

modelNames.desc: What the tool asks for, which is not necessarily what the host has. A name here with no counterpart in models is a tool pointed at a model that is not installed.

models.name: models
models.title: Models from the store that the configured names resolve to
models.desc: Only the names the store actually holds appear here, so a shorter list than modelNames means the tool asks for a model this host cannot serve.

ollama.config.integration.desc: One entry of a user's Ollama integration configuration, recording that a coding tool was pointed at the local server and which models it was given. The `name` field is the key Ollama files the tool under, for example "claude", "codex", "opencode", "cline", "copilot", or "qwen". Reading these answers which assistants on the host send their prompts to a local model rather than to a vendor API, and, through `models`, whether the model each one asks for is actually present in the store.

content.title: Content of the audit_control file

dir.title: Directory where audit log files are stored

expireAfterAge.name: expireAfterAge
expireAfterAge.title: Age threshold from expire-after
expireAfterAge.desc: Age since a trail file was last written after which auditd may remove it, as a duration. Converted as auditd converts it: `s` seconds, `h` hours, `d` days, and `y` years of 364 days plus one day for every fourth year. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no age term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterBytes.name: expireAfterBytes
expireAfterBytes.title: Size threshold from expire-after, in bytes
expireAfterBytes.desc: Aggregate size of all trail files after which auditd may remove the oldest, in bytes. `B` or no suffix is bytes, `K`, `M` and `G` are powers of 1024. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no size term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterOperator.name: expireAfterOperator
expireAfterOperator.title: How the two expire-after thresholds combine
expireAfterOperator.desc: `AND` when a trail file is removed only once both thresholds are exceeded, `OR` when either one is enough. Null for a single threshold, and when expire-after is absent, empty, or a value auditd rejects.

file.name: file
file.title: File resource for the audit_control file

filesz.name: filesz
filesz.title: Maximum size of individual audit log files

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Audit event flags for attributable (user) events

memberClearSflagsMask.name: memberClearSflagsMask
memberClearSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can clear on their processes

memberSetSflagsMask.name: memberSetSflagsMask
memberSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can set on their processes

minRetentionAge.name: minRetentionAge
minRetentionAge.title: Minimum age trail files reach before auditd can remove them
minRetentionAge.desc: Age a trail file is guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove it, whatever the size of the trail, as a duration. Set for an age threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the size threshold alone can remove files (a size on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minRetentionBytes.name: minRetentionBytes
minRetentionBytes.title: Minimum aggregate trail size kept before auditd can remove a file, in bytes
minRetentionBytes.desc: Aggregate size the trail files are guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove one, whatever their age, in bytes. Set for a size threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the age threshold alone can remove files (an age on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minfree.name: minfree
minfree.title: Minimum free space threshold (percentage) before audit warnings

naflags.name: naflags
naflags.title: Audit event flags for non-attributable events

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed parameters from the audit_control file

superuserSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that superusers can set on their processes

openBSMAudit.title: OpenBSM audit_control configuration (macOS and BSD)
openBSMAudit.desc: OpenBSM audit subsystem configuration parsed from the `audit_control` file (pass `path` to override the default location). Exposes the audit event `flags`, log retention (`expireAfter`, `filesz`, `minfree`), and policy parameters that govern which security-relevant events the kernel records. `expireAfter` is also parsed the way auditd reads it: its age and size thresholds (`expireAfterAge`, `expireAfterBytes`), how they combine (`expireAfterOperator`), and what that guarantees about how long trail files survive (`minRetentionAge`, `minRetentionBytes`).

mcpServer.name: mcpServer
mcpServer.title: OpenAI Codex MCP server
mcpServer.desc: Model Context Protocol server Codex connects to, giving the agent access to external tools and data. Servers come from the `[mcp_servers]` tables in config.toml and from installed plugins. Stdio servers run a local command with args; http servers connect to a url. `plugin` records which plugin declared the server (empty for one configured in config.toml) and `hasEnv` whether environment variables (often API keys or tokens) are set, both relevant when auditing what external services the agent can invoke.

model.name: model

modelProvider.title: Configured model provider
modelProvider.desc: The backend that serves the configured model, taken from the `model_provider` key in config.toml (for example "openai"). Empty when unset.

package.title: Package that installed this tool

Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

plugin.title: OpenAI Codex installed plugin
plugin.desc: Plugin dropped into the Codex plugins directory, extending the agent with skills, MCP servers, and hooks. Notable fields for auditing: capabilities and skillNames describe what the plugin can do, while hasMcp and hasHooks flag whether it wires in external MCP servers or executes shell hooks, both of which widen the agent's trust boundary.

repo.name: repo

Exposes the origin remote `url`, the parsed `host` (for example github.com) and `name` (org/repo slug), the checked-out `branch`, all configured `remotes`, and the working-tree root `path`. Repositories are deduplicated by their working-tree root. Sessions whose directory is not a git working tree are omitted.

repos.name: repos

The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional, null when the host cannot be determined.

The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional; null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: OpenHands skill
skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the OpenHands agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills installed for the agent, one resource per discovered SKILL.md file

openhands.title: OpenHands AI agent instance (formerly OpenDevin)
openhands.desc: OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin), an open-source AI software-engineering agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .openhands in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.all-hands.dev/

openhands.skill.name: openhands.skill

allowedTools.name: allowedTools
allowedTools.title: Tools the skill is allowed to use
allowedTools.desc: Tool identifiers parsed from the frontmatter `allowed-tools` field (a comma-separated list), naming the capabilities the skill may invoke such as file edits, shell commands, or web access. Empty when the skill declares no restriction. The key field for reviewing what an installed skill is permitted to do.

argumentHint.name: argumentHint
argumentHint.title: Hint for expected arguments
argumentHint.desc: Usage hint from the frontmatter `argument-hint` field, shown when the skill is invoked. Empty when unset.

content.name: content
content.title: Full raw content of the SKILL.md file
content.desc: Complete Markdown body of the skill, including the YAML frontmatter and the prose instructions the agent follows. Inspect it to review exactly what an installed skill tells the agent to do.

description.name: description
description.title: Skill description
description.desc: Free-text summary from the frontmatter `description` field, stating what the skill does and when the agent should invoke it.

name.name: name
name.title: Skill name
name.desc: Name from the SKILL.md YAML frontmatter `name` field, falling back to the skill's directory name when the frontmatter omits it.

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL identifying the skill's git origin

sha256.name: sha256
sha256.title: SHA-256 hash of the skill content
sha256.desc: Hex-encoded SHA-256 digest of content, for detecting drift or pinning a known-good skill definition against a baseline.

source.name: source
source.title: Filesystem path to the SKILL.md file that defines the skill

openhands.skill.title: OpenHands skill
openhands.skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the OpenHands agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

os.name: os

any.name: any
any.title: Any operating system
any.desc:
The union of every OS root, and the root this provider declares: `_` resolves to it, so a query can reach any resource the provider exposes without naming a platform. The universal fields arrive through the embedded `os.base`; the family-specific ones are aliased onto this resource directly.

A query compiled against this union still says which platform it needs: the compiler narrows the root as members are accessed, so touching only universal members keeps the query portable while touching `iptables` requires a Linux root. See ADR 031.

base.name: base
base.title: Generic operating system information common to all platforms
base.desc:
The universal root of an OS asset: everything present on every supported platform. Embeds `machine` (firmware / SMBIOS hardware identity) and exposes the pretty hostname (or Windows device name), the FQDN-style hostname, environment variables and the resolved PATH list, uptime, the available-OS-update list, the reboot-pending flag, the hypervisor, the machine ID, the system date and timezone, and the `users` and `groups` collections.

The family roots build on it: `os.unix` for the Unix family, `os.linux` and `os.macos` under that, `os.windows` beside it, each carrying only the facilities its family provides. `os.any` is the union of all of them and is the root the provider declares, so `_` resolves to it. Which root a resource hangs off is the statement about where that resource exists, which is why the `alias os.<root>.<resource>` block at the top of this schema is the platform classification: to add a resource you have to place it. Those aliases have to stay contiguous, a comment between two of them fails the parse.

date.name: date
date.title: Current date and timezone of the system
date.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.date, reachable as `_.date`.

env.name: env
env.title: ENV variable contents
env.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.env, reachable as `_.env`.

hostname.name: hostname
hostname.title: Hostname for this OS
hostname.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.hostname, reachable as `_.hostname`.

hypervisor.name: hypervisor
hypervisor.title: Hypervisor for this OS
hypervisor.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.hypervisor, reachable as `_.hypervisor`.

lastUpdate.name: lastUpdate
lastUpdate.title: Time the most recent operating system update was installed
lastUpdate.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.lastUpdate, reachable as `_.lastUpdate`, which documents what the timestamp does and does not cover.

lastUpdateAge.name: lastUpdateAge
lastUpdateAge.title: Time since the most recent operating system update was installed
lastUpdateAge.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.lastUpdateAge, reachable as `_.lastUpdateAge`.

lastUpdateSource.name: lastUpdateSource
lastUpdateSource.title: Record the last-update timestamp was read from
lastUpdateSource.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.lastUpdateSource, reachable as `_.lastUpdateSource`.

linux.name: linux
linux.title: Operating system information for Linux platforms
linux.desc: Extends `os.unix` (and through it, `os.base`) with Linux-only surfaces: the supported packet-filter stacks (`iptables`, `ip6tables`, `nftables`, `ufw`, `firewalld`), the `/etc/fstab` mount table, and the AppArmor mandatory-access-control namespace. Use it to write Linux-specific audits without reaching out to global resource handles.

machineid.name: machineid
machineid.title: Machine ID for this OS
machineid.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.machineid, reachable as `_.machineid`.

macos.name: macos
macos.title: Operating system information for macOS
macos.desc: Extends `os.unix` (and through it, `os.base`) with the facilities only macOS provides: the `macos` surface itself, Safari, `launchd` and the OpenBSM audit subsystem.

name.name: name
name.title: Pretty hostname on macOS/Linux or device name on Windows
name.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.name, reachable as `_.name`.

path.name: path
path.title: PATH variable contents
path.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.path, reachable as `_.path`.

rebootpending.name: rebootpending
rebootpending.title: Whether a reboot is pending
rebootpending.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.rebootpending, reachable as `_.rebootpending`.

rootCertificates.name: rootCertificates
rootCertificates.title: Operating system root certificate trust store
rootCertificates.desc: X.509 root certificates that the asset's operating system trusts for TLS validation, derived from the platform-appropriate trust-store files (e.g. `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` on Debian, `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` on RHEL, the macOS SecTrust store, the Windows Root certificate store). Reads each trust-store file and exposes the parsed `network.certificate` list so audits can pin specific issuers, detect untrusted local additions, or count the trust-store size.

unix.name: unix
unix.title: Operating system information for Unix-like platforms
unix.desc: Extends `os.base` for Unix-family operating systems (macOS, Linux, FreeBSD and similar), carrying the facilities that family provides and Windows does not: `sshd`, `crontab`, `sudo`/`sudoers`, the mount table, the kernel, NFS, ZFS, the classic daemons (`inetd`, `snmpd`, `postfix`, `exim`) and `aide`.

update.name: update
update.title: Operating system update information
update.desc: Single pending OS update: its name, category, severity, whether it requires a restart, and the package format it belongs to. Read from `os.updates` to audit patch state and prioritize outstanding updates by severity.

updates.name: updates
updates.title: List of available OS updates
updates.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.updates, reachable as `_.updates`.

uptime.name: uptime
uptime.title: Current uptime
uptime.desc: Deprecated in favor of os.base.uptime, reachable as `_.uptime`.

windows.name: windows
windows.title: Operating system information for Windows platforms
windows.desc: Extends `os.base` with the facilities only Windows provides: the `windows` surface itself (hotfixes, features, firewall profiles, and the rest), the registry, local security and audit policy, and IIS.

os.title: Operating system information
os.desc: Deprecated in favor of the OS roots. Every field on this resource now lives on `os.base`, which is the universal root of an OS asset, so `_.hostname` or `os.base.hostname` reads what `os.hostname` used to. The fields here keep working for the whole v14 line and are removed in v15; nothing else is attached to `os`, which is only the namespace the roots hang under.

os.any.name: os.any

aide.name: aide
aide.title: AIDE file integrity database
aide.desc: Configuration and database state of AIDE, the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment. `params` holds the settings read from the configuration, `groups` the attribute group definitions, and `rules` the selection lines deciding which paths are watched and which attributes are compared. `database` points at the reference database the next check runs against, and its modification time is the signal worth asserting on: a reference database older than the last package transaction no longer describes the system, so a check against it cannot detect anything that changed in between. Watch for coverage removed by a negative rule, which silently drops a path from an otherwise healthy configuration.

apparmor.name: apparmor
apparmor.title: AppArmor mandatory access control
apparmor.desc: AppArmor status, the loaded profiles and their enforcement modes, and the processes currently under confinement. Use it to confirm AppArmor is active and that security-relevant profiles are in enforce rather than complain or unconfined mode. A host that does not have AppArmor reports `installed` false and confines nothing, so gate a policy on `installed` the way one for SELinux gates on selinux.installed.

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

auditpol.name: auditpol
auditpol.title: Windows audit policies
auditpol.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language and supports looking up a single subcategory by name or GUID.

cgroups.name: cgroups
cgroups.title: Linux control groups (cgroup v2)
cgroups.desc: cgroup hierarchy, available controllers, and the version of cgroups in use. Modern Linux uses cgroup v2 (a single unified hierarchy at /sys/fs/cgroup); v1 hosts and hybrid setups are detected and reported via `version`, but per-controller hierarchies are not modeled. Iterate `list` to query every cgroup on the host, or walk down from `root` to traverse the hierarchy.

crontab.name: crontab
crontab.title: Crontab schedule on the system
crontab.desc: Scheduled cron jobs collected from every source on the host: the system crontab (/etc/crontab), drop-in files under /etc/cron.d and /usr/local/etc/cron.d, and per-user crontabs (/var/spool/cron, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/spool/cron/tabs, /usr/lib/cron/tabs, /var/cron/tabs). The `entries` list shows what runs on a schedule, as which `user`, and with what `command`. Use `entries.where(user == "root")` to focus on privileged jobs. `files` lists the source files the entries were parsed from.

exim.name: exim
exim.title: Exim mail transfer agent configuration
exim.desc: Exim configuration. `params` holds the macros and main-section options parsed from the active config file, covering both the Debian `update-exim4.conf.conf` key/value form and the monolithic `exim.conf` main section (options before the first `begin` block). `localInterfaces` normalizes the local interface list, handling the Debian `dc_local_interfaces` `' ; '`-separated form and the Exim `local_interfaces` list, so policies can compare it directly. By default the per-distribution config location is used; select an alternate file with `exim("/path/to/exim.conf")`.

firewalld.name: firewalld
firewalld.title: firewalld dynamic firewall manager (RHEL/CentOS/Fedora)
firewalld.desc: firewalld daemon state, the default zone, and the full set of configured zones on RHEL, CentOS, and Fedora systems. Check `status` to confirm the daemon is running and `defaultZone` for the zone applied to unclassified interfaces and sources. Enumerate `zones` to audit the per-zone services, ports, and rich rules that make up the effective policy.

fstab.name: fstab
fstab.title: fstab persistent mount table
fstab.desc: Filesystem mount table (/etc/fstab) that defines which devices are mounted where at boot and with what options. Each `entries` row carries the device, mount point, filesystem type, and mount options, so audits can check for hardening flags (nodev, nosuid, noexec) on sensitive mounts. Select an alternate file with `fstab(path: "...")`.

iis.name: iis
iis.title: Internet Information Services web server
iis.desc:
IIS installation on a Windows host: the websites it serves, the application pools that run them, and the configuration in force at each level. Values are reported as IIS resolves them, after machine.config, the root web.config, applicationHost.config, location sections, a site's own web.config and a nested application's web.config have all been applied in order. A setting a site or application overrides therefore reads with the overriding value, not the one applicationHost.config declares.

On a host that does not run IIS, `installed` is false, `config` and `applicationHost` are null, and `sites` and `appPools` are empty. An empty list satisfies `all()`, so a check that iterates sites needs a `iis.sites.length > 0` guard or an `iis.installed` filter to avoid passing on a host that serves nothing.

inetd.name: inetd
inetd.title: inetd super-server namespace
inetd.desc: Namespace hosting `inetd.config`, the entry point for examining which network services the inetd super-server launches on demand.

ip6tables.name: ip6tables
ip6tables.title: IPv6 packet filter (ip6tables)
ip6tables.desc: The host's IPv6 ip6tables ruleset: every `tables` entry (filter, nat, mangle, raw) with its chains and rules, plus shortcuts to the filter table's `input`, `output`, and `forward` chains and their default policies. Audit it alongside `iptables` so IPv6 traffic is filtered as strictly as IPv4.

iptables.name: iptables
iptables.title: IPv4 packet filter (iptables)
iptables.desc: The host's IPv4 iptables ruleset: every `tables` entry (filter, nat, mangle, raw) with its chains and rules, plus shortcuts to the filter table's `input`, `output`, and `forward` chains and their default policies. A default `inputPolicy` of `ACCEPT` with no restricting rules is a common firewall-hardening finding.

kernel.name: kernel
kernel.title: Running kernel and its modules
kernel.desc: Running kernel and its configuration surface. Exposes kernel version info, sysctl `parameters` and `sysctls`, `modules`, installed kernel versions, ASLR state (`aslr`, Linux and FreeBSD), and, on Linux, hardening state (`cmdline`, `taint`, `lockdown`) and the live patches applied in memory (`livepatch`).

launchd.name: launchd
launchd.title: macOS launchd job configurations
launchd.desc: launchd service manager on macOS. The `jobs` collection parses daemon and agent job definitions from their plist files across the system, library, and per-user launchd directories, so audits can review autostarted programs, the accounts they run as, and their launch conditions in one place.

limits.name: limits
limits.title: PAM resource limits configuration (limits.conf)
limits.desc: Soft and hard caps on processes, open files, memory, and other per-user resources, parsed from /etc/security/limits.conf and every .conf file under /etc/security/limits.d. Iterate `entries` to audit for missing or overly permissive limits (e.g. unrestricted core dumps or nofile).

loginconf.name: loginconf
loginconf.title: BSD login class capability database (/etc/login.conf)
loginconf.desc: Login classes parsed from /etc/login.conf on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `loginconf.class` per class. Login classes hold the password policy (password format, expiry, warning period), umask, resource limits, and environment for the accounts assigned to them in /etc/master.passwd. The file uses the getcap(3) format, and the system reads the compiled login.conf.db that `cap_mkdb` builds from it, so an edit takes effect only after `cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf`. Read another file with `loginconf("/path/to/login.conf")`.

logindefs.name: logindefs
logindefs.title: Shadow password suite (login.defs) configuration
logindefs.desc: Password aging, UID/GID ranges, and login policy parameters parsed from /etc/login.defs. The params map exposes settings such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, UMASK, and ENCRYPT_METHOD, which drive account and password-policy audits. Point at an alternate file with the `path` argument.

logrotate.name: logrotate
logrotate.title: logrotate configuration
logrotate.desc: Log rotation configuration parsed from the main logrotate.conf and the fragments under logrotate.d. `globalConfig` holds the directives that apply outside any log block, `entries` holds the per-log-path rotation rules, and `files` lists the configuration files read. Audit rotation frequency, retention counts, and compression to confirm logs are kept long enough and pruned safely.

lsblk.name: lsblk
lsblk.title: Unix block devices (lsblk)
lsblk.desc: Block devices reported by `lsblk`, each carrying its device name, filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount points. Iterate to audit disk layout, filesystem labels, and mount configuration.

luks.name: luks
luks.title: LUKS-encrypted volumes on the host
luks.desc: Block devices that carry a LUKS header, exposing each volume's on-disk format version, cipher, key-derivation parameters, and every keyslot. Both LUKS1 and LUKS2 headers are reported through the same schema; the `version` field on each volume distinguishes them and version-specific fields (label, subsystem, and tokens for LUKS2; AF-splitter stripes for LUKS1) are populated only where they apply.

lvm.name: lvm
lvm.title: Linux Logical Volume Manager
lvm.desc: LVM block-device storage on Linux: physical volumes initialized for LVM, volume groups that aggregate them, and the logical volumes carved out of those groups. Iterate `physicalVolumes`, `volumeGroups`, and `logicalVolumes` to audit LVM layout, free capacity, thin-pool usage, and snapshot relationships.

macos.name: macos
macos.title: macOS-specific operating system surfaces
macos.desc: macOS host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: the machine's `computerName`, per-user and per-host defaults (preferences), the global account/password policy, and installed `systemExtensions`. A starting point for macOS-specific audits alongside the dedicated resources such as firewall, filevault, gatekeeper, and sip.

masterpasswd.name: masterpasswd
masterpasswd.title: BSD password database source (/etc/master.passwd)
masterpasswd.desc: Accounts parsed from /etc/master.passwd on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `masterpasswd.entry` per account. Unlike `users`, which reads the public passwd database, each entry carries the password field, the login class, and the password change and account expiry times, so audits can find accounts with no password, check that passwords are shadowed, and resolve each account's login class settings. The file is readable by root only: a scan without root or `--sudo` returns a permission error, never an empty list. Lines that cannot be parsed are left out and counted in `invalidLines`. Read another file with `masterpasswd("/path/to/master.passwd")`. macOS ships this file too, but its accounts live in Directory Services, so use `users` there.

mdadm.name: mdadm
mdadm.title: Linux software RAID arrays (mdadm)
mdadm.desc: Software RAID arrays managed by mdadm, each with its RAID level, health state, device counts, and resync progress. Iterate `arrays` to audit redundancy and spot degraded or rebuilding arrays. Use `arrays.where(state == "degraded")` to find arrays that have lost a member.

modprobe.name: modprobe
modprobe.title: Kernel module configuration (modprobe.d)
modprobe.desc: Install, remove, blacklist, options, alias, and softdep directives parsed from the modprobe configuration files. Use blacklists to verify that risky kernel modules are prevented from loading and options to audit module parameters. Point at an alternate config with the `path` argument.

mount.name: mount
mount.title: Mount table
mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

nfs.name: nfs
nfs.title: NFS service local state
nfs.desc: Local NFS service viewed from two angles: shares this host declares (`exports`) and NFS volumes this host has mounted (`mounts`). `exports` is parsed from `/etc/exports` using the platform-specific syntax for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and AIX; each row is one `(path, client)` pair so audits like `nfs.exports.where(noRootSquash)` work directly. `mounts` filters the system mount table for NFS file systems and parses NFS-specific options into fields (protocol `version`, `security` flavor, `hardMount`, `readOnly`).

nftables.name: nftables
nftables.title: nftables firewall
nftables.desc: The host's nftables ruleset across all address families (ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge, netdev). Flattened accessors return everything at once: `tables`, `chains` (across all tables), `rules` (across all chains), and named `sets`. nftables is the modern replacement for iptables, so audit it on current distributions to confirm chains have restrictive policies and expected rules.

openBSMAudit.name: openBSMAudit
openBSMAudit.title: OpenBSM audit_control configuration (macOS and BSD)
openBSMAudit.desc: OpenBSM audit subsystem configuration parsed from the `audit_control` file (pass `path` to override the default location).
