Exposes the audit event `flags`, log retention (`expireAfter`, `filesz`, `minfree`), and policy parameters that govern which security-relevant events the kernel records. `expireAfter` is also parsed the way auditd reads it: its age and size thresholds (`expireAfterAge`, `expireAfterBytes`), how they combine (`expireAfterOperator`), and what that guarantees about how long trail files survive (`minRetentionAge`, `minRetentionBytes`).

ovs.name: ovs
ovs.title: Open vSwitch
ovs.desc: Software switch configured through the Open vSwitch database on this host. The bridges, ports, and interfaces fields report the switch as it is running now, joined into the topology the datapath uses, which is the dataplane a CNI plugin builds and Kubernetes only records as intent. Empty on hosts where ovs-vsctl is not installed or the database is not reachable.

polkit.name: polkit
polkit.title: Polkit authorization framework
polkit.desc: System-wide polkit (formerly PolicyKit) authorization state: the `actions` that privileged operations are registered under, the JavaScript `rules` that decide who may invoke them, the legacy local-authority grants in `localAuthorityRules`, and the `adminIdentities` the local authority treats as administrators. Polkit governs whether an unprivileged session may restart a unit, mount a disk, or install a package, so an over-broad grant is a local privilege escalation path. Read `version` before drawing conclusions: polkit 0.106 and later evaluate the JavaScript rules and ignore `.pkla` files, while earlier releases do the reverse.

postfix.name: postfix
postfix.title: Postfix mail transfer agent configuration
postfix.desc: Effective Postfix configuration. `params` reports parameter values from `postconf` when the binary is available (which includes the built-in defaults for parameters not written to the file) and otherwise falls back to parsing main.cf directly (file values only, with `$name` interpolation and continuation lines). `inetInterfaces` is the parsed `inet_interfaces` list and `services` are the daemon definitions from master.cf. By default the per-distribution config locations are used; select an alternate main.cf with `postfix("/path/to/main.cf")`.

powershell.name: powershell
powershell.title: Result of running a PowerShell script on the system
powershell.desc: Ad-hoc PowerShell execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a script string; the resource executes the script via PowerShell on the asset and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. The Windows and cross-platform-PowerShell counterpart to `command` for assertions that need PowerShell-only surface area.

registrykey.name: registrykey
registrykey.title: Windows registry key
registrykey.desc: A Windows registry key selected by `path`, exposing its value entries (`items`), child key names (`children`), and whether the key `exists`. Optionally read a specific user's per-user registry (HKCU) by supplying `userSid`, falling back to their `NTUSER.DAT` profile hive (`ntuserDat`) when that hive is not currently loaded. Select a key with `registrykey(path: "...")`.

safari.name: safari
safari.title: Safari browser (macOS only)
safari.desc: Safari web browser on macOS. The `extensions` collection lists every installed Safari extension across all user accounts on the host, letting audits flag unknown or disabled extensions and verify their provenance.

secpol.name: secpol
secpol.title: Windows local security policy
secpol.desc: Windows local security policy exported via secedit, broken into four maps. `systemaccess` covers password and account-lockout settings (for example MinimumPasswordLength, LockoutBadCount); `eventaudit` holds the legacy audit categories; `registryvalues` exposes security-relevant registry-backed policies; and `privilegerights` maps each user right (for example SeDenyNetworkLogonRight) to the accounts granted it. These are the primary source for CIS-style local policy benchmarks.

selinux.name: selinux
selinux.title: SELinux mandatory access control
selinux.desc: SELinux enforcement mode, configured mode, active policy type, tunable booleans, and loaded policy modules. The runtime `mode` (from getenforce or /sys/fs/selinux on a running system, from /etc/selinux/config in a disk or image scan) may differ from `configMode`, which is what persists across reboot; compare the two to catch a system left permissive at runtime or booted with SELinux disabled.

shadow.name: shadow
shadow.title: Shadow password file (/etc/shadow)
shadow.desc: Per-user password aging, expiration, and lock state parsed from `/etc/shadow`, one `shadow.entry` per account. Audit password policy compliance and find accounts with no expiry, weak aging settings, or locked/disabled passwords.

snmpd.name: snmpd
snmpd.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) namespace
snmpd.desc: Namespace hosting `snmpd.config`, the entry point for examining the effective SNMP daemon configuration.

sriov.name: sriov
sriov.title: SR-IOV network devices
sriov.desc: Single-root I/O virtualization state of the host's network hardware. The physicalFunctions field lists every SR-IOV capable interface with the number of virtual functions it has enabled against the number it supports, and virtualFunctions flattens every virtual function across all of them. This is the realised hardware inventory, so it shows the PCI address, the bound driver, and the per-device link settings that a Kubernetes device plugin only reports as an aggregate count. Empty on hosts with no SR-IOV capable interface.

sshd.name: sshd
sshd.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) namespace
sshd.desc: Namespace hosting `sshd.config`, the entry point for auditing the OpenSSH server's effective settings and Match blocks.

sudo.name: sudo
sudo.title: Sudo binary and runtime metadata
sudo.desc: Installed `sudo` binary: where it lives on disk, the version it reports under `sudo -V`, which plugins are loaded (policy, I/O, audit, approval), whether the build supports Python-based plugins, and the result of `visudo -c` against the sudoers configuration. For sudoers configuration parsing, use the `sudoers` resource directly, or access it via this resource's `sudoers` field.

sudoers.name: sudoers
sudoers.title: sudo authorization configuration
sudoers.desc: User specifications, defaults, and aliases parsed across the sudoers files (/etc/sudoers plus /etc/sudoers.d). Use userSpecs to audit who may run which commands as which users, and defaults to check hardening settings such as env_reset, secure_path, requiretty, and NOPASSWD grants. Point at an alternate root file with the `path` argument.

sysrc.name: sysrc
sysrc.title: FreeBSD rc.conf system configuration
sysrc.desc: FreeBSD service and system configuration merged from rc.conf and rc.conf.local. The `entries` accessor exposes each variable assignment as a structured name/value pair (with the file it came from), so audits can assert on individual settings such as sshd_enable or a firewall being turned on. `content` returns the concatenated raw text. Point at a specific file with `sysrc(path: "...")`.

ufw.name: ufw
ufw.title: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) state and rules
ufw.desc: Uncomplicated Firewall status, default policies, configured rules, and application profiles on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and EPEL systems. Check `status` to confirm the firewall is active, and the `defaultIncoming` / `defaultOutgoing` / `defaultRouted` policies for the baseline stance (a hardened host typically denies incoming by default). Enumerate `rules` to audit the explicit allow/deny entries and `applications` for the service profiles UFW can reference by name.

usb.name: usb
usb.title: USB device inventory (experimental)
usb.desc: USB devices attached to the host, each with its vendor and product IDs, manufacturer, serial number, device class, and connection speed. The `devices` list inventories connected peripherals so you can flag removable storage or unexpected hardware.

windows.name: windows
windows.title: Windows-specific operating system surfaces
windows.desc: Windows host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: consolidated `computerInfo`, installed `hotfixes`, Server roles and features, image `optionalFeatures`, attached `disks`, scheduled tasks, and hardening controls (Device Guard, Exploit Protection, SmartScreen). A starting point for Windows-specific audits.

zfs.name: zfs
zfs.title: ZFS storage pools and datasets
zfs.desc: ZFS storage on the host: the installed `version`, the storage `pools` with their health and capacity, and every `dataset` (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, and bookmarks). Iterate to audit pool health, free capacity, vdev topology, and dataset properties such as compression and encryption.

os.any.title: Any operating system
os.any.desc:
The union of every OS root, and the root this provider declares: `_` resolves to it, so a query can reach any resource the provider exposes without naming a platform. The universal fields arrive through the embedded `os.base`; the family-specific ones are aliased onto this resource directly.

A query compiled against this union still says which platform it needs: the compiler narrows the root as members are accessed, so touching only universal members keeps the query portable while touching `iptables` requires a Linux root. See ADR 031.

os.any.aide.name: aide

configFile.name: configFile
configFile.title: Root configuration file the settings are read from

database.name: database
database.title: Reference database the next check compares against
database.desc: Resolved from `database_in`, with the `file:` prefix stripped. Null when the setting names no readable database, which is also the state before the database is initialized for the first time.

files.name: files
files.title: Every configuration file that contributed, including resolved includes

groups.name: groups
groups.title: Attribute group definitions, as key-value pairs
groups.desc: Maps each group name to its expression exactly as written, for example `NORMAL` to `R+sha512`. Referenced from a rule's `expression` and resolved into its `attributes`.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether AIDE is present on the system
installed.desc: True when an AIDE binary is found. A configuration file left behind by a removed package does not count. Use it to guard integrity-monitoring audits on hosts that ship no AIDE at all.

newDatabase.name: newDatabase
newDatabase.title: Database a fresh initialization writes, resolved from `database_out`

params.name: params
params.title: Settings from the configuration, as key-value pairs
params.desc: Keyed by the option name as written, for example `database_in`, `database_out`, `gzip_dbout`, and `report_url`. A `key = value` line whose key is not a recognized AIDE option is reported in `groups` instead.

rule.name: rule
rule.title: AIDE selection rule
rule.desc: Single selection line from the AIDE configuration: the `path` it applies to, the `attributes` compared for matching entries, the `selection` kind deciding whether the line adds or removes coverage, and the file types it is limited to as `restriction`. Macro references in the path are substituted and the configuration's escapes (`\\.` for `\.`) removed, so `path` is the expression AIDE actually matches. Lines inside an `@@if` block whose condition is false are not rules. A condition that cannot be evaluated, such as `@@if hostname` in an image scan, has both of its branches reported. Executable files reached through `@@x_include` are run, as AIDE runs them, and their output read; on a connection that cannot run commands, such as an image scan, the rules they print are missing.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: Selection rules deciding which paths are checked

version.name: version
version.title: AIDE release reported by the aide binary
version.desc: Requires command execution, so it is null on backends that expose only a filesystem, such as an image scan, and when no aide binary can be run.

os.any.aide.title: AIDE file integrity database
os.any.aide.desc: Configuration and database state of AIDE, the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment. `params` holds the settings read from the configuration, `groups` the attribute group definitions, and `rules` the selection lines deciding which paths are watched and which attributes are compared. `database` points at the reference database the next check runs against, and its modification time is the signal worth asserting on: a reference database older than the last package transaction no longer describes the system, so a check against it cannot detect anything that changed in between. Watch for coverage removed by a negative rule, which silently drops a path from an otherwise healthy configuration.

os.any.apparmor.name: apparmor

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether AppArmor is present on the system

process.name: process
process.title: AppArmor confined process
process.desc: Running process attached to an AppArmor profile, giving its executable path, PID, the applied profile, and the confinement status.

profile.name: profile
profile.title: AppArmor profile
profile.desc: Loaded AppArmor profile and the mode it is running in: enforce (violations blocked), complain (violations logged only), or unconfined.

os.any.apparmor.title: AppArmor mandatory access control
os.any.apparmor.desc: AppArmor status, the loaded profiles and their enforcement modes, and the processes currently under confinement. Use it to confirm AppArmor is active and that security-relevant profiles are in enforce rather than complain or unconfined mode. A host that does not have AppArmor reports `installed` false and confines nothing, so gate a policy on `installed` the way one for SELinux gates on selinux.installed.

os.any.auditpol.name: auditpol

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Windows audit policy entry
entry.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy.subcategory, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language. This entry carries the subcategory name, GUID, inclusion setting, and exclusion setting as reported by the system, plus the setting as `success` and `failure` booleans and as the English `setting`, which are the same in every display language.

os.any.auditpol.title: Windows audit policies
os.any.auditpol.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language and supports looking up a single subcategory by name or GUID.

os.any.cgroups.name: cgroups

controllers.name: controllers
controllers.title: Controllers available on the host (e.g., memory, cpu, io, pids)

list.name: list
list.title: Flat list of every cgroup on the host

version.name: version
version.title: cgroup version in use: 2 (unified), 1 (legacy v1 only), or 0 if cgroups are not available

os.any.cgroups.title: Linux control groups (cgroup v2)
os.any.cgroups.desc: cgroup hierarchy, available controllers, and the version of cgroups in use. Modern Linux uses cgroup v2 (a single unified hierarchy at /sys/fs/cgroup); v1 hosts and hybrid setups are detected and reported via `version`, but per-controller hierarchies are not modeled. Iterate `list` to query every cgroup on the host, or walk down from `root` to traverse the hierarchy.

os.any.crontab.name: crontab

entries.name: entries
entries.title: All cron entries from system and user crontabs

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Individual crontab entry
entry.desc: Single scheduled job parsed from a crontab source. The five schedule fields (`minute`, `hour`, `dayOfMonth`, `month`, `dayOfWeek`) hold the raw cron expressions, `user` is the account the job runs as (taken from the entry for system crontabs, or from the filename for per-user crontabs), and `command` is the line executed. `file` and `lineNumber` locate the entry in its source.

files.name: files
files.title: Files that contain crontab entries

os.any.crontab.title: Crontab schedule on the system
os.any.crontab.desc: Scheduled cron jobs collected from every source on the host: the system crontab (/etc/crontab), drop-in files under /etc/cron.d and /usr/local/etc/cron.d, and per-user crontabs (/var/spool/cron, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/spool/cron/tabs, /usr/lib/cron/tabs, /var/cron/tabs). The `entries` list shows what runs on a schedule, as which `user`, and with what `command`. Use `entries.where(user == "root")` to focus on privileged jobs. `files` lists the source files the entries were parsed from.

os.any.exim.name: exim

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the active Exim configuration file
configPath.desc: On Debian-family systems this is `/etc/exim4/exim4.conf` when that hand-written config exists, otherwise `/etc/exim4/update-exim4.conf.conf`.

localInterfaces.name: localInterfaces
localInterfaces.title: Local interfaces parsed and normalized into a list
localInterfaces.desc: An unset or empty setting means Exim listens on every interface, reported as Exim's own default `::0` and `0.0.0.0`. Macro references such as `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` are resolved. On Debian-family systems the list comes from the generated `/var/lib/exim4/config.autogenerated` that Exim loads, so a `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` in `exim4.conf.localmacros` wins over `dc_local_interfaces`. For the installed Exim's own config, a daemon started with `-oX` reports the interfaces given there (with their `.port` suffix), taken from the running daemons or, when none runs, from `/etc/default/exim4`. Several daemons report every interface they listen on. Empty when no Exim configuration exists.

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed macros and main-section options
params.desc: `.ifdef` and `.ifndef` blocks are evaluated like Exim does, including tests of Exim's built-in feature macros such as `_HAVE_OPENSSL`, which are read from the installed `exim` binary.

os.any.exim.title: Exim mail transfer agent configuration
os.any.exim.desc: Exim configuration. `params` holds the macros and main-section options parsed from the active config file, covering both the Debian `update-exim4.conf.conf` key/value form and the monolithic `exim.conf` main section (options before the first `begin` block). `localInterfaces` normalizes the local interface list, handling the Debian `dc_local_interfaces` `' ; '`-separated form and the Exim `local_interfaces` list, so policies can compare it directly. By default the per-distribution config location is used; select an alternate file with `exim("/path/to/exim.conf")`.

os.any.firewalld.name: firewalld

richrule.name: richrule
richrule.title: firewalld rich rule
richrule.desc: Single firewalld rich rule parsed into its parts: the address family, the source and destination it matches (each with a negation flag for `NOT` address forms), and the action it takes. The full original rule text is kept in `rule`. Rich rules express finer-grained policy than plain service/port entries, so auditing `source`, `sourceInverted`, and `action` together shows exactly which peers are accepted, rejected, or dropped.

status.name: status
status.title: Whether firewalld is running ("running", "failed", "not running", "not installed")
status.desc: "failed" is a daemon that is up but could not apply its ruleset, as `firewall-cmd --state` reports it. Its zones are still listed.

zone.name: zone
zone.title: firewalld zone configuration
zone.desc: Single firewalld zone: the trust level applied to the interfaces and source addresses bound to it. The `target` is the default action for traffic not otherwise matched (default, ACCEPT, REJECT, or DROP), and `active` indicates whether any interfaces or sources are bound. Audit `services`, `ports`, and `protocols` for what the zone permits, `richRules` for expressive per-source rules, and `masquerade` / `forwardPorts` for NAT behavior. Select a zone by name with `firewalld.zone(name: "public")`.

os.any.firewalld.title: firewalld dynamic firewall manager (RHEL/CentOS/Fedora)
os.any.firewalld.desc: firewalld daemon state, the default zone, and the full set of configured zones on RHEL, CentOS, and Fedora systems. Check `status` to confirm the daemon is running and `defaultZone` for the zone applied to unclassified interfaces and sources. Enumerate `zones` to audit the per-zone services, ports, and rich rules that make up the effective policy.

os.any.fstab.name: fstab

entries.name: entries
entries.title: fstab entries defined in this fstab file

entry.name: entry
entry.title: fstab entry for a device and its mount point
entry.desc: Single line of the fstab: the device to mount, where it mounts, its filesystem type, the comma-separated mount options, and the dump/fsck controls. The `options` field is the one audits most often assert on (for example requiring nosuid,nodev,noexec on /tmp or /var).

os.any.fstab.title: fstab persistent mount table
os.any.fstab.desc: Filesystem mount table (/etc/fstab) that defines which devices are mounted where at boot and with what options. Each `entries` row carries the device, mount point, filesystem type, and mount options, so audits can check for hardening flags (nodev, nosuid, noexec) on sensitive mounts. Select an alternate file with `fstab(path: "...")`.

os.any.iis.name: iis

appPool.name: appPool
appPool.title: IIS application pool
appPool.desc: The worker process configuration a site or application runs under: the identity it runs as, when it recycles, and how it reacts to repeated failures. The `name` field selects a pool, for example the "DefaultAppPool" that a stock installation ships.

appPools.name: appPools
appPools.title: Application pools defined on this server
appPools.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed.

application.name: application
application.title: Application mounted under an IIS site
application.desc: An application is a configuration boundary: it runs in its own application pool and its web.config overrides what the site and the server declare. The `path` field is the virtual path it is mounted at, "/" for the site root.

applicationHost.name: applicationHost
applicationHost.title: applicationHost.config, for ownership and permission checks
applicationHost.desc:
The shared configuration file as a file, so its permissions and owner can be audited and its raw text read. Its contents are what IIS starts from, not what it ends up with: a setting overridden by a site or an application still reads here with the server-level value. Use `config`, `iis.site.config` and `iis.application.config` for the values in force.

The typed fields leave credentials behind, but this file does not: it can hold encrypted application pool passwords and machine keys, so reading its content returns whatever it holds. Null when IIS is not installed.

binding.name: binding
binding.title: Address, port and protocol an IIS site answers on

config.name: config
config.title: Configuration in force at server scope
config.desc: The defaults every site inherits unless it overrides them, equivalent to the MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST configuration path. This includes the ASP.NET sections: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, but the server-scope configuration resolves the whole inheritance chain, so they read here with the values a site inherits. Null when IIS is not installed.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: IIS configuration in force at one scope
configuration.desc:
The configuration IIS applies at a single point in its hierarchy, after the whole machine.config, root web.config, applicationHost.config, location, site and application chain has been resolved. This is what the server acts on, which is not what any one configuration file says: reading applicationHost.config directly reports a value a site or application may override, and a check written against that file passes on exactly the override it exists to catch.

The `path` field is the IIS configuration path the values were resolved at, for example "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST" for the server or "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST/Default Web Site" for a site.

A field is null when its section is not declared at this scope. The ASP.NET sections are not such a case: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, and every scope here (the server's included) resolves the inheritance chain, so they carry the effective value at each one.

Each field names the section and attribute it resolves. A setting with no field of its own is reachable at the same place through `sections`, which carries every section this scope declares under its full path.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the web server is present on this host
installed.desc: True when the shared configuration file and the IIS management assembly are both present under %windir%\system32\inetsrv. The assembly ships with the web server itself, so this stays true on an installation that omits the optional management scripting tools.

site.name: site
site.title: Website hosted by IIS
site.desc: A single site: its bindings, the application pool it runs under, the applications mounted beneath it, its log settings, and the configuration in force at the site root. The `name` field is the site name as IIS knows it, which is also what identifies the site in its configuration path.

sites.name: sites
sites.title: Websites hosted by this server
sites.desc: Every site defined on the server, running or stopped. Empty when IIS is not installed, which makes `all()` over this list vacuously true; guard on `length` or on `installed`.

version.name: version
version.title: Version reported by the installation, for example "10.0"
version.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed or the version cannot be read.

virtualDirectory.name: virtualDirectory
virtualDirectory.title: Virtual directory of an IIS application

os.any.iis.title: Internet Information Services web server
os.any.iis.desc:
IIS installation on a Windows host: the websites it serves, the application pools that run them, and the configuration in force at each level. Values are reported as IIS resolves them, after machine.config, the root web.config, applicationHost.config, location sections, a site's own web.config and a nested application's web.config have all been applied in order. A setting a site or application overrides therefore reads with the overriding value, not the one applicationHost.config declares.

On a host that does not run IIS, `installed` is false, `config` and `applicationHost` are null, and `sites` and `appPools` are empty. An empty list satisfies `all()`, so a check that iterates sites needs a `iis.sites.length > 0` guard or an `iis.installed` filter to avoid passing on a host that serves nothing.

os.any.inetd.name: inetd

config.name: config
config.title: inetd super-server configuration
config.desc: Services the inetd (or compatible) super-server is configured to launch on demand. Each active entry pairs a service with its socket type, protocol, wait mode, run-as user, and server program. The configuration is assembled from /etc/inetd.conf together with any drop-in files under /etc/inetd.d. An xinetd configuration, such as inetd.config("/etc/xinetd.conf"), is read with the files it includes, and its entries are the service blocks xinetd runs: blocks with disable = yes, or disabled by the enabled and disabled lists of the defaults block, are left out. A missing configuration yields no entries, so audits such as serviceNames.none("ftp") hold trivially on systems that don't run inetd.

os.any.inetd.title: inetd super-server namespace
os.any.inetd.desc: Namespace hosting `inetd.config`, the entry point for examining which network services the inetd super-server launches on demand.

os.any.ip6tables.name: ip6tables

forwardPolicy.name: forwardPolicy
forwardPolicy.title: Default policy for the FORWARD chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

inputPolicy.name: inputPolicy
inputPolicy.title: Default policy for the INPUT chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

outputPolicy.name: outputPolicy
outputPolicy.title: Default policy for the OUTPUT chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

os.any.ip6tables.title: IPv6 packet filter (ip6tables)
os.any.ip6tables.desc: The host's IPv6 ip6tables ruleset: every `tables` entry (filter, nat, mangle, raw) with its chains and rules, plus shortcuts to the filter table's `input`, `output`, and `forward` chains and their default policies. Audit it alongside `iptables` so IPv6 traffic is filtered as strictly as IPv4.

os.any.iptables.name: iptables

chain.name: chain
chain.title: iptables chain within a table
chain.desc: A chain of ordered `rules` within a table, matched against packets in sequence. Built-in chains (INPUT, OUTPUT, FORWARD, PREROUTING, POSTROUTING) carry a default `policy` applied when no rule matches; user-defined chains have an empty policy and are reached only via a jump target.

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Individual iptables rule entry
entry.desc: A single iptables rule with its packet and byte counters, target action, protocol, input/output interfaces, source and destination addresses, matched ports, conntrack state, TCP flags, and comment. Reached from `iptables.input`, `iptables.output`, or `iptables.forward` to audit individual packet-filter rules, for example finding rules that accept traffic from anywhere with `iptables.input.where(target == "ACCEPT" && source == "0.0.0.0/0")`.

forwardPolicy.name: forwardPolicy
forwardPolicy.title: Default policy for the FORWARD chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

inputPolicy.name: inputPolicy
inputPolicy.title: Default policy for the INPUT chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

outputPolicy.name: outputPolicy
outputPolicy.title: Default policy for the OUTPUT chain (e.g., ACCEPT, DROP)

table.name: table
table.title: iptables table (filter, nat, mangle, raw)
table.desc: One iptables table and the `chains` it contains. The `name` selects the table's purpose: `filter` for packet acceptance/dropping, `nat` for address translation, `mangle` for packet header changes, and `raw` for connection tracking exemptions.

os.any.iptables.title: IPv4 packet filter (iptables)
os.any.iptables.desc: The host's IPv4 iptables ruleset: every `tables` entry (filter, nat, mangle, raw) with its chains and rules, plus shortcuts to the filter table's `input`, `output`, and `forward` chains and their default policies. A default `inputPolicy` of `ACCEPT` with no restricting rules is a common firewall-hardening finding.

os.any.kernel.name: kernel

aslr.name: aslr
aslr.title: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) state (Linux and FreeBSD)

info.name: info
info.title: Active kernel information (version, path, device, arguments)

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Installed kernel versions

livepatch.name: livepatch
livepatch.title: Live patches applied to the running kernel (Linux only)

module.name: module
module.title: System kernel module information
module.desc: Single kernel module: its `name`, in-memory `size`, and whether it is currently `loaded`. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.module(name: "nf_conntrack")`) to check a specific module, or iterate from `kernel.modules` to audit the full loaded-module list. Module names are normalized the way modprobe normalizes them, so `firewire-core` and `firewire_core` select the same module and match a rule written with either spelling. Use `blacklisted`, `installBypass`, and `disabled` to express CIS-style "module must not load" controls without falling back to raw modprobe.d file parsing. Use `onDisk` to tell whether a loadable module file is available for the running kernel even when it isn't currently loaded, and `builtIn` to detect functionality compiled directly into the kernel (which is always active and cannot be blacklisted or unloaded). On FreeBSD, modules carry the names `kldstat -v` lists, such as `msdosfs` or `pci/ena`, including the modules compiled into the kernel; a loaded file name such as `zfs.ko` also selects its module.

parameter.name: parameter
parameter.title: Kernel parameter (sysctl), live and configured
parameter.desc:
One kernel parameter with the value the running kernel uses (`value`) and the value the configuration files will apply at the next boot (`configured`), kept apart so a check can require both. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.parameter("fs.protected_hardlinks")`) or iterate `kernel.sysctls`. Names use the dotted form `sysctl -a` prints; a name written with slashes is accepted too.

Configuration is read from the sysctl.d directories (/etc, /run, /usr/local/lib, /usr/lib, /lib) with the precedence systemd-sysctl applies at boot: a file hides a same-named file in a lower-priority directory, the files are applied in file name order, and the last assignment wins. An explicit assignment beats a glob, and `-name` excludes a parameter from globs. Without systemd-sysctl, /etc/sysctl.conf is applied after the sysctl.d files, as `sysctl --system` does. On BSD and macOS it is /etc/sysctl.conf (and /etc/sysctl.conf.local on FreeBSD).

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Kernel parameters map (sysctl key-value pairs)
parameters.desc: Live values only, as the kernel prints them. Use `sysctls` or `kernel.parameter` for the value the configuration files set as well. Those collapse whitespace in values (the tab in `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` becomes a space), so the same parameter can read differently here.

sysctls.name: sysctls
sysctls.title: Every kernel parameter that is live, configured, or both
sysctls.desc: A parameter set in a configuration file but not exposed by the running kernel, such as one of an unloaded module, is listed with `active` false. A glob assignment is expanded against the live parameters; one that matches none is listed under its pattern.

os.any.kernel.title: Running kernel and its modules
os.any.kernel.desc: Running kernel and its configuration surface. Exposes kernel version info, sysctl `parameters` and `sysctls`, `modules`, installed kernel versions, ASLR state (`aslr`, Linux and FreeBSD), and, on Linux, hardening state (`cmdline`, `taint`, `lockdown`) and the live patches applied in memory (`livepatch`).

os.any.launchd.name: launchd

jobs.name: jobs
jobs.title: All launchd jobs from system and user directories

os.any.launchd.title: macOS launchd job configurations
os.any.launchd.desc: launchd service manager on macOS. The `jobs` collection parses daemon and agent job definitions from their plist files across the system, library, and per-user launchd directories, so audits can review autostarted programs, the accounts they run as, and their launch conditions in one place.

os.any.limits.name: limits

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed limits entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Resource limit entry
entry.desc: Single line from a limits configuration file, giving one domain / type / item / value tuple (e.g. `* hard core 0`).

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the limits configuration

os.any.limits.title: PAM resource limits configuration (limits.conf)
os.any.limits.desc: Soft and hard caps on processes, open files, memory, and other per-user resources, parsed from /etc/security/limits.conf and every .conf file under /etc/security/limits.d. Iterate `entries` to audit for missing or overly permissive limits (e.g. unrestricted core dumps or nofile).

os.any.loginconf.name: loginconf

class.name: class
class.title: Login class from /etc/login.conf
class.desc: One login class record. `capabilities` holds what the record itself writes, `effective` what applies after `tc=` inheritance, and `inherits` the classes it includes. Values keep their text as written (for example `90d` or `022`); boolean capabilities read as true. Select a class with `loginconf.class("default")`, which also matches an alias.

file.name: file
file.title: login.conf file that the classes are read from

os.any.loginconf.title: BSD login class capability database (/etc/login.conf)
os.any.loginconf.desc: Login classes parsed from /etc/login.conf on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `loginconf.class` per class. Login classes hold the password policy (password format, expiry, warning period), umask, resource limits, and environment for the accounts assigned to them in /etc/master.passwd. The file uses the getcap(3) format, and the system reads the compiled login.conf.db that `cap_mkdb` builds from it, so an edit takes effect only after `cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf`. Read another file with `loginconf("/path/to/login.conf")`.

os.any.logindefs.name: logindefs

content.name: content
content.title: Content of the configuration file

file.name: file
file.title: Current configuration file for resource

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed login.defs parameters as a name/value map (e.g. PASS_MAX_DAYS, UMASK, ENCRYPT_METHOD)

os.any.logindefs.title: Shadow password suite (login.defs) configuration
os.any.logindefs.desc: Password aging, UID/GID ranges, and login policy parameters parsed from /etc/login.defs. The params map exposes settings such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, UMASK, and ENCRYPT_METHOD, which drive account and password-policy audits. Point at an alternate file with the `path` argument.

os.any.logrotate.name: logrotate

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Per-file/glob rotation entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Logrotate configuration entry for a specific log path
entry.desc: Rotation rule for one log path or glob. `path` is the log the block applies to and `config` holds every directive inside the block as key-value pairs (e.g. "rotate", "daily", "compress", "maxage"). `file` and `lineNumber` locate the block in its source configuration file.

files.name: files
files.title: List of configuration files (main + logrotate.d fragments)

os.any.logrotate.title: logrotate configuration
os.any.logrotate.desc: Log rotation configuration parsed from the main logrotate.conf and the fragments under logrotate.d. `globalConfig` holds the directives that apply outside any log block, `entries` holds the per-log-path rotation rules, and `files` lists the configuration files read. Audit rotation frequency, retention counts, and compression to confirm logs are kept long enough and pruned safely.

os.any.lsblk.name: lsblk

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Unix block device
entry.desc: Single block device reported by `lsblk`: its device `name`, filesystem type (`fstype`), `label`, UUID, `mountpoints` list, and device `type`. `parents` and `children` walk the device stack (disk, partition, dm-crypt mapping, LVM volume), and `encrypted` reports whether the data on the device passes through a dm-crypt mapping. Filter to audit disk layout and mount configuration, e.g. `lsblk.where(mountpoints.contains("/"))`, or reach the device behind a mount with `mount.point(path: "/").blockDevice`.

os.any.lsblk.title: Unix block devices (lsblk)
os.any.lsblk.desc: Block devices reported by `lsblk`, each carrying its device name, filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount points. Iterate to audit disk layout, filesystem labels, and mount configuration.

os.any.luks.name: luks

keyslot.name: keyslot
keyslot.title: LUKS keyslot
keyslot.desc: One keyslot in a LUKS header: its index, state, and the key-derivation parameters used to wrap the master key. Audit for weak KDFs, low iteration or memory costs, and unexpectedly large numbers of active slots (each active slot is a passphrase that can unlock the volume).

volume.name: volume
volume.title: LUKS-encrypted block device
volume.desc: Single LUKS-formatted block device: its header version, label, master-key size and offset, cipher, and keyslots. Select a volume by its `uuid` (e.g., `luks.volumes.where(uuid == "fd44f17a-...")`) or by the underlying block device's `name`.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: LUKS-formatted block devices on the host

os.any.luks.title: LUKS-encrypted volumes on the host
os.any.luks.desc: Block devices that carry a LUKS header, exposing each volume's on-disk format version, cipher, key-derivation parameters, and every keyslot. Both LUKS1 and LUKS2 headers are reported through the same schema; the `version` field on each volume distinguishes them and version-specific fields (label, subsystem, and tokens for LUKS2; AF-splitter stripes for LUKS1) are populated only where they apply.

os.any.lvm.name: lvm

logicalVolume.name: logicalVolume
logicalVolume.title: LVM logical volume
logicalVolume.desc: Single LVM logical volume: `name`, full device `path`, `uuid`, parent volume group (`volumeGroupName`), attribute flags, size in bytes, snapshot `origin`, and thin-pool data usage. For thin volumes, `poolName` is set; for snapshots, `origin` is the source LV name.

logicalVolumes.name: logicalVolumes
logicalVolumes.title: Logical volumes across all volume groups

physicalVolume.name: physicalVolume
physicalVolume.title: LVM physical volume
physicalVolume.desc: Single block device initialized as an LVM physical volume: device path (`name`), `uuid`, the volume group it belongs to (`volumeGroupName`, empty if unassigned), on-disk `format`, attribute flags, and total/free byte counts.

volumeGroup.name: volumeGroup
volumeGroup.title: LVM volume group
volumeGroup.desc: Single LVM volume group: `name`, `uuid`, attribute flags, total and free byte counts, and the counts of physical volumes, logical volumes, and snapshots it contains. Useful for auditing capacity headroom and group-level policy.

os.any.lvm.title: Linux Logical Volume Manager
os.any.lvm.desc: LVM block-device storage on Linux: physical volumes initialized for LVM, volume groups that aggregate them, and the logical volumes carved out of those groups. Iterate `physicalVolumes`, `volumeGroups`, and `logicalVolumes` to audit LVM layout, free capacity, thin-pool usage, and snapshot relationships.

os.any.macos.name: macos

alf.name: alf
alf.title: macOS application layer firewall (raw ALF preference values)
alf.desc: Raw integer flags read from the Application Layer Firewall plist (`/Library/Preferences/com.apple.alf.plist`). Prefer `macos.firewall`, which decodes these into boolean fields; use this resource only when you need the underlying preference values.

filevault.name: filevault
filevault.title: macOS FileVault full-disk encryption
filevault.desc: FileVault full-disk encryption state: whether it is `enabled`, the current `status`, whether personal and institutional recovery keys exist, and the `users` permitted to unlock the encrypted volume at boot. CIS macOS benchmarks require FileVault enabled.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: macOS application layer firewall
firewall.desc: Decoded Application Layer Firewall configuration: whether the firewall is `enabled`, whether it blocks all incoming connections, stealth mode, logging, the signed-app auto-allow policy, and per-application rules. CIS macOS benchmarks expect the firewall enabled with stealth mode on. See `macos.alf` for the raw preference values.

gatekeeper.name: gatekeeper
gatekeeper.title: macOS Gatekeeper application execution policy
gatekeeper.desc: Gatekeeper policy that controls whether downloaded applications may run: whether assessments are `enabled` and the human-readable `status`. Disabling Gatekeeper lets unsigned or unnotarized software launch without a warning, so benchmarks expect it enabled.

globalAccountPolicies.name: globalAccountPolicies
globalAccountPolicies.title: Global account (password) policy directives applied to all local users

hardware.name: hardware
hardware.title: macOS hardware overview
hardware.desc: Hardware and firmware details reported by `system_profiler`: chip type, model identifiers, installed memory, serial number, and Activation Lock status. Useful for asset inventory and for distinguishing Apple Silicon from Intel Macs in conditional audits.

mdm.name: mdm
mdm.title: macOS MDM (Mobile Device Management) enrollment state
mdm.desc: MDM enrollment state for this Mac: whether it is enrolled, the enrollment server, and whether enrollment was performed via Automated Device Enrollment (formerly DEP) or user-approved. Use `macos.profiles` to enumerate the configuration profiles delivered to the device. Backed by `profiles status -type enrollment`.

profile.name: profile
profile.title: macOS Configuration Profile
profile.desc: Single Configuration Profile: its `identifier`, `uuid`, human-readable `displayName`, `description`, `organization`, `type`, whether it is install-locked (`removalDisallowed`), the scope it applies to (`scope`: `system` or `user`), and the individual `payloads` that carry the actual policy directives.

profiles.name: profiles
profiles.title: macOS configuration profiles installed on the system
profiles.desc: Every Configuration Profile delivered to the device, both MDM-delivered and manually installed `.mobileconfig` payloads, so you can audit what policies are actually in force. Backed by `profiles list -all -output stdout-xml`; requires root to see system-level (`_computerlevel`) profiles, otherwise only the current user's profiles are returned.

sharing.name: sharing
sharing.title: macOS Sharing service state
sharing.desc:
State of each toggle in the unified Sharing panel (System Settings > Sharing on macOS Ventura+, System Preferences > Sharing on older versions). CIS macOS benchmarks require most of these off unless the device explicitly needs the service. Backed by `system_profiler SPSharingDataType`, so the values match exactly what the System Settings UI displays.

`system_profiler SPSharingDataType` also reports `Remote Login` and `Remote Apple Events`; those are intentionally not exposed here because `macos.systemsetup.remoteLogin` and `macos.systemsetup.remoteAppleEvents` already cover them via the `systemsetup` CLI. This resource covers the rest of the panel.

sip.name: sip
sip.title: macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP)
sip.desc: System Integrity Protection state, the kernel-level protection that restricts modification of protected system files and processes even by root. Exposes whether SIP is `enabled` and the raw `status` message from `csrutil status`. Disabling SIP is a significant hardening regression.

softwareupdate.name: softwareupdate
softwareupdate.title: macOS Software Update configuration and pending updates
softwareupdate.desc: Automatic-update policy and the list of updates currently available to install. Policy fields read from `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.SoftwareUpdate.plist` (with `/Library/Managed Preferences/` taking precedence when an MDM configuration profile has been delivered). The `updates` list is produced from `softwareupdate -l --no-scan` so it does not initiate a network check.

systemExtension.name: systemExtension
systemExtension.title: macOS system extension
systemExtension.desc: Installed system extension read from /Library/SystemExtensions/db.plist: its `identifier`, `uuid`, `version`, `teamID` of the signing developer, declared `categories` (such as network or endpoint-security extensions), and `bundlePath`. The `state` string reports the extension's lifecycle, with `enabled` and `active` derived from it. `mdmManaged` is true when the extension or its team is allowlisted by an MDM system-extension policy, which distinguishes centrally approved extensions from user-installed ones.

systemExtensions.name: systemExtensions
systemExtensions.title: Installed system extensions (network, endpoint security, and driver extensions)

systemsetup.name: systemsetup
systemsetup.title: macOS machine settings via the systemsetup CLI
systemsetup.desc: Date/time, sleep and wake, remote login, power, and network-time settings surfaced by the `systemsetup` CLI, with each field mapping to one `systemsetup -get*` query. Requires at least admin privileges to run.

timemachine.name: timemachine
timemachine.title: macOS Time Machine backup configuration
timemachine.desc: Time Machine backup configuration read from its preferences: configured backup destinations, the automatic backup schedule, and the paths excluded from backups, exposed as the raw `preferences` dict.

userHostPreferences.name: userHostPreferences
userHostPreferences.title: Per-user, per-host macOS defaults (ByHost preferences), keyed by preference domain

userPreferences.name: userPreferences
userPreferences.title: Per-user macOS defaults (preferences), keyed by preference domain

xprotect.name: xprotect
xprotect.title: macOS XProtect anti-malware bundle
xprotect.desc:
Version and last-modified timestamp of the XProtect signature bundle (and, when present, the legacy Malware Removal Tool). CIS macOS benchmarks expect XProtect signatures to be current; checking `modified` against the auditor's freshness threshold catches devices that have stopped receiving updates.

XProtect.bundle lives at `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` on modern macOS (with `/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` as the legacy fallback). `mrtVersion` and `mrtModified` are empty or null on macOS 13+ where MRT has been retired in favor of XProtectRemediator.

os.any.macos.title: macOS-specific operating system surfaces
os.any.macos.desc: macOS host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: the machine's `computerName`, per-user and per-host defaults (preferences), the global account/password policy, and installed `systemExtensions`. A starting point for macOS-specific audits alongside the dedicated resources such as firewall, filevault, gatekeeper, and sip.

os.any.masterpasswd.name: masterpasswd

file.name: file
file.title: master.passwd file that the entries are read from

invalidLines.name: invalidLines
invalidLines.title: Number of lines in the file that could not be parsed
invalidLines.desc: Counts the lines left out of the entry list: a line without exactly ten fields, or with a uid, gid, change, or expire field that is not a number. Such a line is never guessed at (a bad uid would otherwise read as 0, which is root), and counting it keeps a shorter list from passing a check silently. `pwd_mkdb` refuses such a file, so a non-zero value also means the password database was not rebuilt from it.

os.any.masterpasswd.title: BSD password database source (/etc/master.passwd)
os.any.masterpasswd.desc: Accounts parsed from /etc/master.passwd on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `masterpasswd.entry` per account. Unlike `users`, which reads the public passwd database, each entry carries the password field, the login class, and the password change and account expiry times, so audits can find accounts with no password, check that passwords are shadowed, and resolve each account's login class settings. The file is readable by root only: a scan without root or `--sudo` returns a permission error, never an empty list. Lines that cannot be parsed are left out and counted in `invalidLines`. Read another file with `masterpasswd("/path/to/master.passwd")`. macOS ships this file too, but its accounts live in Directory Services, so use `users` there.

os.any.mdadm.name: mdadm

array.name: array
array.title: Linux software RAID array
array.desc: Single mdadm array. `level` is the RAID level, `state` is its health, and the device counts (`activeDevices`, `workingDevices`, `failedDevices`, `spareDevices`) together with `resyncProgress` reveal whether the array is healthy, degraded, or rebuilding. `devices` lists the member block devices.

arrays.name: arrays
arrays.title: List of all discovered RAID arrays

device.name: device
device.title: Member device in a software RAID array
device.desc: Single member of an mdadm array. `name` is the block device path, `role` is its slot number in the array layout, and `state` reports its condition (e.g. "active sync", "spare", "faulty").

os.any.mdadm.title: Linux software RAID arrays (mdadm)
os.any.mdadm.desc: Software RAID arrays managed by mdadm, each with its RAID level, health state, device counts, and resync progress. Iterate `arrays` to audit redundancy and spot degraded or rebuilding arrays. Use `arrays.where(state == "degraded")` to find arrays that have lost a member.

os.any.modprobe.name: modprobe

alias.name: alias
alias.title: Kernel module alias directive
alias.desc: A single `alias` line from a modprobe configuration file mapping an alias name or wildcard pattern to a target module. The kernel resolves the alias to `module` when the pattern is requested. A common hardening technique points a module's alias at a no-op (for example aliasing an unused network protocol to `off`) to block on-demand loading.

blacklist.name: blacklist
blacklist.title: Kernel module blacklist directive
blacklist.desc: A single `blacklist` line from a modprobe configuration file that stops a kernel module from being selected automatically. Auditing these confirms unwanted modules (for example `usb-storage`, `cramfs`, or unused filesystem and protocol drivers) are disabled per CIS hardening guidance. `module` is the blacklisted module name and `file`/`lineNumber` locate the declaration.

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the modprobe configuration

install.name: install
install.title: Install directive for module loading
install.desc: One `install` directive from modprobe.d: the module it applies to and the command run in place of the default insmod. A blacklist technique when the command is `/bin/true` or `/bin/false`.

installs.name: installs
installs.title: Install directives (custom commands for loading modules)

option.name: option
option.title: Kernel module options directive
option.desc: A single `options` line from a modprobe configuration file that sets load-time parameters for a kernel module. `parameters` is the raw argument string and `params` parses it into key/value pairs. Used to verify security-relevant module settings, for example that a driver is loaded with a hardened option.

remove.name: remove
remove.title: Remove directive for module unloading
remove.desc: One `remove` directive from modprobe.d: the module it applies to and the command run in place of the default rmmod.

removes.name: removes
removes.title: Remove directives (custom commands for unloading modules)

softdep.name: softdep
softdep.title: Kernel module soft dependency directive
softdep.desc: A single `softdep` line from a modprobe configuration file declaring modules to load before (`pre`) and after (`post`) a given module. Soft dependencies are advisory, so a missing dependency does not block the module from loading.

os.any.modprobe.title: Kernel module configuration (modprobe.d)
os.any.modprobe.desc: Install, remove, blacklist, options, alias, and softdep directives parsed from the modprobe configuration files. Use blacklists to verify that risky kernel modules are prevented from loading and options to audit module parameters. Point at an alternate config with the `path` argument.

os.any.mount.name: mount

point.name: point
point.title: Mount point
point.desc: A single mounted filesystem: the backing `device`, the `path` where it is attached, the `fstype`, mount `options`, whether it is currently `mounted`, and the total, used, and available bytes. Select a mount by path, for example `mount.point(path: "/var")`. On Windows the path matches without regard to case or a trailing backslash, so `mount.point(path: "C:")`, `mount.point(path: "c:\\")` and `mount.point(path: os.base.env["SystemDrive"])` all select the `C:\` volume.

os.any.mount.title: Mount table
os.any.mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

os.any.nfs.name: nfs

export.name: export
export.title: NFS export entry for a single path and client
export.desc: One row of the local NFS export table: the directory being shared (`path`), the client specification it is shared with (`client`, a hostname, IP address, CIDR, wildcard, netgroup, or `*` meaning any client) and the effective export `options` as parsed from `/etc/exports`. `readOnly` is true when the share is exported read-only. `noRootSquash` is true when the share grants remote uid 0 on the share, a classic NFS audit finding.

exports.name: exports
exports.title: NFS exports declared on this host

mount.name: mount
mount.title: NFS client mount
mount.desc: One NFS mount currently active on this host. `device` is the NFS source as the kernel sees it (`server:/remote/path`), split into `server` and `remotePath` for convenience. `mountpoint` is where the share is attached locally. `version` is the negotiated NFS protocol version (for example `3`, `4`, `4.1`, `4.2`); empty when the kernel did not report one. `security` is the authentication flavor, one of `sys`, `krb5`, `krb5i`, `krb5p`, or `none`; empty when unspecified. `hardMount` is true when the mount uses hard semantics (the `soft` option is not set). `readOnly` is true when the mount is `ro`. `options` is the full mount option list as reported by the system.

mounts.name: mounts
mounts.title: NFS mounts currently active on this host

os.any.nfs.title: NFS service local state
os.any.nfs.desc: Local NFS service viewed from two angles: shares this host declares (`exports`) and NFS volumes this host has mounted (`mounts`). `exports` is parsed from `/etc/exports` using the platform-specific syntax for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and AIX; each row is one `(path, client)` pair so audits like `nfs.exports.where(noRootSquash)` work directly. `mounts` filters the system mount table for NFS file systems and parses NFS-specific options into fields (protocol `version`, `security` flavor, `hardMount`, `readOnly`).

os.any.nftables.name: nftables

chain.name: chain
chain.title: nftables chain
chain.desc: Ordered list of rules within a table. A base chain attaches to a kernel hook and carries a type, hook, priority, and default policy, so it decides the fate of packets that fall through all its rules. A regular (non-base) chain is only reached by an explicit jump or goto and leaves those fields empty. Check `isBaseChain` to distinguish the two, and `policy` (accept or drop) to see the default action for a base chain, which is the key setting for a default-deny firewall.

rule.name: rule
rule.title: nftables rule
rule.desc: Single rule within a chain, identified by its handle number. The matching criteria and the action (accept, drop, jump, log, and so on) are parsed into `expr` as structured expression data, and `comment` carries any inline rule comment. Use `chainRef` and `tableRef` to walk back to the chain and table that contain the rule.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: All rules across all tables and chains

set.name: set
set.title: nftables named set or map
set.desc: Named collection of elements referenced by rules in a table, keyed by family, table, and name. A plain set holds a group of values (addresses, ports, MAC addresses) that rules match against, while a map (`isMap` true, `valueType` non-empty) associates each key with a value for verdict or NAT lookups. The `keyType` gives the element data type (for example ipv4_addr, inet_service, ether_addr), `flags` reports set attributes (constant, interval, timeout, dynamic), and `elements` lists the current members as strings.

sets.name: sets
sets.title: All named sets across all tables

table.name: table
table.title: nftables table
table.desc: Top-level container in the nftables ruleset, keyed by address family and name. A table holds the chains, rules, and named sets that make up a firewall configuration. The `family` field selects which protocol the table governs (ip for IPv4, ip6 for IPv6, inet for both, arp, bridge, or netdev), and `flags` reports table attributes such as dormant (rules present but not evaluated), owner, or persist. Traverse `chains`, `rules`, and `sets` to audit the packet-filtering policy defined here.

os.any.nftables.title: nftables firewall
os.any.nftables.desc: The host's nftables ruleset across all address families (ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge, netdev). Flattened accessors return everything at once: `tables`, `chains` (across all tables), `rules` (across all chains), and named `sets`. nftables is the modern replacement for iptables, so audit it on current distributions to confirm chains have restrictive policies and expected rules.

os.any.openBSMAudit.name: openBSMAudit

content.name: content
content.title: Content of the audit_control file

dir.name: dir
dir.title: Directory where audit log files are stored

expireAfterAge.name: expireAfterAge
expireAfterAge.title: Age threshold from expire-after
expireAfterAge.desc: Age since a trail file was last written after which auditd may remove it, as a duration. Converted as auditd converts it: `s` seconds, `h` hours, `d` days, and `y` years of 364 days plus one day for every fourth year. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no age term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterBytes.name: expireAfterBytes
expireAfterBytes.title: Size threshold from expire-after, in bytes
expireAfterBytes.desc: Aggregate size of all trail files after which auditd may remove the oldest, in bytes. `B` or no suffix is bytes, `K`, `M` and `G` are powers of 1024. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no size term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterOperator.name: expireAfterOperator
expireAfterOperator.title: How the two expire-after thresholds combine
expireAfterOperator.desc: `AND` when a trail file is removed only once both thresholds are exceeded, `OR` when either one is enough. Null for a single threshold, and when expire-after is absent, empty, or a value auditd rejects.

file.name: file
file.title: File resource for the audit_control file

filesz.name: filesz
filesz.title: Maximum size of individual audit log files

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Audit event flags for attributable (user) events

memberClearSflagsMask.name: memberClearSflagsMask
memberClearSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can clear on their processes

memberSetSflagsMask.name: memberSetSflagsMask
memberSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can set on their processes

minRetentionAge.name: minRetentionAge
minRetentionAge.title: Minimum age trail files reach before auditd can remove them
minRetentionAge.desc: Age a trail file is guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove it, whatever the size of the trail, as a duration. Set for an age threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the size threshold alone can remove files (a size on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minRetentionBytes.name: minRetentionBytes
minRetentionBytes.title: Minimum aggregate trail size kept before auditd can remove a file, in bytes
minRetentionBytes.desc: Aggregate size the trail files are guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove one, whatever their age, in bytes. Set for a size threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the age threshold alone can remove files (an age on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minfree.name: minfree
minfree.title: Minimum free space threshold (percentage) before audit warnings

naflags.name: naflags
naflags.title: Audit event flags for non-attributable events

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed parameters from the audit_control file

superuserClearSflagsMask.name: superuserClearSflagsMask
superuserClearSflagsMask.title: Flags that superusers can clear on their processes

superuserSetSflagsMask.name: superuserSetSflagsMask
superuserSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that superusers can set on their processes

os.any.openBSMAudit.title: OpenBSM audit_control configuration (macOS and BSD)
os.any.openBSMAudit.desc: OpenBSM audit subsystem configuration parsed from the `audit_control` file (pass `path` to override the default location). Exposes the audit event `flags`, log retention (`expireAfter`, `filesz`, `minfree`), and policy parameters that govern which security-relevant events the kernel records. `expireAfter` is also parsed the way auditd reads it: its age and size thresholds (`expireAfterAge`, `expireAfterBytes`), how they combine (`expireAfterOperator`), and what that guarantees about how long trail files survive (`minRetentionAge`, `minRetentionBytes`).

os.any.ovs.name: ovs

bridge.name: bridge
bridge.title: Open vSwitch bridge
bridge.desc: One bridge of the local switch, selected by name. The failMode field decides what the bridge does when it loses its controller: `secure` keeps the installed flows and forwards nothing new, `standalone` falls back to acting as a learning switch, which forwards traffic no policy authorised. The datapathType, protocols, stpEnabled, and rstpEnabled fields report how the bridge switches, and externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin or the operator wrote. The ports field returns the ports attached to the bridge.

interface.name: interface
interface.title: Open vSwitch interface
interface.desc: One interface of a port, selected by name. The type field reports how the interface reaches the network: an empty type is a system device, `internal` is the bridge's own device, and `vxlan`, `geneve`, or `gre` is a tunnel whose remote end is in options. The adminState and linkState fields report whether the interface is up, and error carries the reason the switch could not open the device, which is how a misconfigured attachment shows up. externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin wrote, which is what ties the interface back to a pod.

port.name: port
port.title: Open vSwitch port
port.desc: One port of a bridge, selected by name. The vlanMode and vlanTag fields report how the port treats VLAN tags: an access port carries a single tag, a trunk port carries the VLANs listed in trunks, and a port with neither carries every VLAN the bridge sees. tagged is false when no tag is set, so an untagged port is not read as VLAN 0. The interfaces field returns the interfaces the port is built from, which is more than one for a bond.

version.name: version
version.title: Open vSwitch version reported by ovs-vsctl

os.any.ovs.title: Open vSwitch
os.any.ovs.desc: Software switch configured through the Open vSwitch database on this host. The bridges, ports, and interfaces fields report the switch as it is running now, joined into the topology the datapath uses, which is the dataplane a CNI plugin builds and Kubernetes only records as intent. Empty on hosts where ovs-vsctl is not installed or the database is not reachable.

os.any.polkit.name: polkit

action.name: action
action.title: Polkit action
action.desc: Single privileged operation polkit can gate, parsed from a `.policy` file in the action directories. `id` is the reverse-DNS action name an application checks (for example `org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units`), and the three `allow` fields hold the implicit authorization that applies when no rule overrides it. `allowAny` is the weakest of the three because it covers subjects with no local seat, including remote sessions, so an action with `allowAny == "yes"` needs no authentication from anyone who can reach the D-Bus interface.

actions.name: actions
actions.title: Actions registered in the polkit action directories

adminIdentities.name: adminIdentities
adminIdentities.title: Identities the local authority treats as administrators
adminIdentities.desc: AdminIdentities from /etc/polkit-1/localauthority.conf.d, for example `unix-group:sudo` or `unix-user:root`. Honored only by polkit 0.105 and earlier. On newer releases administrator selection moves into a rule that calls polkit.addAdminRule, which `rules` reports through `adminRule`.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether polkit is present on the system
installed.desc: True when the polkit daemon (polkitd) or its pkaction or pkexec tool is found. Action and rule directories alone do not count, since systemd and other packages ship files into them without polkit. Use it to guard polkit audits on systems that ship no polkit at all, such as minimal cloud images and container bases.

localAuthorityRule.name: localAuthorityRule
localAuthorityRule.title: Local-authority authorization grant (.pkla)
localAuthorityRule.desc: Single section from a `.pkla` file, the ini-format grant mechanism used by polkit 0.105 and earlier. `identities` lists the users or groups the grant applies to and `actions` the action patterns it covers, while the three `result` fields carry the authorization it produces. Higher-numbered directories override lower-numbered ones, and a grant of `resultAny == "yes"` to a broad group such as `unix-group:users` hands that group the action with no authentication. Ignored outright by polkit 0.106 and later, so read `polkit.version` alongside it.

localAuthorityRules.name: localAuthorityRules
localAuthorityRules.title: Grants from the legacy local-authority .pkla files

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Polkit JavaScript authorization rule file
rule.desc: Single `.rules` file from the polkit rule directories. Polkit evaluates these files in lexicographic order by filename and stops at the first rule returning a result other than NOT_HANDLED, so `order` decides which file wins: a file sorting ahead of the distribution defaults overrides them. `file` carries the path, mode, and ownership, which is what a check for a rule file writable by a non-root account reads. Rule bodies are JavaScript and are not evaluated here. `actionIds` and `results` report the identifiers and result values appearing in the body, so an audit can narrow down which files are worth reading.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: JavaScript authorization rules, in the order polkit evaluates them

version.name: version
version.title: Polkit release reported by pkaction
version.desc: For example `0.105` on older distributions or `124` on current ones. Requires command execution, so it is null on backends that expose only a filesystem, such as an image scan.

os.any.polkit.title: Polkit authorization framework
os.any.polkit.desc: System-wide polkit (formerly PolicyKit) authorization state: the `actions` that privileged operations are registered under, the JavaScript `rules` that decide who may invoke them, the legacy local-authority grants in `localAuthorityRules`, and the `adminIdentities` the local authority treats as administrators. Polkit governs whether an unprivileged session may restart a unit, mount a disk, or install a package, so an over-broad grant is a local privilege escalation path. Read `version` before drawing conclusions: polkit 0.106 and later evaluate the JavaScript rules and ignore `.pkla` files, while earlier releases do the reverse.

os.any.postfix.name: postfix

inetInterfaces.name: inetInterfaces
inetInterfaces.title: Interfaces Postfix listens on, parsed from the inet_interfaces parameter

mainCfPath.name: mainCfPath
mainCfPath.title: Path to the Postfix main.cf configuration file

masterCfPath.name: masterCfPath
masterCfPath.title: Path to the Postfix master.cf configuration file

params.name: params
params.title: Effective Postfix parameters
params.desc: Reported by `postconf` when available (so parameters left at their built-in default still appear); otherwise parsed from main.cf, in which case only values written to the file are present.

service.name: service
service.title: Postfix master.cf service definition
service.desc: Single daemon entry from the Postfix master.cf file: its service name and transport type, the chroot and privilege flags, the wake-up and process limits, and the command it runs. The flag columns carry `y`, `n`, or `-` (use the built-in default). Iterated from `postfix.services`.

os.any.postfix.title: Postfix mail transfer agent configuration
os.any.postfix.desc: Effective Postfix configuration. `params` reports parameter values from `postconf` when the binary is available (which includes the built-in defaults for parameters not written to the file) and otherwise falls back to parsing main.cf directly (file values only, with `$name` interpolation and continuation lines). `inetInterfaces` is the parsed `inet_interfaces` list and `services` are the daemon definitions from master.cf. By default the per-distribution config locations are used; select an alternate main.cf with `postfix("/path/to/main.cf")`.

os.any.powershell.name: powershell

stderr.name: stderr
stderr.title: Standard error output from running the script

stdout.name: stdout
stdout.title: Standard output from running the script

os.any.powershell.title: Result of running a PowerShell script on the system
os.any.powershell.desc: Ad-hoc PowerShell execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a script string; the resource executes the script via PowerShell on the asset and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. The Windows and cross-platform-PowerShell counterpart to `command` for assertions that need PowerShell-only surface area.

os.any.registrykey.name: registrykey

children.name: children
children.title: Names of the immediate child keys under this key

items.name: items
items.title: Value entries in this registry key

ntuserDat.name: ntuserDat
ntuserDat.title: Path to the user's NTUSER.DAT hive file
ntuserDat.desc: Optional. Used with `userSid` to read a user's registry when their hive is not currently loaded, for example a SYSTEM scan running with no interactive session. Typically populated from `user.ntuserDat`.

properties.name: properties
properties.title: Properties of the registry key as a name-to-value map
properties.desc: Deprecated in favor of `items`, which returns structured property entries.

property.name: property
property.title: Windows registry key property
property.desc: A single named value within a registry key: the key `path`, value `name`, whether it `exists`, the registry `type` (for example `REG_SZ`, `REG_DWORD`, `REG_BINARY`, or `REG_MULTI_SZ`), and the parsed `data`. Select a specific value by path and name, or iterate from `registrykey.items`.

userSid.name: userSid
userSid.title: SID of the user whose registry hive to read
userSid.desc: Optional. When set, `path` is interpreted relative to that user's per-user registry (HKCU): the loaded `HKEY_USERS\<sid>` hive when the user is logged in, otherwise the profile's `NTUSER.DAT` (see `ntuserDat`) loaded on demand. Leave empty to treat `path` as an absolute registry path.

os.any.registrykey.title: Windows registry key
os.any.registrykey.desc: A Windows registry key selected by `path`, exposing its value entries (`items`), child key names (`children`), and whether the key `exists`. Optionally read a specific user's per-user registry (HKCU) by supplying `userSid`, falling back to their `NTUSER.DAT` profile hive (`ntuserDat`) when that hive is not currently loaded. Select a key with `registrykey(path: "...")`.

os.any.safari.name: safari
os.any.safari.title: Safari browser (macOS only)
os.any.safari.desc: Safari web browser on macOS. The `extensions` collection lists every installed Safari extension across all user accounts on the host, letting audits flag unknown or disabled extensions and verify their provenance.

os.any.secpol.name: secpol
os.any.secpol.title: Windows local security policy
os.any.secpol.desc: Windows local security policy exported via secedit, broken into four maps. `systemaccess` covers password and account-lockout settings (for example MinimumPasswordLength, LockoutBadCount); `eventaudit` holds the legacy audit categories; `registryvalues` exposes security-relevant registry-backed policies; and `privilegerights` maps each user right (for example SeDenyNetworkLogonRight) to the accounts granted it. These are the primary source for CIS-style local policy benchmarks.

os.any.selinux.name: selinux

boolean.name: boolean
boolean.title: SELinux boolean setting
boolean.desc: One tunable SELinux boolean and its current runtime value (from `getsebool -a` or /sys/fs/selinux/booleans), e.g. httpd_can_network_connect.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether SELinux is installed on the system

mode.name: mode
mode.title: Current enforcement mode: enforcing, permissive, or disabled

module.name: module
module.title: SELinux policy module
module.desc: One installed SELinux policy module from `semodule --list-modules=full`, with its status (enabled or disabled) and priority (higher priority overrides lower for the same module name).

modules.name: modules
modules.title: Installed SELinux policy modules, including disabled ones

policyType.name: policyType
policyType.title: Active policy type (e.g., targeted, mls, minimum)

os.any.selinux.title: SELinux mandatory access control
os.any.selinux.desc: SELinux enforcement mode, configured mode, active policy type, tunable booleans, and loaded policy modules. The runtime `mode` (from getenforce or /sys/fs/selinux on a running system, from /etc/selinux/config in a disk or image scan) may differ from `configMode`, which is what persists across reboot; compare the two to catch a system left permissive at runtime or booted with SELinux disabled.

os.any.shadow.name: shadow

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Shadowed password file entry
entry.desc: A single line from `/etc/shadow`: the username, hashed password field, date of last change, minimum and maximum password age in days, warning period, inactivity period, and account expiry date. Used to audit password aging policy compliance and to detect accounts with no expiry or with locked passwords (a `!` or `*` in the password field).

os.any.shadow.title: Shadow password file (/etc/shadow)
os.any.shadow.desc: Per-user password aging, expiration, and lock state parsed from `/etc/shadow`, one `shadow.entry` per account. Audit password policy compliance and find accounts with no expiry, weak aging settings, or locked/disabled passwords.

os.any.snmpd.name: snmpd

config.name: config
config.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) configuration
config.desc: snmpd.conf settings that govern SNMP access: community strings, VACM users, and listen addresses. The configuration is assembled the way snmpd reads it: the main snmpd.conf, files pulled in by its includeFile and includeDir directives, snmpd.local.conf in the same directory, and the persistent snmpd.conf under /var/lib/snmp. A missing configuration yields empty accessors, so audits such as rwCommunities == [] hold trivially on hosts that don't run snmpd.

os.any.snmpd.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) namespace
os.any.snmpd.desc: Namespace hosting `snmpd.config`, the entry point for examining the effective SNMP daemon configuration.

os.any.sriov.name: sriov

physicalFunction.name: physicalFunction
physicalFunction.title: SR-IOV physical function
physicalFunction.desc: Network interface that supports SR-IOV, selected by its interface name. The numVfs and totalVfs fields report how many virtual functions are enabled against how many the hardware supports, so an interface with numVfs of 0 is capable but unused. The pciAddress, vendorId, deviceId, and driver fields identify the device the way a device-plugin selector does, and macAddress, mtu, and operationalState report the link. The virtualFunctions field returns the virtual functions carved out of this interface.

virtualFunction.name: virtualFunction
virtualFunction.title: SR-IOV virtual function
virtualFunction.desc: One virtual function of an SR-IOV capable interface, selected by its PCI address.
