The driver field reports what the function is bound to, and usesPassthroughDriver marks a function handed to a userspace datapath such as DPDK, which leaves it with no kernel network interface and therefore outside host packet filtering. The spoofChecking, trusted, macAddress, vlanId, and rate fields report the configuration the physical function enforces on the guest, which is the part a workload cannot override. linkConfigured is false when the kernel reports no configuration for the function, so an unreported function is not read as an unprotected one.

virtualFunctions.name: virtualFunctions
virtualFunctions.title: Virtual functions across every physical function

os.any.sriov.title: SR-IOV network devices
os.any.sriov.desc: Single-root I/O virtualization state of the host's network hardware. The physicalFunctions field lists every SR-IOV capable interface with the number of virtual functions it has enabled against the number it supports, and virtualFunctions flattens every virtual function across all of them. This is the realised hardware inventory, so it shows the PCI address, the bound driver, and the per-device link settings that a Kubernetes device plugin only reports as an aggregate count. Empty on hosts with no SR-IOV capable interface.

os.any.sshd.name: sshd

config.name: config
config.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) configuration
config.desc: OpenSSH server settings parsed from sshd_config (and any Include files), plus the effective values reported by `sshd -T`. Surfaces `ciphers`, `macs`, `kexs`, and `hostkeyalgorithms` for cryptographic hardening checks, `permitRootLogin` for root-access policy, and `blocks` for the conditional Match blocks. Compare the configured values (`ciphers`) against the effective ones (`effectiveCiphers`) to catch overrides applied at runtime. The default file is /etc/ssh/sshd_config, or C:\ProgramData\ssh\sshd_config on Windows.

os.any.sshd.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) namespace
os.any.sshd.desc: Namespace hosting `sshd.config`, the entry point for auditing the OpenSSH server's effective settings and Match blocks.

os.any.sudo.name: sudo

implementation.name: implementation
implementation.title: Which sudo implementation the binary is: "sudo" or "sudo-rs"
implementation.desc: "sudo" is the C implementation from sudo.ws. "sudo-rs" is the Rust reimplementation that recent Ubuntu releases install as `sudo`. It reads the same sudoers files but supports a subset of the options, has no plugins, and rejects settings such as `logfile`, `log_input`, `log_output`, and `requiretty`. Null when sudo is not installed or `sudo -V` output is not recognized.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether sudo is installed and executable

ioPlugins.name: ioPlugins
ioPlugins.title: I/O plugins (e.g., sudoers_io for log_input / log_output)

path.name: path
path.title: Path to the sudo binary
path.desc: Filesystem-resolved location of the `sudo` binary on the asset (e.g., `/usr/bin/sudo`). Empty when sudo is not installed; check `installed` rather than testing this field for emptiness.

plugin.name: plugin
plugin.title: A sudo plugin reported by `sudo -V`
plugin.desc: One loaded sudo plugin, identified by name and type (policy, I/O, audit, or approval) with its version and, when reported, the path to the .so file backing it.

policyPlugin.name: policyPlugin
policyPlugin.title: Policy plugin (typically sudoers_policy). Null when none is loaded.

pythonSupport.name: pythonSupport
pythonSupport.title: Whether the build supports Python-based plugins

validate.name: validate
validate.title: Result of `visudo -c`. Null when sudoers files cannot be read (e.g., running unprivileged against a mode-0440 /etc/sudoers).

validation.name: validation
validation.title: Result of validating sudoers configuration with `visudo -c`
validation.desc: Syntax-check outcome for the sudoers files: `valid` is true when `visudo -c` exits cleanly, and `errors` lists every parse error otherwise.

version.name: version
version.title: Version string reported by `sudo -V` (e.g., "1.9.5p3")
version.desc: The version of the implementation named by `implementation`: a sudo.ws release such as "1.9.5p3", or a sudo-rs release such as "0.2.13". The two number independently, so compare a version only after checking `implementation`. A distribution package revision that sudo-rs appends (e.g., "-0ubuntu1.2") is not included.

os.any.sudo.title: Sudo binary and runtime metadata
os.any.sudo.desc: Installed `sudo` binary: where it lives on disk, the version it reports under `sudo -V`, which plugins are loaded (policy, I/O, audit, approval), whether the build supports Python-based plugins, and the result of `visudo -c` against the sudoers configuration. For sudoers configuration parsing, use the `sudoers` resource directly, or access it via this resource's `sudoers` field.

os.any.sudoers.name: sudoers

alias.name: alias
alias.title: Sudoers alias definition
alias.desc: One alias declaration (User_Alias, Host_Alias, Cmnd_Alias, or Runas_Alias) and the members assigned to it, used to expand aliases referenced in user specifications.

content.name: content
content.title: Raw contents of all sudoers files

default.name: default
default.title: Sudoers default setting
default.desc: One `Defaults` directive from the sudoers configuration, giving the parameter, its value and operation, the scope it applies at, and whether it is negated. Covers hardening flags such as env_reset and secure_path.

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the sudoers configuration

userSpec.name: userSpec
userSpec.title: Sudoers user specification (permission entry)
userSpec.desc: Single sudoers permission rule: which users, on which hosts, may run which commands, as which run-as users/groups, under which tags (e.g. NOPASSWD). The building block for auditing privilege grants.

os.any.sudoers.title: sudo authorization configuration
os.any.sudoers.desc: User specifications, defaults, and aliases parsed across the sudoers files (/etc/sudoers plus /etc/sudoers.d). Use userSpecs to audit who may run which commands as which users, and defaults to check hardening settings such as env_reset, secure_path, requiretty, and NOPASSWD grants. Point at an alternate root file with the `path` argument.

os.any.sysrc.name: sysrc

content.name: content
content.title: Raw contents of all rc.conf files

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed key-value entries from all rc.conf files

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Single rc.conf variable entry
entry.desc: One variable assignment from an rc.conf file: its `name`, `value`, and the `file` it was defined in. The source file matters because a setting in rc.conf.local overrides the same name in rc.conf.

files.name: files
files.title: List of rc.conf files that make up the configuration

os.any.sysrc.title: FreeBSD rc.conf system configuration
os.any.sysrc.desc: FreeBSD service and system configuration merged from rc.conf and rc.conf.local. The `entries` accessor exposes each variable assignment as a structured name/value pair (with the file it came from), so audits can assert on individual settings such as sshd_enable or a firewall being turned on. `content` returns the concatenated raw text. Point at a specific file with `sysrc(path: "...")`.

os.any.ufw.name: ufw

application.name: application
application.title: UFW application profile from /etc/ufw/applications.d/
application.desc: Named application profile that maps a service to the ports it needs, so UFW rules can reference it by name instead of listing ports. Each profile carries a `name` (for example "Nginx Full"), a human-readable `title` and `description`, and the `ports` specification it opens.

defaultRouted.name: defaultRouted
defaultRouted.title: Default policy for routed (forwarded) traffic
defaultRouted.desc: Read from DEFAULT_FORWARD_POLICY in /etc/default/ufw and reported with UFW policy names: "deny" for DROP, "allow" for ACCEPT, or "reject". This is the configured policy, so it never returns "disabled" or the raw iptables name "drop", even though `ufw status verbose` prints `disabled (routed)` while IP forwarding is off in the kernel. Compare against "deny" for a hardened stance, and read `kernel.parameters["net.ipv4.ip_forward"]` to check forwarding itself.

logging.name: logging
logging.title: Logging level (off, low, medium, high, full)

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Individual UFW rule
rule.desc: Single UFW rule as reported by `ufw status`, covering the action taken, the traffic direction, and the addresses, ports, protocol, and interface it matches. The `action` (ALLOW, DENY, REJECT, LIMIT), `direction`, and `port`/`from`/`to` fields together describe what the rule permits or blocks; `ipv6` flags IPv6 rules, and `raw` preserves the original text.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: All UFW rules
rules.desc: Read from user.rules and user6.rules in /etc/ufw on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/lib/ufw on Fedora and EPEL.

status.name: status
status.title: Whether UFW is active ("active", "inactive", "not installed")
status.desc: "not installed" when neither the ufw command nor ufw-init is present, including a package that was removed but not purged and left /etc/ufw/ufw.conf behind. The command is looked up in /usr/sbin, /sbin, and /usr/local/sbin, where the upstream tarball installs it. Where commands can run, "active" means the ufw rules are loaded, as `ufw status` reports, not only that ufw.conf sets ENABLED=yes. Fedora and EPEL ship ENABLED=yes on a firewall that was never enabled. Asking ufw needs root. Image scans read ENABLED from ufw.conf.

os.any.ufw.title: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) state and rules
os.any.ufw.desc: Uncomplicated Firewall status, default policies, configured rules, and application profiles on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and EPEL systems. Check `status` to confirm the firewall is active, and the `defaultIncoming` / `defaultOutgoing` / `defaultRouted` policies for the baseline stance (a hardened host typically denies incoming by default). Enumerate `rules` to audit the explicit allow/deny entries and `applications` for the service profiles UFW can reference by name.

os.any.usb.name: usb

device.name: device
device.title: Experimental: USB device
device.desc: Single attached USB device. `vendorId` and `productId` identify the hardware model, `class`/`className` give its function (e.g. mass storage, HID, hub), `serial` uniquely identifies the unit where the device reports one, and `isRemovable` distinguishes hot-pluggable peripherals from fixed internal devices.

os.any.usb.title: USB device inventory (experimental)
os.any.usb.desc: USB devices attached to the host, each with its vendor and product IDs, manufacturer, serial number, device class, and connection speed. The `devices` list inventories connected peripherals so you can flag removable storage or unexpected hardware.

os.any.windows.name: windows

acl.name: acl
acl.title: Windows access control list
acl.desc:
Discretionary access control list of a filesystem object, selected by `path`, for example `windows.acl("C:\\inetpub")` or `windows.acl(path: "C:\\Windows\\System32\\dns")`. Exposes the object's owner and primary group, whether it still inherits permissions from its parent, the security descriptor in SDDL form, and every access control entry with the principal it applies to and the rights it grants or denies.

This is the Windows counterpart of `file.permissions`, which models a POSIX mode and cannot express an access control entry, an inherited permission, or the difference between an owner and a principal. Also reachable as `file.acl` so it composes with `files.find`.

Each entry carries both the raw `rightsMask` and named predicates derived from it (`allowsWrite`, `allowsFullControl`, and so on). Prefer the predicates: the `rights` label is unreliable, since .NET renders a mask containing generic bits as a bare number rather than a name, and a principal granted Modify is a writer whose label does not contain the word Write.

auditPolicy.name: auditPolicy
auditPolicy.title: Windows advanced audit policy
auditPolicy.desc: Effective Windows advanced audit policy: every audit subcategory together with whether success and failure events are audited. Subcategory names and categories are reported in English regardless of the OS display language, so the same audit works unchanged on localized systems. Iterate the subcategories to assert audit coverage, for example `windows.auditPolicy.where(category == "Account Logon").all(success)`, or select a single subcategory with windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.

bitlocker.name: bitlocker
bitlocker.title: Windows BitLocker drive encryption
bitlocker.desc: BitLocker Drive Encryption state across volumes: the encryption, lock, and protection status of each `volume`, plus the BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings under `policy`. Use it to verify that OS and data drives are encrypted and protected.

certificate.name: certificate
certificate.title: Certificate in a Windows certificate store
certificate.desc: Single certificate as it sits in one store: the `store` holding it, the `location` that scopes it to the machine or to one account, its `thumbprint`, and whether the store also holds the matching private key. `store` carries the trust decision rather than the certificate itself. A certificate in Root is trusted as a certification authority, one in Disallowed is explicitly distrusted, and one in TrustedPublisher lets code it signed run without prompting, so the same certificate means different things in different stores. Read `certificate` for the subject, issuer, validity dates and extensions.

certificates.name: certificates
certificates.title: Certificates held in the Windows certificate stores

computerInfo.name: computerInfo
computerInfo.title: A consolidated object of system and operating system properties

defender.name: defender
defender.title: Microsoft Defender Antivirus
defender.desc: Complete runtime status and configuration of Microsoft Defender Antivirus, so policies can assert on every Defender security control. The `status` field exposes the live engine, signature, and protection state reported by Get-MpComputerStatus (real-time protection, behavior monitoring, network inspection, tamper protection, scan ages, and signature freshness). The `preferences` field exposes the configurable policy reported by Get-MpPreference, grouped into scan, real-time, cloud-delivered protection, signature-update, threat-action, controlled-folder-access, network-protection, and remediation settings, plus exclusions and Attack Surface Reduction rules. The `threats` and `threatDetections` fields expose the recorded threat history. On systems without Defender (for example servers running a third-party antivirus) these fields resolve to null rather than failing the query.

deviceGuard.name: deviceGuard
deviceGuard.title: Device Guard policy (Virtualization-Based Security, HVCI, and Credential Guard)

disk.name: disk
disk.title: Disk attached to a Windows computer
disk.desc: A physical or virtual disk as Windows Storage Management reports it through the MSFT_Disk class. Covers identity (`number`, `friendlyName`, `serialNumber`, `uniqueId`), capacity (`size` in bytes), how the disk is attached (`busType`), how it is laid out (`partitionStyle`), whether it holds the boot or system partition, and its offline, read-only, operational, and health state. For example, `windows.disks.where(isBoot).all(size >= 64 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)` checks the capacity of the disk Windows runs from.

disks.name: disks
disks.title: Disks attached to this computer, as reported by Windows Storage Management
disks.desc: Physical and virtual disks from the MSFT_Disk class, the same set that Get-Disk lists: size, bus type, partition style, and whether the disk holds the boot or system partition. `windows.disks.where(isBoot)` selects the disk that holds the running Windows installation.

dnsServer.name: dnsServer
dnsServer.title: Windows DNS Server
dnsServer.desc: Configuration of the Windows DNS Server role: global server settings, recursion, resolver cache hardening, forwarders, root hints, response rate limiting, stale record scavenging, event and debug logging, and every zone the server hosts together with its zone transfer, dynamic update and DNSSEC signing configuration. Backed by the DnsServer PowerShell module, which is read once per scan in a single batched call rather than one call per field. Every field requires the DNS Server role to be installed; gate an audit on `windows.serverFeature(name: "DNS").installed` so the checks do not run on hosts that are not name servers. That gate narrows an audit but does not close it: a host where the role was added and the restart has not happened yet reports the feature as installed while the management module is still absent, and every field here reports an error on such a host rather than a configuration. Complements the client-side `dns` resource in the network provider, which resolves names through the public DNS system and cannot see a server's own configuration.

driver.name: driver
driver.title: Windows kernel or file system driver
driver.desc: Single driver registered with the service control manager: the service `name` it loads under, the on-disk `path` of its image, the `startMode` that decides when it loads, and whether it is currently `running`. `signed` and `signer` carry the Authenticode verdict on the image, which is what a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver audit reads, and `purl` identifies the driver for vulnerability matching in the same pkg:windows-driver namespace as windows.printerDriver.

drivers.name: drivers
drivers.title: Kernel and file system drivers registered on the machine

eventlog.name: eventlog
eventlog.title: Windows Event Log channel configuration
eventlog.desc: Size, retention policy and collection state of a single Windows Event Log channel. The `name` field selects the channel by its log name, for example `windows.eventlog(name: "Security")`, `windows.eventlog(name: "Application")` or a modern provider channel such as `windows.eventlog(name: "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational")`. `maxSizeKB` reports the maximum log file size in KB and `retention` decodes how the channel behaves when that size is reached. `retention` reads the registry alone, so it works on a connection that cannot run commands. `enabled`, `logFilePath`, `isClassicLog` and `recordCount` report the live channel state and need a connection that can run commands.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: Windows Firewall (Advanced Security)
firewall.desc: Windows Firewall with Advanced Security posture: the global settings, the per-profile defaults (Domain, Private, Public), and every configured firewall rule. Use `profiles` to assert that the firewall is enabled and blocks inbound traffic by default on each profile, and `rules` to audit which allow/block rules are active. Backed by the `Get-NetFirewallProfile` and `Get-NetFirewallRule` PowerShell cmdlets, read from the ActiveStore: the effective policy, local configuration merged with Group Policy.

hotfix.name: hotfix
hotfix.title: Windows hotfix
hotfix.desc: Single installed Windows hotfix (a Quick Fix Engineering update): its `hotfixId` (for example "KB5034441"), the `description` type of the fix, the knowledge-base `caption` URL, the `installedOn` date, and the account that installed it. Audit patch compliance across `windows.hotfixes`, for example `windows.hotfixes.where(installedOn > time.now - 30*time.day)`.

logonSession.name: logonSession
logonSession.title: Windows logon session
logonSession.desc: Single active logon session as the Local Security Authority reports it: the `logonType` that created it, the `authenticationPackage` that authenticated it, the account it runs as, and when it started. `logonType` and its readable form `logonTypeName` carry most of the audit value, since a session's type says how it was established: 10 is an incoming Remote Desktop logon, 3 is a network logon, and 9 is a session created with alternate credentials. `authenticationPackage` reports whether the session was authenticated with Kerberos or fell back to NTLM.

lsa.name: lsa
lsa.title: Windows Local Security Authority (LSA) security policy
lsa.desc: Local Security Authority configuration that backs the "Network access", "Network security", and related security options under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. These values control anonymous access restrictions, blank-password use, LAN Manager authentication level, NTLM hashing, LSA protection (RunAsPPL), and audit behavior, including whether the system halts when it cannot write security audits. On/off settings are exposed as booleans and graded settings (such as the LAN Manager authentication level) as integers. NTLM (MSV1_0 and WDigest) settings are grouped under `ntlm` and the Netlogon secure-channel settings under `secureChannel`. The FIPS algorithm policy, the Kerberos supported encryption types, the LDAP signing and channel-binding requirements, and the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) minimum password length limit are read from their own keys and exposed directly on this resource. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, letting checks assert on configured-vs-default precisely.

optionalFeature.name: optionalFeature
optionalFeature.title: Windows optional feature (desktop-only)
optionalFeature.desc: Windows optional feature reported by `Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online`, the desktop equivalent of server roles. Select one by its feature name, for example `windows.optionalFeature(name: "SMB1Protocol")`, to check whether a legacy or risky feature (such as SMBv1, Telnet client, or PowerShell v2) is turned on. `enabled` is the simple boolean; `state` carries the underlying DISM feature state for more granular checks.

optionalFeatures.name: optionalFeatures
optionalFeatures.title: Information about optional features in a Windows image.

powershell.name: powershell
powershell.title: Windows PowerShell logging policy
powershell.desc: PowerShell logging settings configured via Group Policy under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell: Script Block Logging, Module Logging, Transcription, and the machine execution policy, together with the system lockdown state that decides the session language mode. The policy settings are GPO-only values with no effective fallback, so when a value is absent the corresponding field is null, which is distinguishable from an explicit 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

printerDrivers.name: printerDrivers
printerDrivers.title: Print drivers registered with the Windows spooler
printerDrivers.desc: Print drivers as the spooler reports them, with the vendor version, the manufacturer, the print environment each is registered under, and the INF the package was installed from. Use it to assert which drivers are present and at which version. Drivers are read from the spooler rather than from installed software, because a driver delivered as an INF/CAB package lands in the driver store and creates no Add/Remove Programs entry, so a software inventory cannot see it while the spooler is still loading it.

rdp.name: rdp
rdp.title: Windows Remote Desktop / Terminal Services configuration
rdp.desc: Effective Remote Desktop (Terminal Services) policy posture: whether Network Level Authentication is required, the negotiated security layer and minimum client encryption level, device and resource redirection toggles, credential handling, and session idle / disconnection time limits. Each field resolves the Group Policy value (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft \Windows NT\Terminal Services) first, then the per-listener configuration (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp), and finally the documented Windows default when neither is set, so audits can assert the effective state without handling missing registry values.

schannel.name: schannel
schannel.title: Windows Schannel TLS configuration
schannel.desc:
Schannel (Secure Channel) TLS cipher-suite, supported-group, and signature-algorithm configuration that backs the Microsoft TLS/SSL stack, read from the effective local Schannel store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Cryptography\Configuration\Local\SSL. The 00010002 subkey holds the ordered cipher-suite list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value and the ordered elliptic-curve / supported-group list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `EccCurves` value, the same list `Get-TlsEccCurve` reports. The 00010003 subkey holds the ordered signature-algorithm list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value. On Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 the supported-group list is where post-quantum ML-KEM key-exchange groups (for example secp256r1_mlkem768) appear once enabled.

When a key or value is absent (the common case on older Windows, on systems using the default order, and on non-Windows platforms) the list accessors resolve to an empty list and pqcKeyExchangeEnabled resolves to false rather than failing.

The protocols, ciphers, hashes, and keyExchangeAlgorithms lists come from the separate per-algorithm override store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL. Windows applies a built-in default to every algorithm that has no override there, and that default differs between Windows releases, so an absent registry value does not mean the algorithm is off. Each list therefore always contains the well-known algorithm names, whether or not the registry mentions them, and reports configured as false with a null enablement for the ones it does not. Write audits against configured and the enablement fields together, for example `windows.schannel.protocols.where(name == "TLS 1.0").all(clientConfigured && clientEnabled == false)`, so a host that never set the value fails instead of passing on a null.

scheduledTask.name: scheduledTask
scheduledTask.title: Windows Task Scheduler task
scheduledTask.desc: Registered task from the Windows Task Scheduler: its identity (`name`, `path`, `uri`), run `state`, whether it is `enabled`, descriptive metadata (`description`, `author`), and the security context it runs under via `principal`. The `actions` it executes, the `triggers` that launch it, and its full `settings` are exposed as nested resources, while `lastRunTime`, `nextRunTime`, `lastTaskResult`, and `missedRuns` report the most recent run-time information. Audit which tasks run, as whom, and on what schedule, for example `windows.scheduledTasks.where(enabled).where(principal.runLevel == "Highest")` surfaces enabled tasks running with the highest available privileges.

security.name: security
security.title: Windows registered security products
security.desc: Antivirus, anti-spyware, and firewall providers registered with the Windows Security Center. Use `products` to verify that an up-to-date, enabled security product is present, for example `windows.security.products.where(type == "antivirus").any(productState == "on")`.

serverFeature.name: serverFeature
serverFeature.title: Windows Server role, role service, or feature
serverFeature.desc: Installable Windows Server component reported by `Get-WindowsFeature`. Select one by its command name, for example `windows.serverFeature(name: "Web-Server")`, to check whether a role such as IIS, DNS, or Hyper-V is present. `installed` is the simple boolean check, while `installState` distinguishes fully installed from removed or available-for-install states.

serverFeatures.name: serverFeatures
serverFeatures.title: Information about Windows Server roles, role services, and features that are available for installation and installed on a specified server.

smb.name: smb
smb.title: Windows SMB (Server Message Block) server
smb.desc: SMB shares published by the host, active inbound client sessions, and outbound connections to other SMB servers, along with the server and client registry hardening configuration and whether the deprecated SMBv1 driver is still enabled. Backed by the `Get-SmbShare`, `Get-SmbSession`, and `Get-SmbConnection` PowerShell cmdlets plus registry reads.

spooler.name: spooler
spooler.title: Windows Print Spooler security configuration
spooler.desc:
Hardening-relevant state of the Windows Print Spooler and printing subsystem. The fields are sourced from the Group Policy printer keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers (and its PointAndPrint, RPC, IPP, and WPP subkeys), the machine-wide HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print key, and the spooler service start configuration under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Spooler. These controls address the PrintNightmare and related spooler vulnerabilities: whether the service is disabled, whether remote RPC is accepted, and how Point-and-Print driver installation is restricted.

Integer settings that are not present in the registry resolve to null so "not configured" is distinguishable from an explicit value of 0 (important because several controls, for example registerRemoteRpcEndpoint == 0, are compliant precisely when set to 0). Boolean settings resolve to their documented Windows default when the value is absent.

telemetry.name: telemetry
telemetry.title: Windows diagnostic data (telemetry) and consumer cloud-content policy
telemetry.desc: Effective Windows privacy and telemetry posture read from the Group Policy keys HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DataCollection and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CloudContent. These are GPO-only DWORD values. The diagnostic data level is a graded integer; the remaining settings are on/off booleans. Every field is nullable so that an absent value (the policy is not configured) is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

tpm.name: tpm
tpm.title: Windows Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
tpm.desc: Trusted Platform Module state: whether a TPM is present, ready for use, enabled, and activated, along with its manufacturer, its major specification version, its dictionary-attack lockout state, and whether Windows provisions it automatically. Presence and a 2.0 specification version are prerequisites for Windows 11 readiness and several BitLocker and device-health controls, and a locked out or unprovisioned TPM is present without being usable. On a system without a TPM the fields resolve cleanly (present is false) rather than erroring.

uac.name: uac
uac.title: Windows User Account Control (UAC) policy
uac.desc: User Account Control settings that back the "User Account Control" security options, read from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, together with the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy value in the same key that governs UAC remote restrictions for local accounts. These control whether Admin Approval Mode is on, how administrators and standard users are prompted for elevation, whether prompts use the secure desktop, installer detection, UIAccess restrictions, file and registry virtualization, and whether remote connections by local administrators receive a filtered token. On/off settings are exposed as booleans, with any non-zero DWORD reading true, and the two prompt behaviors as integers. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, and each field names the Windows default that applies when it is absent. Checks on a setting whose secure state is the default should therefore accept null, for example `windows.uac.localAccountTokenFilterPolicy != true`.

update.name: update
update.title: Windows Update Agent
update.desc: How a Windows host receives updates and what it has applied or has pending. The `config` field surfaces Windows Update Agent configuration and freshness (the effective catalog source, WSUS settings, the last successful detection / download / install times, and whether a reboot is pending). `installed` lists the updates the agent has applied (the installed-KB history), and `available` lists updates the agent has found but not yet installed, answered from the cache of its last detection rather than a live scan. Configuration is read from the registry and works even on connections that cannot run commands; the installed and available collections fall back to the Windows Update Agent COM API when commands are available.

winrm.name: winrm
winrm.title: Windows Remote Management (WinRM)
winrm.desc: Effective WinRM (Windows Remote Management) policy posture for both the WinRM client and service, plus the WinRS remote shell setting and the WinRM service start mode. The client and service settings are read from the Group Policy key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM; these are GPO-only values with no per-listener effective fallback, so when a value is absent the documented Windows default applies. `serviceStartMode` reflects HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinRM\Start. Those fields are read from the registry, so they are available even on connections that cannot run commands. `listeners`, `client.trustedHosts`, `service.ipv4Filter` and `service.ipv6Filter` report the live WS-Management configuration instead and need a connection that can run commands.

os.any.windows.title: Windows-specific operating system surfaces
os.any.windows.desc: Windows host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: consolidated `computerInfo`, installed `hotfixes`, Server roles and features, image `optionalFeatures`, attached `disks`, scheduled tasks, and hardening controls (Device Guard, Exploit Protection, SmartScreen). A starting point for Windows-specific audits.

os.any.zfs.name: zfs

dataset.name: dataset
dataset.title: ZFS dataset (filesystem, volume, snapshot, or bookmark)
dataset.desc: Single ZFS dataset: full `name`, `type` (filesystem, volume, snapshot, bookmark), used/available/referenced bytes, `mountpoint`, compression algorithm and ratio, `mounted` flag, record size, quota, reservation, `origin` snapshot for clones, creation time, encryption algorithm, full `properties` map, and `snapshots` list. Initialize by name or iterate from `zfs.datasets`.

datasets.name: datasets
datasets.title: All ZFS datasets (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, bookmarks)

pool.name: pool
pool.title: ZFS storage pool
pool.desc: Single ZFS storage pool: `name`, `guid`, health status, total/allocated/free bytes, fragmentation percentage, space utilization, deduplication ratio, read-only flag, auto-expand/replace/trim settings, the top-level `vdevs` topology, and the full `properties` map. Initialize by name (e.g., `zfs.pool(name: "tank")`) or iterate from `zfs.pools`.

version.name: version
version.title: ZFS version string
version.desc: The OpenZFS release, for example `zfs-2.2.2-1`. ZFS on Linux before 0.8 reports the release of its loaded kernel module, for example `zfs-kmod-0.6.5.6-0ubuntu28`. Oracle Solaris names its ZFS release by the pool version instead, for example `53`.

os.any.zfs.title: ZFS storage pools and datasets
os.any.zfs.desc: ZFS storage on the host: the installed `version`, the storage `pools` with their health and capacity, and every `dataset` (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, and bookmarks). Iterate to audit pool health, free capacity, vdev topology, and dataset properties such as compression and encryption.

os.base.name: os.base

agentskills.name: agentskills
agentskills.title: Agent Skills under a directory
agentskills.desc: Skills that follow the Agent Skills specification (https://agentskills.io/specification), independent of the agent that loads them. The `path` field selects the directory searched, for example `agentskills(path: "/home/alice/src/my-skills")`. Every SKILL.md below it is a skill, including skills nested in plugin directories; the files inside a skill, `.git`, and `node_modules` are not searched. Use it to validate a skills repository against the specification or to inventory the skills in a checkout.

ai.name: ai
ai.title: AI Model Cache
ai.desc: Locally cached AI models discovered from tools such as Ollama, Hugging Face Hub, LM Studio, GPT4All, PyTorch Hub, Keras, TensorFlow Hub, and Jan, plus the Gemini Nano model Google Chrome downloads for its built-in AI features. Iterate `models` to audit which AI models are present on the system, their sizes, file formats, publishers, and licenses.

aider.name: aider
aider.title: Aider coding assistant instance
aider.desc: Aider, a command-line AI pair-programming tool, configured on the host through .aider.conf.yml in the user's home. Queryable through it are the configured model and whether the configuration file stores provider API keys, along with the package that installed the tool and the runtime it runs in. Pass configPath to target another configuration file. URL: https://aider.chat/

antigravity.name: antigravity
antigravity.title: Antigravity (Google) instance
antigravity.desc: Antigravity, Google's agentic development platform, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .gemini/antigravity in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://antigravity.google/

apache2.name: apache2
apache2.title: Apache2 HTTP Server
apache2.desc: Apache HTTP Server daemon version as reported by the apache2/httpd binary. Use apache2.conf for the parsed configuration, including directives, loaded modules, virtual hosts, and access-control blocks.

apt.name: apt
apt.title: Advanced Package Tool (APT) configuration
apt.desc: Debian/Ubuntu package management configuration. `repos` enumerates every configured APT repository across `/etc/apt/sources.list` and the `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` directory, parsing both the classic one-line format and the deb822 `.sources` format. Audit repository trust from there: each `apt.repo` reports whether it is marked `trusted` (signature checks bypassed) and the `signedBy` keyring that pins which key may sign it. `apt.config` holds APT's configuration.

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

augment.name: augment
augment.title: Augment Code instance
augment.desc: Augment Code, an AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .augment in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.augmentcode.com/

authorizedkeys.name: authorizedkeys
authorizedkeys.title: SSH authorized_keys file
authorizedkeys.desc: Single `authorized_keys` file: its path, the `file` reference, the raw `content` string, and the parsed `entry` list where each entry surfaces the line number, key type, key material, label, and any `command=` / `from=` / `no-port-forwarding` SSH options. Select the file by absolute path, for example `authorizedkeys(path: "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys")`, or reach it per account through the `user` resource, whose `authorizedkeys` field resolves each user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` automatically (for example `users.where(name == "root") { authorizedkeys { list { key } } }`). Used to audit which keys actually grant SSH access to a given user and to detect entries with no source or command restrictions.

bind9.name: bind9
bind9.title: BIND 9 DNS Server
bind9.desc: Parsed named.conf configuration with every include expanded, which is where distributions keep the parts worth auditing: named.conf.options and named.conf.local on Debian and Ubuntu, /etc/named.conf.local on Red Hat. Covers the global options block, every zone declared at the top level or inside a view, named address-match lists, and TSIG keys. The files field lists every file that contributed, so permission and ownership checks reach the whole configuration rather than the entry point. Pass a path, as in `bind9("/etc/named.conf")`, to read a config outside the default locations.

cassandra.name: cassandra
cassandra.title: Apache Cassandra Server
cassandra.desc: Cassandra server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use cassandra.conf for the parsed cassandra.yaml, covering authentication and authorization, client and internode encryption, at-rest encryption, audit logging, network binding, and the feature toggles that widen the query surface. JMX exposure lives in a shell script rather than in cassandra.yaml, so it is reached through cassandra.env, and the snitch topology through cassandra.rackdc.

chrome.name: chrome
chrome.title: Chromium-family browsers (Chrome, Brave, Edge variants)
chrome.desc: Installed browser extensions across all users and profiles for Chromium-based browsers. The `extensions` field lists every extension with its manifest metadata and permissions, and `extensionContentScripts` lists the content scripts those extensions inject into web pages. Useful for auditing risky permissions and unexpected or side-loaded extensions.

cline.name: cline
cline.title: Cline AI agent instance
cline.desc: Cline AI coding agent installed on the host. Queryable through it are the installed skills (read from the shared ~/.agents/skills directory), along with the package that installed the agent and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://cline.bot/

cloud.name: cloud
cloud.title: Cloud-asset metadata
cloud.desc: Cloud provider hosting the asset and the instance metadata it exposes. The `provider` field names the platform (aws, azure, gcp), and `instance` reaches the per-instance metadata read from the cloud's metadata service.

command.name: command
command.title: Result of running a shell command on the system
command.desc: Ad-hoc command execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a shell command string; the resource executes the command through the connection (local exec, SSH, container exec, and similar) and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. Used as a fall-back when there isn't a more specific resource for a piece of system state, and for assertions on tool versions or command-line probes.

containerd.name: containerd
containerd.title: containerd container runtime
containerd.desc: The containerd of a host or Kubernetes node (kubeadm, kind, K3s, RKE2, MicroK8s, k0s, and Docker's own containerd): its version, the configuration it runs with, and the containers it manages. The configuration is read from `configFile` and the files it imports, merged the way containerd merges them, and settings no file sets report containerd's built-in default, as each field says. Configuration fields read files only, so they also work on images and mounted filesystems. The registry audit is `containerd.registryHosts.none(skipVerify)`.

continuedev.name: continuedev
continuedev.title: Continue (open-source AI coding assistant) instance
continuedev.desc: Continue, an open-source AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .continue in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://continue.dev/

crio.name: crio
crio.title: CRI-O container runtime
crio.desc: The CRI-O container runtime of a Kubernetes node (OpenShift, MicroShift, and Kubernetes set up with CRI-O): its version, its effective configuration with the security defaults it applies to every container, and the containers it runs. `configuration` is what the running CRI-O reports; without a running CRI-O it is merged from `configFiles`.

cursor.name: cursor
cursor.title: Cursor editor (AI-powered) instance
cursor.desc: Cursor AI code editor installed on the host. Queryable through it are the configured MCP servers, the global and project rules that steer the assistant, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. Useful for auditing what tools and instructions govern the AI assistant. URL: https://www.cursor.com/

date.name: date
date.title: Current date and timezone of the system

docker.name: docker
docker.title: Docker host
docker.desc: Images and containers managed by the local Docker daemon. The `images` field lists every image stored on the host with its ID, tags, digests, size, and labels; `containers` lists running and stopped containers with their state, image, command, and labels. Use it to audit what is deployed on a Docker host, for example `docker.containers.where(status == /Up/)` for currently running workloads. `daemon` reports the configuration the Docker daemon runs with.

edr.name: edr
edr.title: Endpoint detection and response agents
edr.desc:
Endpoint security agents recognized on this asset. products lists every agent that was found, each carrying the packages, services, processes, and system extensions that make it up, so a report can name the vendor and the component that is unhealthy. installed and healthy answer the fleet-wide questions directly, letting an audit assert on one field instead of enumerating vendors per platform. Agents are recognized on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Recognized agents. Select one by its `id`, for example `edr.products.where(id == "sentinelone")`. An agent not listed here is not reported, so installed reads false on an asset protected only by an unlisted product.

| id | Product | Vendor | Category | Windows | Linux | macOS |
|---|---|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `crowdstrike-falcon` | CrowdStrike Falcon | CrowdStrike | edr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `sentinelone` | SentinelOne | SentinelOne | edr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `eset` | ESET Endpoint Security | ESET | epp | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `microsoft-defender` | Microsoft Defender Antivirus | Microsoft | av | ✓ | | |
| `wazuh` | Wazuh Agent | Wazuh | edr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `sophos` | Sophos Endpoint | Sophos | edr | ✓ | | |
| `cortex-xdr` | Cortex XDR | Palo Alto Networks | xdr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `watchguard-epdr` | WatchGuard EPDR | WatchGuard | epp | ✓ | | |
| `malwarebytes` | Malwarebytes Endpoint Agent | Malwarebytes | epp | ✓ | | ✓ |

file.name: file
file.title: File on the system
file.desc: Single file referenced by absolute path. Surfaces the path itself, the basename and dirname, an `exists` flag, the `content` string, the file's size in bytes, an `empty` predicate, the owning `user` and `group` as references, and a structured `permissions` resource that explodes the POSIX mode into named user / group / other read / write / execute bits, the SUID / SGID / sticky bits, the `isFile` / `isDirectory` / `isSymlink` discriminators, and a printed mode string. The unit of file-level audits and the building block most config-file resources read through. Select a file by path, for example `file("/etc/ssh/sshd_config")`.

files.name: files
files.title: File search and discovery namespace
files.desc: Empty namespace whose only purpose is to host `files.find`, so audits can write `files.find(...) {...}` to locate files on the asset rather than enumerating known paths.

firefox.name: firefox
firefox.title: Firefox-family browsers
firefox.desc: Installed browser addons discovered across every user account and profile for Firefox and its derivatives (Firefox Developer Edition, Nightly, LibreWolf, Waterfox, Floorp, Zen, Tor Browser, and Mullvad Browser). Iterate `addons` to inventory extensions and themes, spot disabled or side-loaded addons, and review the API permissions and host origins each addon requests. Mozilla-shipped system addons, locales, and dictionaries are filtered out.

gemini.name: gemini
gemini.title: Gemini CLI (Google) instance
gemini.desc: Google Gemini command-line tool installed on the host. Queryable through it are the authentication type, the settings dictionary, the configured MCP servers, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the tool and the runtime it executes in. Useful for auditing how the assistant authenticates and what tools it can reach. URL: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli

goose.name: goose
goose.title: Goose AI agent (Block) instance
goose.desc: Goose AI agent from Block installed on the host. Queryable through it are the active provider and model, whether telemetry is enabled, the configured extensions, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the agent and the runtime it executes in. Useful for auditing which model backend and extensions the agent uses. URL: https://block.github.io/goose/

group.name: group
group.title: Group on the system
group.desc: Single local group: numeric GID (or SID on Windows), group name, and the `members` list of users in the group. Used to audit privileged-group membership (`sudo`, `wheel`, `docker`, `adm`, and so on) and to confirm only expected accounts are present.

haproxy.name: haproxy
haproxy.title: HAProxy load balancer
haproxy.desc: HAProxy daemon version and configuration. The configuration covers the global section, defaults blocks, frontends, backends, listens, the servers behind each backend, and supporting sections (resolvers, userlists, peers).

idp.name: idp
idp.title: Identity provider this device belongs to
idp.desc: The identity providers the device is joined to, bound to, or registered with, alongside mdm for its management and edr for its endpoint protection. A device can belong to several at once (for example a hybrid join to Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID), so each one is its own field and is null when the device does not belong to it. Independent of MDM enrollment: a device can belong to an identity provider without being enrolled in an MDM service, and the other way round. Microsoft Entra ID is detected on Windows client editions, and Active Directory on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Others (for example FreeIPA, LDAP/Kerberos realms, or JumpCloud) can be added as fields later. This is the device's own identity, not the user-facing federation an `idp` resource describes in the SaaS providers.

ipAddress.name: ipAddress
ipAddress.title: IP address (v4 or v6) with networking details
ipAddress.desc: IP address plus its network context: the address itself, the subnet it belongs to, the address in CIDR notation, the broadcast address, and the gateway. Works for both IPv4 and IPv6.

jboss.name: jboss
jboss.title: JBoss EAP / WildFly application server
jboss.desc:
Locates a JBoss installation through JBOSS_HOME and exposes the server configuration it holds: the management section (management interfaces, security realms, the audit log and access control), the network interfaces and socket bindings, the password vault, and the subsystems declared in each profile. Nothing here needs a running JVM or the management CLI, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Both operating modes are covered. In standalone mode `config` is the profile the server is actually started with — which is not always standalone.xml, since `--server-config` selects one of the four shipped profiles. In domain mode `config` is domain.xml and `host` is the host controller's host.xml, which is where a domain keeps its management interfaces and security realms.

Every nested collection (profiles, subsystems, interfaces, socket bindings, security realms, management interfaces, audit handlers, connectors, log handlers) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-realm server keeps working when a second realm is added.

Pass `init(home: "...")` to point at an installation the discovery does not find, and `init(configFile: "...")` to read a profile other than the active one.

jetbrains.name: jetbrains
jetbrains.title: JetBrains IDE plugins
jetbrains.desc: Plugins discovered across every user account and every installed JetBrains product (IntelliJ IDEA, GoLand, PyCharm, Rider, WebStorm, CLion, DataGrip, DataSpell, PhpStorm, RubyMine, RustRover and the rest). Iterate `plugins` to inventory what extends each IDE, tell a plugin that ships with the product from one a user added, see whether the IDE currently loads it, and find plugins pinned to an IDE build older than the one installed. `paths` lists the plugin directories that were searched.

junie.name: junie
junie.title: Junie (JetBrains AI agent) instance
junie.desc: Junie, JetBrains' AI coding agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .junie in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.jetbrains.com/junie/

kilocode.title: Kilo Code AI agent instance
kilocode.desc: Kilo Code, an open-source AI coding agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .kilocode in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://kilocode.ai/
