kiro.title: Kiro CLI (AWS) instance
kiro.desc: Kiro AI coding agent from AWS installed on the host. Queryable through it are the installed skills, along with the package that installed the tool and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://kiro.dev/

kubelet.name: kubelet
kubelet.title: Kubernetes kubelet on this node
kubelet.desc: The kubelet agent running on this node, with its security-relevant settings resolved from the config file merged with the live process's CLI flags (CLI flags take precedence). The fields map to CIS Kubernetes benchmark controls: anonymous authentication, authorization mode, client CA, the read-only port, streaming timeouts, certificate rotation, and the TLS cipher/version floor. `configuration` returns the full merged configuration as a dict.

lastUpdate.name: lastUpdate
lastUpdate.title: Time the most recent operating system update was installed
lastUpdate.desc:
Newest completed update the platform's own update mechanism recorded for software the operating system vendor ships: a vendor package upgrade in dnf's transaction log or dnf5's transaction history (the transaction's end time), a completed apt upgrade run (timestamped by its End-Date), a completed `apk upgrade` run that upgraded at least one package (timestamped by when it started, the only time apk records), a macOS update in the install history, or a Windows Update Agent entry for a Windows product. Software that is not the operating system does not count, so a .NET or Office update on Windows, a third-party rpm such as Docker or Grafana, and an operator running `apt install` or `apk add` are all excluded, and so is definition data (XProtect on macOS, Defender signatures on Windows) that lands daily or weekly. Installing a package is not updating the operating system, so a first-time install never advances this timestamp, on any platform.

Null on containers and container images, which are rebuilt rather than patched, so the newest install inside one dates the image build rather than any patching of the workload. Null too wherever the asset keeps no record of a completed update that can be attributed to the vendor: an rpm host whose package manager writes no transaction log (yum-era RHEL, Photon), a SUSE host whose zypper history holds no update run, image-based systems that update by swapping the OS image (Bottlerocket, CoreOS), a Debian host whose apt history has rotated away or whose newest history log cannot be read, a Windows host whose update agent history cannot be read, an Alpine host whose apk-tools writes no transaction log (Alpine 3.22 and earlier), and pacman. A timestamp materially in the future (a skewed clock, a misread timezone) also reads null rather than reporting the asset as freshly patched. An inferred, incomplete or ambiguous answer would report a different fact than the one asked for, so the field reads null instead of answering loosely.

Null is not false, so guard on it rather than comparing straight through: `os.lastUpdate != null && (time.now - os.lastUpdate).days < 30`.

lastUpdateAge.name: lastUpdateAge
lastUpdateAge.title: Time since the most recent operating system update was installed
lastUpdateAge.desc: A duration, like `uptime`, so `os.lastUpdateAge.days` reads the patch age directly. Measured once, when the field is first read, and held for the rest of the scan rather than tracking the clock, the same way `uptime` behaves. For an age relative to a specific moment, subtract instead: `time.now - os.lastUpdate`. Null whenever `lastUpdate` is null.

lastUpdateSource.name: lastUpdateSource
lastUpdateSource.title: Record the last-update timestamp was read from
lastUpdateSource.desc: One of "dnf-rpm-log", "dnf5-history", "apt-security", "apt-history", "apk-log", "macos-install-history", "windows-update-agent", or "nixos-generation". Every one of them names an exact, completed install event, so this reports provenance rather than precision, and how tightly the vendor attribution holds is what separates them. "apt-security" is a completed unattended-upgrades run, whose default origin is the distribution's security pocket, which makes it the closest an asset comes to recording a vendor security advisory without an external advisory database; "apt-history" is an operator-run full upgrade, which vendor packages dominate but which can also carry a third-party repository. "apk-log" is the same kind of operator-run upgrade on Alpine, and "zypp-history" on SUSE: a `zypper update`, `zypper patch` or `zypper dist-upgrade` run that installed at least one package, timestamped by its last install. `zypper install` does not count, even when it satisfies a patch. A policy that demands the vendor security channel can require "apt-security", where a looser one takes any non-null answer. Null whenever `lastUpdate` is null.

mariadb.name: mariadb
mariadb.title: MariaDB Server
mariadb.desc: MariaDB server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use mariadb.conf for the parsed option files, including option groups, server and client scope options, Galera cluster settings, TLS material, and the per-user option files under home directories.

mdm.name: mdm
mdm.title: Mobile device management enrollment
mdm.desc: MDM enrollment state for this asset on macOS and Windows. enrolled, vendor, and serverUrl answer the fleet-wide questions without a per-platform query, for example `mdm.enrolled && mdm.vendor == "intune"`, and method says how the device was enrolled. On any other platform enrolled is false.

memory.name: memory
memory.title: Physical and virtual memory of the running system
memory.desc: Installed physical memory, the physical memory still available, and the committed virtual memory against its commit limit, all in bytes and read in one snapshot. Used for operational inventory and for usage checks such as `memory.available * 100 / memory.total > 10` and `memory.committed * 100 / memory.commitLimit < 80`. Supported on Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, and Solaris. A value the platform does not keep reads as null: macOS and NetBSD have no commit accounting, and FreeBSD reports no commit limit. Asset types that do not run a live system, such as container images and disk snapshots, report the fields as not applicable.

mongodb.name: mongodb
mongodb.title: MongoDB Server
mongodb.desc: MongoDB server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use mongodb.conf for the parsed configuration file, covering network binding, TLS material, authentication and authorization, auditing, encryption at rest, replication, and query profiling.

mysql.name: mysql
mysql.title: MySQL Server
mysql.desc: MySQL server version and distribution as reported by the installed server binary. Percona Server is reported here too, since it shares MySQL's option file layout and binary names. Use mysql.conf for the parsed option files, including option groups, server and client scope options, TLS material, and the per-user option files under home directories. MariaDB installations are covered by the mariadb resource.

name.name: name
name.title: Pretty Hostname on macOS/Linux or device name on Windows

network.name: network
network.title: Network configuration of this system
network.desc: Host networking view: the network interfaces and their addresses, the routing table (including default routes), the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses detected across interfaces, the primary addresses chosen by the default route, and the ARP / NDP neighbor cache.

nginx.name: nginx
nginx.title: Nginx HTTP Server
nginx.desc: Nginx daemon version and the modules compiled into the binary. Use nginx.conf for the parsed configuration, including server blocks, upstream pools, and listen addresses.

openclaw.name: openclaw
openclaw.title: OpenClaw AI agent instance
openclaw.desc: OpenClaw, an AI coding agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .openclaw in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://openclaw.ai/

opencode.name: opencode
opencode.title: OpenCode AI coding assistant instance
opencode.desc: OpenCode, an open-source terminal AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .config/opencode in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://opencode.ai/

openhands.name: openhands
openhands.title: OpenHands AI agent instance (formerly OpenDevin)
openhands.desc: OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin), an open-source AI software-engineering agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .openhands in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.all-hands.dev/

package.name: package
package.title: Installed package on the platform or OS
package.desc: Single package known to the asset's native package manager (rpm, deb, apk, pkg, msi, nuget, pacman, and so on). Surfaces the package name, description, currently-installed `version`, architecture, epoch, package format, install status, package URL, the CPE list mapping the package to NVD identifiers, the package origin, the latest `available` version known to the package manager, the `installed` and `outdated` flags, the file inventory the package contributed, and the package vendor. The unit of asset-level package audits and the join key for vulnerability correlation.

packages.name: packages
packages.title: All packages installed on the system
packages.desc: Collection of every `package` known to the asset's native package manager(s). The entry point for fleet-wide patch audits, banned-package checks, and inventory exports.

pi.name: pi
pi.title: Pi AI agent instance
pi.desc: Pi, an AI coding agent, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .pi/agent in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://pi.dev/

pkg.name: pkg
pkg.title: FreeBSD pkg configuration
pkg.desc: FreeBSD package manager configuration. `repos` enumerates every repository pkg would use, read from `/etc/pkg/` and then `/usr/local/etc/pkg/repos/` and merged the way pkg merges them, so a later file redefining a repository by name overrides only the keys it sets. Audit repository trust from there: each `pkg.repo` reports the `signatureType` pkg verifies it with and the key material that verification reads.

podman.name: podman
podman.title: Podman container engine
podman.desc: Workloads managed by Podman, together with the engine settings that apply to all of them. `rootless` reports whether the engine runs without root, which changes what a container escape is worth, and `seccompEnabled`, `apparmorEnabled`, and `selinuxEnabled` report which confinement mechanisms the host makes available. `containers`, `images`, `pods`, `volumes`, and `networks` inventory the workloads themselves. On RedHat-family hosts Podman is the default engine and Docker is often absent, so this is where those workloads are found.

port.name: port
port.title: Single TCP/UDP port on the system
port.desc: Single network socket: its protocol, local address and port, connection state, and (where the OS reports it) the owning process and the remote peer. The `state` field distinguishes listening sockets from established connections, `process` links to the program holding the socket, and `tls` probes the endpoint for a TLS configuration. Central to exposure audits, for example finding listening ports bound to a non-loopback address.

ports.name: ports
ports.title: All TCP/UDP ports on the system
ports.desc: Collection of all network sockets, both listening and connected. The `listening` accessor narrows the set to sockets in the listen state, which is the usual starting point for an exposure audit (for example `ports.listening.where(address != "127.0.0.1")`).

privatekey.name: privatekey
privatekey.title: Private key on disk
privatekey.desc: PEM-encoded private key file: the `file` reference, the raw PEM `pem` payload, and an `encrypted` flag indicating whether the key is passphrase-protected. `publicKeyAlgorithm` and `publicKeyBits` describe the key material. Used to inventory SSH or service-account keys discovered on the asset and to flag unencrypted private keys stored in user home directories.

process.name: process
process.title: Single process on the system
process.desc: Running process identified by its PID. Exposes the executable path, the full command line it was invoked with, its current state, and a map of additional per-process flags. Select a process with `process(pid: 1)`.

processes.name: processes
processes.title: All processes running on the system
processes.desc: Collection of every running process, for filtering by executable, command line, user, or state. For example `processes.where(executable == "/usr/sbin/sshd")` finds all instances of a daemon, or filter on state to spot zombie or stopped processes.

python.name: python
python.title: Python package inventory
python.desc: Installed Python packages discovered on the host. `packages` lists every package found and `toplevel` narrows that to packages that were explicitly installed rather than pulled in as dependencies. Pass `path` to scan a specific site-packages location instead of the default locations. Used for software inventory and vulnerability correlation.

roo.name: roo
roo.title: Roo Code editor instance
roo.desc: Roo Code AI coding agent installed on the host. Queryable through it are the installed skills, along with the package that installed the tool and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://roocode.com/

service.name: service
service.title: Service on the system
service.desc: Single init/service-manager unit (systemd, SysV, launchd, and others), selected by name (e.g., `service(name: "sshd")`). Exposes install, enable, and run state plus the unit type and mask/static metadata, so you can assert that required services run and unwanted ones stay off.

services.name: services
services.title: All services configured on the system
services.desc: Collection of every service across the asset's init/service manager. Filter it to find running-but-unwanted or disabled-but-required services, e.g. `services.where(running == true)`.

squid.name: squid
squid.title: Squid caching proxy
squid.desc: Squid proxy server version reported by the daemon binary. Use `squid.conf` to inspect the full configuration including ACLs, access rules, listen ports, cache peers, refresh patterns, and any fragments pulled in by `include` directives (for example the contents of `/etc/squid/conf.d/*.conf`).

tomcat.name: tomcat
tomcat.title: Apache Tomcat
tomcat.desc:
Locates a Tomcat installation through CATALINA_HOME / CATALINA_BASE and exposes its on-disk configuration: server.xml, the global web.xml and context.xml, catalina.properties, logging.properties, tomcat-users.xml, and the applications deployed under each Host's appBase. Nothing here needs a running JVM, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Every nested collection (services, connectors, engines, hosts, valves, realms, listeners, contexts, users, webapps) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-Connector server keeps working when a second Connector is added.

Pass `init(home: "...", base: "...")` to point at a non-default layout.

trae.name: trae
trae.title: Trae AI assistant (ByteDance) instance
trae.desc: Trae, ByteDance's AI-powered IDE assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .trae in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://trae.ai/

user.name: user
user.title: User account on the system
user.desc: Single local user account: numeric UID and primary GID (Windows SID where applicable), name, home directory, configured login shell, and an `enabled` flag. Surfaces the primary `group` reference, the `authorizedkeys` resource that parses the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, the SSH private keys discovered in the user's home, and a `loggedIn` predicate that reflects whether the user currently has an active session. Used for identity audits, dormant-account hygiene, and SSH-key inventories.

vscode.name: vscode
vscode.title: Visual Studio Code (and forks)
vscode.desc: Installed editor extensions discovered across all users for VS Code and compatible forks (Cursor, Windsurf, and similar). Iterate `extensions` to inventory what is installed per editor, review publishers and versions, and identify untrusted or outdated extensions. `paths` lists the extension directories that were searched.

vulnmgmt.name: vulnmgmt
vulnmgmt.title: Asset vulnerability assessment
vulnmgmt.desc: Vulnerability data Mondoo derives for an asset by joining its installed-package inventory and platform identity against the curated CVE and advisory feed. Exposes every CVE affecting the asset, every vendor advisory that mentions one of those CVEs, the affected packages with their currently-installed and patched-available versions, the timestamp of the last assessment run, and the rolled-up CVSS statistics: the surface used to score asset risk and to drive patch-status policies.

warp.name: warp
warp.title: Warp AI terminal instance
warp.desc: Warp, an AI-powered terminal, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Warp reads skills from the shared .agents/skills directory in each user's home rather than its own .warp config directory; pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.warp.dev/

windsurf.name: windsurf
windsurf.title: Windsurf editor (Codeium) instance
windsurf.desc: Windsurf AI code editor from Codeium installed on the host. Queryable through it are the global rules and memories that steer the assistant, the configured MCP servers, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://windsurf.com/

winget.name: winget
winget.title: Windows Package Manager (winget)
winget.desc: Whether winget is installed on a Windows host and whether it can run as the SYSTEM account, where it often cannot. installed, version, and path come from the Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller package that ships winget.exe, found in the AppX package repository and the WindowsApps folder without running winget. missingDependencies lists the framework packages its manifest requires that the machine does not have, and systemUsable combines these checks, for example `winget.installed && winget.systemUsable`. sources lists the package sources winget uses for the SYSTEM account. On any other platform installed and systemUsable are false.

yum.name: yum
yum.title: Yum/DNF package manager
yum.desc: Configuration of the yum/dnf package manager on RedHat-family systems. `vars` exposes the variables defined across `/etc/yum.conf` and the `.repo` files (for example `$releasever` and `$basearch`) and `repos` lists every configured repository as `yum.repo` entries.

zed.name: zed
zed.title: Zed editor instance
zed.desc: Zed code editor installed on the host. Queryable through it are the workspace settings dictionary and the names of installed extensions, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://zed.dev/

os.base.title: Generic operating system information common to all platforms
os.base.desc:
The universal root of an OS asset: everything present on every supported platform. Embeds `machine` (firmware / SMBIOS hardware identity) and exposes the pretty hostname (or Windows device name), the FQDN-style hostname, environment variables and the resolved PATH list, uptime, the available-OS-update list, the reboot-pending flag, the hypervisor, the machine ID, the system date and timezone, and the `users` and `groups` collections.

The family roots build on it: `os.unix` for the Unix family, `os.linux` and `os.macos` under that, `os.windows` beside it, each carrying only the facilities its family provides. `os.any` is the union of all of them and is the root the provider declares, so `_` resolves to it. Which root a resource hangs off is the statement about where that resource exists, which is why the `alias os.<root>.<resource>` block at the top of this schema is the platform classification: to add a resource you have to place it. Those aliases have to stay contiguous, a comment between two of them fails the parse.

os.base.agentskills.name: agentskills

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Agent skill defined by a SKILL.md file
skill.desc: A skill directory as the Agent Skills specification defines it. The frontmatter fields hold the values exactly as written, with no fallbacks, so a missing or malformed value can be checked: `name` is empty when the frontmatter omits it, and `errors` explains a frontmatter that cannot be read. `directory` is what the specification requires `name` to equal, `files` lists the bundled scripts, references, and assets, and `sha256` pins the definition.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills found under the directory, one per SKILL.md file

os.base.agentskills.title: Agent Skills under a directory
os.base.agentskills.desc: Skills that follow the Agent Skills specification (https://agentskills.io/specification), independent of the agent that loads them. The `path` field selects the directory searched, for example `agentskills(path: "/home/alice/src/my-skills")`. Every SKILL.md below it is a skill, including skills nested in plugin directories; the files inside a skill, `.git`, and `node_modules` are not searched. Use it to validate a skills repository against the specification or to inventory the skills in a checkout.

os.base.ai.name: ai

model.name: model
model.title: AI Model
model.desc: Single locally cached AI model. The `name` field identifies the model and `source` indicates which tool cached it (for example `"ollama"`, `"huggingface"`, `"lmstudio"`, `"gpt4all"`, `"pytorch"`, `"keras"`, `"tfhub"`, `"jan"`, or `"chrome"`). Use `ai.models.where(source == "ollama")` to filter by source, or inspect `size` and `modifiedAt` to find the largest or most recently used models on the system.

models.name: models
models.title: All locally cached AI models across all supported sources

os.base.ai.title: AI Model Cache
os.base.ai.desc: Locally cached AI models discovered from tools such as Ollama, Hugging Face Hub, LM Studio, GPT4All, PyTorch Hub, Keras, TensorFlow Hub, and Jan, plus the Gemini Nano model Google Chrome downloads for its built-in AI features. Iterate `models` to audit which AI models are present on the system, their sizes, file formats, publishers, and licenses.

os.base.aider.name: aider

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Aider configuration file

hasApiKeys.name: hasApiKeys
hasApiKeys.title: Whether the configuration file stores provider API keys
hasApiKeys.desc: True when `openai-api-key`, `anthropic-api-key`, or any `api-key` entry holds a value. The keys themselves are never returned.

model.name: model
model.title: Configured default model
model.desc: The `model` key of the configuration file, for example "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4" or "ollama/qwen2.5-coder". Empty when unset.

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional, null when the host cannot be determined.

os.base.aider.title: Aider coding assistant instance
os.base.aider.desc: Aider, a command-line AI pair-programming tool, configured on the host through .aider.conf.yml in the user's home. Queryable through it are the configured model and whether the configuration file stores provider API keys, along with the package that installed the tool and the runtime it runs in. Pass configPath to target another configuration file. URL: https://aider.chat/

os.base.antigravity.name: antigravity

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Antigravity configuration directory

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional; null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Antigravity skill
skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the Antigravity agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills installed for the agent, one resource per discovered SKILL.md file

os.base.antigravity.title: Antigravity (Google) instance
os.base.antigravity.desc: Antigravity, Google's agentic development platform, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .gemini/antigravity in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://antigravity.google/

os.base.apache2.name: apache2

conf.name: conf
conf.title: Apache2 HTTP Server configuration
conf.desc: Parsed Apache configuration covering flat directives, loaded modules, virtual hosts, and Directory / Location access-control blocks, merged across the main config and every Include fragment. Also surfaces hardening-relevant settings such as ServerTokens, ServerSignature, TraceEnable, and response security headers. Pass `init(path: "...")` to point at a non-default config file.

os.base.apache2.title: Apache2 HTTP Server
os.base.apache2.desc: Apache HTTP Server daemon version as reported by the apache2/httpd binary. Use apache2.conf for the parsed configuration, including directives, loaded modules, virtual hosts, and access-control blocks.

os.base.apt.name: apt

config.name: config
config.title: APT configuration
config.desc: APT's effective configuration, as APT itself resolves it: its built-in defaults merged with `/etc/apt/apt.conf` and every file in `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/`, read from `apt-config dump`. `params` holds every option with its full name as the key (e.g. `Acquire::http::Proxy`) and the unquoted value; a list option such as `DPkg::Pre-Invoke` holds its items joined by newlines. The bool fields audit repository trust and package selection: they parse values the way APT does (`1`/`0`, `true`/`false`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off`) and fall back to APT's documented default when the option is not set. Reading the configuration needs `apt-config`; where it cannot run, `params` and the bool fields are an error rather than defaults.

repo.name: repo
repo.title: APT software repository
repo.desc: A single configured APT repository parsed from a sources list: its package `type` (`deb` for binary or `deb-src` for source), the `url` it fetches from, the `distribution` (suite) and `components` it pulls, and the `file` that declares it. The security-relevant fields are `trusted`, true when the entry carries `[trusted=yes]`, which disables signature verification, and `signedBy`, the keyring path pinning which key may sign the repository. `allowInsecure`, `allowWeak`, `allowDowngradeToInsecure`, `checkValidUntil` and `checkDate` are the entry's own trust options, which override the matching apt.config option for this repository; each is null when the entry does not set it. `enabled` is false for entries commented out in a one-line sources file or marked `Enabled: no` in a deb822 file.

os.base.apt.title: Advanced Package Tool (APT) configuration
os.base.apt.desc: Debian/Ubuntu package management configuration. `repos` enumerates every configured APT repository across `/etc/apt/sources.list` and the `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` directory, parsing both the classic one-line format and the deb822 `.sources` format. Audit repository trust from there: each `apt.repo` reports whether it is marked `trusted` (signature checks bypassed) and the `signedBy` keyring that pins which key may sign it. `apt.config` holds APT's configuration.

os.base.augment.name: augment

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Augment configuration directory

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional; null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Augment skill
skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the Augment agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills installed for the agent, one resource per discovered SKILL.md file

os.base.augment.title: Augment Code instance
os.base.augment.desc: Augment Code, an AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .augment in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.augmentcode.com/

os.base.authorizedkeys.name: authorizedkeys

content.name: content
content.title: Key file content

entry.name: entry
entry.title: SSH authorized key
entry.desc: Single entry from an `authorized_keys` file: the source line number, key type, key material, label, and any SSH options such as `command=`, `from=`, or `no-port-forwarding`. Used to audit which keys grant SSH access to a user and to flag entries that lack source or command restrictions.

file.name: file
file.title: Key file

os.base.authorizedkeys.title: SSH authorized_keys file
os.base.authorizedkeys.desc: Single `authorized_keys` file: its path, the `file` reference, the raw `content` string, and the parsed `entry` list where each entry surfaces the line number, key type, key material, label, and any `command=` / `from=` / `no-port-forwarding` SSH options. Select the file by absolute path, for example `authorizedkeys(path: "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys")`, or reach it per account through the `user` resource, whose `authorizedkeys` field resolves each user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` automatically (for example `users.where(name == "root") { authorizedkeys { list { key } } }`). Used to audit which keys actually grant SSH access to a given user and to detect entries with no source or command restrictions.

os.base.bind9.name: bind9

acl.name: acl
acl.title: BIND 9 address-match list
acl.desc: A list declared with acl and referenced by name from the options block or a zone, so a check that resolves a name like "trusted" can see what it stands for.

acls.name: acls
acls.title: Named address-match lists declared with acl

allowQuery.name: allowQuery
allowQuery.title: Hosts allowed to query the server (allow-query)

allowTransfer.name: allowTransfer
allowTransfer.title: Hosts allowed to transfer zones (allow-transfer)
allowTransfer.desc: An unrestricted transfer hands a copy of every zone to anyone who asks, which is why hardening guidance starts here.

allowUpdate.name: allowUpdate
allowUpdate.title: Hosts allowed to submit dynamic updates (allow-update)

alsoNotify.name: alsoNotify
alsoNotify.title: Secondaries notified of zone changes beyond the zone NS records (also-notify)
alsoNotify.desc: Notifications carry the fact that a zone changed, so the list is worth checking against the secondaries that are supposed to receive them.

channel.name: channel
channel.title: BIND 9 logging channel
channel.desc: One channel of the logging block, naming where records go and how much of them is kept.

channels.name: channels
channels.title: Logging channels declared inside the logging block

dnssecKey.name: dnssecKey
dnssecKey.title: A DNSSEC key pair on disk
dnssecKey.desc: One entry per `K<zone>.+<algorithm>+<tag>.key` file `dnssec-keygen` wrote. The private half is reported as a file so its mode and owner can be checked; its contents are never read.

dnssecKeys.name: dnssecKeys
dnssecKeys.title: DNSSEC key files found on disk
dnssecKeys.desc: The key pairs `dnssec-keygen` writes, looked for in the key-directory option, then the working directory, then the well-known locations. No named.conf statement names them individually, so they are found rather than declared.

dnssecValidation.name: dnssecValidation
dnssecValidation.title: dnssec-validation setting ("yes", "no", or "auto"; empty when unset)

file.name: file
file.title: Primary configuration file
file.desc: The file named loads: the -c argument of the running named, or when named is not running, of the systemd service that starts it with OPTIONS from /etc/default/named, /etc/default/bind9, or /etc/sysconfig/named. Without a -c argument, the distribution's default location.

files.name: files
files.title: Every file that contributes to the running configuration
files.desc: The primary file plus each one it pulls in, directly or through a chain of includes, so ownership and permission checks cover the fragments a zone or a key is actually declared in.

key.name: key
key.title: BIND 9 TSIG key
key.desc: A key used to authenticate transfers, dynamic updates, and rndc. The shared secret is not among the fields.

keys.name: keys
keys.title: TSIG keys declared with key
keys.desc: A key reports its name and algorithm. The shared secret is left behind, so this field carries no key material. The file the key is declared in is still a file like any other, and its content is readable through it.

listenOn.name: listenOn
listenOn.title: Addresses the server listens on for IPv4 (listen-on)

listenOnPort.name: listenOnPort
listenOnPort.title: Port the IPv4 listener is bound to
listenOnPort.desc: The port modifier of listen-on, as in `listen-on port 5353 { ... }`. 0 when the statement does not set one, in which case BIND listens on 53.

listenOnV6.name: listenOnV6
listenOnV6.title: Addresses the server listens on for IPv6 (listen-on-v6)

listenOnV6Port.name: listenOnV6Port
listenOnV6Port.title: Port the IPv6 listener is bound to
listenOnV6Port.desc: 0 when listen-on-v6 does not set one, in which case BIND listens on 53.

logCategories.name: logCategories
logCategories.title: Logging categories and the channels each is sent to
logCategories.desc: The category name maps to its channel list, so `queries` mapping to a channel is what says query logging is on.

params.name: params
params.title: Every scalar statement of the options block, as written
params.desc: Carries the settings without a field of their own here, so a check can reach a statement this resource does not model. A list-valued statement is not in here: its value is a block, and flattening it to a string would invent a value the file does not have.

recursion.name: recursion
recursion.title: Whether the server answers recursive queries
recursion.desc: BIND defaults to recursion for a server that does not say otherwise, so this reads true when the statement is absent. An authoritative server that has not turned recursion off is an open resolver.

version.name: version
version.title: Version string reported in a version.bind query
version.desc: Empty when the statement is absent, which means the real version is reported. A server that hides it sets this, often to "none" or a made-up string. `version "";` also reads empty, so check for a version key in params to tell it from an absent statement.

zone.name: zone
zone.title: BIND 9 zone
zone.desc: One zone declaration. The name field selects the zone as it appears in named.conf, for example `bind9.zones.where(name == "example.com")`.

zones.name: zones
zones.title: Zones this server answers for
zones.desc: Zones declared at the top level and inside every view. The view a zone belongs to is on the zone itself, so a server that splits its answers still reports one list.

os.base.bind9.title: BIND 9 DNS Server
os.base.bind9.desc: Parsed named.conf configuration with every include expanded, which is where distributions keep the parts worth auditing: named.conf.options and named.conf.local on Debian and Ubuntu, /etc/named.conf.local on Red Hat. Covers the global options block, every zone declared at the top level or inside a view, named address-match lists, and TSIG keys. The files field lists every file that contributed, so permission and ownership checks reach the whole configuration rather than the entry point. Pass a path, as in `bind9("/etc/named.conf")`, to read a config outside the default locations.

os.base.cassandra.name: cassandra

conf.name: conf
conf.title: Apache Cassandra cassandra.yaml file
conf.desc:
Settings from the main Cassandra configuration file on disk, useful for auditing the cluster's declared posture without a CQL session or credentials, and for detecting drift between the file and a running node that has not been restarted since it was edited. The file is a nested YAML document and has no include mechanism, so a parse reads exactly one file and `params` holds the whole tree as written.

Convenience fields flatten the branches that carry security posture: authentication and authorization, client and internode encryption, encryption at rest, audit and full query logging, network binding, the feature toggles that widen the query surface, and storage durability. Each reports the value the server would use, so an option left out of the file reads as the server default rather than as empty. That matters most where the default is permissive: `authenticator` and `authorizer` both default to their AllowAll variants, which authenticate nobody and authorize everybody.

Option names follow Cassandra 4.1 and later, which renamed most of cassandra.yaml. Settings that name an implementation class are read in both shapes the server accepts, a bare class name and a mapping carrying `class_name`. By default the file is located by probing the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu, RPM, and tarball installations; pass an explicit path with `cassandra.conf("/path/to/cassandra.yaml")`.

env.name: env
env.title: Apache Cassandra cassandra-env.sh file
env.desc:
JMX exposure and the JVM system properties the launch script sets, read from cassandra-env.sh. Cassandra keeps its JMX posture in this shell script rather than in cassandra.yaml, and it is not reported by the running server either, so this file is the only place the settings can be audited. `localJmx` is the consequential one: Cassandra ships with JMX bound to localhost, and turning that off exposes a port that can read and write cluster state, run nodetool operations, and, with full query log archiving on, execute shell commands.

The file is a script rather than a configuration file, and it ships with both a localhost-only and a remote branch of JMX settings present in the text. The `if [ "$LOCAL_JMX" = "yes" ]` conditional that selects between them is resolved, so `properties` holds only what the live branch sets and `jmxAuthenticate` reports the value that actually applies. Any other conditional in the file is treated as taken. Permissions on the files named by `jmxPasswordFile` and `jmxAccessFile` are worth checking alongside these, through the file resource. By default the script is located by probing the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu, RPM, and tarball installations; pass an explicit path with `cassandra.env("/path/to/cassandra-env.sh")`.

rackdc.name: rackdc
rackdc.title: Apache Cassandra cassandra-rackdc.properties file
rackdc.desc: Data center and rack this node reports to the cluster, which the rack-aware snitches read to place replicas. A wrong or default value here puts replicas that were meant to be spread across failure domains onto the same one, and it decides which links `internodeEncryption` set to dc or rack considers internal. By default the file is located by probing the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu, RPM, and tarball installations; pass an explicit path with `cassandra.rackdc("/path/to/cassandra-rackdc.properties")`.

version.name: version
version.title: Cassandra version (e.g., "5.0.2")
version.desc: Read by running the server binary, so it reports nothing over a transport that cannot run commands. The configuration files the other cassandra resources read are unaffected, since they come off the filesystem.

os.base.cassandra.title: Apache Cassandra Server
os.base.cassandra.desc: Cassandra server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use cassandra.conf for the parsed cassandra.yaml, covering authentication and authorization, client and internode encryption, at-rest encryption, audit logging, network binding, and the feature toggles that widen the query surface. JMX exposure lives in a shell script rather than in cassandra.yaml, so it is reached through cassandra.env, and the snitch topology through cassandra.rackdc.

os.base.chrome.name: chrome

extension.name: extension
extension.title: Chrome browser extension
extension.desc: Single installed Chromium-family browser extension and its manifest metadata: the `identifier`, `name`, `version`, requested `permissions` and `optionalPermissions`, on-disk `path`, owning `profile` and `browser`, whether it came from the Web Store, whether it is `enabled`, and the declared content scripts. Audits use the permissions and `fromWebstore` fields to flag over-privileged or unvetted extensions.

extensionContentScript.name: extensionContentScript
extensionContentScript.title: Chrome extension content script
extensionContentScript.desc: Content script declared by a Chrome-family extension: a JavaScript file the extension injects into pages whose URLs match a pattern. Each record ties the injected `script` to the `match` pattern that triggers it and to the owning extension (`identifier`, `version`) and user (`uid`), so you can audit which extensions run code against which sites and flag broad patterns such as `<all_urls>`.

extensionContentScripts.name: extensionContentScripts
extensionContentScripts.title: All content scripts from all Chrome extensions across all profiles and users

extensions.name: extensions
extensions.title: All installed Chrome extensions across all profiles and users

os.base.chrome.title: Chromium-family browsers (Chrome, Brave, Edge variants)
os.base.chrome.desc: Installed browser extensions across all users and profiles for Chromium-based browsers. The `extensions` field lists every extension with its manifest metadata and permissions, and `extensionContentScripts` lists the content scripts those extensions inject into web pages. Useful for auditing risky permissions and unexpected or side-loaded extensions.

os.base.cline.name: cline

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Cline configuration directory

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional, null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Cline skill
skill.desc: Skill defined by a SKILL.md file that packages task instructions for the agent. The allowedTools list bounds which tools the skill may invoke, argumentHint documents its expected arguments, and content holds the full definition. Use sha256 to detect tampering.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Installed skills

os.base.cline.title: Cline AI agent instance
os.base.cline.desc: Cline AI coding agent installed on the host. Queryable through it are the installed skills (read from the shared ~/.agents/skills directory), along with the package that installed the agent and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://cline.bot/

os.base.cloud.name: cloud
os.base.cloud.title: Cloud-asset metadata
os.base.cloud.desc: Cloud provider hosting the asset and the instance metadata it exposes. The `provider` field names the platform (aws, azure, gcp), and `instance` reaches the per-instance metadata read from the cloud's metadata service.

os.base.command.name: command

command.name: command
command.title: Command string that was run

stderr.name: stderr
stderr.title: Standard error output from running the command

stdout.name: stdout
stdout.title: Standard output from running the command

os.base.command.title: Result of running a shell command on the system
os.base.command.desc: Ad-hoc command execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a shell command string; the resource executes the command through the connection (local exec, SSH, container exec, and similar) and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. Used as a fall-back when there isn't a more specific resource for a piece of system state, and for assertions on tool versions or command-line probes.

os.base.containerd.name: containerd

configFile.name: configFile
configFile.title: Main configuration file
configFile.desc: The file the running containerd's `--config` flag names. Otherwise the first that exists of /etc/containerd/config.toml and the files K3s, RKE2, MicroK8s and k0s generate, or /etc/containerd/config.toml when none exists, since containerd runs without one.

configVersion.name: configVersion
configVersion.title: Configuration format version: 1, 2 (containerd 1.x and 2.x), 3 (containerd 2.x), or 4 (containerd 2.3 and later)
configVersion.desc: From the files, otherwise the version of containerd's built-in defaults. Null when no file sets it and the containerd version is unknown.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: Settings from the configuration files
configuration.desc: Keyed as in the files, with the `imports` merged in the way containerd merges them. Holds only what the files set, no defaults. Registry credentials (`auth`, `auths`) and registry headers are left out.

container.name: container
container.title: Single containerd container
container.desc: A container managed by containerd, identified by `id` within its `namespace`, with its `image` reference, lifecycle `status`, process `pid`, `labels`, the `runtime` handling it (e.g. `io.containerd.runc.v2`), and the `snapshotter` providing its filesystem. The confinement fields are read from the OCI runtime spec the container was created with: capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, the host namespaces it shares, its mounts and resource limits. For a Kubernetes container they also name its pod, for example `containerd.containers.where(privileged) { podNamespace podName name }`. The pod sandbox (pause) containers are listed too.

containers.name: containers
containers.title: All containers across every containerd namespace

defaultRuntime.name: defaultRuntime
defaultRuntime.title: Runtime handler Kubernetes containers use unless they ask for another; containerd's default is "runc"

deviceOwnershipFromSecurityContext.name: deviceOwnershipFromSecurityContext
deviceOwnershipFromSecurityContext.title: Whether devices a pod mounts are owned by the pod's user and group rather than by root; containerd's default is false

disableApparmor.name: disableApparmor
disableApparmor.title: Whether AppArmor is turned off for all containers; containerd's default is false

disabledPlugins.name: disabledPlugins
disabledPlugins.title: Plugins containerd does not load (for example "io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri" for Docker's containerd)

enableUnprivilegedIcmp.name: enableUnprivilegedIcmp
enableUnprivilegedIcmp.title: Whether pods may send ICMP echo requests without a capability
enableUnprivilegedIcmp.desc: Sets net.ipv4.ping_group_range to every group in every pod. containerd 2.x defaults to true, 1.x to false. Null when no file sets it and the containerd version is unknown.

enableUnprivilegedPorts.name: enableUnprivilegedPorts
enableUnprivilegedPorts.title: Whether pods may bind ports below 1024 without a capability
enableUnprivilegedPorts.desc: Sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start to 0 in every pod. containerd 2.x defaults to true, 1.x to false. Null when no file sets it and the containerd version is unknown.

files.name: files
files.title: Configuration files, in the order containerd applies them
files.desc: `configFile` followed by the files its `imports` name, and the files those import, each overriding the ones before. Empty when `configFile` does not exist.

grpcAddress.name: grpcAddress
grpcAddress.title: Path of the socket containerd serves its API on; containerd's default is "/run/containerd/containerd.sock"

grpcGid.name: grpcGid
grpcGid.title: Group ID that owns the API socket; containerd's default is 0

grpcTcpAddress.name: grpcTcpAddress
grpcTcpAddress.title: TCP address containerd also serves its API on; empty when it serves the socket only

grpcUid.name: grpcUid
grpcUid.title: User ID that owns the API socket; containerd's default is 0

image.name: image
image.title: Image stored by containerd
image.desc: An image reference in a containerd namespace, with the `digest` and `mediaType` of its manifest or index, the `platforms` it is published for, and its `labels`. The configuration fields come from the image built for the host's platform: `configDigest` (the image ID Kubernetes reports), `size`, `createdAt`, `os`, `architecture`, `user` and `runsAsRoot`, `entrypoint`, `cmd`, `exposedPorts`, and the `layers`. They are null when containerd does not store that image's content, for example `containerd.images.where(runsAsRoot == false) { name user }`.

images.name: images
images.title: All images across every containerd namespace
images.desc: Kubernetes keeps its images in the `k8s.io` namespace. An image stored under several references is listed once for each, for example `containerd.images.where(namespace == "k8s.io" && runsAsRoot) { name }`.

process.name: process
process.title: Running containerd process; null when containerd is not running or the process list cannot be read

registryConfigPaths.name: registryConfigPaths
registryConfigPaths.title: Directories containerd looks up registry host configurations (`hosts.toml`) in
registryConfigPaths.desc: From the CRI `registry.config_path`, in the order they are tried. When neither it nor the deprecated `registry.mirrors` is set, containerd 2.x reads /etc/containerd/certs.d and /etc/docker/certs.d, and containerd 1.x none. Null when no file sets it and the containerd version is unknown.

registryHost.name: registryHost
registryHost.title: Registry host containerd pulls images from
registryHost.desc: A host of a registry namespace: a `[host."<url>"]` entry of the namespace's `hosts.toml`, tried in the order listed, or the namespace's `server`, tried last.

registryHosts.name: registryHosts
registryHosts.title: Registry hosts containerd pulls Kubernetes images from
registryHosts.desc: Read from the `hosts.toml` files in `registryConfigPaths` or, when no directory is configured, from the deprecated `registry.mirrors` and `registry.configs` settings.

restrictOomScoreAdj.name: restrictOomScoreAdj
restrictOomScoreAdj.title: Whether containerd caps the OOM score adjustment of containers at its own; containerd's default is false

root.name: root
root.title: Root directory of containerd's persistent data; containerd's default is "/var/lib/containerd"

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: containerd runtime handler
runtime.desc: A `containerd.runtimes.<name>` entry of the CRI configuration: the runtime a Kubernetes pod runs with when its RuntimeClass names this handler, or by default.

runtimes.name: runtimes
runtimes.title: Runtime handlers Kubernetes pods can run with

sandboxImage.name: sandboxImage
sandboxImage.title: Image of the pod sandbox (pause) container
sandboxImage.desc: Null when no file sets it and the containerd version is unknown, since the built-in default changes between releases.

selinuxEnabled.name: selinuxEnabled
selinuxEnabled.title: Whether containers run with SELinux labeling; containerd's default is false

snapshotter.name: snapshotter
snapshotter.title: Snapshotter that unpacks images for Kubernetes pods; containerd's default is "overlayfs"

state.name: state
state.title: Directory of containerd's transient state; containerd's default is "/run/containerd"

streamAddress.name: streamAddress
streamAddress.title: Listen address of the CRI streaming server for exec, attach and port forwarding
streamAddress.desc: containerd defaults to "127.0.0.1", so that only the kubelet on the node can reach it. Any other address exposes the server to the network.

streamPort.name: streamPort
streamPort.title: Port the CRI streaming server listens on; 0, containerd's default, picks a free port

streamTlsEnabled.name: streamTlsEnabled
streamTlsEnabled.title: Whether the CRI streaming server serves TLS; containerd's default is false

tolerateMissingHugetlbController.name: tolerateMissingHugetlbController
tolerateMissingHugetlbController.title: Whether containers start when the hugetlb cgroup controller is missing; containerd's default is true

version.name: version
version.title: containerd version (for example "2.2.0")
version.desc: Reported by the containerd binary. Null when it cannot be run, as on an image or a mounted filesystem.

os.base.containerd.title: containerd container runtime
os.base.containerd.desc: The containerd of a host or Kubernetes node (kubeadm, kind, K3s, RKE2, MicroK8s, k0s, and Docker's own containerd): its version, the configuration it runs with, and the containers it manages. The configuration is read from `configFile` and the files it imports, merged the way containerd merges them, and settings no file sets report containerd's built-in default, as each field says. Configuration fields read files only, so they also work on images and mounted filesystems. The registry audit is `containerd.registryHosts.none(skipVerify)`.

os.base.continuedev.name: continuedev

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Continue configuration directory

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional; null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Continue skill
skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the Continue agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills installed for the agent, one resource per discovered SKILL.md file

os.base.continuedev.title: Continue (open-source AI coding assistant) instance
os.base.continuedev.desc: Continue, an open-source AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Skills are scanned under the configuration directory (default .continue in the user's home); pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://continue.dev/

os.base.crio.name: crio

apparmorProfile.name: apparmorProfile
apparmorProfile.title: AppArmor profile applied to containers that set none (for example "crio-default")

configFiles.name: configFiles
configFiles.title: Configuration files, in the order CRI-O applies them
configFiles.desc: /etc/crio/crio.conf when present, then every file in /etc/crio/crio.conf.d and its subdirectories in name order, hidden files included, each overriding the ones before.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: Effective CRI-O configuration
configuration.desc: The configuration the running CRI-O reports, with its defaults filled in. Without a running CRI-O, merged from `configFiles`, which holds only what they set.

container.name: container
container.title: CRI-O container
container.desc: A container CRI-O runs for a Kubernetes pod, with its pod (`podName`, `podNamespace`, `sandboxId`), its image, and how it is confined: read from the OCI runtime spec CRI-O created it with (its capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor and SELinux settings, user, and resource limits) and from its pod sandbox (the host namespaces it shares). The spec is stored on the node, so these fields also work when CRI-O is stopped and on a scanned image or filesystem. For example `crio.containers.where(privileged || hostPID) { podNamespace podName name }`.

containers.name: containers
containers.title: Containers CRI-O runs, without the pod sandboxes that hold them

defaultCapabilities.name: defaultCapabilities
defaultCapabilities.title: Capabilities every container gets by default (for example "CAP_CHOWN")
defaultCapabilities.desc: In upper case with the CAP_ prefix, however the configuration spells them.

defaultRuntime.name: defaultRuntime
defaultRuntime.title: Runtime handler containers use unless they ask for another (for example "crun" or "runc")

defaultSysctls.name: defaultSysctls
defaultSysctls.title: Sysctls set in every pod (for example "net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0")

image.name: image
image.title: Image stored by CRI-O
image.desc: An image in CRI-O's containers/storage, selected by its `id`, with the `names` and `repoDigests` it is known by and its `size`. The configuration fields describe what a container started from it runs: `user` and `runsAsRoot`, `entrypoint` and `cmd`, `exposedPorts`, its `labels`, and the platform (`os`, `architecture`, `variant`) and build time (`createdAt`). They are null when the image's configuration is not stored. `containers` lists the containers created from it, for example `crio.images.where(runsAsRoot && containers.length > 0) { names }`.

images.name: images
images.title: Images CRI-O stores
images.desc: Read from containers/storage under `crio.root` (by default /var/lib/containers/storage), for example `crio.images.where(runsAsRoot) { names }`.

namespaceSignaturePolicies.name: namespaceSignaturePolicies
namespaceSignaturePolicies.title: Signature policies for the pods of single Kubernetes namespaces
namespaceSignaturePolicies.desc: The `<namespace>.json` files in `crio.image.signature_policy_dir`. A pod in a namespace with its own policy is verified against that policy instead of `signaturePolicy`.

namespaceSignaturePolicy.name: namespaceSignaturePolicy
namespaceSignaturePolicy.title: Signature policy CRI-O applies to the pods of one Kubernetes namespace

readOnly.name: readOnly
readOnly.title: Whether containers run with a read-only root filesystem by default

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: CRI-O runtime handler
runtime.desc: A `[crio.runtime.runtimes.<name>]` entry: the low-level runtime CRI-O runs a container with when a pod's RuntimeClass names it, or by default.

runtimes.name: runtimes
runtimes.title: Runtime handlers CRI-O can run containers with

seccompProfile.name: seccompProfile
seccompProfile.title: Seccomp profile applied to containers that set none; empty is CRI-O's built-in default profile

selinux.name: selinux
selinux.title: Whether CRI-O runs containers with SELinux labeling

signaturePolicy.name: signaturePolicy
signaturePolicy.title: Image signature policy CRI-O verifies pulled images against
signaturePolicy.desc: From `crio.image.signature_policy`, by default /etc/containers/policy.json, or /usr/share/containers/policy.json when only that one exists. Null when the policy file cannot be read.

streamAddress.name: streamAddress
streamAddress.title: Listen address of the streaming server for exec, attach and port forwarding
streamAddress.desc: CRI-O defaults to "127.0.0.1", so that only the kubelet on the node can reach it. Any other address exposes the server to the network.

streamPort.name: streamPort
streamPort.title: Port the streaming server listens on; 0 picks a free port

streamTlsEnabled.name: streamTlsEnabled
streamTlsEnabled.title: Whether the streaming server serves TLS

os.base.crio.title: CRI-O container runtime
os.base.crio.desc: The CRI-O container runtime of a Kubernetes node (OpenShift, MicroShift, and Kubernetes set up with CRI-O): its version, its effective configuration with the security defaults it applies to every container, and the containers it runs. `configuration` is what the running CRI-O reports; without a running CRI-O it is merged from `configFiles`.

os.base.cursor.name: cursor

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Cursor configuration directory

mcpServer.name: mcpServer
mcpServer.title: Cursor MCP server configuration
mcpServer.desc: Model Context Protocol server Cursor is configured to use. Stdio servers run a local command; sse and streamable-http servers connect to a url. `type` reports the transport and the hasEnv flag reports whether environment variables (often holding API keys or tokens) are configured for the server.

mcpServers.name: mcpServers
mcpServers.title: MCP servers the editor connects to

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

repo.name: repo
repo.title: Cursor workspace repository
repo.desc: Git repository backing a workspace folder opened in Cursor, derived from the editor's opened-folder history and resolved through its `.git/config`. Exposes the origin remote `url`, the parsed `host` (for example github.com) and `name` (org/repo slug), the checked-out `branch`, all configured `remotes`, and the working-tree root `path`. Repositories are deduplicated by their working-tree root. Opened folders that are not git working trees are omitted.

repos.name: repos
repos.title: Git repositories backing the opened workspaces

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Cursor rule file
rule.desc: Rule file that injects standing instructions into the Cursor assistant's context, either globally or scoped to a project. The content field holds the full rule text, which shapes how the AI behaves and is worth reviewing for injected or unexpected directives.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: Cursor rules (global and project-scoped) that steer the assistant

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional, null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Cursor skill
skill.desc: Skill defined by a SKILL.md file that packages task instructions for the assistant. The allowedTools list bounds which tools the skill may invoke, argumentHint documents its expected arguments, and content holds the full definition. Use sha256 to detect tampering.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Installed skills

os.base.cursor.title: Cursor editor (AI-powered) instance
os.base.cursor.desc: Cursor AI code editor installed on the host. Queryable through it are the configured MCP servers, the global and project rules that steer the assistant, and any installed skills, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. Useful for auditing what tools and instructions govern the AI assistant. URL: https://www.cursor.com/

os.base.docker.name: docker

container.name: container
container.title: Single Docker container on the host
container.desc: A container on the Docker host, running or stopped, with its `state`, `status`, source `image`, startup `command`, and `labels`. The confinement settings describe what the container can reach on the host: `privileged` disables nearly every confinement at once, `capAdd` and `capDrop` adjust the capability set, `seccompProfile`, `apparmorProfile`, and `noNewPrivileges` report the process restrictions, and the namespace modes (`networkMode`, `pidMode`, `ipcMode`, `utsMode`, `usernsMode`, `cgroupnsMode`) report which host namespaces it shares. `mounts`, `devices`, and `ports` list what of the host is exposed inside it, for example `docker.containers.none(mounts.any(hostPath == "/var/run/docker.sock"))` finds containers that control the Docker daemon. Filter by state, for example `docker.containers.where(state == "running")`.

containers.name: containers
containers.title: All Docker containers on the host, running and stopped

daemon.name: daemon
daemon.title: Configuration of the Docker Engine daemon on the host

file.name: file
file.title: Dockerfile parser
file.desc: Parsed contents of a Dockerfile, giving structured access to every build instruction rather than the raw text. The `stages` field breaks a multi-stage build into its `FROM`/`RUN`/`COPY`/`ENV`/`EXPOSE`/`USER`/ `HEALTHCHECK` instructions, `instructions` returns them in file order, and `finalStage` points at the stage that produces the image. Select a file with `docker.file(path: "/path/to/Dockerfile")` and audit it, for example `docker.file("Dockerfile").stages.all(runsAsRoot == false)`.

image.name: image
image.title: Single Docker image on the host
image.desc: An image stored on the Docker host, with its content-addressable `id`, the `tags` and `repoDigests` it is known by, its `size`, and its `labels`. The image configuration reports what a container started from it runs: `user` and `runsAsRoot`, `entrypoint` and `cmd`, `exposedPorts`, the health check, and the platform (`os`, `architecture`, `variant`) and build time (`createdAt`). `containers` lists the containers created from it. Use it to inventory images and check provenance, for example `docker.images.where(tags.none(_ == /latest/))` to find images not pinned to a floating tag, or `docker.images.where(runsAsRoot)` to find images whose containers run as root unless told otherwise.

images.name: images
images.title: All Docker images stored on the host

network.name: network
network.title: Docker network
network.desc: A network defined on the Docker host, selected by `name`, for example `docker.network(name: "bridge")`. `internal` marks a network with no route to the outside, `subnets` holds the address ranges containers on it receive, and for the bridge driver `icc`, `ipMasquerade`, and `hostBindingIpv4` report whether containers on the network can reach each other, whether their traffic leaves through the host's address, and the address published ports bind to. `containers` lists the containers connected to it, for example `docker.networks.where(internal == false) { name containers.length }`.

networks.name: networks
networks.title: All networks defined on the Docker host, including the predefined bridge, host, and none

volume.name: volume
volume.title: Docker volume
volume.desc: A volume stored on the Docker host, selected by `name`, for example `docker.volume(name: "pgdata")`. `mountpoint` is the host path backing the volume, which is what a container writing to the volume ultimately writes to, and `containers` lists the containers that mount it, for example `docker.volumes.where(containers.length == 0)` for volumes nothing uses.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: All volumes stored on the Docker host, named and anonymous

os.base.docker.title: Docker host
os.base.docker.desc: Images and containers managed by the local Docker daemon. The `images` field lists every image stored on the host with its ID, tags, digests, size, and labels; `containers` lists running and stopped containers with their state, image, command, and labels. Use it to audit what is deployed on a Docker host, for example `docker.containers.where(status == /Up/)` for currently running workloads. `daemon` reports the configuration the Docker daemon runs with.

os.base.edr.name: edr

healthy.name: healthy
healthy.title: Whether every installed agent is running, and enabled to start at boot where the platform reports it

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether at least one recognized agent is installed

product.name: product
product.title: Endpoint security agent
product.desc: A single agent recognized on this asset. The `id` field selects the product, for example `edr.products.where(id == "crowdstrike-falcon")`. installed, running, and enabled report the agent's own components, and healthy combines them for the platform the asset runs. Fields the vendor does not report are null rather than zero, so a check that reads signatureAge on an agent that publishes no content version fails instead of passing against a made-up value.

products.name: products
products.title: Every recognized endpoint security agent found on this asset

os.base.edr.title: Endpoint detection and response agents
os.base.edr.desc:
Endpoint security agents recognized on this asset. products lists every agent that was found, each carrying the packages, services, processes, and system extensions that make it up, so a report can name the vendor and the component that is unhealthy. installed and healthy answer the fleet-wide questions directly, letting an audit assert on one field instead of enumerating vendors per platform. Agents are recognized on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Recognized agents. Select one by its `id`, for example `edr.products.where(id == "sentinelone")`. An agent not listed here is not reported, so installed reads false on an asset protected only by an unlisted product.
