| `sentinelone` | SentinelOne | SentinelOne | edr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `eset` | ESET Endpoint Security | ESET | epp | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `microsoft-defender` | Microsoft Defender Antivirus | Microsoft | av | ✓ | | |
| `wazuh` | Wazuh Agent | Wazuh | edr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `sophos` | Sophos Endpoint | Sophos | edr | ✓ | | |
| `cortex-xdr` | Cortex XDR | Palo Alto Networks | xdr | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `watchguard-epdr` | WatchGuard EPDR | WatchGuard | epp | ✓ | | |
| `malwarebytes` | Malwarebytes Endpoint Agent | Malwarebytes | epp | ✓ | | ✓ |

os.base.file.name: file

acl.name: acl
acl.title: Windows access control list for this file
acl.desc: Null on systems that do not use Windows security descriptors. Use it together with `files.find` to answer who may write to a set of paths, for example `files.find(from: "C:\\inetpub", type: "directory") { acl { ... } }`. On POSIX systems read `permissions` instead.

basename.name: basename
basename.title: Filename without path prefix of this file

content.name: content
content.title: Contents of this file

context.name: context
context.title: File context is a range of lines/columns in a file

dirname.name: dirname
dirname.title: Path to the folder containing this file

exists.name: exists
exists.title: Whether this file exists on the system

path.name: path
path.title: Location of the file on the system

size.name: size
size.title: Size of this file on disk in bytes

os.base.file.title: File on the system
os.base.file.desc: Single file referenced by absolute path. Surfaces the path itself, the basename and dirname, an `exists` flag, the `content` string, the file's size in bytes, an `empty` predicate, the owning `user` and `group` as references, and a structured `permissions` resource that explodes the POSIX mode into named user / group / other read / write / execute bits, the SUID / SGID / sticky bits, the `isFile` / `isDirectory` / `isSymlink` discriminators, and a printed mode string. The unit of file-level audits and the building block most config-file resources read through. Select a file by path, for example `file("/etc/ssh/sshd_config")`.

os.base.files.name: files

find.name: find
find.title: File search results
find.desc: Files discovered by a recursive filesystem walk rooted at `from`. Narrow the walk with `type` (file, directory, device, and so on), `regex` (path/name pattern), `permissions` (octal mode floor), `name` (filename glob), `depth` (maximum traversal depth), and `xdev` (whether to cross into other mounted filesystems). Resolves to the matching `[]file` list, so content, ownership, and permission checks can be layered on the result. For example `files.find(from: "/etc", type: "file", permissions: 0o002) { path }` finds every world-writable file under /etc.

os.base.files.title: File search and discovery namespace
os.base.files.desc: Empty namespace whose only purpose is to host `files.find`, so audits can write `files.find(...) {...}` to locate files on the asset rather than enumerating known paths.

os.base.firefox.name: firefox

addon.name: addon
addon.title: Firefox browser addon
addon.desc: Single addon installed in a Firefox-family profile, parsed from the profile's extensions.json. Beyond `name`, `version`, and `type`, the record exposes enablement state (`active`, `userDisabled`, `disabled`), where it came from (`sourceUri`, `location`), whether auto-update is on (`autoupdate`), and the combined API `permissions` and host origins it was granted, so you can audit addon trust and overreach per user.

addons.name: addons
addons.title: All installed Firefox addons across all profiles and users

policies.name: policies
policies.title: Firefox enterprise policy configuration
policies.desc:
Effective enterprise policy configuration for a managed Firefox installation — the settings an administrator deploys to lock the browser down (TLS floor, telemetry, private browsing, sanitize-on-shutdown, locked preferences, and so on). Firefox shows this state at `about:policies`; this resource resolves it off-host from the policy file and, on Windows, additionally from the Mozilla policy keys in the registry.

`params` holds the normalized policy set — the contents of the top-level "policies" object — in the same shape regardless of which platform or source it came from, so one check works everywhere. `inputs` exposes the unmerged sources for hosts where an operator needs to see what each one contributed on its own.

Precedence follows Firefox. On Windows the registry and the policy file are combined with the registry winning per top-level policy key, and the merge is shallow: if the registry sets a policy at all, the file's entire object for that policy is discarded rather than merged into. On Linux and macOS Firefox reads exactly one policy file — on Linux the administrator-owned `/etc/firefox/policies/policies.json` outranks the install prefix, and the files are never merged with each other. Flathub's Firefox ignores both and reads `policies/policies.json` in its `org.mozilla.firefox.systemconfig` extension (`/var/lib/flatpak/extension/...`, or a user's own `~/.local/share/flatpak/extension/...`, which replaces the system one for that user). Those locations are used when the flatpak is the only Firefox on the host; when a distribution Firefox is installed too, the resource reports the distribution Firefox.

A host with no enterprise policy anywhere is the normal unmanaged state, not an error: `configured` is false, `source` is empty, and `params` is null.

unreadableAddons.name: unreadableAddons
unreadableAddons.title: Number of addon records that could not be read
unreadableAddons.desc: Counts the entries skipped while decoding every profile's extensions.json, for example an entry holding a value of a type the record does not describe, plus one for each extensions.json and each user's home the scan was not permitted to read (another user's home on a non-root scan). Those are left out of addons rather than failing the whole list, so any value above zero means addons is an incomplete view of what is installed.

os.base.firefox.title: Firefox-family browsers
os.base.firefox.desc: Installed browser addons discovered across every user account and profile for Firefox and its derivatives (Firefox Developer Edition, Nightly, LibreWolf, Waterfox, Floorp, Zen, Tor Browser, and Mullvad Browser). Iterate `addons` to inventory extensions and themes, spot disabled or side-loaded addons, and review the API permissions and host origins each addon requests. Mozilla-shipped system addons, locales, and dictionaries are filtered out.

Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in

The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. provider.name: provider

os.base.group.name: group

members.name: members
members.title: Users who are members of this group

os.base.group.title: Group on the system
os.base.group.desc: Single local group: numeric GID (or SID on Windows), group name, and the `members` list of users in the group. Used to audit privileged-group membership (`sudo`, `wheel`, `docker`, `adm`, and so on) and to confirm only expected accounts are present.

os.base.haproxy.name: haproxy

config.name: config
config.title: HAProxy configuration
config.desc: Parsed haproxy.cfg, every other file haproxy loads with `-f` (read from the running haproxy process or the haproxy systemd service and its environment files; a directory loads its `*.cfg` files), and every file pulled in by `!include` / `!includeglob` directives (HAProxy 2.4+). Exposes each section as a dedicated resource, plus a raw view over every section for types that are not modeled. Pass `init(path: "...")` to point at a non-default config file.

version.name: version
version.title: HAProxy version string extracted from the haproxy binary (e.g., "2.8.4-1")

os.base.haproxy.title: HAProxy load balancer
os.base.haproxy.desc: HAProxy daemon version and configuration. The configuration covers the global section, defaults blocks, frontends, backends, listens, the servers behind each backend, and supporting sections (resolvers, userlists, peers).

os.base.idp.name: idp

activeDirectory.name: activeDirectory
activeDirectory.title: Active Directory domain membership, null when the device is not a member of a domain

entra.name: entra
entra.title: Microsoft Entra ID membership, null when the device has no Entra device identity

joined.name: joined
joined.title: Whether the device belongs to any recognized identity provider
joined.desc: True when the device belongs to at least one. False when every identity provider looked for on the platform was read and none has the device as a member. Null where no identity provider is read, and where Active Directory membership is looked for but cannot be read, such as a Linux scan without root, which cannot read sssd.conf, or a scan of a Windows disk image: no complete lookup happened there, so the device may well be a member.

os.base.idp.title: Identity provider this device belongs to
os.base.idp.desc: The identity providers the device is joined to, bound to, or registered with, alongside mdm for its management and edr for its endpoint protection. A device can belong to several at once (for example a hybrid join to Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID), so each one is its own field and is null when the device does not belong to it. Independent of MDM enrollment: a device can belong to an identity provider without being enrolled in an MDM service, and the other way round. Microsoft Entra ID is detected on Windows client editions, and Active Directory on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Others (for example FreeIPA, LDAP/Kerberos realms, or JumpCloud) can be added as fields later. This is the device's own identity, not the user-facing federation an `idp` resource describes in the SaaS providers.

auditHandler.title: <file-handler> or <syslog-handler> of a JBoss audit log

configDir.name: configDir

os.base.jboss.title: JBoss EAP / WildFly application server
os.base.jboss.desc:
Locates a JBoss installation through JBOSS_HOME and exposes the server configuration it holds: the management section (management interfaces, security realms, the audit log and access control), the network interfaces and socket bindings, the password vault, and the subsystems declared in each profile. Nothing here needs a running JVM or the management CLI, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Both operating modes are covered. In standalone mode `config` is the profile the server is actually started with — which is not always standalone.xml, since `--server-config` selects one of the four shipped profiles. In domain mode `config` is domain.xml and `host` is the host controller's host.xml, which is where a domain keeps its management interfaces and security realms.

Every nested collection (profiles, subsystems, interfaces, socket bindings, security realms, management interfaces, audit handlers, connectors, log handlers) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-realm server keeps working when a second realm is added.

Pass `init(home: "...")` to point at an installation the discovery does not find, and `init(configFile: "...")` to read a profile other than the active one.

os.base.kubelet.title: Kubernetes kubelet on this node

os.base.mariadb.name: mariadb

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MariaDB option files
conf.desc:
Options from the MariaDB server option file chain on disk, useful for auditing settings as they are written to the file before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the on-disk configuration and a running server. The `!include` and `!includedir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in contribute to `sections`, and option names are normalized so `-` and `_` are interchangeable, matching how the server treats them.

Options stay grouped as the server reads them. `sections` holds every option group and `serverOptions` merges the groups mariadbd reads: `[mysqld]`, `[server]`, `[mariadb]`, `[mariadbd]` (from 10.4), `[client-server]`, `[galera]` on a server built with wsrep (from 10.1, whether or not wsrep is on), and the version-suffixed groups for the installed server version, such as `[mariadb-11.4]` on 11.4, or `[mariadb-11]` from 11.8.7 and 12.3.2 on. That set is not an extension of MySQL's, because packaged fragments since 11.0 configure the server under `[mariadbd]` and ship no `[mysqld]` group at all. `galeraOptions` also breaks out `[galera]` on its own so cluster transport settings stay separable, and `clientOptions` merges the client groups, where a `password` option means credentials are stored in the file.

By default the option files are the ones the server reads: those named with `--defaults-file` or `--defaults-extra-file` on the command line of the running server or of its systemd unit, or else every default option file the installed server binary lists, in its order, including the server account's `~/.my.cnf`. Where the binary cannot be run, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. The resource returns nothing when the host runs MySQL rather than MariaDB, or runs no database server at all. The installed server binary decides, so option files that a client library ships (such as `[client-mariadb]` on a RHEL host running MySQL) do not. Pass an explicit path with `mariadb.conf("/etc/mysql/mariadb.cnf")` to parse a file regardless of which product it belongs to.

`serverOptions` applies the options on that command line over the files. A setting made at runtime with `SET GLOBAL` is not visible here, and an option nothing sets reads null rather than zero.

os.base.mariadb.title: MariaDB Server
os.base.mariadb.desc: MariaDB server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use mariadb.conf for the parsed option files, including option groups, server and client scope options, Galera cluster settings, TLS material, and the per-user option files under home directories.

enrolled.title: Whether the device is enrolled in an MDM service

intune.title: Intune details, null unless the device is enrolled in Microsoft Intune

method.title: How the device was enrolled, null when it is not enrolled
method.desc: automated for Apple Automated Device Enrollment or Windows Autopilot, policy for Windows Group Policy auto-enrollment, and user for an enrollment a user started.

serverUrl.title: URL of the MDM server, null when the device is not enrolled

vendor.title: MDM vendor recognized from the enrollment server
vendor.desc: One of intune, jamf, kandji, mosyle, workspaceone, simplemdm, addigy, hexnode, or jumpcloud. Null when the device is not enrolled or the server is not one of these.

os.base.mdm.title: Mobile device management enrollment
os.base.mdm.desc: MDM enrollment state for this asset on macOS and Windows. enrolled, vendor, and serverUrl answer the fleet-wide questions without a per-platform query, for example `mdm.enrolled && mdm.vendor == "intune"`, and method says how the device was enrolled. On any other platform enrolled is false.

os.base.memory.name: memory

available.name: available
available.title: Physical memory available for new allocations without paging, in bytes
available.desc: Free memory plus memory the system can reclaim at once, such as clean file cache. On Windows, the Memory\Available Bytes performance counter (free, zeroed, and standby pages). On Linux, MemAvailable, which kernels before 3.14 do not report. On macOS, free, file-backed, and purgeable pages. On FreeBSD, free and inactive pages. On NetBSD, free and cached file pages. On Solaris, the freemem page count.

commitLimit.name: commitLimit
commitLimit.title: Maximum committed virtual memory, in bytes
commitLimit.desc: On Windows, the Memory\Commit Limit performance counter: physical memory plus the current size of all paging files, rising if a paging file is allowed to grow. On Linux, CommitLimit, which the kernel enforces only with vm.overcommit_memory set to 2. On Solaris, the used plus available totals of swap -s, a limit Solaris always enforces. Null on macOS, FreeBSD, and NetBSD.

committed.name: committed
committed.title: Committed virtual memory, in bytes
committed.desc: Virtual memory the system has promised to back with physical memory or swap. On Windows, the Memory\Committed Bytes performance counter. On Linux, Committed_AS. On FreeBSD, vm.swap_reserved. On Solaris, the used total of swap -s (allocated plus reserved). Null on macOS and NetBSD.

total.name: total
total.title: Physical memory visible to the operating system, in bytes
total.desc: Installed memory minus what firmware and hardware reserve. On Windows, TotalVisibleMemorySize of Win32_OperatingSystem. On Linux, MemTotal in /proc/meminfo. On macOS, hw.memsize. On FreeBSD, hw.physmem. On NetBSD, hw.physmem64. On Solaris, the physmem page count.

os.base.memory.title: Physical and virtual memory of the running system
os.base.memory.desc: Installed physical memory, the physical memory still available, and the committed virtual memory against its commit limit, all in bytes and read in one snapshot. Used for operational inventory and for usage checks such as `memory.available * 100 / memory.total > 10` and `memory.committed * 100 / memory.commitLimit < 80`. Supported on Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, and Solaris. A value the platform does not keep reads as null: macOS and NetBSD have no commit accounting, and FreeBSD reports no commit limit. Asset types that do not run a live system, such as container images and disk snapshots, report the fields as not applicable.

os.base.mongodb.name: mongodb

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MongoDB configuration file
conf.desc:
Settings from mongod.conf as written on disk, useful for auditing the configuration before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the file and a running server. The file is a nested YAML document and has no include mechanism, so a parse reads exactly one file and `params` holds the whole tree as written. A file in the legacy `name = value` format the server also reads (`bind_ip`, `auth`, `sslMode`), as shipped in /etc/mongodb.conf by older Debian and Ubuntu packages, is translated into the same tree, and options with no YAML counterpart stay at the top level under their legacy names.

Convenience fields flatten the branches that carry security posture: network binding, TLS material, authentication and authorization, the setParameter block, the audit log, the system log, storage, process management, replication and sharding, and query profiling. Each reports the value the server would use, so an option left out of the file reads as the server default rather than as empty. That matters most where the default is permissive: javascriptEnabled and enableLocalhostAuthBypass are both on unless the file turns them off.

Options written under the pre-4.2 `net.ssl` tree are reported through the `tls` fields, since the server still accepts them as aliases. By default the file is located by probing the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu, RPM, and Homebrew installations; pass an explicit path with `mongodb.conf("/path/to/mongod.conf")`.

version.name: version
version.title: MongoDB version (e.g., "7.0.14")
version.desc: Read by running the server binary, so it reports nothing over a transport that cannot run commands. The configuration file mongodb.conf reads is unaffected, since it comes off the filesystem.

os.base.mongodb.title: MongoDB Server
os.base.mongodb.desc: MongoDB server version as reported by the installed server binary. Use mongodb.conf for the parsed configuration file, covering network binding, TLS material, authentication and authorization, auditing, encryption at rest, replication, and query profiling.

os.base.mysql.name: mysql

conf.name: conf
conf.title: MySQL option files
conf.desc:
Options from the MySQL server option file chain on disk, useful for auditing settings as they are written to the file before the server has been restarted, for example to detect drift between the on-disk configuration and a running server. The `!include` and `!includedir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in contribute to `sections`, and option names are normalized so `-` and `_` are interchangeable, matching how the server treats them.

Options stay grouped as the server reads them. `sections` holds every option group, `serverOptions` merges the groups mysqld itself reads (`[mysqld]`, `[server]`, the version-suffixed group for the installed server version, such as `[mysqld-8.0]` on 8.0, and `[mysql_cluster]` where the build reads it), and `clientOptions` merges `[client]`, `[mysql]`, and `[client-server]`, where a `password` option means credentials are stored in the file. Convenience views cover networking, TLS, authentication and password policy, filesystem privileges, logging, binary logging and replication, and encryption at rest. `userFiles` reports the per-user option files under home directories.

By default the option files are the ones the server reads: those named with `--defaults-file` or `--defaults-extra-file` on the command line of the running server or of its systemd unit, or else every default option file the installed server binary lists, in its order, including the server account's `~/.my.cnf`. Where the binary cannot be run, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. The resource returns nothing when the host runs MariaDB rather than MySQL, or runs no database server at all. The installed server binary decides, so option files that a client library ships (such as `[client-mariadb]` on a RHEL host running MySQL) do not. Pass an explicit path with `mysql.conf("/etc/mysql/my.cnf")` to parse a file regardless of which product it belongs to.

`serverOptions` applies the options on that command line over the files, and then the settings `SET PERSIST` wrote to `mysqld-auto.cnf` in the data directory, which the server applies last. A setting made at runtime with `SET GLOBAL` is not visible here, and an option nothing sets reads null rather than zero. An option belonging to a plugin or component the server does not load (`validate_password.*` without the component, `audit_log_*` on a server without the audit plugin, a `loose-` option the version does not know) is reported as written but has no effect on the server.

flavor.name: flavor
flavor.title: Distribution the server binary belongs to
flavor.desc: Either "mysql" or "percona". Empty when no server binary could be read. The binary name does not determine this: MariaDB also installs a binary called mysqld, and it is excluded here.

os.base.mysql.title: MySQL Server
os.base.mysql.desc: MySQL server version and distribution as reported by the installed server binary. Percona Server is reported here too, since it shares MySQL's option file layout and binary names. Use mysql.conf for the parsed option files, including option groups, server and client scope options, TLS material, and the per-user option files under home directories. MariaDB installations are covered by the mariadb resource.

os.base.network.name: network

ipv4.name: ipv4
ipv4.title: All IPv4 addresses detected on host interfaces

ipv6.name: ipv6
ipv6.title: All IPv6 addresses detected on host interfaces

primaryIPv4.name: primaryIPv4

os.base.package.name: package

arch.name: arch
arch.title: Architecture of this package (e.g., x86_64, arm64, noarch)
arch.desc: On macOS, the architecture of the application's executable: arm64, x86_64, or universal. Empty when it is not a Mach-O binary.

available.name: available
available.title: Latest version the package manager reports as available

cpes.name: cpes
cpes.title: Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) for the package

epoch.name: epoch
epoch.title: Epoch of this package (version-comparison tiebreaker; empty when unset)

files.name: files
files.title: Package-manager records that evidence this package
files.desc:
The file, directory, or database entry the package manager recorded this package in, usually a single record. It is provenance for the package entry, not the list of files the package installed on disk, so it does not answer which package owns a given path.

The record is per-backend:

dpkg      /var/lib/dpkg/info/<name>.list rpm       the rpm database directory, %{_dbpath} apk       /lib/apk/db/installed pacman    the local database entry for the package xbps      the package's own file list, which reports the installed paths pkg       the files the package installed, as `pkg query %Fp` lists them (FreeBSD, DragonFly BSD) macOS     the application bundle path Windows   the install location from the uninstall registry

Empty on package managers with no such record, among them flatpak, snap, homebrew, nix, gentoo, and the NetBSD and OpenBSD package tools.

format.name: format
format.title: Format of this package (e.g., rpm, deb)
format.desc: Empty for an abstract package synthesized from a tool install (see the `package` accessor on tool resources such as `cursor` or `claude.code`): it has no package-manager format and does not appear in `packages`.

installDate.name: installDate
installDate.title: Package install date
installDate.desc:
Time the installed version of the package was placed on this asset. Populated from %{INSTALLTIME} (rpm), the install-date field of the xbps database, the install time in the FreeBSD pkg database, the InstallDate column of the Windows Uninstall registry, and on dpkg from two sources in order. On macOS, the install time in the installer receipt of the package that installed the application: /var/db/receipts for pkg installers and the App Store, /Library/Apple/System/Library/Receipts for Apple packages from Software Update such as XProtect.

On dpkg, first the install, upgrade and `status installed` lines of /var/log/dpkg.log and its rotations. Second, for a package those logs do not mention, the modification time of its file list, /var/lib/dpkg/info/<name>.list or <name>:<arch>.list. dpkg rewrites that file when it unpacks the package, so it holds the time of the last install, upgrade or reinstall, as rpm's install time does. It also moves when a later package takes over one of the package's files, so it can be later than the install but not earlier.

On macOS it is null for applications no receipt claims: the ones that ship with the OS, and those copied into place from a disk image or archive. It is also null when the receipt names another version than the one installed, because the application updated itself after the package was installed. Null on backends with no install-time source at all (apk, pacman) and on any package no source covers.

installScope.name: installScope
installScope.title: Install scope of this package: "machine" or "user"
installScope.desc: "machine" for a package installed system-wide, visible to every user. "user" for one installed into a single user's own profile, which an unattended or SYSTEM-run scan cannot see without reading that user's registry hive directly. Populated for Windows packages read from the Uninstall registry key: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE is "machine"; HKCU or a specific user's hive under HKEY_USERS is "user". Windows appx packages, the .NET Framework runtime, and hotfixes are always "machine", since none of those sources carry per-user attribution. On macOS, "user" for an application inside a user's home directory. Empty on platforms with no such concept. Query-only: not carried into the SBOM output.

installUser.name: installUser
installUser.title: User owning a user-scope install
installUser.desc: Local user a package with `installScope` "user" belongs to: on Windows matched on the installing SID, on macOS on the home directory's owner. Null for machine-scope installs and accounts that no longer exist.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the package is installed

license.name: license
license.title: Package license
license.desc: SPDX license expression (or upstream-reported license string). Eagerly populated where the package manager has it inline (rpm %{LICENSE}, apk APKINDEX, pacman desc, FreeBSD pkg); fetched on demand for dpkg (parses /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/copyright). Empty when no source exists (e.g. Windows registry DisplayName). FreeBSD pkg records its own license names, joined with OR or AND as the package declares, for example `ART10 OR GPLv1+`.

macos.name: macos
macos.title: macOS application details; null for anything that is not a macOS application

name.name: name
name.title: Name of the package
name.desc: On macOS, the application's display name as Finder shows it.

origin.name: origin
origin.title: Package origin, may include version if available (optional)
origin.desc:
Set to "unknown" for an abstract package synthesized from a tool install (see the `package` accessor on tool resources): the installing source could not be identified. A known origin means the package is manager-tracked and listed in `packages`.

The exact meaning is per-backend, so compare it against values you know the backend emits rather than across platforms:

flatpak       the remote it was installed from, e.g. "flathub" freebsd       the ports origin path, e.g. "security/sudo" netbsd        PKGPATH macOS         how the bundle was obtained, as classified by Gatekeeper: "apple", "mac_app_store", "ios_app_store", "identified_developer", or "unknown"

On macOS this distinguishes App Store installs from everything else, which matters when choosing an update path: an App Store app cannot be upgraded with `brew upgrade`.

outdated.name: outdated
outdated.title: Whether a newer version than the installed one is available

pinned.name: pinned
pinned.title: Whether the package is held at its current version
pinned.desc:
True when the package manager is configured not to upgrade it: a dpkg or opkg hold, a dnf or yum versionlock, or a zypper lock. An outdated package that is pinned is a deliberate state rather than a missed patch, and it will not receive a security update until the pin is released.

Read from the package manager's own files, so it answers the same way on a running host, a container image and a mounted filesystem. Debian's apt preferences are priorities rather than holds and do not set this. False on package managers with no lock mechanism, where it means there is no such thing rather than not checked.

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL (purl) identifier for this package
purl.desc: On macOS, qualifiers present when known: `arch` (for now the host's architecture), `bundle-id`, `team-id`, `app-store=true`, `install-scope=user`.

status.name: status
status.title: Status of this package (e.g., if it is needed)

version.name: version
version.title: Currently installed version of the package

os.base.package.title: Installed package on the platform or OS
os.base.package.desc: Single package known to the asset's native package manager (rpm, deb, apk, pkg, msi, nuget, pacman, and so on). Surfaces the package name, description, currently-installed `version`, architecture, epoch, package format, install status, package URL, the CPE list mapping the package to NVD identifiers, the package origin, the latest `available` version known to the package manager, the `installed` and `outdated` flags, the file inventory the package contributed, and the package vendor. The unit of asset-level package audits and the join key for vulnerability correlation.

os.base.packages.name: packages
os.base.packages.title: All packages installed on the system
os.base.packages.desc: Collection of every `package` known to the asset's native package manager(s). The entry point for fleet-wide patch audits, banned-package checks, and inventory exports.

os.base.pkg.name: pkg

repo.name: repo
repo.title: FreeBSD pkg repository
repo.desc: A single repository pkg would use, named by the configuration block that declares it and merged across every file that redefines that name. `url` is where packages are fetched from, `enabled` reports whether pkg consults the repository, `mirrorType` how mirrors are resolved, and `priority` which repository wins when several offer the same package. The security-relevant field is `signatureType`: `none` means pkg installs from the repository without verifying a signature. `fingerprints` and `pubkey` carry the key material the other two schemes verify against.

os.base.pkg.title: FreeBSD pkg configuration
os.base.pkg.desc: FreeBSD package manager configuration. `repos` enumerates every repository pkg would use, read from `/etc/pkg/` and then `/usr/local/etc/pkg/repos/` and merged the way pkg merges them, so a later file redefining a repository by name overrides only the keys it sets. Audit repository trust from there: each `pkg.repo` reports the `signatureType` pkg verifies it with and the key material that verification reads.

os.base.podman.name: podman

apparmorEnabled.name: apparmorEnabled
apparmorEnabled.title: Whether AppArmor confinement is available to containers

cgroupManager.name: cgroupManager
cgroupManager.title: Cgroup manager driving resource limits (e.g., systemd, cgroupfs)

cgroupVersion.name: cgroupVersion
cgroupVersion.title: Cgroup hierarchy version in use (e.g., v1, v2)

container.name: container
container.title: Podman container
container.desc: Single container managed by Podman, selected by `id`. The privilege fields describe what the container can reach on the host: `privileged` disables nearly every confinement at once, `effectiveCapabilities` is the capability set the main process actually starts with, and `securityOptions` records where a seccomp, AppArmor, or SELinux profile was turned off. Prefer `effectiveCapabilities` and `boundingCapabilities` over `capAdd` and `capDrop` for an audit: the engine folds a dropped capability into the resulting set rather than echoing it back, so a dropped capability leaves `capDrop` empty while the effective set shrinks. `seccompProfile`, `apparmorProfile`, and `noNewPrivileges` report the process restrictions, the namespace modes (`networkMode`, `pidMode`, `ipcMode`, `utsMode`, `usernsMode`, `cgroupnsMode`) report which host namespaces it shares, and `mounts`, `devices`, and `ports` list what of the host is exposed inside it, for example `podman.containers.none(mounts.any(hostPath == /podman\.sock$/))` finds containers that control the Podman service.

image.name: image
image.title: Podman image
image.desc: Single image stored by Podman, selected by `id`. `names` holds every reference the image is tagged with and `repoDigests` the content-addressed references it was pulled by, which is what pins an image to an exact build rather than to a moving tag.

images.name: images
images.title: All images stored on the host

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the podman binary is present on the system

network.name: network
network.title: Podman network
network.desc: Network defined by Podman, selected by `name`. `internal` marks a network with no route to the outside, and `subnets` holds the address ranges containers on it receive.

networkBackend.name: networkBackend
networkBackend.title: Network backend in use (e.g., netavark, cni)

networks.name: networks
networks.title: All networks defined on the host

ociRuntime.name: ociRuntime
ociRuntime.title: OCI runtime that starts containers (e.g., crun, runc)

pod.name: pod
pod.title: Podman pod
pod.desc: Group of containers sharing namespaces, selected by `id`. Every pod runs an infrastructure container that owns the shared namespaces, reported by `infraContainer`, and the workload containers are reported by `containers`.

pods.name: pods
pods.title: All pods defined on the host

rootless.name: rootless
rootless.title: Whether the engine runs without root privileges
rootless.desc: A rootless engine maps container root to an unprivileged host account, so a container escape lands with far less authority than under a rootful engine.

seccompEnabled.name: seccompEnabled
seccompEnabled.title: Whether seccomp filtering is available to containers

seccompProfilePath.name: seccompProfilePath
seccompProfilePath.title: Path of the default seccomp profile applied to containers

selinuxEnabled.name: selinuxEnabled
selinuxEnabled.title: Whether SELinux confinement is available to containers

storageDriver.name: storageDriver
storageDriver.title: Storage driver backing container filesystems (e.g., overlay, vfs)

version.name: version
version.title: Podman release reported by the engine (e.g., 5.3.1)

volume.name: volume
volume.title: Podman volume
volume.desc: Storage volume defined by Podman, selected by `name`. `mountpoint` is the host path backing the volume, which is what a container writing to the volume ultimately writes to.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: All volumes defined on the host

os.base.podman.title: Podman container engine
os.base.podman.desc: Workloads managed by Podman, together with the engine settings that apply to all of them. `rootless` reports whether the engine runs without root, which changes what a container escape is worth, and `seccompEnabled`, `apparmorEnabled`, and `selinuxEnabled` report which confinement mechanisms the host makes available. `containers`, `images`, `pods`, `volumes`, and `networks` inventory the workloads themselves. On RedHat-family hosts Podman is the default engine and Docker is often absent, so this is where those workloads are found.

os.base.port.name: port

port.name: port
port.title: Port number

tls.name: tls

Central to exposure audits, for example finding listening ports bound to a non-loopback address.

file.name: file

path.name: path
path.title: Path to the private key file
path.desc: Deprecated in favor of the `file` field.

publicKeyAlgorithm.name: publicKeyAlgorithm
publicKeyAlgorithm.title: Public key algorithm of the key material (e.g., RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, DSA)

os.base.privatekey.title: Private key on disk
os.base.privatekey.desc: PEM-encoded private key file: the `file` reference, the raw PEM `pem` payload, and an `encrypted` flag indicating whether the key is passphrase-protected. `publicKeyAlgorithm` and `publicKeyBits` describe the key material. Used to inventory SSH or service-account keys discovered on the asset and to flag unencrypted private keys stored in user home directories.

base.title: Instance directory (CATALINA_BASE); equals home in a single-instance install

connector.name: connector
connector.title: Tomcat <Connector> element
connector.desc: Boolean and numeric fields carry Tomcat's documented default when the attribute is absent, so they describe the connector's effective behavior. Use `params` to tell an absent attribute from an explicitly declared one.

context.name: context
context.title: Parsed conf/context.xml, the global context defaults; null when absent

home.name: home
home.title: Installation directory (CATALINA_HOME); empty when no installation is found

host.name: host
host.title: Tomcat <Host> element
host.desc: Boolean fields carry Tomcat's documented default when the attribute is absent — autoDeploy, deployOnStartup, deployXML and unpackWARs all default to true. Use `params` to tell an absent attribute from a declared one.

realm.name: realm
realm.title: Tomcat <Realm> element
realm.desc: Realms nest: a LockOutRealm wraps the realm that actually authenticates, so `realms` walks the inner realms instead of leaving them unreachable.

server.name: server
server.title: Parsed conf/server.xml; null when the installation has none

valve.name: valve
valve.title: Tomcat <Valve> element, wherever it is declared (Engine, Host or Context)

version.name: version
version.title: Tomcat version (e.g., "10.1.34"); empty when it cannot be read from disk

webXml.name: webXml
webXml.title: Parsed conf/web.xml, the global deployment descriptor; null when absent

webapp.name: webapp
webapp.title: Application deployed under a Tomcat Host's appBase

webapps.name: webapps
webapps.title: Applications deployed under each Host's appBase (exploded directories)

webxml.name: webxml
webxml.title: Tomcat deployment descriptor (conf/web.xml or an application's WEB-INF/web.xml)
webxml.desc: Nested XML is exposed as dicts whose keys are the camelCase spelling of the element name, so `<transport-guarantee>` reads as `transportGuarantee`.

os.base.tomcat.title: Apache Tomcat
os.base.tomcat.desc:
Locates a Tomcat installation through CATALINA_HOME / CATALINA_BASE and exposes its on-disk configuration: server.xml, the global web.xml and context.xml, catalina.properties, logging.properties, tomcat-users.xml, and the applications deployed under each Host's appBase. Nothing here needs a running JVM, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Every nested collection (services, connectors, engines, hosts, valves, realms, listeners, contexts, users, webapps) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-Connector server keeps working when a second Connector is added.

Pass `init(home: "...", base: "...")` to point at a non-default layout.

os.base.trae.title: Trae AI assistant (ByteDance) instance

Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://trae.ai/

os.base.user.name: user

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether the account is enabled (not locked or disabled)

hasLoginShell.name: hasLoginShell
hasLoginShell.title: Whether the account's shell starts an interactive session
hasLoginShell.desc: False when shell is `nologin`, `false`, or `true` in /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, or /usr/sbin (so both /sbin/nologin and /usr/sbin/nologin, and both /bin/false and /usr/bin/false, count). True for every other shell, including an empty one, which means /bin/sh. /etc/shells is not consulted: login and sshd do not read it, and some distributions list /bin/false in it. Null on Windows.

loggedIn.name: loggedIn
loggedIn.title: Whether the user currently has an active login session

ntuserDat.name: ntuserDat
ntuserDat.title: Path to this user's NTUSER.DAT registry hive file (Windows)
ntuserDat.desc: The per-user registry hive on disk, located at `<home>\NTUSER.DAT`. Pass it together with `sid` to `registrykey`/`registrykey.property` to read a user's HKCU settings even when their hive is not loaded, for example a SYSTEM scan running with no interactive session. Empty on non-Windows platforms or when the home directory is unknown.

shell.name: shell
shell.title: Login shell configured for the user (e.g., /bin/bash, /usr/sbin/nologin)

sshkeys.name: sshkeys
sshkeys.title: Private SSH keys discovered in the user's home directory

system.name: system
system.title: Whether this is a system account rather than an interactive user
system.desc: On Linux, true when uid is below UID_MIN, or above UID_MAX and at most 65535 outside the systemd-homed range 60001 to 60513. The upper band holds `nobody` (65534), Debian's static allocations (60000 to 64999) and systemd dynamic service users; uids above 65535 are container and directory-service ranges and count as regular users. UID_MIN and UID_MAX come from /etc/login.defs (or /usr/etc/login.defs when /etc has none), defaulting to 1000 and 60000 when the file is absent or a value is unset or unparsable. Root (uid 0) counts as a system account. On macOS, true when uid is below 500, which covers root, the `_`-prefixed service accounts, and `nobody` (-2). On FreeBSD, true when uid is below minuid, or above maxuid and at most 65535, which covers root, the service accounts and `nobody` (65534). minuid and maxuid come from /etc/pw.conf, defaulting to 1000 and 32000 like pw(8) when the file is absent or a value is unset or unparsable. Null on Windows and on other Unix platforms, which have no common convention. Combine with hasLoginShell to find service accounts that can log in, for example `users.where(system && name != "root").none(hasLoginShell)`.

os.base.user.title: User account on the system
os.base.user.desc: Single local user account: numeric UID and primary GID (Windows SID where applicable), name, home directory, configured login shell, and an `enabled` flag. Surfaces the primary `group` reference, the `authorizedkeys` resource that parses the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, the SSH private keys discovered in the user's home, and a `loggedIn` predicate that reflects whether the user currently has an active session. Used for identity audits, dormant-account hygiene, and SSH-key inventories.

paths.name: paths

os.base.vscode.title: Visual Studio Code (and forks)

Iterate `extensions` to inventory what is installed per editor, review publishers and versions, and identify untrusted or outdated extensions. `paths` lists the extension directories that were searched.

os.base.vulnmgmt.title: Asset vulnerability assessment

Exposes every CVE affecting the asset, every vendor advisory that mentions one of those CVEs, the affected packages with their currently-installed and patched-available versions, the timestamp of the last assessment run, and the rolled-up CVSS statistics: the surface used to score asset risk and to drive patch-status policies.

os.base.windsurf.name: windsurf

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Windsurf configuration directory

mcpServer.name: mcpServer
mcpServer.title: Windsurf MCP server configuration
mcpServer.desc: Model Context Protocol server Windsurf is configured to use. Stdio servers launch a local command with args; sse servers connect to a url. `type` reports the transport and hasEnv whether environment variables (often holding API keys or tokens) are configured for the server.

mcpServers.name: mcpServers
mcpServers.title: MCP servers the editor connects to

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

repo.name: repo

Exposes the origin remote `url`, the parsed `host` (for example github.com) and `name` (org/repo slug), the checked-out `branch`, all configured `remotes`, and the working-tree root `path`. os.base.winget.name: winget

architecture.name: architecture
architecture.title: Processor architecture of the App Installer package, for example x64 or arm64

enabledByPolicy.name: enabledByPolicy
enabledByPolicy.title: Whether Group Policy allows winget to run
enabledByPolicy.desc: False when the EnableAppInstaller or EnableWindowsPackageManagerCommandLineInterfaces policy is set to disabled.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether a winget.exe the machine can run is present

missingDependencies.name: missingDependencies
missingDependencies.title: Framework packages App Installer requires that are not present
missingDependencies.desc: Each entry names a PackageDependency from the package manifest that no package on the machine satisfies with the same architecture (or neutral) and at least the required version, as `<name> >= <minVersion>`. Null when winget is not installed or its manifest cannot be read.

packageFullName.name: packageFullName
packageFullName.title: Full name of the App Installer package

path.name: path
path.title: Path to winget.exe, null when winget is not installed

source.name: source
source.title: winget package source

sources.name: sources
sources.title: Package sources winget uses for the SYSTEM account
sources.desc: The defaults (msstore, winget, winget-font) unless Group Policy disables them, sources added by Group Policy, and sources added or removed for the SYSTEM account, filtered by the allowed-sources policy.

systemUsable.name: systemUsable
systemUsable.title: Whether winget can run as the SYSTEM account
systemUsable.desc: True when winget.exe is present for an architecture the machine runs, every framework package the manifest requires is present, and Group Policy does not disable winget. False whenever Group Policy disables winget. Otherwise null when the package manifest cannot be read. This is a read-only check: winget is not started.

version.name: version
version.title: Version of winget.exe
version.desc: The product version of winget.exe, which is what `winget --version` reports, for example 1.29.380.0. It can be higher than the App Installer package version in packageFullName. When the file version cannot be read, the package version is reported. Null when winget is not installed.

os.base.winget.title: Windows Package Manager (winget)
os.base.winget.desc: Whether winget is installed on a Windows host and whether it can run as the SYSTEM account, where it often cannot. installed, version, and path come from the Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller package that ships winget.exe, found in the AppX package repository and the WindowsApps folder without running winget. missingDependencies lists the framework packages its manifest requires that the machine does not have, and systemUsable combines these checks, for example `winget.installed && winget.systemUsable`. sources lists the package sources winget uses for the SYSTEM account. On any other platform installed and systemUsable are false.

os.base.yum.name: yum

config.name: config
config.title: Yum/DNF global configuration
config.desc: System-wide package manager configuration: the `[main]` section of `/etc/yum.conf`, or `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf` on dnf-based systems. Use `gpgcheck` and `localPkgGpgcheck` to assert that package signature verification is enforced for every repository and for locally installed packages, a core CIS supply-chain control; `repoGpgcheck` extends that to repository metadata. The bool accessors report the value the package manager uses: the directive in the file, on dnf 5 applied over the drop-in files in `/usr/share/dnf5/libdnf.conf.d` and `/etc/dnf/libdnf5.conf.d` (on dnf 5 `gpgcheck` reads `pkg_gpgcheck`, the option it is another name for), and the package manager's default when no file sets it. `params` exposes every `[main]` directive of the file as a raw string map for settings without a dedicated accessor. Select an alternate file with `yum.config(path: "...")`; drop-in files do not apply to it. Where the file does not exist and no yum or dnf is installed, or a file named with `path` does not exist, `content`, `params` and the bool fields are null.

repo.name: repo
repo.title: Yum repository
repo.desc: A single configured yum/dnf repository as reported by `yum -v repolist all`, or `dnf5 repo info --all` on dnf 5 hosts such as Fedora 41+ and Amazon Linux 2027: its `id`, human-readable `name`, `status`, `baseurl` list, expiry indicator, backing configuration `file`, `revision`, package count, size, mirror list, and whether it is currently `enabled`. Select a repository by ID, for example `yum.repo(id: "baseos")`.

repos.name: repos
repos.title: List of all configured Yum repositories

vars.name: vars
vars.title: Variables available for substitution in yum/dnf repository configuration
vars.desc: The built-in `arch`, `basearch`, and `releasever` as dnf computes them, plus the custom variables defined on disk: one file per variable in `/etc/yum/vars` and `/etc/dnf/vars` (dnf 4), or `/usr/share/dnf5/vars.d` and `/etc/dnf/vars` (dnf 5), named after the file with the file's first line as the value. A variable in `/etc/dnf/vars` overrides one of the same name in the other directory, and a custom variable overrides a built-in one, the same way dnf resolves them. The built-in variables come from dnf's Python API, yum's on RHEL 7 and older, or `dnf5 --dump-variables`, and are missing where none of these can run, such as image scans.

os.base.yum.title: Yum/DNF package manager
os.base.yum.desc: Configuration of the yum/dnf package manager on RedHat-family systems. `vars` exposes the variables defined across `/etc/yum.conf` and the `.repo` files (for example `$releasever` and `$basearch`) and `repos` lists every configured repository as `yum.repo` entries.

repos.name: repos
repos.title: Git repositories backing the opened workspaces

runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. settings.name: settings
settings.title: Full settings dictionary parsed from the Zed configuration

os.base.zed.title: Zed editor instance
os.base.zed.desc: Zed code editor installed on the host. Queryable through it are the workspace settings dictionary and the names of installed extensions, along with the package that installed the editor and the runtime it executes in. URL: https://zed.dev/

os.date.name: os.date
os.date.title: Operating system date and timezone information
os.date.desc: Current system clock time and the configured timezone string (e.g., "America/New_York", "UTC"). Used to verify that clocks are synchronized and that the correct timezone is set.

os.linux.name: os.linux

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

cgroups.name: cgroups
cgroups.title: Linux control groups (cgroup v2)
cgroups.desc: cgroup hierarchy, available controllers, and the version of cgroups in use. Modern Linux uses cgroup v2 (a single unified hierarchy at /sys/fs/cgroup); v1 hosts and hybrid setups are detected and reported via `version`, but per-controller hierarchies are not modeled. Iterate `list` to query every cgroup on the host, or walk down from `root` to traverse the hierarchy.

limits.name: limits
limits.title: PAM resource limits configuration (limits.conf)
limits.desc: Soft and hard caps on processes, open files, memory, and other per-user resources, parsed from /etc/security/limits.conf and every .conf file under /etc/security/limits.d. Iterate `entries` to audit for missing or overly permissive limits (e.g. unrestricted core dumps or nofile).

logindefs.name: logindefs
logindefs.title: Shadow password suite (login.defs) configuration
logindefs.desc: Password aging, UID/GID ranges, and login policy parameters parsed from /etc/login.defs. The params map exposes settings such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, UMASK, and ENCRYPT_METHOD, which drive account and password-policy audits. Point at an alternate file with the `path` argument.

lsblk.name: lsblk
lsblk.title: Unix block devices (lsblk)
lsblk.desc: Block devices reported by `lsblk`, each carrying its device name, filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount points. Iterate to audit disk layout, filesystem labels, and mount configuration.

luks.name: luks
luks.title: LUKS-encrypted volumes on the host
luks.desc: Block devices that carry a LUKS header, exposing each volume's on-disk format version, cipher, key-derivation parameters, and every keyslot. Both LUKS1 and LUKS2 headers are reported through the same schema; the `version` field on each volume distinguishes them and version-specific fields (label, subsystem, and tokens for LUKS2; AF-splitter stripes for LUKS1) are populated only where they apply.

lvm.name: lvm
lvm.title: Linux Logical Volume Manager
lvm.desc: LVM block-device storage on Linux: physical volumes initialized for LVM, volume groups that aggregate them, and the logical volumes carved out of those groups. Iterate `physicalVolumes`, `volumeGroups`, and `logicalVolumes` to audit LVM layout, free capacity, thin-pool usage, and snapshot relationships.

mdadm.name: mdadm
mdadm.title: Linux software RAID arrays (mdadm)
mdadm.desc: Software RAID arrays managed by mdadm, each with its RAID level, health state, device counts, and resync progress. Iterate `arrays` to audit redundancy and spot degraded or rebuilding arrays. Use `arrays.where(state == "degraded")` to find arrays that have lost a member.

modprobe.name: modprobe
modprobe.title: Kernel module configuration (modprobe.d)
modprobe.desc: Install, remove, blacklist, options, alias, and softdep directives parsed from the modprobe configuration files. Use blacklists to verify that risky kernel modules are prevented from loading and options to audit module parameters. Point at an alternate config with the `path` argument.

ovs.name: ovs
ovs.title: Open vSwitch
ovs.desc: Software switch configured through the Open vSwitch database on this host. The bridges, ports, and interfaces fields report the switch as it is running now, joined into the topology the datapath uses, which is the dataplane a CNI plugin builds and Kubernetes only records as intent. Empty on hosts where ovs-vsctl is not installed or the database is not reachable.

polkit.name: polkit
polkit.title: Polkit authorization framework
polkit.desc: System-wide polkit (formerly PolicyKit) authorization state: the `actions` that privileged operations are registered under, the JavaScript `rules` that decide who may invoke them, the legacy local-authority grants in `localAuthorityRules`, and the `adminIdentities` the local authority treats as administrators. Polkit governs whether an unprivileged session may restart a unit, mount a disk, or install a package, so an over-broad grant is a local privilege escalation path. Read `version` before drawing conclusions: polkit 0.106 and later evaluate the JavaScript rules and ignore `.pkla` files, while earlier releases do the reverse.

selinux.name: selinux
selinux.title: SELinux mandatory access control
selinux.desc: SELinux enforcement mode, configured mode, active policy type, tunable booleans, and loaded policy modules. The runtime `mode` (from getenforce or /sys/fs/selinux on a running system, from /etc/selinux/config in a disk or image scan) may differ from `configMode`, which is what persists across reboot; compare the two to catch a system left permissive at runtime or booted with SELinux disabled.

shadow.name: shadow
shadow.title: Shadow password file (/etc/shadow)
shadow.desc: Per-user password aging, expiration, and lock state parsed from `/etc/shadow`, one `shadow.entry` per account. Audit password policy compliance and find accounts with no expiry, weak aging settings, or locked/disabled passwords.

sriov.name: sriov
sriov.title: SR-IOV network devices
sriov.desc: Single-root I/O virtualization state of the host's network hardware. The physicalFunctions field lists every SR-IOV capable interface with the number of virtual functions it has enabled against the number it supports, and virtualFunctions flattens every virtual function across all of them. This is the realised hardware inventory, so it shows the PCI address, the bound driver, and the per-device link settings that a Kubernetes device plugin only reports as an aggregate count. Empty on hosts with no SR-IOV capable interface.

os.linux.title: Operating system information for Linux platforms
os.linux.desc: Extends `os.unix` (and through it, `os.base`) with Linux-only surfaces: the supported packet-filter stacks (`iptables`, `ip6tables`, `nftables`, `ufw`, `firewalld`), the `/etc/fstab` mount table, and the AppArmor mandatory-access-control namespace. Use it to write Linux-specific audits without reaching out to global resource handles.

os.linux.cgroups.name: cgroups

controllers.name: controllers
controllers.title: Controllers available on the host (e.g., memory, cpu, io, pids)

list.name: list
list.title: Flat list of every cgroup on the host

version.name: version
version.title: cgroup version in use: 2 (unified), 1 (legacy v1 only), or 0 if cgroups are not available

os.linux.cgroups.title: Linux control groups (cgroup v2)
os.linux.cgroups.desc: cgroup hierarchy, available controllers, and the version of cgroups in use. Modern Linux uses cgroup v2 (a single unified hierarchy at /sys/fs/cgroup); v1 hosts and hybrid setups are detected and reported via `version`, but per-controller hierarchies are not modeled. Iterate `list` to query every cgroup on the host, or walk down from `root` to traverse the hierarchy.

os.linux.limits.name: limits

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed limits entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Resource limit entry
entry.desc: Single line from a limits configuration file, giving one domain / type / item / value tuple (e.g. `* hard core 0`).

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the limits configuration

os.linux.limits.title: PAM resource limits configuration (limits.conf)
os.linux.limits.desc: Soft and hard caps on processes, open files, memory, and other per-user resources, parsed from /etc/security/limits.conf and every .conf file under /etc/security/limits.d. Iterate `entries` to audit for missing or overly permissive limits (e.g. unrestricted core dumps or nofile).

os.linux.logindefs.name: logindefs

content.name: content
content.title: Content of the configuration file

file.name: file
file.title: Current configuration file for resource

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed login.defs parameters as a name/value map (e.g. PASS_MAX_DAYS, UMASK, ENCRYPT_METHOD)

os.linux.logindefs.title: Shadow password suite (login.defs) configuration
os.linux.logindefs.desc: Password aging, UID/GID ranges, and login policy parameters parsed from /etc/login.defs. The params map exposes settings such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, UMASK, and ENCRYPT_METHOD, which drive account and password-policy audits. Point at an alternate file with the `path` argument.

os.linux.lsblk.name: lsblk

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Unix block device
entry.desc: Single block device reported by `lsblk`: its device `name`, filesystem type (`fstype`), `label`, UUID, `mountpoints` list, and device `type`. `parents` and `children` walk the device stack (disk, partition, dm-crypt mapping, LVM volume), and `encrypted` reports whether the data on the device passes through a dm-crypt mapping. Filter to audit disk layout and mount configuration, e.g. `lsblk.where(mountpoints.contains("/"))`, or reach the device behind a mount with `mount.point(path: "/").blockDevice`.

os.linux.lsblk.title: Unix block devices (lsblk)
os.linux.lsblk.desc: Block devices reported by `lsblk`, each carrying its device name, filesystem type, label, UUID, and mount points. Iterate to audit disk layout, filesystem labels, and mount configuration.

os.linux.luks.name: luks

keyslot.name: keyslot
keyslot.title: LUKS keyslot
keyslot.desc: One keyslot in a LUKS header: its index, state, and the key-derivation parameters used to wrap the master key. Audit for weak KDFs, low iteration or memory costs, and unexpectedly large numbers of active slots (each active slot is a passphrase that can unlock the volume).

volume.name: volume
volume.title: LUKS-encrypted block device
volume.desc: Single LUKS-formatted block device: its header version, label, master-key size and offset, cipher, and keyslots. Select a volume by its `uuid` (e.g., `luks.volumes.where(uuid == "fd44f17a-...")`) or by the underlying block device's `name`.

volumes.name: volumes
volumes.title: LUKS-formatted block devices on the host

os.linux.luks.title: LUKS-encrypted volumes on the host
os.linux.luks.desc: Block devices that carry a LUKS header, exposing each volume's on-disk format version, cipher, key-derivation parameters, and every keyslot. Both LUKS1 and LUKS2 headers are reported through the same schema; the `version` field on each volume distinguishes them and version-specific fields (label, subsystem, and tokens for LUKS2; AF-splitter stripes for LUKS1) are populated only where they apply.

os.linux.lvm.name: lvm

logicalVolume.name: logicalVolume
logicalVolume.title: LVM logical volume
logicalVolume.desc: Single LVM logical volume: `name`, full device `path`, `uuid`, parent volume group (`volumeGroupName`), attribute flags, size in bytes, snapshot `origin`, and thin-pool data usage. For thin volumes, `poolName` is set; for snapshots, `origin` is the source LV name.

logicalVolumes.name: logicalVolumes
logicalVolumes.title: Logical volumes across all volume groups

physicalVolume.name: physicalVolume
physicalVolume.title: LVM physical volume
physicalVolume.desc: Single block device initialized as an LVM physical volume: device path (`name`), `uuid`, the volume group it belongs to (`volumeGroupName`, empty if unassigned), on-disk `format`, attribute flags, and total/free byte counts.

volumeGroup.name: volumeGroup
volumeGroup.title: LVM volume group
volumeGroup.desc: Single LVM volume group: `name`, `uuid`, attribute flags, total and free byte counts, and the counts of physical volumes, logical volumes, and snapshots it contains. Useful for auditing capacity headroom and group-level policy.

os.linux.lvm.title: Linux Logical Volume Manager
os.linux.lvm.desc: LVM block-device storage on Linux: physical volumes initialized for LVM, volume groups that aggregate them, and the logical volumes carved out of those groups. Iterate `physicalVolumes`, `volumeGroups`, and `logicalVolumes` to audit LVM layout, free capacity, thin-pool usage, and snapshot relationships.

os.linux.mdadm.name: mdadm

array.name: array
array.title: Linux software RAID array
array.desc: Single mdadm array. `level` is the RAID level, `state` is its health, and the device counts (`activeDevices`, `workingDevices`, `failedDevices`, `spareDevices`) together with `resyncProgress` reveal whether the array is healthy, degraded, or rebuilding. `devices` lists the member block devices.

arrays.name: arrays
arrays.title: List of all discovered RAID arrays

device.name: device
device.title: Member device in a software RAID array
device.desc: Single member of an mdadm array. `name` is the block device path, `role` is its slot number in the array layout, and `state` reports its condition (e.g. "active sync", "spare", "faulty").

os.linux.mdadm.title: Linux software RAID arrays (mdadm)
os.linux.mdadm.desc: Software RAID arrays managed by mdadm, each with its RAID level, health state, device counts, and resync progress. Iterate `arrays` to audit redundancy and spot degraded or rebuilding arrays. Use `arrays.where(state == "degraded")` to find arrays that have lost a member.

os.linux.modprobe.name: modprobe

alias.name: alias
alias.title: Kernel module alias directive
alias.desc: A single `alias` line from a modprobe configuration file mapping an alias name or wildcard pattern to a target module. The kernel resolves the alias to `module` when the pattern is requested. A common hardening technique points a module's alias at a no-op (for example aliasing an unused network protocol to `off`) to block on-demand loading.

blacklist.name: blacklist
blacklist.title: Kernel module blacklist directive
blacklist.desc: A single `blacklist` line from a modprobe configuration file that stops a kernel module from being selected automatically. Auditing these confirms unwanted modules (for example `usb-storage`, `cramfs`, or unused filesystem and protocol drivers) are disabled per CIS hardening guidance. `module` is the blacklisted module name and `file`/`lineNumber` locate the declaration.

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the modprobe configuration

install.name: install
install.title: Install directive for module loading
install.desc: One `install` directive from modprobe.d: the module it applies to and the command run in place of the default insmod. A blacklist technique when the command is `/bin/true` or `/bin/false`.

installs.name: installs
installs.title: Install directives (custom commands for loading modules)

option.name: option
option.title: Kernel module options directive
option.desc: A single `options` line from a modprobe configuration file that sets load-time parameters for a kernel module. `parameters` is the raw argument string and `params` parses it into key/value pairs. Used to verify security-relevant module settings, for example that a driver is loaded with a hardened option.

remove.name: remove
remove.title: Remove directive for module unloading
remove.desc: One `remove` directive from modprobe.d: the module it applies to and the command run in place of the default rmmod.

removes.name: removes
removes.title: Remove directives (custom commands for unloading modules)

softdep.name: softdep
softdep.title: Kernel module soft dependency directive
softdep.desc: A single `softdep` line from a modprobe configuration file declaring modules to load before (`pre`) and after (`post`) a given module. Soft dependencies are advisory, so a missing dependency does not block the module from loading.

os.linux.modprobe.title: Kernel module configuration (modprobe.d)
os.linux.modprobe.desc: Install, remove, blacklist, options, alias, and softdep directives parsed from the modprobe configuration files. Use blacklists to verify that risky kernel modules are prevented from loading and options to audit module parameters. Point at an alternate config with the `path` argument.

os.linux.ovs.name: ovs

bridge.name: bridge
bridge.title: Open vSwitch bridge
bridge.desc: One bridge of the local switch, selected by name. The failMode field decides what the bridge does when it loses its controller: `secure` keeps the installed flows and forwards nothing new, `standalone` falls back to acting as a learning switch, which forwards traffic no policy authorised. The datapathType, protocols, stpEnabled, and rstpEnabled fields report how the bridge switches, and externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin or the operator wrote. The ports field returns the ports attached to the bridge.

interface.name: interface
interface.title: Open vSwitch interface
interface.desc: One interface of a port, selected by name. The type field reports how the interface reaches the network: an empty type is a system device, `internal` is the bridge's own device, and `vxlan`, `geneve`, or `gre` is a tunnel whose remote end is in options. The adminState and linkState fields report whether the interface is up, and error carries the reason the switch could not open the device, which is how a misconfigured attachment shows up. externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin wrote, which is what ties the interface back to a pod.

port.name: port
port.title: Open vSwitch port
port.desc: One port of a bridge, selected by name. The vlanMode and vlanTag fields report how the port treats VLAN tags: an access port carries a single tag, a trunk port carries the VLANs listed in trunks, and a port with neither carries every VLAN the bridge sees. tagged is false when no tag is set, so an untagged port is not read as VLAN 0. The interfaces field returns the interfaces the port is built from, which is more than one for a bond.

version.name: version
version.title: Open vSwitch version reported by ovs-vsctl

os.linux.ovs.title: Open vSwitch
os.linux.ovs.desc: Software switch configured through the Open vSwitch database on this host. The bridges, ports, and interfaces fields report the switch as it is running now, joined into the topology the datapath uses, which is the dataplane a CNI plugin builds and Kubernetes only records as intent. Empty on hosts where ovs-vsctl is not installed or the database is not reachable.

os.linux.polkit.name: polkit

action.name: action
action.title: Polkit action
action.desc: Single privileged operation polkit can gate, parsed from a `.policy` file in the action directories. `id` is the reverse-DNS action name an application checks (for example `org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units`), and the three `allow` fields hold the implicit authorization that applies when no rule overrides it. `allowAny` is the weakest of the three because it covers subjects with no local seat, including remote sessions, so an action with `allowAny == "yes"` needs no authentication from anyone who can reach the D-Bus interface.

actions.name: actions
actions.title: Actions registered in the polkit action directories

adminIdentities.name: adminIdentities
adminIdentities.title: Identities the local authority treats as administrators
adminIdentities.desc: AdminIdentities from /etc/polkit-1/localauthority.conf.d, for example `unix-group:sudo` or `unix-user:root`. Honored only by polkit 0.105 and earlier. On newer releases administrator selection moves into a rule that calls polkit.addAdminRule, which `rules` reports through `adminRule`.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether polkit is present on the system
installed.desc: True when the polkit daemon (polkitd) or its pkaction or pkexec tool is found. Action and rule directories alone do not count, since systemd and other packages ship files into them without polkit. Use it to guard polkit audits on systems that ship no polkit at all, such as minimal cloud images and container bases.

localAuthorityRule.name: localAuthorityRule
localAuthorityRule.title: Local-authority authorization grant (.pkla)
localAuthorityRule.desc: Single section from a `.pkla` file, the ini-format grant mechanism used by polkit 0.105 and earlier. `identities` lists the users or groups the grant applies to and `actions` the action patterns it covers, while the three `result` fields carry the authorization it produces. Higher-numbered directories override lower-numbered ones, and a grant of `resultAny == "yes"` to a broad group such as `unix-group:users` hands that group the action with no authentication. Ignored outright by polkit 0.106 and later, so read `polkit.version` alongside it.

localAuthorityRules.name: localAuthorityRules
localAuthorityRules.title: Grants from the legacy local-authority .pkla files

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Polkit JavaScript authorization rule file
rule.desc: Single `.rules` file from the polkit rule directories. Polkit evaluates these files in lexicographic order by filename and stops at the first rule returning a result other than NOT_HANDLED, so `order` decides which file wins: a file sorting ahead of the distribution defaults overrides them. `file` carries the path, mode, and ownership, which is what a check for a rule file writable by a non-root account reads. Rule bodies are JavaScript and are not evaluated here. `actionIds` and `results` report the identifiers and result values appearing in the body, so an audit can narrow down which files are worth reading.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: JavaScript authorization rules, in the order polkit evaluates them

version.name: version
version.title: Polkit release reported by pkaction
version.desc: For example `0.105` on older distributions or `124` on current ones. Requires command execution, so it is null on backends that expose only a filesystem, such as an image scan.

os.linux.polkit.title: Polkit authorization framework
os.linux.polkit.desc: System-wide polkit (formerly PolicyKit) authorization state: the `actions` that privileged operations are registered under, the JavaScript `rules` that decide who may invoke them, the legacy local-authority grants in `localAuthorityRules`, and the `adminIdentities` the local authority treats as administrators. Polkit governs whether an unprivileged session may restart a unit, mount a disk, or install a package, so an over-broad grant is a local privilege escalation path. Read `version` before drawing conclusions: polkit 0.106 and later evaluate the JavaScript rules and ignore `.pkla` files, while earlier releases do the reverse.

os.linux.selinux.name: selinux

boolean.name: boolean
boolean.title: SELinux boolean setting
boolean.desc: One tunable SELinux boolean and its current runtime value (from `getsebool -a` or /sys/fs/selinux/booleans), e.g. httpd_can_network_connect.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether SELinux is installed on the system

mode.name: mode
mode.title: Current enforcement mode: enforcing, permissive, or disabled

module.name: module
module.title: SELinux policy module
module.desc: One installed SELinux policy module from `semodule --list-modules=full`, with its status (enabled or disabled) and priority (higher priority overrides lower for the same module name).

modules.name: modules
modules.title: Installed SELinux policy modules, including disabled ones

policyType.name: policyType
policyType.title: Active policy type (e.g., targeted, mls, minimum)

os.linux.selinux.title: SELinux mandatory access control
os.linux.selinux.desc: SELinux enforcement mode, configured mode, active policy type, tunable booleans, and loaded policy modules. The runtime `mode` (from getenforce or /sys/fs/selinux on a running system, from /etc/selinux/config in a disk or image scan) may differ from `configMode`, which is what persists across reboot; compare the two to catch a system left permissive at runtime or booted with SELinux disabled.

os.linux.shadow.name: shadow

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Shadowed password file entry
entry.desc: A single line from `/etc/shadow`: the username, hashed password field, date of last change, minimum and maximum password age in days, warning period, inactivity period, and account expiry date. Used to audit password aging policy compliance and to detect accounts with no expiry or with locked passwords (a `!` or `*` in the password field).

os.linux.shadow.title: Shadow password file (/etc/shadow)
os.linux.shadow.desc: Per-user password aging, expiration, and lock state parsed from `/etc/shadow`, one `shadow.entry` per account. Audit password policy compliance and find accounts with no expiry, weak aging settings, or locked/disabled passwords.

os.linux.sriov.name: sriov

physicalFunction.name: physicalFunction
physicalFunction.title: SR-IOV physical function
physicalFunction.desc: Network interface that supports SR-IOV, selected by its interface name. The numVfs and totalVfs fields report how many virtual functions are enabled against how many the hardware supports, so an interface with numVfs of 0 is capable but unused. The pciAddress, vendorId, deviceId, and driver fields identify the device the way a device-plugin selector does, and macAddress, mtu, and operationalState report the link. The virtualFunctions field returns the virtual functions carved out of this interface.

virtualFunction.name: virtualFunction
virtualFunction.title: SR-IOV virtual function
virtualFunction.desc: One virtual function of an SR-IOV capable interface, selected by its PCI address. The driver field reports what the function is bound to, and usesPassthroughDriver marks a function handed to a userspace datapath such as DPDK, which leaves it with no kernel network interface and therefore outside host packet filtering. The spoofChecking, trusted, macAddress, vlanId, and rate fields report the configuration the physical function enforces on the guest, which is the part a workload cannot override. linkConfigured is false when the kernel reports no configuration for the function, so an unreported function is not read as an unprotected one.

virtualFunctions.name: virtualFunctions
virtualFunctions.title: Virtual functions across every physical function

os.linux.sriov.title: SR-IOV network devices
os.linux.sriov.desc: Single-root I/O virtualization state of the host's network hardware. The physicalFunctions field lists every SR-IOV capable interface with the number of virtual functions it has enabled against the number it supports, and virtualFunctions flattens every virtual function across all of them.
