This is the realised hardware inventory, so it shows the PCI address, the bound driver, and the per-device link settings that a Kubernetes device plugin only reports as an aggregate count. Empty on hosts with no SR-IOV capable interface.

os.macos.name: os.macos

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

launchd.name: launchd
launchd.title: macOS launchd job configurations
launchd.desc: launchd service manager on macOS. The `jobs` collection parses daemon and agent job definitions from their plist files across the system, library, and per-user launchd directories, so audits can review autostarted programs, the accounts they run as, and their launch conditions in one place.

macos.name: macos
macos.title: macOS-specific operating system surfaces
macos.desc: macOS host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: the machine's `computerName`, per-user and per-host defaults (preferences), the global account/password policy, and installed `systemExtensions`. A starting point for macOS-specific audits alongside the dedicated resources such as firewall, filevault, gatekeeper, and sip.

openBSMAudit.name: openBSMAudit
openBSMAudit.title: OpenBSM audit_control configuration (macOS and BSD)
openBSMAudit.desc: OpenBSM audit subsystem configuration parsed from the `audit_control` file (pass `path` to override the default location). Exposes the audit event `flags`, log retention (`expireAfter`, `filesz`, `minfree`), and policy parameters that govern which security-relevant events the kernel records. `expireAfter` is also parsed the way auditd reads it: its age and size thresholds (`expireAfterAge`, `expireAfterBytes`), how they combine (`expireAfterOperator`), and what that guarantees about how long trail files survive (`minRetentionAge`, `minRetentionBytes`).

safari.name: safari
safari.title: Safari browser (macOS only)
safari.desc: Safari web browser on macOS. The `extensions` collection lists every installed Safari extension across all user accounts on the host, letting audits flag unknown or disabled extensions and verify their provenance.

usb.name: usb
usb.title: USB device inventory (experimental)
usb.desc: USB devices attached to the host, each with its vendor and product IDs, manufacturer, serial number, device class, and connection speed. The `devices` list inventories connected peripherals so you can flag removable storage or unexpected hardware.

os.macos.title: Operating system information for macOS
os.macos.desc: Extends `os.unix` (and through it, `os.base`) with the facilities only macOS provides: the `macos` surface itself, Safari, `launchd` and the OpenBSM audit subsystem.

os.macos.launchd.name: launchd

jobs.name: jobs
jobs.title: All launchd jobs from system and user directories

os.macos.launchd.title: macOS launchd job configurations
os.macos.launchd.desc: launchd service manager on macOS. The `jobs` collection parses daemon and agent job definitions from their plist files across the system, library, and per-user launchd directories, so audits can review autostarted programs, the accounts they run as, and their launch conditions in one place.

os.macos.macos.name: macos

alf.name: alf
alf.title: macOS application layer firewall (raw ALF preference values)
alf.desc: Raw integer flags read from the Application Layer Firewall plist (`/Library/Preferences/com.apple.alf.plist`). Prefer `macos.firewall`, which decodes these into boolean fields; use this resource only when you need the underlying preference values.

filevault.name: filevault
filevault.title: macOS FileVault full-disk encryption
filevault.desc: FileVault full-disk encryption state: whether it is `enabled`, the current `status`, whether personal and institutional recovery keys exist, and the `users` permitted to unlock the encrypted volume at boot. CIS macOS benchmarks require FileVault enabled.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: macOS application layer firewall
firewall.desc: Decoded Application Layer Firewall configuration: whether the firewall is `enabled`, whether it blocks all incoming connections, stealth mode, logging, the signed-app auto-allow policy, and per-application rules. CIS macOS benchmarks expect the firewall enabled with stealth mode on. See `macos.alf` for the raw preference values.

gatekeeper.name: gatekeeper
gatekeeper.title: macOS Gatekeeper application execution policy
gatekeeper.desc: Gatekeeper policy that controls whether downloaded applications may run: whether assessments are `enabled` and the human-readable `status`. Disabling Gatekeeper lets unsigned or unnotarized software launch without a warning, so benchmarks expect it enabled.

globalAccountPolicies.name: globalAccountPolicies
globalAccountPolicies.title: Global account (password) policy directives applied to all local users

hardware.name: hardware
hardware.title: macOS hardware overview
hardware.desc: Hardware and firmware details reported by `system_profiler`: chip type, model identifiers, installed memory, serial number, and Activation Lock status. Useful for asset inventory and for distinguishing Apple Silicon from Intel Macs in conditional audits.

mdm.name: mdm
mdm.title: macOS MDM (Mobile Device Management) enrollment state
mdm.desc: MDM enrollment state for this Mac: whether it is enrolled, the enrollment server, and whether enrollment was performed via Automated Device Enrollment (formerly DEP) or user-approved. Use `macos.profiles` to enumerate the configuration profiles delivered to the device. Backed by `profiles status -type enrollment`.

profile.name: profile
profile.title: macOS Configuration Profile
profile.desc: Single Configuration Profile: its `identifier`, `uuid`, human-readable `displayName`, `description`, `organization`, `type`, whether it is install-locked (`removalDisallowed`), the scope it applies to (`scope`: `system` or `user`), and the individual `payloads` that carry the actual policy directives.

profiles.name: profiles
profiles.title: macOS configuration profiles installed on the system
profiles.desc: Every Configuration Profile delivered to the device, both MDM-delivered and manually installed `.mobileconfig` payloads, so you can audit what policies are actually in force. Backed by `profiles list -all -output stdout-xml`; requires root to see system-level (`_computerlevel`) profiles, otherwise only the current user's profiles are returned.

sharing.name: sharing
sharing.title: macOS Sharing service state
sharing.desc:
State of each toggle in the unified Sharing panel (System Settings > Sharing on macOS Ventura+, System Preferences > Sharing on older versions). CIS macOS benchmarks require most of these off unless the device explicitly needs the service. Backed by `system_profiler SPSharingDataType`, so the values match exactly what the System Settings UI displays.

`system_profiler SPSharingDataType` also reports `Remote Login` and `Remote Apple Events`; those are intentionally not exposed here because `macos.systemsetup.remoteLogin` and `macos.systemsetup.remoteAppleEvents` already cover them via the `systemsetup` CLI. This resource covers the rest of the panel.

sip.name: sip
sip.title: macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP)
sip.desc: System Integrity Protection state, the kernel-level protection that restricts modification of protected system files and processes even by root. Exposes whether SIP is `enabled` and the raw `status` message from `csrutil status`. Disabling SIP is a significant hardening regression.

softwareupdate.name: softwareupdate
softwareupdate.title: macOS Software Update configuration and pending updates
softwareupdate.desc: Automatic-update policy and the list of updates currently available to install. Policy fields read from `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.SoftwareUpdate.plist` (with `/Library/Managed Preferences/` taking precedence when an MDM configuration profile has been delivered). The `updates` list is produced from `softwareupdate -l --no-scan` so it does not initiate a network check.

systemExtension.name: systemExtension
systemExtension.title: macOS system extension
systemExtension.desc: Installed system extension read from /Library/SystemExtensions/db.plist: its `identifier`, `uuid`, `version`, `teamID` of the signing developer, declared `categories` (such as network or endpoint-security extensions), and `bundlePath`. The `state` string reports the extension's lifecycle, with `enabled` and `active` derived from it. `mdmManaged` is true when the extension or its team is allowlisted by an MDM system-extension policy, which distinguishes centrally approved extensions from user-installed ones.

systemExtensions.name: systemExtensions
systemExtensions.title: Installed system extensions (network, endpoint security, and driver extensions)

systemsetup.name: systemsetup
systemsetup.title: macOS machine settings via the systemsetup CLI
systemsetup.desc: Date/time, sleep and wake, remote login, power, and network-time settings surfaced by the `systemsetup` CLI, with each field mapping to one `systemsetup -get*` query. Requires at least admin privileges to run.

timemachine.name: timemachine
timemachine.title: macOS Time Machine backup configuration
timemachine.desc: Time Machine backup configuration read from its preferences: configured backup destinations, the automatic backup schedule, and the paths excluded from backups, exposed as the raw `preferences` dict.

userHostPreferences.name: userHostPreferences
userHostPreferences.title: Per-user, per-host macOS defaults (ByHost preferences), keyed by preference domain

userPreferences.name: userPreferences
userPreferences.title: Per-user macOS defaults (preferences), keyed by preference domain

xprotect.name: xprotect
xprotect.title: macOS XProtect anti-malware bundle
xprotect.desc:
Version and last-modified timestamp of the XProtect signature bundle (and, when present, the legacy Malware Removal Tool). CIS macOS benchmarks expect XProtect signatures to be current; checking `modified` against the auditor's freshness threshold catches devices that have stopped receiving updates.

XProtect.bundle lives at `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` on modern macOS (with `/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle` as the legacy fallback). `mrtVersion` and `mrtModified` are empty or null on macOS 13+ where MRT has been retired in favor of XProtectRemediator.

os.macos.macos.title: macOS-specific operating system surfaces
os.macos.macos.desc: macOS host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: the machine's `computerName`, per-user and per-host defaults (preferences), the global account/password policy, and installed `systemExtensions`. A starting point for macOS-specific audits alongside the dedicated resources such as firewall, filevault, gatekeeper, and sip.

os.macos.openBSMAudit.name: openBSMAudit

content.name: content
content.title: Content of the audit_control file

dir.name: dir
dir.title: Directory where audit log files are stored

expireAfterAge.name: expireAfterAge
expireAfterAge.title: Age threshold from expire-after
expireAfterAge.desc: Age since a trail file was last written after which auditd may remove it, as a duration. Converted as auditd converts it: `s` seconds, `h` hours, `d` days, and `y` years of 364 days plus one day for every fourth year. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no age term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterBytes.name: expireAfterBytes
expireAfterBytes.title: Size threshold from expire-after, in bytes
expireAfterBytes.desc: Aggregate size of all trail files after which auditd may remove the oldest, in bytes. `B` or no suffix is bytes, `K`, `M` and `G` are powers of 1024. Read from the first expire-after line, as auditd does. Null when expire-after is absent, empty, has no size term, or is a value auditd rejects.

expireAfterOperator.name: expireAfterOperator
expireAfterOperator.title: How the two expire-after thresholds combine
expireAfterOperator.desc: `AND` when a trail file is removed only once both thresholds are exceeded, `OR` when either one is enough. Null for a single threshold, and when expire-after is absent, empty, or a value auditd rejects.

file.name: file
file.title: File resource for the audit_control file

filesz.name: filesz
filesz.title: Maximum size of individual audit log files

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Audit event flags for attributable (user) events

memberClearSflagsMask.name: memberClearSflagsMask
memberClearSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can clear on their processes

memberSetSflagsMask.name: memberSetSflagsMask
memberSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that non-superusers can set on their processes

minRetentionAge.name: minRetentionAge
minRetentionAge.title: Minimum age trail files reach before auditd can remove them
minRetentionAge.desc: Age a trail file is guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove it, whatever the size of the trail, as a duration. Set for an age threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the size threshold alone can remove files (a size on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minRetentionBytes.name: minRetentionBytes
minRetentionBytes.title: Minimum aggregate trail size kept before auditd can remove a file, in bytes
minRetentionBytes.desc: Aggregate size the trail files are guaranteed to reach before expire-after lets auditd remove one, whatever their age, in bytes. Set for a size threshold on its own or joined with `AND`. Null when the age threshold alone can remove files (an age on its own, or joined with `OR`), and when expire-after is absent, empty, sets no nonzero threshold, or is a value auditd rejects. A zero threshold is one auditd ignores.

minfree.name: minfree
minfree.title: Minimum free space threshold (percentage) before audit warnings

naflags.name: naflags
naflags.title: Audit event flags for non-attributable events

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed parameters from the audit_control file

superuserClearSflagsMask.name: superuserClearSflagsMask
superuserClearSflagsMask.title: Flags that superusers can clear on their processes

superuserSetSflagsMask.name: superuserSetSflagsMask
superuserSetSflagsMask.title: Flags that superusers can set on their processes

os.macos.openBSMAudit.title: OpenBSM audit_control configuration (macOS and BSD)
os.macos.openBSMAudit.desc: OpenBSM audit subsystem configuration parsed from the `audit_control` file (pass `path` to override the default location). Exposes the audit event `flags`, log retention (`expireAfter`, `filesz`, `minfree`), and policy parameters that govern which security-relevant events the kernel records. `expireAfter` is also parsed the way auditd reads it: its age and size thresholds (`expireAfterAge`, `expireAfterBytes`), how they combine (`expireAfterOperator`), and what that guarantees about how long trail files survive (`minRetentionAge`, `minRetentionBytes`).

os.macos.safari.name: safari
os.macos.safari.title: Safari browser (macOS only)
os.macos.safari.desc: Safari web browser on macOS. The `extensions` collection lists every installed Safari extension across all user accounts on the host, letting audits flag unknown or disabled extensions and verify their provenance.

os.macos.usb.name: usb

device.name: device
device.title: Experimental: USB device
device.desc: Single attached USB device. `vendorId` and `productId` identify the hardware model, `class`/`className` give its function (e.g. mass storage, HID, hub), `serial` uniquely identifies the unit where the device reports one, and `isRemovable` distinguishes hot-pluggable peripherals from fixed internal devices.

os.macos.usb.title: USB device inventory (experimental)
os.macos.usb.desc: USB devices attached to the host, each with its vendor and product IDs, manufacturer, serial number, device class, and connection speed. The `devices` list inventories connected peripherals so you can flag removable storage or unexpected hardware.

os.rootCertificates.name: os.rootCertificates

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that define these certificates

unparseable.name: unparseable
unparseable.title: Number of certificates in the trust-store files that could not be parsed
unparseable.desc: Counts the certificate blocks skipped while decoding the trust-store files, for example a truncated or malformed certificate. Those blocks are left out of the list rather than failing the whole store, so any value above zero means the list is an incomplete view of what the platform trusts.

os.rootCertificates.title: Operating system root certificate trust store
os.rootCertificates.desc: X.509 root certificates that the asset's operating system trusts for TLS validation, derived from the platform-appropriate trust-store files (e.g. `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` on Debian, `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt` on RHEL, the macOS SecTrust store, the Windows Root certificate store). Reads each trust-store file and exposes the parsed `network.certificate` list so audits can pin specific issuers, detect untrusted local additions, or count the trust-store size.

os.unix.name: os.unix

aide.name: aide
aide.title: AIDE file integrity database
aide.desc: Configuration and database state of AIDE, the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment. `params` holds the settings read from the configuration, `groups` the attribute group definitions, and `rules` the selection lines deciding which paths are watched and which attributes are compared. `database` points at the reference database the next check runs against, and its modification time is the signal worth asserting on: a reference database older than the last package transaction no longer describes the system, so a check against it cannot detect anything that changed in between. Watch for coverage removed by a negative rule, which silently drops a path from an otherwise healthy configuration.

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

crontab.name: crontab
crontab.title: Crontab schedule on the system
crontab.desc: Scheduled cron jobs collected from every source on the host: the system crontab (/etc/crontab), drop-in files under /etc/cron.d and /usr/local/etc/cron.d, and per-user crontabs (/var/spool/cron, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/spool/cron/tabs, /usr/lib/cron/tabs, /var/cron/tabs). The `entries` list shows what runs on a schedule, as which `user`, and with what `command`. Use `entries.where(user == "root")` to focus on privileged jobs. `files` lists the source files the entries were parsed from.

exim.name: exim
exim.title: Exim mail transfer agent configuration
exim.desc: Exim configuration. `params` holds the macros and main-section options parsed from the active config file, covering both the Debian `update-exim4.conf.conf` key/value form and the monolithic `exim.conf` main section (options before the first `begin` block). `localInterfaces` normalizes the local interface list, handling the Debian `dc_local_interfaces` `' ; '`-separated form and the Exim `local_interfaces` list, so policies can compare it directly. By default the per-distribution config location is used; select an alternate file with `exim("/path/to/exim.conf")`.

inetd.name: inetd
inetd.title: inetd super-server namespace
inetd.desc: Namespace hosting `inetd.config`, the entry point for examining which network services the inetd super-server launches on demand.

kernel.name: kernel
kernel.title: Running kernel and its modules
kernel.desc: Running kernel and its configuration surface. Exposes kernel version info, sysctl `parameters` and `sysctls`, `modules`, installed kernel versions, ASLR state (`aslr`, Linux and FreeBSD), and, on Linux, hardening state (`cmdline`, `taint`, `lockdown`) and the live patches applied in memory (`livepatch`).

loginconf.name: loginconf
loginconf.title: BSD login class capability database (/etc/login.conf)
loginconf.desc: Login classes parsed from /etc/login.conf on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `loginconf.class` per class. Login classes hold the password policy (password format, expiry, warning period), umask, resource limits, and environment for the accounts assigned to them in /etc/master.passwd. The file uses the getcap(3) format, and the system reads the compiled login.conf.db that `cap_mkdb` builds from it, so an edit takes effect only after `cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf`. Read another file with `loginconf("/path/to/login.conf")`.

logrotate.name: logrotate
logrotate.title: logrotate configuration
logrotate.desc: Log rotation configuration parsed from the main logrotate.conf and the fragments under logrotate.d. `globalConfig` holds the directives that apply outside any log block, `entries` holds the per-log-path rotation rules, and `files` lists the configuration files read. Audit rotation frequency, retention counts, and compression to confirm logs are kept long enough and pruned safely.

masterpasswd.name: masterpasswd
masterpasswd.title: BSD password database source (/etc/master.passwd)
masterpasswd.desc: Accounts parsed from /etc/master.passwd on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `masterpasswd.entry` per account. Unlike `users`, which reads the public passwd database, each entry carries the password field, the login class, and the password change and account expiry times, so audits can find accounts with no password, check that passwords are shadowed, and resolve each account's login class settings. The file is readable by root only: a scan without root or `--sudo` returns a permission error, never an empty list. Lines that cannot be parsed are left out and counted in `invalidLines`. Read another file with `masterpasswd("/path/to/master.passwd")`. macOS ships this file too, but its accounts live in Directory Services, so use `users` there.

mount.name: mount
mount.title: Mount table
mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

nfs.name: nfs
nfs.title: NFS service local state
nfs.desc: Local NFS service viewed from two angles: shares this host declares (`exports`) and NFS volumes this host has mounted (`mounts`). `exports` is parsed from `/etc/exports` using the platform-specific syntax for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and AIX; each row is one `(path, client)` pair so audits like `nfs.exports.where(noRootSquash)` work directly. `mounts` filters the system mount table for NFS file systems and parses NFS-specific options into fields (protocol `version`, `security` flavor, `hardMount`, `readOnly`).

postfix.name: postfix
postfix.title: Postfix mail transfer agent configuration
postfix.desc: Effective Postfix configuration. `params` reports parameter values from `postconf` when the binary is available (which includes the built-in defaults for parameters not written to the file) and otherwise falls back to parsing main.cf directly (file values only, with `$name` interpolation and continuation lines). `inetInterfaces` is the parsed `inet_interfaces` list and `services` are the daemon definitions from master.cf. By default the per-distribution config locations are used; select an alternate main.cf with `postfix("/path/to/main.cf")`.

snmpd.name: snmpd
snmpd.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) namespace
snmpd.desc: Namespace hosting `snmpd.config`, the entry point for examining the effective SNMP daemon configuration.

sshd.name: sshd
sshd.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) namespace
sshd.desc: Namespace hosting `sshd.config`, the entry point for auditing the OpenSSH server's effective settings and Match blocks.

sudo.name: sudo
sudo.title: Sudo binary and runtime metadata
sudo.desc: Installed `sudo` binary: where it lives on disk, the version it reports under `sudo -V`, which plugins are loaded (policy, I/O, audit, approval), whether the build supports Python-based plugins, and the result of `visudo -c` against the sudoers configuration. For sudoers configuration parsing, use the `sudoers` resource directly, or access it via this resource's `sudoers` field.

sudoers.name: sudoers
sudoers.title: sudo authorization configuration
sudoers.desc: User specifications, defaults, and aliases parsed across the sudoers files (/etc/sudoers plus /etc/sudoers.d). Use userSpecs to audit who may run which commands as which users, and defaults to check hardening settings such as env_reset, secure_path, requiretty, and NOPASSWD grants. Point at an alternate root file with the `path` argument.

sysrc.name: sysrc
sysrc.title: FreeBSD rc.conf system configuration
sysrc.desc: FreeBSD service and system configuration merged from rc.conf and rc.conf.local. The `entries` accessor exposes each variable assignment as a structured name/value pair (with the file it came from), so audits can assert on individual settings such as sshd_enable or a firewall being turned on. `content` returns the concatenated raw text. Point at a specific file with `sysrc(path: "...")`.

zfs.name: zfs
zfs.title: ZFS storage pools and datasets
zfs.desc: ZFS storage on the host: the installed `version`, the storage `pools` with their health and capacity, and every `dataset` (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, and bookmarks). Iterate to audit pool health, free capacity, vdev topology, and dataset properties such as compression and encryption.

os.unix.title: Operating system information for Unix-like platforms
os.unix.desc: Extends `os.base` for Unix-family operating systems (macOS, Linux, FreeBSD and similar), carrying the facilities that family provides and Windows does not: `sshd`, `crontab`, `sudo`/`sudoers`, the mount table, the kernel, NFS, ZFS, the classic daemons (`inetd`, `snmpd`, `postfix`, `exim`) and `aide`.

os.unix.aide.name: aide

configFile.name: configFile
configFile.title: Root configuration file the settings are read from

database.name: database
database.title: Reference database the next check compares against
database.desc: Resolved from `database_in`, with the `file:` prefix stripped. Null when the setting names no readable database, which is also the state before the database is initialized for the first time.

files.name: files
files.title: Every configuration file that contributed, including resolved includes

groups.name: groups
groups.title: Attribute group definitions, as key-value pairs
groups.desc: Maps each group name to its expression exactly as written, for example `NORMAL` to `R+sha512`. Referenced from a rule's `expression` and resolved into its `attributes`.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether AIDE is present on the system
installed.desc: True when an AIDE binary is found. A configuration file left behind by a removed package does not count. Use it to guard integrity-monitoring audits on hosts that ship no AIDE at all.

newDatabase.name: newDatabase
newDatabase.title: Database a fresh initialization writes, resolved from `database_out`

params.name: params
params.title: Settings from the configuration, as key-value pairs
params.desc: Keyed by the option name as written, for example `database_in`, `database_out`, `gzip_dbout`, and `report_url`. A `key = value` line whose key is not a recognized AIDE option is reported in `groups` instead.

rule.name: rule
rule.title: AIDE selection rule
rule.desc: Single selection line from the AIDE configuration: the `path` it applies to, the `attributes` compared for matching entries, the `selection` kind deciding whether the line adds or removes coverage, and the file types it is limited to as `restriction`. Macro references in the path are substituted and the configuration's escapes (`\\.` for `\.`) removed, so `path` is the expression AIDE actually matches. Lines inside an `@@if` block whose condition is false are not rules. A condition that cannot be evaluated, such as `@@if hostname` in an image scan, has both of its branches reported. Executable files reached through `@@x_include` are run, as AIDE runs them, and their output read; on a connection that cannot run commands, such as an image scan, the rules they print are missing.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: Selection rules deciding which paths are checked

version.name: version
version.title: AIDE release reported by the aide binary
version.desc: Requires command execution, so it is null on backends that expose only a filesystem, such as an image scan, and when no aide binary can be run.

os.unix.aide.title: AIDE file integrity database
os.unix.aide.desc: Configuration and database state of AIDE, the Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment. `params` holds the settings read from the configuration, `groups` the attribute group definitions, and `rules` the selection lines deciding which paths are watched and which attributes are compared. `database` points at the reference database the next check runs against, and its modification time is the signal worth asserting on: a reference database older than the last package transaction no longer describes the system, so a check against it cannot detect anything that changed in between. Watch for coverage removed by a negative rule, which silently drops a path from an otherwise healthy configuration.

os.unix.crontab.name: crontab

entries.name: entries
entries.title: All cron entries from system and user crontabs

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Individual crontab entry
entry.desc: Single scheduled job parsed from a crontab source. The five schedule fields (`minute`, `hour`, `dayOfMonth`, `month`, `dayOfWeek`) hold the raw cron expressions, `user` is the account the job runs as (taken from the entry for system crontabs, or from the filename for per-user crontabs), and `command` is the line executed. `file` and `lineNumber` locate the entry in its source.

files.name: files
files.title: Files that contain crontab entries

os.unix.crontab.title: Crontab schedule on the system
os.unix.crontab.desc: Scheduled cron jobs collected from every source on the host: the system crontab (/etc/crontab), drop-in files under /etc/cron.d and /usr/local/etc/cron.d, and per-user crontabs (/var/spool/cron, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/spool/cron/tabs, /usr/lib/cron/tabs, /var/cron/tabs). The `entries` list shows what runs on a schedule, as which `user`, and with what `command`. Use `entries.where(user == "root")` to focus on privileged jobs. `files` lists the source files the entries were parsed from.

os.unix.exim.name: exim

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the active Exim configuration file
configPath.desc: On Debian-family systems this is `/etc/exim4/exim4.conf` when that hand-written config exists, otherwise `/etc/exim4/update-exim4.conf.conf`.

localInterfaces.name: localInterfaces
localInterfaces.title: Local interfaces parsed and normalized into a list
localInterfaces.desc: An unset or empty setting means Exim listens on every interface, reported as Exim's own default `::0` and `0.0.0.0`. Macro references such as `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` are resolved. On Debian-family systems the list comes from the generated `/var/lib/exim4/config.autogenerated` that Exim loads, so a `MAIN_LOCAL_INTERFACES` in `exim4.conf.localmacros` wins over `dc_local_interfaces`. For the installed Exim's own config, a daemon started with `-oX` reports the interfaces given there (with their `.port` suffix), taken from the running daemons or, when none runs, from `/etc/default/exim4`. Several daemons report every interface they listen on. Empty when no Exim configuration exists.

params.name: params
params.title: Parsed macros and main-section options
params.desc: `.ifdef` and `.ifndef` blocks are evaluated like Exim does, including tests of Exim's built-in feature macros such as `_HAVE_OPENSSL`, which are read from the installed `exim` binary.

os.unix.exim.title: Exim mail transfer agent configuration
os.unix.exim.desc: Exim configuration. `params` holds the macros and main-section options parsed from the active config file, covering both the Debian `update-exim4.conf.conf` key/value form and the monolithic `exim.conf` main section (options before the first `begin` block). `localInterfaces` normalizes the local interface list, handling the Debian `dc_local_interfaces` `' ; '`-separated form and the Exim `local_interfaces` list, so policies can compare it directly. By default the per-distribution config location is used; select an alternate file with `exim("/path/to/exim.conf")`.

os.unix.inetd.name: inetd

config.name: config
config.title: inetd super-server configuration
config.desc: Services the inetd (or compatible) super-server is configured to launch on demand. Each active entry pairs a service with its socket type, protocol, wait mode, run-as user, and server program. The configuration is assembled from /etc/inetd.conf together with any drop-in files under /etc/inetd.d. An xinetd configuration, such as inetd.config("/etc/xinetd.conf"), is read with the files it includes, and its entries are the service blocks xinetd runs: blocks with disable = yes, or disabled by the enabled and disabled lists of the defaults block, are left out. A missing configuration yields no entries, so audits such as serviceNames.none("ftp") hold trivially on systems that don't run inetd.

os.unix.inetd.title: inetd super-server namespace
os.unix.inetd.desc: Namespace hosting `inetd.config`, the entry point for examining which network services the inetd super-server launches on demand.

os.unix.kernel.name: kernel

aslr.name: aslr
aslr.title: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) state (Linux and FreeBSD)

info.name: info
info.title: Active kernel information (version, path, device, arguments)

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Installed kernel versions

livepatch.name: livepatch
livepatch.title: Live patches applied to the running kernel (Linux only)

module.name: module
module.title: System kernel module information
module.desc: Single kernel module: its `name`, in-memory `size`, and whether it is currently `loaded`. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.module(name: "nf_conntrack")`) to check a specific module, or iterate from `kernel.modules` to audit the full loaded-module list. Module names are normalized the way modprobe normalizes them, so `firewire-core` and `firewire_core` select the same module and match a rule written with either spelling. Use `blacklisted`, `installBypass`, and `disabled` to express CIS-style "module must not load" controls without falling back to raw modprobe.d file parsing. Use `onDisk` to tell whether a loadable module file is available for the running kernel even when it isn't currently loaded, and `builtIn` to detect functionality compiled directly into the kernel (which is always active and cannot be blacklisted or unloaded). On FreeBSD, modules carry the names `kldstat -v` lists, such as `msdosfs` or `pci/ena`, including the modules compiled into the kernel; a loaded file name such as `zfs.ko` also selects its module.

parameter.name: parameter
parameter.title: Kernel parameter (sysctl), live and configured
parameter.desc:
One kernel parameter with the value the running kernel uses (`value`) and the value the configuration files will apply at the next boot (`configured`), kept apart so a check can require both. Initialize by name (e.g., `kernel.parameter("fs.protected_hardlinks")`) or iterate `kernel.sysctls`. Names use the dotted form `sysctl -a` prints; a name written with slashes is accepted too.

Configuration is read from the sysctl.d directories (/etc, /run, /usr/local/lib, /usr/lib, /lib) with the precedence systemd-sysctl applies at boot: a file hides a same-named file in a lower-priority directory, the files are applied in file name order, and the last assignment wins. An explicit assignment beats a glob, and `-name` excludes a parameter from globs. Without systemd-sysctl, /etc/sysctl.conf is applied after the sysctl.d files, as `sysctl --system` does. On BSD and macOS it is /etc/sysctl.conf (and /etc/sysctl.conf.local on FreeBSD).

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Kernel parameters map (sysctl key-value pairs)
parameters.desc: Live values only, as the kernel prints them. Use `sysctls` or `kernel.parameter` for the value the configuration files set as well. Those collapse whitespace in values (the tab in `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` becomes a space), so the same parameter can read differently here.

sysctls.name: sysctls
sysctls.title: Every kernel parameter that is live, configured, or both
sysctls.desc: A parameter set in a configuration file but not exposed by the running kernel, such as one of an unloaded module, is listed with `active` false. A glob assignment is expanded against the live parameters; one that matches none is listed under its pattern.

os.unix.kernel.title: Running kernel and its modules
os.unix.kernel.desc: Running kernel and its configuration surface. Exposes kernel version info, sysctl `parameters` and `sysctls`, `modules`, installed kernel versions, ASLR state (`aslr`, Linux and FreeBSD), and, on Linux, hardening state (`cmdline`, `taint`, `lockdown`) and the live patches applied in memory (`livepatch`).

os.unix.loginconf.name: loginconf

class.name: class
class.title: Login class from /etc/login.conf
class.desc: One login class record. `capabilities` holds what the record itself writes, `effective` what applies after `tc=` inheritance, and `inherits` the classes it includes. Values keep their text as written (for example `90d` or `022`); boolean capabilities read as true. Select a class with `loginconf.class("default")`, which also matches an alias.

file.name: file
file.title: login.conf file that the classes are read from

os.unix.loginconf.title: BSD login class capability database (/etc/login.conf)
os.unix.loginconf.desc: Login classes parsed from /etc/login.conf on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `loginconf.class` per class. Login classes hold the password policy (password format, expiry, warning period), umask, resource limits, and environment for the accounts assigned to them in /etc/master.passwd. The file uses the getcap(3) format, and the system reads the compiled login.conf.db that `cap_mkdb` builds from it, so an edit takes effect only after `cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf`. Read another file with `loginconf("/path/to/login.conf")`.

os.unix.logrotate.name: logrotate

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Per-file/glob rotation entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Logrotate configuration entry for a specific log path
entry.desc: Rotation rule for one log path or glob. `path` is the log the block applies to and `config` holds every directive inside the block as key-value pairs (e.g. "rotate", "daily", "compress", "maxage"). `file` and `lineNumber` locate the block in its source configuration file.

files.name: files
files.title: List of configuration files (main + logrotate.d fragments)

os.unix.logrotate.title: logrotate configuration
os.unix.logrotate.desc: Log rotation configuration parsed from the main logrotate.conf and the fragments under logrotate.d. `globalConfig` holds the directives that apply outside any log block, `entries` holds the per-log-path rotation rules, and `files` lists the configuration files read. Audit rotation frequency, retention counts, and compression to confirm logs are kept long enough and pruned safely.

os.unix.masterpasswd.name: masterpasswd

file.name: file
file.title: master.passwd file that the entries are read from

invalidLines.name: invalidLines
invalidLines.title: Number of lines in the file that could not be parsed
invalidLines.desc: Counts the lines left out of the entry list: a line without exactly ten fields, or with a uid, gid, change, or expire field that is not a number. Such a line is never guessed at (a bad uid would otherwise read as 0, which is root), and counting it keeps a shorter list from passing a check silently. `pwd_mkdb` refuses such a file, so a non-zero value also means the password database was not rebuilt from it.

os.unix.masterpasswd.title: BSD password database source (/etc/master.passwd)
os.unix.masterpasswd.desc: Accounts parsed from /etc/master.passwd on FreeBSD, DragonFly, OpenBSD, and NetBSD, one `masterpasswd.entry` per account. Unlike `users`, which reads the public passwd database, each entry carries the password field, the login class, and the password change and account expiry times, so audits can find accounts with no password, check that passwords are shadowed, and resolve each account's login class settings. The file is readable by root only: a scan without root or `--sudo` returns a permission error, never an empty list. Lines that cannot be parsed are left out and counted in `invalidLines`. Read another file with `masterpasswd("/path/to/master.passwd")`. macOS ships this file too, but its accounts live in Directory Services, so use `users` there.

os.unix.mount.name: mount

point.name: point
point.title: Mount point
point.desc: A single mounted filesystem: the backing `device`, the `path` where it is attached, the `fstype`, mount `options`, whether it is currently `mounted`, and the total, used, and available bytes. Select a mount by path, for example `mount.point(path: "/var")`. On Windows the path matches without regard to case or a trailing backslash, so `mount.point(path: "C:")`, `mount.point(path: "c:\\")` and `mount.point(path: os.base.env["SystemDrive"])` all select the `C:\` volume.

os.unix.mount.title: Mount table
os.unix.mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

os.unix.nfs.name: nfs

export.name: export
export.title: NFS export entry for a single path and client
export.desc: One row of the local NFS export table: the directory being shared (`path`), the client specification it is shared with (`client`, a hostname, IP address, CIDR, wildcard, netgroup, or `*` meaning any client) and the effective export `options` as parsed from `/etc/exports`. `readOnly` is true when the share is exported read-only. `noRootSquash` is true when the share grants remote uid 0 on the share, a classic NFS audit finding.

exports.name: exports
exports.title: NFS exports declared on this host

mount.name: mount
mount.title: NFS client mount
mount.desc: One NFS mount currently active on this host. `device` is the NFS source as the kernel sees it (`server:/remote/path`), split into `server` and `remotePath` for convenience. `mountpoint` is where the share is attached locally. `version` is the negotiated NFS protocol version (for example `3`, `4`, `4.1`, `4.2`); empty when the kernel did not report one. `security` is the authentication flavor, one of `sys`, `krb5`, `krb5i`, `krb5p`, or `none`; empty when unspecified. `hardMount` is true when the mount uses hard semantics (the `soft` option is not set). `readOnly` is true when the mount is `ro`. `options` is the full mount option list as reported by the system.

mounts.name: mounts
mounts.title: NFS mounts currently active on this host

os.unix.nfs.title: NFS service local state
os.unix.nfs.desc: Local NFS service viewed from two angles: shares this host declares (`exports`) and NFS volumes this host has mounted (`mounts`). `exports` is parsed from `/etc/exports` using the platform-specific syntax for Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, and AIX; each row is one `(path, client)` pair so audits like `nfs.exports.where(noRootSquash)` work directly. `mounts` filters the system mount table for NFS file systems and parses NFS-specific options into fields (protocol `version`, `security` flavor, `hardMount`, `readOnly`).

os.unix.postfix.name: postfix

inetInterfaces.name: inetInterfaces
inetInterfaces.title: Interfaces Postfix listens on, parsed from the inet_interfaces parameter

mainCfPath.name: mainCfPath
mainCfPath.title: Path to the Postfix main.cf configuration file

masterCfPath.name: masterCfPath
masterCfPath.title: Path to the Postfix master.cf configuration file

params.name: params
params.title: Effective Postfix parameters
params.desc: Reported by `postconf` when available (so parameters left at their built-in default still appear); otherwise parsed from main.cf, in which case only values written to the file are present.

service.name: service
service.title: Postfix master.cf service definition
service.desc: Single daemon entry from the Postfix master.cf file: its service name and transport type, the chroot and privilege flags, the wake-up and process limits, and the command it runs. The flag columns carry `y`, `n`, or `-` (use the built-in default). Iterated from `postfix.services`.

os.unix.postfix.title: Postfix mail transfer agent configuration
os.unix.postfix.desc: Effective Postfix configuration. `params` reports parameter values from `postconf` when the binary is available (which includes the built-in defaults for parameters not written to the file) and otherwise falls back to parsing main.cf directly (file values only, with `$name` interpolation and continuation lines). `inetInterfaces` is the parsed `inet_interfaces` list and `services` are the daemon definitions from master.cf. By default the per-distribution config locations are used; select an alternate main.cf with `postfix("/path/to/main.cf")`.

os.unix.snmpd.name: snmpd

config.name: config
config.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) configuration
config.desc: snmpd.conf settings that govern SNMP access: community strings, VACM users, and listen addresses. The configuration is assembled the way snmpd reads it: the main snmpd.conf, files pulled in by its includeFile and includeDir directives, snmpd.local.conf in the same directory, and the persistent snmpd.conf under /var/lib/snmp. A missing configuration yields empty accessors, so audits such as rwCommunities == [] hold trivially on hosts that don't run snmpd.

os.unix.snmpd.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) namespace
os.unix.snmpd.desc: Namespace hosting `snmpd.config`, the entry point for examining the effective SNMP daemon configuration.

os.unix.sshd.name: sshd

config.name: config
config.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) configuration
config.desc: OpenSSH server settings parsed from sshd_config (and any Include files), plus the effective values reported by `sshd -T`. Surfaces `ciphers`, `macs`, `kexs`, and `hostkeyalgorithms` for cryptographic hardening checks, `permitRootLogin` for root-access policy, and `blocks` for the conditional Match blocks. Compare the configured values (`ciphers`) against the effective ones (`effectiveCiphers`) to catch overrides applied at runtime. The default file is /etc/ssh/sshd_config, or C:\ProgramData\ssh\sshd_config on Windows.

os.unix.sshd.title: OpenSSH server (sshd) namespace
os.unix.sshd.desc: Namespace hosting `sshd.config`, the entry point for auditing the OpenSSH server's effective settings and Match blocks.

os.unix.sudo.name: sudo

implementation.name: implementation
implementation.title: Which sudo implementation the binary is: "sudo" or "sudo-rs"
implementation.desc: "sudo" is the C implementation from sudo.ws. "sudo-rs" is the Rust reimplementation that recent Ubuntu releases install as `sudo`. It reads the same sudoers files but supports a subset of the options, has no plugins, and rejects settings such as `logfile`, `log_input`, `log_output`, and `requiretty`. Null when sudo is not installed or `sudo -V` output is not recognized.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether sudo is installed and executable

ioPlugins.name: ioPlugins
ioPlugins.title: I/O plugins (e.g., sudoers_io for log_input / log_output)

path.name: path
path.title: Path to the sudo binary
path.desc: Filesystem-resolved location of the `sudo` binary on the asset (e.g., `/usr/bin/sudo`). Empty when sudo is not installed; check `installed` rather than testing this field for emptiness.

plugin.name: plugin
plugin.title: A sudo plugin reported by `sudo -V`
plugin.desc: One loaded sudo plugin, identified by name and type (policy, I/O, audit, or approval) with its version and, when reported, the path to the .so file backing it.

policyPlugin.name: policyPlugin
policyPlugin.title: Policy plugin (typically sudoers_policy). Null when none is loaded.

pythonSupport.name: pythonSupport
pythonSupport.title: Whether the build supports Python-based plugins

validate.name: validate
validate.title: Result of `visudo -c`. Null when sudoers files cannot be read (e.g., running unprivileged against a mode-0440 /etc/sudoers).

validation.name: validation
validation.title: Result of validating sudoers configuration with `visudo -c`
validation.desc: Syntax-check outcome for the sudoers files: `valid` is true when `visudo -c` exits cleanly, and `errors` lists every parse error otherwise.

version.name: version
version.title: Version string reported by `sudo -V` (e.g., "1.9.5p3")
version.desc: The version of the implementation named by `implementation`: a sudo.ws release such as "1.9.5p3", or a sudo-rs release such as "0.2.13". The two number independently, so compare a version only after checking `implementation`. A distribution package revision that sudo-rs appends (e.g., "-0ubuntu1.2") is not included.

os.unix.sudo.title: Sudo binary and runtime metadata
os.unix.sudo.desc: Installed `sudo` binary: where it lives on disk, the version it reports under `sudo -V`, which plugins are loaded (policy, I/O, audit, approval), whether the build supports Python-based plugins, and the result of `visudo -c` against the sudoers configuration. For sudoers configuration parsing, use the `sudoers` resource directly, or access it via this resource's `sudoers` field.

os.unix.sudoers.name: sudoers

alias.name: alias
alias.title: Sudoers alias definition
alias.desc: One alias declaration (User_Alias, Host_Alias, Cmnd_Alias, or Runas_Alias) and the members assigned to it, used to expand aliases referenced in user specifications.

content.name: content
content.title: Raw contents of all sudoers files

default.name: default
default.title: Sudoers default setting
default.desc: One `Defaults` directive from the sudoers configuration, giving the parameter, its value and operation, the scope it applies at, and whether it is negated. Covers hardening flags such as env_reset and secure_path.

files.name: files
files.title: List of files that make up the sudoers configuration

userSpec.name: userSpec
userSpec.title: Sudoers user specification (permission entry)
userSpec.desc: Single sudoers permission rule: which users, on which hosts, may run which commands, as which run-as users/groups, under which tags (e.g. NOPASSWD). The building block for auditing privilege grants.

os.unix.sudoers.title: sudo authorization configuration
os.unix.sudoers.desc: User specifications, defaults, and aliases parsed across the sudoers files (/etc/sudoers plus /etc/sudoers.d). Use userSpecs to audit who may run which commands as which users, and defaults to check hardening settings such as env_reset, secure_path, requiretty, and NOPASSWD grants. Point at an alternate root file with the `path` argument.

os.unix.sysrc.name: sysrc

content.name: content
content.title: Raw contents of all rc.conf files

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed key-value entries from all rc.conf files

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Single rc.conf variable entry
entry.desc: One variable assignment from an rc.conf file: its `name`, `value`, and the `file` it was defined in. The source file matters because a setting in rc.conf.local overrides the same name in rc.conf.

files.name: files
files.title: List of rc.conf files that make up the configuration

os.unix.sysrc.title: FreeBSD rc.conf system configuration
os.unix.sysrc.desc: FreeBSD service and system configuration merged from rc.conf and rc.conf.local. The `entries` accessor exposes each variable assignment as a structured name/value pair (with the file it came from), so audits can assert on individual settings such as sshd_enable or a firewall being turned on. `content` returns the concatenated raw text. Point at a specific file with `sysrc(path: "...")`.

os.unix.zfs.name: zfs

dataset.name: dataset
dataset.title: ZFS dataset (filesystem, volume, snapshot, or bookmark)
dataset.desc: Single ZFS dataset: full `name`, `type` (filesystem, volume, snapshot, bookmark), used/available/referenced bytes, `mountpoint`, compression algorithm and ratio, `mounted` flag, record size, quota, reservation, `origin` snapshot for clones, creation time, encryption algorithm, full `properties` map, and `snapshots` list. Initialize by name or iterate from `zfs.datasets`.

datasets.name: datasets
datasets.title: All ZFS datasets (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, bookmarks)

pool.name: pool
pool.title: ZFS storage pool
pool.desc: Single ZFS storage pool: `name`, `guid`, health status, total/allocated/free bytes, fragmentation percentage, space utilization, deduplication ratio, read-only flag, auto-expand/replace/trim settings, the top-level `vdevs` topology, and the full `properties` map. Initialize by name (e.g., `zfs.pool(name: "tank")`) or iterate from `zfs.pools`.

version.name: version
version.title: ZFS version string
version.desc: The OpenZFS release, for example `zfs-2.2.2-1`. ZFS on Linux before 0.8 reports the release of its loaded kernel module, for example `zfs-kmod-0.6.5.6-0ubuntu28`. Oracle Solaris names its ZFS release by the pool version instead, for example `53`.

os.unix.zfs.title: ZFS storage pools and datasets
os.unix.zfs.desc: ZFS storage on the host: the installed `version`, the storage `pools` with their health and capacity, and every `dataset` (filesystems, volumes, snapshots, and bookmarks). Iterate to audit pool health, free capacity, vdev topology, and dataset properties such as compression and encryption.

os.update.name: os.update

restart.name: restart
restart.title: Whether a restart is required to complete the update

os.update.title: Operating system update information
os.update.desc: Single pending OS update: its name, category, severity, whether it requires a restart, and the package format it belongs to. Read from `os.updates` to audit patch state and prioritize outstanding updates by severity.

os.windows.name: os.windows

asset.name: asset
asset.title: Asset this root belongs to
asset.desc: Platform, version, identity and labels of the asset this root describes.

auditpol.name: auditpol
auditpol.title: Windows audit policies
auditpol.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language and supports looking up a single subcategory by name or GUID.

iis.name: iis
iis.title: Internet Information Services web server
iis.desc:
IIS installation on a Windows host: the websites it serves, the application pools that run them, and the configuration in force at each level. Values are reported as IIS resolves them, after machine.config, the root web.config, applicationHost.config, location sections, a site's own web.config and a nested application's web.config have all been applied in order. A setting a site or application overrides therefore reads with the overriding value, not the one applicationHost.config declares.

On a host that does not run IIS, `installed` is false, `config` and `applicationHost` are null, and `sites` and `appPools` are empty. An empty list satisfies `all()`, so a check that iterates sites needs a `iis.sites.length > 0` guard or an `iis.installed` filter to avoid passing on a host that serves nothing.

mount.name: mount
mount.title: Mount table
mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

powershell.name: powershell
powershell.title: Result of running a PowerShell script on the system
powershell.desc: Ad-hoc PowerShell execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a script string; the resource executes the script via PowerShell on the asset and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. The Windows and cross-platform-PowerShell counterpart to `command` for assertions that need PowerShell-only surface area.

registrykey.name: registrykey
registrykey.title: Windows registry key
registrykey.desc: A Windows registry key selected by `path`, exposing its value entries (`items`), child key names (`children`), and whether the key `exists`. Optionally read a specific user's per-user registry (HKCU) by supplying `userSid`, falling back to their `NTUSER.DAT` profile hive (`ntuserDat`) when that hive is not currently loaded. Select a key with `registrykey(path: "...")`.

secpol.name: secpol
secpol.title: Windows local security policy
secpol.desc: Windows local security policy exported via secedit, broken into four maps. `systemaccess` covers password and account-lockout settings (for example MinimumPasswordLength, LockoutBadCount); `eventaudit` holds the legacy audit categories; `registryvalues` exposes security-relevant registry-backed policies; and `privilegerights` maps each user right (for example SeDenyNetworkLogonRight) to the accounts granted it. These are the primary source for CIS-style local policy benchmarks.

windows.name: windows
windows.title: Windows-specific operating system surfaces
windows.desc: Windows host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: consolidated `computerInfo`, installed `hotfixes`, Server roles and features, image `optionalFeatures`, attached `disks`, scheduled tasks, and hardening controls (Device Guard, Exploit Protection, SmartScreen). A starting point for Windows-specific audits.

os.windows.title: Operating system information for Windows platforms
os.windows.desc: Extends `os.base` with the facilities only Windows provides: the `windows` surface itself (hotfixes, features, firewall profiles, and the rest), the registry, local security and audit policy, and IIS.

os.windows.auditpol.name: auditpol

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Windows audit policy entry
entry.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy.subcategory, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language. This entry carries the subcategory name, GUID, inclusion setting, and exclusion setting as reported by the system, plus the setting as `success` and `failure` booleans and as the English `setting`, which are the same in every display language.

os.windows.auditpol.title: Windows audit policies
os.windows.auditpol.desc: Deprecated in favor of windows.auditPolicy, which reports subcategory names and categories in English regardless of the OS display language and supports looking up a single subcategory by name or GUID.

os.windows.iis.name: iis

appPool.name: appPool
appPool.title: IIS application pool
appPool.desc: The worker process configuration a site or application runs under: the identity it runs as, when it recycles, and how it reacts to repeated failures. The `name` field selects a pool, for example the "DefaultAppPool" that a stock installation ships.

appPools.name: appPools
appPools.title: Application pools defined on this server
appPools.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed.

application.name: application
application.title: Application mounted under an IIS site
application.desc: An application is a configuration boundary: it runs in its own application pool and its web.config overrides what the site and the server declare. The `path` field is the virtual path it is mounted at, "/" for the site root.

applicationHost.name: applicationHost
applicationHost.title: applicationHost.config, for ownership and permission checks
applicationHost.desc:
The shared configuration file as a file, so its permissions and owner can be audited and its raw text read. Its contents are what IIS starts from, not what it ends up with: a setting overridden by a site or an application still reads here with the server-level value. Use `config`, `iis.site.config` and `iis.application.config` for the values in force.

The typed fields leave credentials behind, but this file does not: it can hold encrypted application pool passwords and machine keys, so reading its content returns whatever it holds. Null when IIS is not installed.

binding.name: binding
binding.title: Address, port and protocol an IIS site answers on

config.name: config
config.title: Configuration in force at server scope
config.desc: The defaults every site inherits unless it overrides them, equivalent to the MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST configuration path. This includes the ASP.NET sections: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, but the server-scope configuration resolves the whole inheritance chain, so they read here with the values a site inherits. Null when IIS is not installed.

configuration.name: configuration
configuration.title: IIS configuration in force at one scope
configuration.desc:
The configuration IIS applies at a single point in its hierarchy, after the whole machine.config, root web.config, applicationHost.config, location, site and application chain has been resolved. This is what the server acts on, which is not what any one configuration file says: reading applicationHost.config directly reports a value a site or application may override, and a check written against that file passes on exactly the override it exists to catch.

The `path` field is the IIS configuration path the values were resolved at, for example "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST" for the server or "MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST/Default Web Site" for a site.

A field is null when its section is not declared at this scope. The ASP.NET sections are not such a case: they are declared in machine.config and the root web.config, and every scope here (the server's included) resolves the inheritance chain, so they carry the effective value at each one.

Each field names the section and attribute it resolves. A setting with no field of its own is reachable at the same place through `sections`, which carries every section this scope declares under its full path.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the web server is present on this host
installed.desc: True when the shared configuration file and the IIS management assembly are both present under %windir%\system32\inetsrv. The assembly ships with the web server itself, so this stays true on an installation that omits the optional management scripting tools.

site.name: site
site.title: Website hosted by IIS
site.desc: A single site: its bindings, the application pool it runs under, the applications mounted beneath it, its log settings, and the configuration in force at the site root. The `name` field is the site name as IIS knows it, which is also what identifies the site in its configuration path.

sites.name: sites
sites.title: Websites hosted by this server
sites.desc: Every site defined on the server, running or stopped. Empty when IIS is not installed, which makes `all()` over this list vacuously true; guard on `length` or on `installed`.

version.name: version
version.title: Version reported by the installation, for example "10.0"
version.desc: Empty when IIS is not installed or the version cannot be read.

virtualDirectory.name: virtualDirectory
virtualDirectory.title: Virtual directory of an IIS application

os.windows.iis.title: Internet Information Services web server
os.windows.iis.desc:
IIS installation on a Windows host: the websites it serves, the application pools that run them, and the configuration in force at each level. Values are reported as IIS resolves them, after machine.config, the root web.config, applicationHost.config, location sections, a site's own web.config and a nested application's web.config have all been applied in order. A setting a site or application overrides therefore reads with the overriding value, not the one applicationHost.config declares.

On a host that does not run IIS, `installed` is false, `config` and `applicationHost` are null, and `sites` and `appPools` are empty. An empty list satisfies `all()`, so a check that iterates sites needs a `iis.sites.length > 0` guard or an `iis.installed` filter to avoid passing on a host that serves nothing.

os.windows.mount.name: mount

point.name: point
point.title: Mount point
point.desc: A single mounted filesystem: the backing `device`, the `path` where it is attached, the `fstype`, mount `options`, whether it is currently `mounted`, and the total, used, and available bytes. Select a mount by path, for example `mount.point(path: "/var")`. On Windows the path matches without regard to case or a trailing backslash, so `mount.point(path: "C:")`, `mount.point(path: "c:\\")` and `mount.point(path: os.base.env["SystemDrive"])` all select the `C:\` volume.

os.windows.mount.title: Mount table
os.windows.mount.desc: Every mounted filesystem on the host as a list of `mount.point` entries, each with its backing device, mount path, filesystem type, options, and capacity. Filter it to surface findings such as temporary or removable-media mounts missing `nosuid`, `nodev`, or `noexec` options. On Windows each volume access path is one entry: drive letters (`C:\`), volumes mounted into an NTFS folder (`C:\mnt\data`), and volumes with no access path at their volume GUID path (`\\?\Volume{...}\`), read from the running system. The Windows volume table cannot be read from an image or a mounted disk.

os.windows.powershell.name: powershell

stderr.name: stderr
stderr.title: Standard error output from running the script

stdout.name: stdout
stdout.title: Standard output from running the script

os.windows.powershell.title: Result of running a PowerShell script on the system
os.windows.powershell.desc: Ad-hoc PowerShell execution as an MQL resource. Initialized with a script string; the resource executes the script via PowerShell on the asset and surfaces the captured `stdout`, `stderr`, and `exitcode`. The Windows and cross-platform-PowerShell counterpart to `command` for assertions that need PowerShell-only surface area.

os.windows.registrykey.name: registrykey

children.name: children
children.title: Names of the immediate child keys under this key

items.name: items
items.title: Value entries in this registry key

ntuserDat.name: ntuserDat
ntuserDat.title: Path to the user's NTUSER.DAT hive file
ntuserDat.desc: Optional. Used with `userSid` to read a user's registry when their hive is not currently loaded, for example a SYSTEM scan running with no interactive session. Typically populated from `user.ntuserDat`.

properties.name: properties
properties.title: Properties of the registry key as a name-to-value map
properties.desc: Deprecated in favor of `items`, which returns structured property entries.

property.name: property
property.title: Windows registry key property
property.desc: A single named value within a registry key: the key `path`, value `name`, whether it `exists`, the registry `type` (for example `REG_SZ`, `REG_DWORD`, `REG_BINARY`, or `REG_MULTI_SZ`), and the parsed `data`. Select a specific value by path and name, or iterate from `registrykey.items`.

userSid.name: userSid
userSid.title: SID of the user whose registry hive to read
userSid.desc: Optional. When set, `path` is interpreted relative to that user's per-user registry (HKCU): the loaded `HKEY_USERS\<sid>` hive when the user is logged in, otherwise the profile's `NTUSER.DAT` (see `ntuserDat`) loaded on demand. Leave empty to treat `path` as an absolute registry path.

os.windows.registrykey.title: Windows registry key
os.windows.registrykey.desc: A Windows registry key selected by `path`, exposing its value entries (`items`), child key names (`children`), and whether the key `exists`. Optionally read a specific user's per-user registry (HKCU) by supplying `userSid`, falling back to their `NTUSER.DAT` profile hive (`ntuserDat`) when that hive is not currently loaded. Select a key with `registrykey(path: "...")`.

os.windows.secpol.name: secpol
os.windows.secpol.title: Windows local security policy
os.windows.secpol.desc: Windows local security policy exported via secedit, broken into four maps. `systemaccess` covers password and account-lockout settings (for example MinimumPasswordLength, LockoutBadCount); `eventaudit` holds the legacy audit categories; `registryvalues` exposes security-relevant registry-backed policies; and `privilegerights` maps each user right (for example SeDenyNetworkLogonRight) to the accounts granted it. These are the primary source for CIS-style local policy benchmarks.

os.windows.windows.name: windows

acl.name: acl
acl.title: Windows access control list
acl.desc:
Discretionary access control list of a filesystem object, selected by `path`, for example `windows.acl("C:\\inetpub")` or `windows.acl(path: "C:\\Windows\\System32\\dns")`. Exposes the object's owner and primary group, whether it still inherits permissions from its parent, the security descriptor in SDDL form, and every access control entry with the principal it applies to and the rights it grants or denies.

This is the Windows counterpart of `file.permissions`, which models a POSIX mode and cannot express an access control entry, an inherited permission, or the difference between an owner and a principal. Also reachable as `file.acl` so it composes with `files.find`.

Each entry carries both the raw `rightsMask` and named predicates derived from it (`allowsWrite`, `allowsFullControl`, and so on). Prefer the predicates: the `rights` label is unreliable, since .NET renders a mask containing generic bits as a bare number rather than a name, and a principal granted Modify is a writer whose label does not contain the word Write.

auditPolicy.name: auditPolicy
auditPolicy.title: Windows advanced audit policy
auditPolicy.desc: Effective Windows advanced audit policy: every audit subcategory together with whether success and failure events are audited. Subcategory names and categories are reported in English regardless of the OS display language, so the same audit works unchanged on localized systems. Iterate the subcategories to assert audit coverage, for example `windows.auditPolicy.where(category == "Account Logon").all(success)`, or select a single subcategory with windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.

bitlocker.name: bitlocker
bitlocker.title: Windows BitLocker drive encryption
bitlocker.desc: BitLocker Drive Encryption state across volumes: the encryption, lock, and protection status of each `volume`, plus the BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings under `policy`. Use it to verify that OS and data drives are encrypted and protected.

certificate.name: certificate
certificate.title: Certificate in a Windows certificate store
certificate.desc: Single certificate as it sits in one store: the `store` holding it, the `location` that scopes it to the machine or to one account, its `thumbprint`, and whether the store also holds the matching private key. `store` carries the trust decision rather than the certificate itself. A certificate in Root is trusted as a certification authority, one in Disallowed is explicitly distrusted, and one in TrustedPublisher lets code it signed run without prompting, so the same certificate means different things in different stores. Read `certificate` for the subject, issuer, validity dates and extensions.

certificates.name: certificates
certificates.title: Certificates held in the Windows certificate stores

computerInfo.name: computerInfo
computerInfo.title: A consolidated object of system and operating system properties

defender.name: defender
defender.title: Microsoft Defender Antivirus
defender.desc: Complete runtime status and configuration of Microsoft Defender Antivirus, so policies can assert on every Defender security control. The `status` field exposes the live engine, signature, and protection state reported by Get-MpComputerStatus (real-time protection, behavior monitoring, network inspection, tamper protection, scan ages, and signature freshness). The `preferences` field exposes the configurable policy reported by Get-MpPreference, grouped into scan, real-time, cloud-delivered protection, signature-update, threat-action, controlled-folder-access, network-protection, and remediation settings, plus exclusions and Attack Surface Reduction rules. The `threats` and `threatDetections` fields expose the recorded threat history. On systems without Defender (for example servers running a third-party antivirus) these fields resolve to null rather than failing the query.

deviceGuard.name: deviceGuard
deviceGuard.title: Device Guard policy (Virtualization-Based Security, HVCI, and Credential Guard)

disk.name: disk
disk.title: Disk attached to a Windows computer
disk.desc: A physical or virtual disk as Windows Storage Management reports it through the MSFT_Disk class. Covers identity (`number`, `friendlyName`, `serialNumber`, `uniqueId`), capacity (`size` in bytes), how the disk is attached (`busType`), how it is laid out (`partitionStyle`), whether it holds the boot or system partition, and its offline, read-only, operational, and health state. For example, `windows.disks.where(isBoot).all(size >= 64 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)` checks the capacity of the disk Windows runs from.

disks.name: disks
disks.title: Disks attached to this computer, as reported by Windows Storage Management
disks.desc: Physical and virtual disks from the MSFT_Disk class, the same set that Get-Disk lists: size, bus type, partition style, and whether the disk holds the boot or system partition. `windows.disks.where(isBoot)` selects the disk that holds the running Windows installation.

dnsServer.name: dnsServer
dnsServer.title: Windows DNS Server
dnsServer.desc: Configuration of the Windows DNS Server role: global server settings, recursion, resolver cache hardening, forwarders, root hints, response rate limiting, stale record scavenging, event and debug logging, and every zone the server hosts together with its zone transfer, dynamic update and DNSSEC signing configuration. Backed by the DnsServer PowerShell module, which is read once per scan in a single batched call rather than one call per field. Every field requires the DNS Server role to be installed; gate an audit on `windows.serverFeature(name: "DNS").installed` so the checks do not run on hosts that are not name servers. That gate narrows an audit but does not close it: a host where the role was added and the restart has not happened yet reports the feature as installed while the management module is still absent, and every field here reports an error on such a host rather than a configuration. Complements the client-side `dns` resource in the network provider, which resolves names through the public DNS system and cannot see a server's own configuration.

driver.name: driver
driver.title: Windows kernel or file system driver
driver.desc: Single driver registered with the service control manager: the service `name` it loads under, the on-disk `path` of its image, the `startMode` that decides when it loads, and whether it is currently `running`. `signed` and `signer` carry the Authenticode verdict on the image, which is what a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver audit reads, and `purl` identifies the driver for vulnerability matching in the same pkg:windows-driver namespace as windows.printerDriver.

drivers.name: drivers
drivers.title: Kernel and file system drivers registered on the machine

eventlog.name: eventlog
eventlog.title: Windows Event Log channel configuration
eventlog.desc: Size, retention policy and collection state of a single Windows Event Log channel. The `name` field selects the channel by its log name, for example `windows.eventlog(name: "Security")`, `windows.eventlog(name: "Application")` or a modern provider channel such as `windows.eventlog(name: "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational")`. `maxSizeKB` reports the maximum log file size in KB and `retention` decodes how the channel behaves when that size is reached. `retention` reads the registry alone, so it works on a connection that cannot run commands. `enabled`, `logFilePath`, `isClassicLog` and `recordCount` report the live channel state and need a connection that can run commands.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: Windows Firewall (Advanced Security)
firewall.desc: Windows Firewall with Advanced Security posture: the global settings, the per-profile defaults (Domain, Private, Public), and every configured firewall rule. Use `profiles` to assert that the firewall is enabled and blocks inbound traffic by default on each profile, and `rules` to audit which allow/block rules are active. Backed by the `Get-NetFirewallProfile` and `Get-NetFirewallRule` PowerShell cmdlets, read from the ActiveStore: the effective policy, local configuration merged with Group Policy.

hotfix.name: hotfix
hotfix.title: Windows hotfix
hotfix.desc: Single installed Windows hotfix (a Quick Fix Engineering update): its `hotfixId` (for example "KB5034441"), the `description` type of the fix, the knowledge-base `caption` URL, the `installedOn` date, and the account that installed it. Audit patch compliance across `windows.hotfixes`, for example `windows.hotfixes.where(installedOn > time.now - 30*time.day)`.

logonSession.name: logonSession
logonSession.title: Windows logon session
logonSession.desc: Single active logon session as the Local Security Authority reports it: the `logonType` that created it, the `authenticationPackage` that authenticated it, the account it runs as, and when it started. `logonType` and its readable form `logonTypeName` carry most of the audit value, since a session's type says how it was established: 10 is an incoming Remote Desktop logon, 3 is a network logon, and 9 is a session created with alternate credentials. `authenticationPackage` reports whether the session was authenticated with Kerberos or fell back to NTLM.

lsa.name: lsa
lsa.title: Windows Local Security Authority (LSA) security policy
lsa.desc: Local Security Authority configuration that backs the "Network access", "Network security", and related security options under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. These values control anonymous access restrictions, blank-password use, LAN Manager authentication level, NTLM hashing, LSA protection (RunAsPPL), and audit behavior, including whether the system halts when it cannot write security audits. On/off settings are exposed as booleans and graded settings (such as the LAN Manager authentication level) as integers. NTLM (MSV1_0 and WDigest) settings are grouped under `ntlm` and the Netlogon secure-channel settings under `secureChannel`.
