The FIPS algorithm policy, the Kerberos supported encryption types, the LDAP signing and channel-binding requirements, and the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) minimum password length limit are read from their own keys and exposed directly on this resource. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, letting checks assert on configured-vs-default precisely.

optionalFeature.name: optionalFeature
optionalFeature.title: Windows optional feature (desktop-only)
optionalFeature.desc: Windows optional feature reported by `Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online`, the desktop equivalent of server roles. Select one by its feature name, for example `windows.optionalFeature(name: "SMB1Protocol")`, to check whether a legacy or risky feature (such as SMBv1, Telnet client, or PowerShell v2) is turned on. `enabled` is the simple boolean; `state` carries the underlying DISM feature state for more granular checks.

optionalFeatures.name: optionalFeatures
optionalFeatures.title: Information about optional features in a Windows image.

powershell.name: powershell
powershell.title: Windows PowerShell logging policy
powershell.desc: PowerShell logging settings configured via Group Policy under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell: Script Block Logging, Module Logging, Transcription, and the machine execution policy, together with the system lockdown state that decides the session language mode. The policy settings are GPO-only values with no effective fallback, so when a value is absent the corresponding field is null, which is distinguishable from an explicit 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

printerDrivers.name: printerDrivers
printerDrivers.title: Print drivers registered with the Windows spooler
printerDrivers.desc: Print drivers as the spooler reports them, with the vendor version, the manufacturer, the print environment each is registered under, and the INF the package was installed from. Use it to assert which drivers are present and at which version. Drivers are read from the spooler rather than from installed software, because a driver delivered as an INF/CAB package lands in the driver store and creates no Add/Remove Programs entry, so a software inventory cannot see it while the spooler is still loading it.

rdp.name: rdp
rdp.title: Windows Remote Desktop / Terminal Services configuration
rdp.desc: Effective Remote Desktop (Terminal Services) policy posture: whether Network Level Authentication is required, the negotiated security layer and minimum client encryption level, device and resource redirection toggles, credential handling, and session idle / disconnection time limits. Each field resolves the Group Policy value (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft \Windows NT\Terminal Services) first, then the per-listener configuration (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp), and finally the documented Windows default when neither is set, so audits can assert the effective state without handling missing registry values.

schannel.name: schannel
schannel.title: Windows Schannel TLS configuration
schannel.desc:
Schannel (Secure Channel) TLS cipher-suite, supported-group, and signature-algorithm configuration that backs the Microsoft TLS/SSL stack, read from the effective local Schannel store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Cryptography\Configuration\Local\SSL. The 00010002 subkey holds the ordered cipher-suite list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value and the ordered elliptic-curve / supported-group list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `EccCurves` value, the same list `Get-TlsEccCurve` reports. The 00010003 subkey holds the ordered signature-algorithm list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value. On Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 the supported-group list is where post-quantum ML-KEM key-exchange groups (for example secp256r1_mlkem768) appear once enabled.

When a key or value is absent (the common case on older Windows, on systems using the default order, and on non-Windows platforms) the list accessors resolve to an empty list and pqcKeyExchangeEnabled resolves to false rather than failing.

The protocols, ciphers, hashes, and keyExchangeAlgorithms lists come from the separate per-algorithm override store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL. Windows applies a built-in default to every algorithm that has no override there, and that default differs between Windows releases, so an absent registry value does not mean the algorithm is off. Each list therefore always contains the well-known algorithm names, whether or not the registry mentions them, and reports configured as false with a null enablement for the ones it does not. Write audits against configured and the enablement fields together, for example `windows.schannel.protocols.where(name == "TLS 1.0").all(clientConfigured && clientEnabled == false)`, so a host that never set the value fails instead of passing on a null.

scheduledTask.name: scheduledTask
scheduledTask.title: Windows Task Scheduler task
scheduledTask.desc: Registered task from the Windows Task Scheduler: its identity (`name`, `path`, `uri`), run `state`, whether it is `enabled`, descriptive metadata (`description`, `author`), and the security context it runs under via `principal`. The `actions` it executes, the `triggers` that launch it, and its full `settings` are exposed as nested resources, while `lastRunTime`, `nextRunTime`, `lastTaskResult`, and `missedRuns` report the most recent run-time information. Audit which tasks run, as whom, and on what schedule, for example `windows.scheduledTasks.where(enabled).where(principal.runLevel == "Highest")` surfaces enabled tasks running with the highest available privileges.

security.name: security
security.title: Windows registered security products
security.desc: Antivirus, anti-spyware, and firewall providers registered with the Windows Security Center. Use `products` to verify that an up-to-date, enabled security product is present, for example `windows.security.products.where(type == "antivirus").any(productState == "on")`.

serverFeature.name: serverFeature
serverFeature.title: Windows Server role, role service, or feature
serverFeature.desc: Installable Windows Server component reported by `Get-WindowsFeature`. Select one by its command name, for example `windows.serverFeature(name: "Web-Server")`, to check whether a role such as IIS, DNS, or Hyper-V is present. `installed` is the simple boolean check, while `installState` distinguishes fully installed from removed or available-for-install states.

serverFeatures.name: serverFeatures
serverFeatures.title: Information about Windows Server roles, role services, and features that are available for installation and installed on a specified server.

smb.name: smb
smb.title: Windows SMB (Server Message Block) server
smb.desc: SMB shares published by the host, active inbound client sessions, and outbound connections to other SMB servers, along with the server and client registry hardening configuration and whether the deprecated SMBv1 driver is still enabled. Backed by the `Get-SmbShare`, `Get-SmbSession`, and `Get-SmbConnection` PowerShell cmdlets plus registry reads.

spooler.name: spooler
spooler.title: Windows Print Spooler security configuration
spooler.desc:
Hardening-relevant state of the Windows Print Spooler and printing subsystem. The fields are sourced from the Group Policy printer keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers (and its PointAndPrint, RPC, IPP, and WPP subkeys), the machine-wide HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print key, and the spooler service start configuration under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Spooler. These controls address the PrintNightmare and related spooler vulnerabilities: whether the service is disabled, whether remote RPC is accepted, and how Point-and-Print driver installation is restricted.

Integer settings that are not present in the registry resolve to null so "not configured" is distinguishable from an explicit value of 0 (important because several controls, for example registerRemoteRpcEndpoint == 0, are compliant precisely when set to 0). Boolean settings resolve to their documented Windows default when the value is absent.

telemetry.name: telemetry
telemetry.title: Windows diagnostic data (telemetry) and consumer cloud-content policy
telemetry.desc: Effective Windows privacy and telemetry posture read from the Group Policy keys HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DataCollection and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CloudContent. These are GPO-only DWORD values. The diagnostic data level is a graded integer; the remaining settings are on/off booleans. Every field is nullable so that an absent value (the policy is not configured) is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

tpm.name: tpm
tpm.title: Windows Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
tpm.desc: Trusted Platform Module state: whether a TPM is present, ready for use, enabled, and activated, along with its manufacturer, its major specification version, its dictionary-attack lockout state, and whether Windows provisions it automatically. Presence and a 2.0 specification version are prerequisites for Windows 11 readiness and several BitLocker and device-health controls, and a locked out or unprovisioned TPM is present without being usable. On a system without a TPM the fields resolve cleanly (present is false) rather than erroring.

uac.name: uac
uac.title: Windows User Account Control (UAC) policy
uac.desc: User Account Control settings that back the "User Account Control" security options, read from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, together with the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy value in the same key that governs UAC remote restrictions for local accounts. These control whether Admin Approval Mode is on, how administrators and standard users are prompted for elevation, whether prompts use the secure desktop, installer detection, UIAccess restrictions, file and registry virtualization, and whether remote connections by local administrators receive a filtered token. On/off settings are exposed as booleans, with any non-zero DWORD reading true, and the two prompt behaviors as integers. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, and each field names the Windows default that applies when it is absent. Checks on a setting whose secure state is the default should therefore accept null, for example `windows.uac.localAccountTokenFilterPolicy != true`.

update.name: update
update.title: Windows Update Agent
update.desc: How a Windows host receives updates and what it has applied or has pending. The `config` field surfaces Windows Update Agent configuration and freshness (the effective catalog source, WSUS settings, the last successful detection / download / install times, and whether a reboot is pending). `installed` lists the updates the agent has applied (the installed-KB history), and `available` lists updates the agent has found but not yet installed, answered from the cache of its last detection rather than a live scan. Configuration is read from the registry and works even on connections that cannot run commands; the installed and available collections fall back to the Windows Update Agent COM API when commands are available.

winrm.name: winrm
winrm.title: Windows Remote Management (WinRM)
winrm.desc: Effective WinRM (Windows Remote Management) policy posture for both the WinRM client and service, plus the WinRS remote shell setting and the WinRM service start mode. The client and service settings are read from the Group Policy key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM; these are GPO-only values with no per-listener effective fallback, so when a value is absent the documented Windows default applies. `serviceStartMode` reflects HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinRM\Start. Those fields are read from the registry, so they are available even on connections that cannot run commands. `listeners`, `client.trustedHosts`, `service.ipv4Filter` and `service.ipv6Filter` report the live WS-Management configuration instead and need a connection that can run commands.

os.windows.windows.title: Windows-specific operating system surfaces
os.windows.windows.desc: Windows host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: consolidated `computerInfo`, installed `hotfixes`, Server roles and features, image `optionalFeatures`, attached `disks`, scheduled tasks, and hardening controls (Device Guard, Exploit Protection, SmartScreen). A starting point for Windows-specific audits.

ovs.name: ovs

bridge.name: bridge
bridge.title: Open vSwitch bridge
bridge.desc: One bridge of the local switch, selected by name. The failMode field decides what the bridge does when it loses its controller: `secure` keeps the installed flows and forwards nothing new, `standalone` falls back to acting as a learning switch, which forwards traffic no policy authorised. The datapathType, protocols, stpEnabled, and rstpEnabled fields report how the bridge switches, and externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin or the operator wrote. The ports field returns the ports attached to the bridge.

interface.name: interface
interface.title: Open vSwitch interface
interface.desc: One interface of a port, selected by name. The type field reports how the interface reaches the network: an empty type is a system device, `internal` is the bridge's own device, and `vxlan`, `geneve`, or `gre` is a tunnel whose remote end is in options. The adminState and linkState fields report whether the interface is up, and error carries the reason the switch could not open the device, which is how a misconfigured attachment shows up. externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin wrote, which is what ties the interface back to a pod.

port.name: port
port.title: Open vSwitch port
port.desc: One port of a bridge, selected by name. The vlanMode and vlanTag fields report how the port treats VLAN tags: an access port carries a single tag, a trunk port carries the VLANs listed in trunks, and a port with neither carries every VLAN the bridge sees. tagged is false when no tag is set, so an untagged port is not read as VLAN 0. The interfaces field returns the interfaces the port is built from, which is more than one for a bond.

version.name: version
version.title: Open vSwitch version reported by ovs-vsctl

ovs.title: Open vSwitch
ovs.desc: Software switch configured through the Open vSwitch database on this host. The bridges, ports, and interfaces fields report the switch as it is running now, joined into the topology the datapath uses, which is the dataplane a CNI plugin builds and Kubernetes only records as intent. Empty on hosts where ovs-vsctl is not installed or the database is not reachable.

ovs.bridge.name: ovs.bridge

datapathType.name: datapathType
datapathType.title: Datapath the bridge runs on (system, netdev)

externalIds.name: externalIds
externalIds.title: Tags written into the external_ids column

failMode.name: failMode
failMode.title: Behaviour when the bridge has no controller connection
failMode.desc: `secure` keeps the installed flows, `standalone` falls back to a learning switch. Empty when no fail mode is set, which the switch treats as standalone.

otherConfig.name: otherConfig
otherConfig.title: Settings written into the other_config column

protocols.name: protocols
protocols.title: OpenFlow versions the bridge accepts (for example OpenFlow13)

rstpEnabled.name: rstpEnabled
rstpEnabled.title: Whether Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol is enabled

stpEnabled.name: stpEnabled
stpEnabled.title: Whether Spanning Tree Protocol is enabled

ovs.bridge.title: Open vSwitch bridge
ovs.bridge.desc: One bridge of the local switch, selected by name. The failMode field decides what the bridge does when it loses its controller: `secure` keeps the installed flows and forwards nothing new, `standalone` falls back to acting as a learning switch, which forwards traffic no policy authorised. The datapathType, protocols, stpEnabled, and rstpEnabled fields report how the bridge switches, and externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin or the operator wrote. The ports field returns the ports attached to the bridge.

ovs.interface.name: ovs.interface

adminState.name: adminState
adminState.title: Administrative state reported by the switch (up, down)

bridgeName.name: bridgeName
bridgeName.title: Name of the bridge the interface reaches, empty when no bridge claims it

error.name: error
error.title: Reason the switch could not open the device, empty when it is healthy

externalIds.name: externalIds
externalIds.title: Tags written into the external_ids column

linkState.name: linkState
linkState.title: Link state reported by the switch (up, down)

mtu.name: mtu
mtu.title: Maximum transmission unit of the interface

ofport.name: ofport
ofport.title: OpenFlow port number, -1 when the switch could not assign one

options.name: options
options.title: Type-specific settings, such as the remote_ip of a tunnel

port.name: port
port.title: Port the interface belongs to (null when no port claims it)

portName.name: portName
portName.title: Name of the port the interface belongs to, empty when no port claims it

type.name: type
type.title: Interface type, empty for a system device (internal, vxlan, geneve, gre, patch, ...)

ovs.interface.title: Open vSwitch interface
ovs.interface.desc: One interface of a port, selected by name. The type field reports how the interface reaches the network: an empty type is a system device, `internal` is the bridge's own device, and `vxlan`, `geneve`, or `gre` is a tunnel whose remote end is in options. The adminState and linkState fields report whether the interface is up, and error carries the reason the switch could not open the device, which is how a misconfigured attachment shows up. externalIds carries the tags the CNI plugin wrote, which is what ties the interface back to a pod.

ovs.port.name: ovs.port

bridge.name: bridge
bridge.title: Bridge the port is attached to (null when no bridge claims it)

bridgeName.name: bridgeName
bridgeName.title: Name of the bridge the port is attached to, empty when no bridge claims it

externalIds.name: externalIds
externalIds.title: Tags written into the external_ids column

interfaces.name: interfaces
interfaces.title: Interfaces the port is built from

otherConfig.name: otherConfig
otherConfig.title: Settings written into the other_config column

tagged.name: tagged
tagged.title: Whether a VLAN tag is set on the port
tagged.desc: False means the port carries every VLAN the bridge sees, which is not the same as carrying VLAN 0.

trunks.name: trunks
trunks.title: VLAN IDs a trunk port carries

vlanMode.name: vlanMode
vlanMode.title: VLAN handling of the port (access, native-tagged, native-untagged, trunk)

vlanTag.name: vlanTag
vlanTag.title: VLAN ID of an access port, 0 when no tag is set

ovs.port.title: Open vSwitch port
ovs.port.desc: One port of a bridge, selected by name. The vlanMode and vlanTag fields report how the port treats VLAN tags: an access port carries a single tag, a trunk port carries the VLANs listed in trunks, and a port with neither carries every VLAN the bridge sees. tagged is false when no tag is set, so an untagged port is not read as VLAN 0. The interfaces field returns the interfaces the port is built from, which is more than one for a bond.

package.name: package

arch.name: arch
arch.title: Architecture of this package (e.g., x86_64, arm64, noarch)
arch.desc: On macOS, the architecture of the application's executable: arm64, x86_64, or universal. Empty when it is not a Mach-O binary.

available.name: available
available.title: Latest version the package manager reports as available

cpes.name: cpes
cpes.title: Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) for the package

epoch.name: epoch
epoch.title: Epoch of this package (version-comparison tiebreaker; empty when unset)

files.name: files
files.title: Package-manager records that evidence this package
files.desc:
The file, directory, or database entry the package manager recorded this package in, usually a single record. It is provenance for the package entry, not the list of files the package installed on disk, so it does not answer which package owns a given path.

The record is per-backend:

dpkg      /var/lib/dpkg/info/<name>.list rpm       the rpm database directory, %{_dbpath} apk       /lib/apk/db/installed pacman    the local database entry for the package xbps      the package's own file list, which reports the installed paths pkg       the files the package installed, as `pkg query %Fp` lists them (FreeBSD, DragonFly BSD) macOS     the application bundle path Windows   the install location from the uninstall registry

Empty on package managers with no such record, among them flatpak, snap, homebrew, nix, gentoo, and the NetBSD and OpenBSD package tools.

format.name: format
format.title: Format of this package (e.g., rpm, deb)
format.desc: Empty for an abstract package synthesized from a tool install (see the `package` accessor on tool resources such as `cursor` or `claude.code`): it has no package-manager format and does not appear in `packages`.

installDate.name: installDate
installDate.title: Package install date
installDate.desc:
Time the installed version of the package was placed on this asset. Populated from %{INSTALLTIME} (rpm), the install-date field of the xbps database, the install time in the FreeBSD pkg database, the InstallDate column of the Windows Uninstall registry, and on dpkg from two sources in order. On macOS, the install time in the installer receipt of the package that installed the application: /var/db/receipts for pkg installers and the App Store, /Library/Apple/System/Library/Receipts for Apple packages from Software Update such as XProtect.

On dpkg, first the install, upgrade and `status installed` lines of /var/log/dpkg.log and its rotations. Second, for a package those logs do not mention, the modification time of its file list, /var/lib/dpkg/info/<name>.list or <name>:<arch>.list. dpkg rewrites that file when it unpacks the package, so it holds the time of the last install, upgrade or reinstall, as rpm's install time does. It also moves when a later package takes over one of the package's files, so it can be later than the install but not earlier.

On macOS it is null for applications no receipt claims: the ones that ship with the OS, and those copied into place from a disk image or archive. It is also null when the receipt names another version than the one installed, because the application updated itself after the package was installed. Null on backends with no install-time source at all (apk, pacman) and on any package no source covers.

installScope.name: installScope
installScope.title: Install scope of this package: "machine" or "user"
installScope.desc: "machine" for a package installed system-wide, visible to every user. "user" for one installed into a single user's own profile, which an unattended or SYSTEM-run scan cannot see without reading that user's registry hive directly. Populated for Windows packages read from the Uninstall registry key: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE is "machine"; HKCU or a specific user's hive under HKEY_USERS is "user". Windows appx packages, the .NET Framework runtime, and hotfixes are always "machine", since none of those sources carry per-user attribution. On macOS, "user" for an application inside a user's home directory. Empty on platforms with no such concept. Query-only: not carried into the SBOM output.

installUser.name: installUser
installUser.title: User owning a user-scope install
installUser.desc: Local user a package with `installScope` "user" belongs to: on Windows matched on the installing SID, on macOS on the home directory's owner. Null for machine-scope installs and accounts that no longer exist.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the package is installed

license.name: license
license.title: Package license
license.desc: SPDX license expression (or upstream-reported license string). Eagerly populated where the package manager has it inline (rpm %{LICENSE}, apk APKINDEX, pacman desc, FreeBSD pkg); fetched on demand for dpkg (parses /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/copyright). Empty when no source exists (e.g. Windows registry DisplayName). FreeBSD pkg records its own license names, joined with OR or AND as the package declares, for example `ART10 OR GPLv1+`.

macos.name: macos
macos.title: macOS application details; null for anything that is not a macOS application

name.name: name
name.title: Name of the package
name.desc: On macOS, the application's display name as Finder shows it.

origin.name: origin
origin.title: Package origin, may include version if available (optional)
origin.desc:
Set to "unknown" for an abstract package synthesized from a tool install (see the `package` accessor on tool resources): the installing source could not be identified. A known origin means the package is manager-tracked and listed in `packages`.

The exact meaning is per-backend, so compare it against values you know the backend emits rather than across platforms:

flatpak       the remote it was installed from, e.g. "flathub" freebsd       the ports origin path, e.g. "security/sudo" netbsd        PKGPATH macOS         how the bundle was obtained, as classified by Gatekeeper: "apple", "mac_app_store", "ios_app_store", "identified_developer", or "unknown"

On macOS this distinguishes App Store installs from everything else, which matters when choosing an update path: an App Store app cannot be upgraded with `brew upgrade`.

outdated.name: outdated
outdated.title: Whether a newer version than the installed one is available

pinned.name: pinned
pinned.title: Whether the package is held at its current version
pinned.desc:
True when the package manager is configured not to upgrade it: a dpkg or opkg hold, a dnf or yum versionlock, or a zypper lock. An outdated package that is pinned is a deliberate state rather than a missed patch, and it will not receive a security update until the pin is released.

Read from the package manager's own files, so it answers the same way on a running host, a container image and a mounted filesystem. Debian's apt preferences are priorities rather than holds and do not set this. False on package managers with no lock mechanism, where it means there is no such thing rather than not checked.

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL (purl) identifier for this package
purl.desc: On macOS, qualifiers present when known: `arch` (for now the host's architecture), `bundle-id`, `team-id`, `app-store=true`, `install-scope=user`.

conf.name: conf
conf.title: PAM (pluggable authentication module) configuration
conf.desc: Aggregate view of the PAM service configuration: one file per service, read from `/etc/pam.d` or, for a service with no file there, from the distribution defaults in `/usr/lib/pam.d` or `/usr/etc/pam.d`, the same order PAM uses. The legacy single-file `/etc/pam.conf` is read only when none of those directories exists. `entries` returns parsed service entries keyed by service, each carrying its type, control, and module; `modules` deduplicates the modules loaded across every service. Used to audit authentication policy, such as which services enforce `pam_faillock` or `pam_pwquality`. `pam.conf("<path>")` reads a single file instead: one whose lines start with the type, as in a pam.d directory or an authselect profile under `/etc/authselect/custom`, or one whose lines start with the service name, as in `/etc/pam.conf`.

module.name: module
module.title: PAM module aggregated view
module.desc:
Single PAM module viewed across every service that loads it. The `params` dict merges `key=value` options from every line that uses this module (last-write-wins per key) so audits like `pam.module("pam_faillock").params["deny"]` work without iterating `pam.conf.entries`. `enabled` is true when any service entry loads the module with a non-skip control.

Initialize by module name (e.g. `pam.module(name: "pam_faillock")`) or iterate `pam.modules` for every distinct module name seen across the parsed PAM configuration.

pam.conf.name: pam.conf

content.name: content
content.title: The raw PAM configuration (across all files)

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed service entries keyed by service name

exists.name: exists
exists.title: Whether PAM configuration is present on the system
exists.desc: True when any of the `/etc/pam.d`, `/usr/lib/pam.d`, or `/usr/etc/pam.d` directories or the `/etc/pam.conf` file exists. Use it to guard PAM audits on hosts that ship no PAM configuration, such as container-optimized OS images.

files.name: files

files.desc: The file PAM loads for each service. A service file in `/etc/pam.d` shadows the one of the same name in `/usr/lib/pam.d` or `/usr/etc/pam.d`, so only the `/etc/pam.d` copy is listed.

modules.name: modules
modules.title: All PAM modules loaded across every service (deduplicated by name)

service.name: service
service.title: PAM service configuration
service.desc: PAM configuration for a single service selected by name, for example `pam.conf.service(name: "su")` or `pam.conf.service(name: "sshd")`. The service is resolved from its `/etc/pam.d/<name>` file, falling back to `/usr/lib/pam.d/<name>` and then `/usr/etc/pam.d/<name>` as PAM does, or from the lines naming it in the legacy single-file `/etc/pam.conf`. `entries` are the parsed lines for that service and `modules` aggregates the modules it loads keyed by name, so audits such as `pam.conf.service(name: "su").modules["pam_wheel"].params["use_uid"]` work without filtering `pam.conf.entries` by file path.

serviceEntry.title: A single entry within a PAM service configuration

services.title: Services configured via PAM

pam.conf.desc: Aggregate view of the PAM service configuration: one file per service, read from `/etc/pam.d` or, for a service with no file there, from the distribution defaults in `/usr/lib/pam.d` or `/usr/etc/pam.d`, the same order PAM uses. The legacy single-file `/etc/pam.conf` is read only when none of those directories exists. `entries` returns parsed service entries keyed by service, each carrying its type, control, and module; `modules` deduplicates the modules loaded across every service. Used to audit authentication policy, such as which services enforce `pam_faillock` or `pam_pwquality`. `pam.conf("<path>")` reads a single file instead: one whose lines start with the type, as in a pam.d directory or an authselect profile under `/etc/authselect/custom`, or one whose lines start with the service name, as in `/etc/pam.conf`.

pam.conf.service.name: pam.conf.service

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed entries for this service, in source order
entries.desc: The lines of the service's own file. An include line is an entry here; `stack` has the lines it brings in.

modules.name: modules
modules.title: Modules this service runs, keyed by canonical module name
modules.desc: Aggregated over `stack`, so modules pulled in through an include are listed. Each value aggregates every entry that loads the module (last-write-wins per option), so `modules["pam_wheel"].params["use_uid"]` and `modules["pam_wheel"].enabled` answer module-level questions without iterating `stack`.

path.name: path
path.title: Path of the configuration file the service is defined in
path.desc: `/etc/pam.d/<name>` on systems that use the pam.d directory, `/usr/lib/pam.d/<name>` or `/usr/etc/pam.d/<name>` when the service has only a distribution default, or `/etc/pam.conf` when the service comes from the legacy single file. Empty when no such service is configured.

stack.name: stack
stack.title: Entries PAM runs for this service, with includes expanded
stack.desc: In order: `@include <file>` brings in every line of the file, and `<type> include <file>` and `<type> substack <file>` bring in the file's lines of that type, nested includes expanded the same way. A relative file name is looked up in the pam.d directories as a service is. Each entry's `service` names the file it came from, such as `/etc/pam.d/common-auth`. An included file that does not exist is an error, since PAM then fails the service.

pam.conf.service.title: PAM service configuration
pam.conf.service.desc: PAM configuration for a single service selected by name, for example `pam.conf.service(name: "su")` or `pam.conf.service(name: "sshd")`. The service is resolved from its `/etc/pam.d/<name>` file, falling back to `/usr/lib/pam.d/<name>` and then `/usr/etc/pam.d/<name>` as PAM does, or from the lines naming it in the legacy single-file `/etc/pam.conf`. `entries` are the parsed lines for that service and `modules` aggregates the modules it loads keyed by name, so audits such as `pam.conf.service(name: "su").modules["pam_wheel"].params["use_uid"]` work without filtering `pam.conf.entries` by file path.

pam.conf.serviceEntry.name: pam.conf.serviceEntry

control.name: control
control.title: Control field (e.g., required, requisite, sufficient, optional, or a bracketed [value=action] expression)

ignoreMissing.name: ignoreMissing
ignoreMissing.title: Whether PAM skips the line silently when its module cannot be loaded
ignoreMissing.desc: True when the type is written with a leading `-`, such as `-auth sufficient pam_sss.so`.

lineNumber.name: lineNumber
lineNumber.title: Line number the entry was read from
lineNumber.desc: Zero-based: the first line of the file is 0. Every other lineNumber in this provider counts from 1, including limits.entry, logrotate.entry, crontab.entry, sudoers and modprobe, so subtract nothing here and add nothing there when comparing against a text editor. The value forms part of the entry's identity, so it is kept as it is rather than renumbered.

options.name: options
options.title: Configuration options for pam service entry

pamType.name: pamType
pamType.title: PAM entry type (e.g., auth, account, password, session)
pamType.desc: Without the leading `-` that marks a line PAM skips silently when the module is missing (see ignoreMissing), so `-session optional pam_systemd.so` has the type `session`. `@include` for an include line.

params.name: params
params.title: Options parsed into key/value pairs
params.desc: `key=value` options become map entries (key lower-cased); bare flags such as `use_uid` map to an empty string, so `params["use_uid"] != null` works as an existence check. When the same key appears more than once the last occurrence wins, matching how PAM evaluates duplicate options. The raw `options` list is retained unchanged.

service.name: service
service.title: Service the entry belongs to
service.desc: The path of the file the line came from, such as `/etc/pam.d/su` or `/usr/lib/pam.d/su`, or the service name in the first column when read from the single-file `/etc/pam.conf`.

pam.conf.serviceEntry.title: A single entry within a PAM service configuration

pam.module.name: pam.module

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether any entry runs the module with a control that acts on its result
enabled.desc: True for `required`, `requisite`, `sufficient`, `optional`, and any bracketed control with an action other than `ignore`, such as `[success=2 default=ignore]` or `[default=die]`. False only when every entry's bracketed control ignores every return value, as `[default=ignore]` or `[success=ignore default=ignore]` do.

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Every service entry that loads this module
entries.desc: The full list across every service file, in source order. Each entry carries its originating `service`, `lineNumber`, `pamType`, `control`, and raw `options` so callers can drill back into the underlying line if `params` aggregation isn't enough.

name.name: name
name.title: Module name as it appears after `<type> <control>`
name.desc: Examples: `pam_unix`, `pam_faillock`, `pam_pwquality`. The `.so` suffix and any leading path are stripped so lookups by short name work consistently.

params.name: params
params.title: All key=value options aggregated across every service entry that loads this module
params.desc: The same option key appearing on multiple lines is last-write-wins in source order (matching how PAM itself evaluates duplicate flags, where the later line wins). Bare options (no `=`) are present in the map with an empty string value so `params["use_authtok"] != null` works as an existence check.

pam.module.title: PAM module aggregated view
pam.module.desc:
Single PAM module viewed across every service that loads it. The `params` dict merges `key=value` options from every line that uses this module (last-write-wins per key) so audits like `pam.module("pam_faillock").params["deny"]` work without iterating `pam.conf.entries`. `enabled` is true when any service entry loads the module with a non-skip control.

Initialize by module name (e.g. `pam.module(name: "pam_faillock")`) or iterate `pam.modules` for every distinct module name seen across the parsed PAM configuration.

polkit.name: polkit

action.name: action
action.title: Polkit action
action.desc: Single privileged operation polkit can gate, parsed from a `.policy` file in the action directories. `id` is the reverse-DNS action name an application checks (for example `org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units`), and the three `allow` fields hold the implicit authorization that applies when no rule overrides it. `allowAny` is the weakest of the three because it covers subjects with no local seat, including remote sessions, so an action with `allowAny == "yes"` needs no authentication from anyone who can reach the D-Bus interface.

actions.name: actions
actions.title: Actions registered in the polkit action directories

adminIdentities.name: adminIdentities
adminIdentities.title: Identities the local authority treats as administrators
adminIdentities.desc: AdminIdentities from /etc/polkit-1/localauthority.conf.d, for example `unix-group:sudo` or `unix-user:root`. Honored only by polkit 0.105 and earlier. On newer releases administrator selection moves into a rule that calls polkit.addAdminRule, which `rules` reports through `adminRule`.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether polkit is present on the system
installed.desc: True when the polkit daemon (polkitd) or its pkaction or pkexec tool is found. Action and rule directories alone do not count, since systemd and other packages ship files into them without polkit. Use it to guard polkit audits on systems that ship no polkit at all, such as minimal cloud images and container bases.

localAuthorityRule.name: localAuthorityRule
localAuthorityRule.title: Local-authority authorization grant (.pkla)
localAuthorityRule.desc: Single section from a `.pkla` file, the ini-format grant mechanism used by polkit 0.105 and earlier. `identities` lists the users or groups the grant applies to and `actions` the action patterns it covers, while the three `result` fields carry the authorization it produces. Higher-numbered directories override lower-numbered ones, and a grant of `resultAny == "yes"` to a broad group such as `unix-group:users` hands that group the action with no authentication. Ignored outright by polkit 0.106 and later, so read `polkit.version` alongside it.

localAuthorityRules.name: localAuthorityRules
localAuthorityRules.title: Grants from the legacy local-authority .pkla files

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Polkit JavaScript authorization rule file
rule.desc: Single `.rules` file from the polkit rule directories. Polkit evaluates these files in lexicographic order by filename and stops at the first rule returning a result other than NOT_HANDLED, so `order` decides which file wins: a file sorting ahead of the distribution defaults overrides them. `file` carries the path, mode, and ownership, which is what a check for a rule file writable by a non-root account reads. Rule bodies are JavaScript and are not evaluated here. `actionIds` and `results` report the identifiers and result values appearing in the body, so an audit can narrow down which files are worth reading.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: JavaScript authorization rules, in the order polkit evaluates them

version.name: version
version.title: Polkit release reported by pkaction
version.desc: For example `0.105` on older distributions or `124` on current ones. Requires command execution, so it is null on backends that expose only a filesystem, such as an image scan.

polkit.title: Polkit authorization framework
polkit.desc: System-wide polkit (formerly PolicyKit) authorization state: the `actions` that privileged operations are registered under, the JavaScript `rules` that decide who may invoke them, the legacy local-authority grants in `localAuthorityRules`, and the `adminIdentities` the local authority treats as administrators. Polkit governs whether an unprivileged session may restart a unit, mount a disk, or install a package, so an over-broad grant is a local privilege escalation path. Read `version` before drawing conclusions: polkit 0.106 and later evaluate the JavaScript rules and ignore `.pkla` files, while earlier releases do the reverse.

conf.name: conf
conf.title: PostgreSQL postgresql.conf file
conf.desc: Settings from the main PostgreSQL configuration file on disk, useful for auditing directives as they are written to the file (before the server has been reloaded), for example to detect drift between the on-disk configuration and a running server. The `include`, `include_if_exists`, and `include_dir` directives are resolved so the fragments they pull in are flattened into a single `params` map. `listenAddresses`, `port`, `sslEnabled`, `sslCertFile`, `sslKeyFile`, `sslCaFile`, `dataDirectory`, `hbaFile`, and `identFile` are convenience views into common directives. Pair with `postgresql.hba` and `postgresql.ident` for the auxiliary configuration files. By default the file is the one a running postmaster or a postgresql systemd unit points at (so a data directory relocated with `Environment=PGDATA=` is found), then the first of the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations; pass an explicit path with `postgresql.conf("/path/to/postgresql.conf")`.

hba.name: hba
hba.title: PostgreSQL pg_hba.conf file
hba.desc: Host-based authentication rules as written on disk. Each non-blank, non-comment line becomes a `postgresql.hba.rule` entry with the file's order preserved (rule matching is first-rule-wins in PostgreSQL, so order is significant). The `include`, `include_if_exists`, and `include_dir` directives (PostgreSQL 16 and later) are resolved, so the rules of an included file appear in place of the directive. Audit the entries to flag insecure `authMethod` values (`trust`, `password`) or overly broad client `address` ranges. `rules` is null when no pg_hba.conf was found. By default the file is the one the server loads: `hba_file` from `postgresql.conf`, or pg_hba.conf in the data directory. Without a postgresql.conf, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. Pass an explicit path with `postgresql.hba(path: "/path/to/pg_hba.conf")`.

ident.name: ident
ident.title: PostgreSQL pg_ident.conf file
ident.desc: User-name mapping rules as written on disk. Mappings translate an external authenticated identity (Kerberos principal, SSL CN, OS username) into a PostgreSQL role for the `ident`, `peer`, `gss`, and `cert` authentication methods. The `include`, `include_if_exists`, and `include_dir` directives (PostgreSQL 16 and later) are resolved. `mappings` is null when no pg_ident.conf was found. By default the file is the one the server loads: `ident_file` from `postgresql.conf`, or pg_ident.conf in the data directory. Without a postgresql.conf, the well-known paths for Debian/Ubuntu and RPM installations are probed. Pass an explicit path with `postgresql.ident(path: "/path/to/pg_ident.conf")`.

action.name: action
action.title: rsyslog output action
action.desc: Destination where rsyslog ships matched log lines. Surfaces modern `action(type="omfwd" target="…" …)` statements, alone or after a filter (`*.* action(…)`, `if … then action(…)`, `& action(…)`), and legacy targets such as `*.* @@host:514` or `:msg, contains, "x" /var/log/x.log`. For a legacy target, `type`, `target`, `protocol`, and `template` come from the token's syntax, and the `$Action*` directives that precede it fill `queue`, `parameters`, and `tlsEnabled`. Use it to confirm that remote forwarding uses TCP with TLS rather than plaintext UDP.

conf.name: conf
conf.title: rsyslog daemon configuration
conf.desc: Effective settings across the main file and included fragments. The `modules`, `inputs`, `actions`, and `rules` fields parse the configuration into structured form so audits can assert on individual statements without regex over raw text. Each entry carries `sourceFile` and `sourceLine` so findings can point back at the fragment that introduced the directive.

input.name: input
input.title: rsyslog input source
input.desc: Configured input, the module instance that pulls log lines into rsyslog. Surfaces both legacy single-directive forms (e.g. `$InputTCPServerRun 514`) and modern RainerScript blocks (`input(type="imtcp" port="514" ruleset="…")`). Use it to audit which listeners are open, on what ports and addresses, and whether network inputs accept TLS.

module.name: module
module.title: rsyslog loaded module
module.desc: Single module load: modern `module(load="imtcp" KeepAlive="on")` or legacy `$ModLoad imtcp`. Modern declarations carry their full parameter dict; legacy declarations carry only the module name (parameters is empty). The module name follows rsyslog conventions: `im*` for inputs, `om*` for outputs, `mm*` for message modifications, `pm*` for parsers.

rule.name: rule
rule.title: rsyslog selector rule
rule.desc:
Selector-based `<facility>.<severity> <target>` routing rule, the form that ships in every default rsyslog config. The target is a legacy token or an `action(…)` statement. Filters without a selector (`if … then …`, `:property, …`) have no rule; their actions are in `rsyslog.conf.actions`.

Selector grammar covered:
- Simple: `auth.info /var/log/auth.log`
- Facility list: `auth,authpriv.* /var/log/auth.log`
- Multi-selector: `*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none /var/log/messages` (each selector becomes its own rule)
- Negation: `auth,authpriv.none` → `negate = true`
- Wildcards: `*.*` and `auth.*`

ruleset.name: ruleset
ruleset.title: rsyslog ruleset
ruleset.desc: A named set of rules and actions that processes messages from the inputs bound to it. Statements outside any `ruleset()` block belong to the default ruleset `RSYSLOG_DefaultRuleset`, which also serves every input without a `ruleset=` binding. The `actions` and `inputs` fields connect listeners to destinations, for example to find where messages received on a network port end up.

rsyslog.action.name: rsyslog.action

condition.name: condition
condition.title: Filter expression that must match for this action to run
condition.desc: The `if` expression or property filter (`:msg, contains, "error"`) as written, joined with the conditions of any enclosing `if` blocks, and negated for an `else` branch. Empty when the action runs for every message that reaches it, or when a selector is its only filter (see rules).

fileCreateMode.name: fileCreateMode
fileCreateMode.title: File creation mode for an omfile action, for example `0640`
fileCreateMode.desc: From the action's `fileCreateMode`, else `module(load="builtin:omfile" fileCreateMode=...)`. A legacy file target uses the most recent `$FileCreateMode` instead, since rsyslog applies that directive to legacy targets only. `0644` when nothing sets it. The mode as configured, before the process umask is applied. Empty for other action types.

fileGroup.name: fileGroup
fileGroup.title: Group of files an omfile action creates
fileGroup.desc: From `fileGroup` (or `fileGroupNum`), resolved like fileCreateMode. Empty when not set.

fileOwner.name: fileOwner
fileOwner.title: Owner of files an omfile action creates
fileOwner.desc: From `fileOwner` (or `fileOwnerNum`), resolved like fileCreateMode. Empty when not set, in which case files are owned by the user rsyslogd runs as.

isRemote.name: isRemote
isRemote.title: Whether this action delivers messages to another host
isRemote.desc: True for network output modules: omfwd, omrelp, omhttp, omkafka, omelasticsearch, omgssapi, omudpspoof, omamqp1, omrabbitmq, omazureeventhubs, omclickhouse, omhiredis, ommongodb, ommysql, ompgsql, omlibdbi, omsnmp, and ommail.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: All parameters as a dict
parameters.desc: Modern actions carry every key/value pair other than `type` and the `queue.*` settings, with lowercase keys. Legacy targets carry `action.resumeretrycount` from `$ActionResumeRetryCount`, and TCP forwards the `$ActionSendStreamDriver*` settings in effect (`streamdrivermode`, `streamdriverauthmode`, ...).

port.name: port
port.title: Port a network action connects to
port.desc: From `port=` or the legacy `@@host:port`. omfwd and omrelp default to 514 when no port is given; 0 for actions that are not network actions.

protocol.name: protocol
protocol.title: Transport protocol for network actions: `"tcp"`, `"udp"`, or empty

queue.name: queue
queue.title: Action-level queue configuration, empty when no queue is configured
queue.desc: Carries the modern `queue.*` parameters as `{type, filename, size, saveonshutdown, ...}` (the exact key set depends on the queue type). For a legacy target, the `$ActionQueue*` directives just before it (`$ActionQueueType LinkedList` becomes `type`).

resumeRetryCount.name: resumeRetryCount
resumeRetryCount.title: Number of times a suspended action is retried before messages are dropped
resumeRetryCount.desc: From `action.resumeRetryCount` or the legacy `$ActionResumeRetryCount`. `-1` retries forever. Null when not configured, in which case rsyslog does not retry.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: Selector rules that route messages to this action

sourceFile.name: sourceFile
sourceFile.title: Absolute path of the file this directive was read from

streamDriver.name: streamDriver
streamDriver.title: Stream driver a TCP forward uses, for example `gtls` or `ossl`
streamDriver.desc: From the action's `StreamDriver`, the legacy `$ActionSendStreamDriver`, or the global `DefaultNetstreamDriver`, in that order. Empty for UDP forwards, other action types, and when none of these is set (plain TCP).

streamDriverAuthMode.name: streamDriverAuthMode
streamDriverAuthMode.title: Peer authentication mode a TCP forward's stream driver uses
streamDriverAuthMode.desc: For example `x509/name`, `x509/fingerprint`, `x509/certvalid`, or `anon`. From the action's `StreamDriverAuthMode` or the legacy `$ActionSendStreamDriverAuthMode`. Empty when not set, in which case the stream driver applies its own default.

target.name: target
target.title: Destination of the action
target.desc: For omfile a filesystem path; for omfwd a `host` or `host:port`; for omusrmsg a comma-separated user list (or `*` for wall); for omhttp / omkafka the relevant URL or broker list. Legacy prefixes such as `@@`, `-`, `|`, and `:omrelp:` are removed.

template.name: template
template.title: Template name applied to messages, empty when the default is used

tlsEnabled.name: tlsEnabled
tlsEnabled.title: Whether TLS is configured for this action
tlsEnabled.desc: True when the modern form sets `StreamDriverMode="1"`, or when a legacy TCP forward (`@@host`) follows `$ActionSendStreamDriverMode 1` with no `$ResetConfigVariables` in between. Included files count at the point of their include.

type.name: type
type.title: Action module type (e.g. omfwd, omfile, omusrmsg, omhttp, omkafka)

rsyslog.action.title: rsyslog output action
rsyslog.action.desc: Destination where rsyslog ships matched log lines. Surfaces modern `action(type="omfwd" target="…" …)` statements, alone or after a filter (`*.* action(…)`, `if … then action(…)`, `& action(…)`), and legacy targets such as `*.* @@host:514` or `:msg, contains, "x" /var/log/x.log`. For a legacy target, `type`, `target`, `protocol`, and `template` come from the token's syntax, and the `$Action*` directives that precede it fill `queue`, `parameters`, and `tlsEnabled`. Use it to confirm that remote forwarding uses TCP with TLS rather than plaintext UDP.

rsyslog.conf.name: rsyslog.conf

content.title: Raw contents of this rsyslog service configuration

path.name: path

rules.name: rules
rules.title: Legacy selector-based routing rules (facility.severity → target)

sourceFile.name: sourceFile

users.name: users

users.desc: Each entry carries the access the directive grants and the minimum security level it requires, so audits such as users.none(access == "rw" && securityLevel == "noauth") hold only when no user can write without authentication. snmpd.config.title: Net-SNMP daemon (snmpd) configuration
snmpd.config.desc: snmpd.conf settings that govern SNMP access: community strings, VACM users, and listen addresses. The configuration is assembled the way snmpd reads it: the main snmpd.conf, files pulled in by its includeFile and includeDir directives, snmpd.local.conf in the same directory, and the persistent snmpd.conf under /var/lib/snmp. A missing configuration yields empty accessors, so audits such as rwCommunities == [] hold trivially on hosts that don't run snmpd.

cortex.title: Snowflake Cortex Code instance
cortex.desc: Snowflake Cortex Code, Snowflake's AI coding assistant, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. conf.name: conf

conf.desc: Parsed Squid configuration covering directives, access control lists, listen ports, cache peers, cache directories, refresh patterns, authentication parameters, and access logs from `squid.conf` together with every fragment pulled in by `include` directives. physicalFunction.name: physicalFunction
physicalFunction.title: SR-IOV physical function
physicalFunction.desc: Network interface that supports SR-IOV, selected by its interface name. The numVfs and totalVfs fields report how many virtual functions are enabled against how many the hardware supports, so an interface with numVfs of 0 is capable but unused. The pciAddress, vendorId, deviceId, and driver fields identify the device the way a device-plugin selector does, and macAddress, mtu, and operationalState report the link. The virtualFunctions field returns the virtual functions carved out of this interface.

virtualFunction.name: virtualFunction
virtualFunction.title: SR-IOV virtual function
virtualFunction.desc: One virtual function of an SR-IOV capable interface, selected by its PCI address. The driver field reports what the function is bound to, and usesPassthroughDriver marks a function handed to a userspace datapath such as DPDK, which leaves it with no kernel network interface and therefore outside host packet filtering. The spoofChecking, trusted, macAddress, vlanId, and rate fields report the configuration the physical function enforces on the guest, which is the part a workload cannot override. linkConfigured is false when the kernel reports no configuration for the function, so an unreported function is not read as an unprotected one.

virtualFunctions.name: virtualFunctions
virtualFunctions.title: Virtual functions across every physical function

sriov.title: SR-IOV network devices
sriov.desc: Single-root I/O virtualization state of the host's network hardware. The physicalFunctions field lists every SR-IOV capable interface with the number of virtual functions it has enabled against the number it supports, and virtualFunctions flattens every virtual function across all of them. This is the realised hardware inventory, so it shows the PCI address, the bound driver, and the per-device link settings that a Kubernetes device plugin only reports as an aggregate count. Empty on hosts with no SR-IOV capable interface.

config.desc: OpenSSH server settings parsed from sshd_config (and any Include files), plus the effective values reported by `sshd -T`. Surfaces `ciphers`, `macs`, `kexs`, and `hostkeyalgorithms` for cryptographic hardening checks, `permitRootLogin` for root-access policy, and `blocks` for the conditional Match blocks. Compare the configured values (`ciphers`) against the effective ones (`effectiveCiphers`) to catch overrides applied at runtime. implementation.desc: "sudo" is the C implementation from sudo.ws. "sudo-rs" is the Rust reimplementation that recent Ubuntu releases install as `sudo`. It reads the same sudoers files but supports a subset of the options, has no plugins, and rejects settings such as `logfile`, `log_input`, `log_output`, and `requiretty`. content.title: Raw contents of all rc.conf files

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Parsed key-value entries from all rc.conf files

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Single rc.conf variable entry
entry.desc: One variable assignment from an rc.conf file: its `name`, `value`, and the `file` it was defined in. The source file matters because a setting in rc.conf.local overrides the same name in rc.conf.

files.name: files
files.title: List of rc.conf files that make up the configuration

sysrc.title: FreeBSD rc.conf system configuration
sysrc.desc: FreeBSD service and system configuration merged from rc.conf and rc.conf.local. The `entries` accessor exposes each variable assignment as a structured name/value pair (with the file it came from), so audits can assert on individual settings such as sshd_enable or a firewall being turned on. `content` returns the concatenated raw text. Point at a specific file with `sysrc(path: "...")`.

sysrc.entry.name: sysrc.entry

file.name: file
file.title: File where this entry is defined

sysrc.entry.title: Single rc.conf variable entry
sysrc.entry.desc: One variable assignment from an rc.conf file: its `name`, `value`, and the `file` it was defined in. The source file matters because a setting in rc.conf.local overrides the same name in rc.conf.

boot.name: boot
boot.title: systemd-boot bootloader state
boot.desc: State of the systemd-boot bootloader: whether it is `installed` on the EFI system partition, whether it is `active`, meaning it is what booted this host, the `version` it reports, the `espPath` and `bootPath` it was found at, and the `selectedEntry` the host booted from. `installed`, `version`, `espPath` and `bootPath` are read from the files on the EFI system partition, so they resolve on an image or a mounted filesystem. `active` and `selectedEntry` are read from the EFI variables systemd-boot sets as it runs, so they are null where no booted system can be observed. Useful for asserting which bootloader a host boots with, and for finding a second bootloader left installed beside the one in use.

coredump.name: coredump
coredump.title: systemd-coredump core dump handling
coredump.desc: Core dump handling by systemd-coredump: whether it is `active`, meaning the kernel hands core dumps to it, and the effective `storage`, `processSizeMax` and `externalSizeMax` settings merged the way systemd merges them from coredump.conf and every coredump.conf.d drop-in under /etc, /run, /usr/local/lib and /usr/lib. The contributing `files` and the merged raw `params` are exposed too. Useful for asserting that core dumps are neither stored nor processed, for example `systemd.coredump.storage == "none" && systemd.coredump.processSizeMax == 0`.

resolved.name: resolved
resolved.title: systemd-resolved DNS resolver state
resolved.desc: Global DNS resolution configuration provided by systemd-resolved: whether the daemon is `active`, the effective DNS servers (`dns`) and `fallbackDns`, search `domains`, DNSSEC and DNS-over-TLS modes, LLMNR and multicast-DNS settings, the resolv.conf mode, and whether caching is enabled. Backed by `resolvectl status` (`systemd-resolve --status` before systemd 239) for the Global scope, with what that report leaves out read from resolved.conf and its drop-ins. Useful for asserting that DNSSEC or DNS-over-TLS is enforced.

socket.name: socket
socket.title: systemd socket unit
socket.desc: Single socket-activated unit, selected by name (e.g., `systemd.socket(name: "sshd")`). Exposes the listen addresses/ports, the service it activates, and enable/mask/run state, so you can audit which sockets expose network services.

sockets.name: sockets
sockets.title: All systemd socket units on the system
sockets.desc: Collection of every socket-activated unit, for listen-address and activation-target audits.

target.name: target
target.title: systemd target unit
target.desc: Single systemd target: its load state, active state, the unit file's enabled/disabled state, fragment path on disk, and the dependency lists (`wants`, `requires`, `after`, `before`) that determine which other units the target pulls in or orders around. Iterated from `systemd.targets`.

targets.name: targets
targets.title: All systemd target units on the system
targets.desc: Collection of every target unit, for auditing boot ordering, the default target, and dependency wiring.

timer.name: timer
timer.title: systemd timer unit
timer.desc: Single systemd timer, selected by name (e.g., `systemd.timer(name: "logrotate")`). Exposes the schedule, the unit it activates, enable/mask/static state, and whether it is currently running, so you can audit scheduled maintenance and update jobs.

timers.name: timers
timers.title: All systemd timer units on the system
timers.desc: Collection of every timer, for filtering by schedule, activation target, or status.

timesyncd.name: timesyncd
timesyncd.title: systemd-timesyncd NTP client state
timesyncd.desc: SNTP client state provided by systemd-timesyncd: whether the daemon is `active`, whether the system clock is currently `synchronized`, the configured `servers` and `fallbackServers`, the currently selected NTP `serverName` and `serverAddress`, the current poll interval, and the leap-second status. Only a running daemon reports its servers, poll interval and leap status, so those fields are null while systemd-timesyncd is not active. Useful for asserting that time is synchronized to an approved source.

unit.name: unit
unit.title: systemd unit execution and sandboxing settings
unit.desc: Single systemd unit with the execution and confinement settings from its unit file and drop-ins, selected by full name including the suffix (e.g. `systemd.unit(name: "sshd.service")`). `user` and the `protect`, `private`, and `restrict` settings describe how much of the host the unit can reach: a unit running as root with `noNewPrivileges` false and `protectSystem` set to `no` has the whole system available to it once the service is compromised. `capabilityBoundingSet` and `systemCallFilter` narrow that further, and `fragmentPath` locates the unit file the values came from. These settings belong to units that start a process, so they are empty for a unit type that does not, such as a target.

units.name: units
units.title: All systemd service units on the system
units.desc: Collection of every service unit with its execution and confinement settings. Service units are the ones that start a process and so the ones these settings apply to; a socket, timer, or target is reached through `systemd.socket`, `systemd.timer`, and `systemd.target` instead. Filter it to find daemons running unconfined, for example `systemd.units.where(user == "" && noNewPrivileges == false)`.

systemd.boot.name: systemd.boot

active.name: active
active.title: Whether systemd-boot booted this host
active.desc: True when the running system was booted by systemd-boot, which the bootloader states in an EFI variable as it hands control to the kernel. Null where no EFI variables are readable, such as an image or filesystem scan, since a bootloader that cannot be observed booting is neither in use nor out of use.

bootPath.name: bootPath
bootPath.title: Path the boot entries are read from
bootPath.desc: The extended boot loader partition where the host keeps one, and the EFI system partition otherwise.

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Boot entries the bootloader offers on the next boot
entries.desc: Read from both sources systemd-boot takes entries from: the Boot Loader Specification files under `loader/entries`, and the unified kernel images under `EFI/Linux`, which carry their command line inside the image and have no entry file at all. Null when neither source yields an entry, since a host whose boot entries cannot be read has none to report rather than an empty list of them, which would satisfy every assertion made over the entries. Null as well when systemd-boot is neither installed nor booted this host, since the entry files then belong to another boot loader, such as GRUB on the Red Hat family.

entry.name: entry
entry.title: systemd-boot boot entry
entry.desc: Single boot entry, from a Boot Loader Specification file under `loader/entries` or a unified kernel image under `EFI/Linux`. `parameters` and `flags` hold the kernel command line split into key-value directives and bare tokens, so a check can assert on a parameter such as audit without matching text. `cmdline` keeps the command line as it appears and `kernel` names the kernel the entry boots. `bootable` is the distinction a control over boot parameters rests on, since only an entry that boots an operating system carries parameters to audit. `signed` reports whether a unified kernel image carries a signature, which is what Secure Boot verifies.

espPath.name: espPath
espPath.title: Path to the EFI system partition
espPath.desc: Where the bootloaders are installed, which is `/efi`, `/boot` or `/boot/efi`. Empty on a legacy BIOS host, including one that carries an empty `EFI` directory on its root filesystem, and on a scan that cannot read the partition.

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the systemd-boot binary is installed on the EFI system partition
installed.desc: Read from the EFI system partition, so it holds on an image or a mounted filesystem. A host where this is true and `active` is false carries a bootloader it does not boot with.

selectedEntry.name: selectedEntry
selectedEntry.title: Identifier of the boot entry the host booted from
selectedEntry.desc: Names the entry systemd-boot selected, such as `arch.conf` for an entry file or the file name of a unified kernel image. Null where no EFI variables are readable.

version.name: version
version.title: systemd-boot version
version.desc: Version the bootloader states for itself, such as `257.13-1.fc42`, read from the binary on the EFI system partition. Empty when systemd-boot is not installed.

systemd.boot.title: systemd-boot bootloader state
systemd.boot.desc: State of the systemd-boot bootloader: whether it is `installed` on the EFI system partition, whether it is `active`, meaning it is what booted this host, the `version` it reports, the `espPath` and `bootPath` it was found at, and the `selectedEntry` the host booted from. `installed`, `version`, `espPath` and `bootPath` are read from the files on the EFI system partition, so they resolve on an image or a mounted filesystem. `active` and `selectedEntry` are read from the EFI variables systemd-boot sets as it runs, so they are null where no booted system can be observed. Useful for asserting which bootloader a host boots with, and for finding a second bootloader left installed beside the one in use.

systemd.boot.entry.name: systemd.boot.entry

bootable.name: bootable
bootable.title: Whether the entry boots an operating system
bootable.desc: True for a normal or recovery entry, which are the entries a control over kernel parameters applies to. False for a memory test and an entry that boots no kernel at all.

cmdline.name: cmdline
cmdline.title: Kernel command line
cmdline.desc: The options line of an entry file, or the command line built into a unified kernel image.

flags.name: flags
flags.title: Bare kernel command line tokens, such as ro, quiet, or single

initrd.name: initrd
initrd.title: Initrd path
initrd.desc: The initrd line of an entry file. Empty for a unified kernel image, which carries its initrd inside the image.

kernel.name: kernel
kernel.title: Kernel image the entry boots
kernel.desc: The linux line of an entry file, or the kernel release recorded inside a unified kernel image.

kind.name: kind
kind.title: Entry role
kind.desc: One of `normal`, `recovery`, `memtest`, or `other`. `other` covers an entry that boots no kernel, such as one that opens the firmware settings or chainloads another operating system.

parameterValues.name: parameterValues
parameterValues.title: Every value of each kernel command line parameter
parameterValues.desc: Values of each key-value token in command-line order, for a parameter the kernel reads once per occurrence, such as console.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.title: Kernel command line parameters
parameters.desc: Key-value tokens from the kernel command line. When a parameter appears more than once the last occurrence wins, which is how the kernel reads most of them. `parameterValues` keeps every occurrence.

signed.name: signed
signed.title: Whether the image carries a signature
signed.desc: True when a unified kernel image carries an Authenticode signature, which is what Secure Boot verifies before handing over to it. False for an entry file, which points at a kernel it does not itself sign.

source.name: source
source.title: Path of the file the entry was read from

unifiedKernelImage.name: unifiedKernelImage
unifiedKernelImage.title: Whether the entry is a unified kernel image
unifiedKernelImage.desc: A unified kernel image is one signed executable holding the kernel, the initrd and the command line, discovered under `EFI/Linux` rather than declared by an entry file.

systemd.boot.entry.title: systemd-boot boot entry
systemd.boot.entry.desc: Single boot entry, from a Boot Loader Specification file under `loader/entries` or a unified kernel image under `EFI/Linux`. `parameters` and `flags` hold the kernel command line split into key-value directives and bare tokens, so a check can assert on a parameter such as audit without matching text. `cmdline` keeps the command line as it appears and `kernel` names the kernel the entry boots. `bootable` is the distinction a control over boot parameters rests on, since only an entry that boots an operating system carries parameters to audit. `signed` reports whether a unified kernel image carries a signature, which is what Secure Boot verifies.

systemd.coredump.name: systemd.coredump

active.name: active
active.title: Whether systemd-coredump receives the kernel's core dumps
active.desc: True when the kernel core pattern (/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) pipes core dumps to a systemd-coredump binary, false when it names anything else. Null when the core pattern cannot be read, such as on a container image. Inside a container this reflects the host kernel's pattern.

externalSizeMax.name: externalSizeMax
externalSizeMax.title: Maximum size of a core dump saved to disk with external storage, in bytes
externalSizeMax.desc: -1 when set to `infinity` or to a size of 8E or more. Null when no file sets a valid value, in which case systemd applies its compiled default, the same as for `processSizeMax`.

files.name: files
files.title: Configuration files that contribute to the effective settings
files.desc: In the order systemd applies them: the main coredump.conf (the first found in /etc/systemd, /run/systemd, /usr/local/lib/systemd, /usr/lib/systemd), then the coredump.conf.d/*.conf drop-ins from those directories sorted by file name. A drop-in in a higher-priority directory masks one with the same name in a lower-priority directory. Empty when no file exists.

params.name: params
params.title: Merged settings of the [Coredump] section
params.desc: Raw values as written, where the last assignment across `files` wins. Values systemd would reject still appear here; the typed fields apply systemd's parsing.

processSizeMax.name: processSizeMax
processSizeMax.title: Maximum size of a core dump that is processed, in bytes
processSizeMax.desc: Core dumps above this size get no stack trace, so 0 means none is processed. Sizes accept systemd's base-1024 suffixes (K, M, G, T, P, E); systemd does not accept `infinity` here, and a size of 8E or more reads as -1. Null when no file sets a valid value, in which case systemd applies its compiled default: 32G on 64-bit systems (1G on 32-bit) since systemd 251, 2G on earlier versions.

storage.name: storage
storage.title: Where core dumps are stored
storage.desc: One of `none`, `external` (files in /var/lib/systemd/coredump) or `journal`. The last valid Storage assignment wins; systemd matches the value case-sensitively and ignores anything else. When no file sets it, this is systemd's default, `external`, if systemd-coredump is installed, and null if it is not.

systemd.coredump.title: systemd-coredump core dump handling
systemd.coredump.desc: Core dump handling by systemd-coredump: whether it is `active`, meaning the kernel hands core dumps to it, and the effective `storage`, `processSizeMax` and `externalSizeMax` settings merged the way systemd merges them from coredump.conf and every coredump.conf.d drop-in under /etc, /run, /usr/local/lib and /usr/lib. The contributing `files` and the merged raw `params` are exposed too. Useful for asserting that core dumps are neither stored nor processed, for example `systemd.coredump.storage == "none" && systemd.coredump.processSizeMax == 0`.

dns.name: dns
dns.title: Effective DNS server addresses for the Global scope

dnssec.name: dnssec
dnssec.title: DNSSEC mode
dnssec.desc: One of `yes`, `no`, or `allow-downgrade`: the mode the host requests, whether or not the current upstream server supports DNSSEC.

fallbackDns.name: fallbackDns
fallbackDns.title: Fallback DNS servers used when no Link or Global DNS is configured

systemd.resolved.title: systemd-resolved DNS resolver state
systemd.resolved.desc: Global DNS resolution configuration provided by systemd-resolved: whether the daemon is `active`, the effective DNS servers (`dns`) and `fallbackDns`, search `domains`, DNSSEC and DNS-over-TLS modes, LLMNR and multicast-DNS settings, the resolv.conf mode, and whether caching is enabled. Backed by `resolvectl status` (`systemd-resolve --status` before systemd 239) for the Global scope, with what that report leaves out read from resolved.conf and its drop-ins. Useful for asserting that DNSSEC or DNS-over-TLS is enforced.

systemd.socket.name: systemd.socket

accept.name: accept
accept.title: Whether the socket accepts connections (inetd-style, one service instance per connection)

activates.name: activates
activates.title: The unit that this socket activates (e.g., "dbus.service")

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether the socket is enabled (starts at boot)

installed.name: installed
installed.title: Whether the socket unit file is installed

listenAddresses.name: listenAddresses
listenAddresses.title: Addresses, paths, or ports this socket listens on

masked.name: masked
masked.title: Whether the socket is masked (symlinked to /dev/null so it cannot start)

name.name: name
name.title: Name of the socket unit (without .socket suffix)

running.name: running
running.title: Whether the socket is currently active

static.name: static
static.title: Whether the socket is static (unit file has no [Install] section)

systemd.socket.title: systemd socket unit
systemd.socket.desc: Single socket-activated unit, selected by name (e.g., `systemd.socket(name: "sshd")`). Exposes the listen addresses/ports, the service it activates, and enable/mask/run state, so you can audit which sockets expose network services.

systemd.sockets.name: systemd.sockets
systemd.sockets.title: All systemd socket units on the system

procSubset.name: procSubset

procSubset.desc: Either `all` or `pid`, where `pid` hides the entries in /proc that are not processes.

systemCallFilterIsDenylist.name: systemCallFilterIsDenylist

umask.name: umask
umask.title: File mode creation mask the unit starts with (UMask, e.g. 0022)

unitFileState.name: unitFileState
unitFileState.title: Unit file state (e.g., enabled, disabled, static, masked)

user.name: user

systemd.unit.title: systemd unit execution and sandboxing settings
systemd.unit.desc: Single systemd unit with the execution and confinement settings from its unit file and drop-ins, selected by full name including the suffix (e.g. `systemd.unit(name: "sshd.service")`). `user` and the `protect`, `private`, and `restrict` settings describe how much of the host the unit can reach: a unit running as root with `noNewPrivileges` false and `protectSystem` set to `no` has the whole system available to it once the service is compromised. `capabilityBoundingSet` and `systemCallFilter` narrow that further, and `fragmentPath` locates the unit file the values came from. These settings belong to units that start a process, so they are empty for a unit type that does not, such as a target.

systemd.units.name: systemd.units

systemd.units.desc: Collection of every service unit with its execution and confinement settings. Service units are the ones that start a process and so the ones these settings apply to; a socket, timer, or target is reached through `systemd.socket`, `systemd.timer`, and `systemd.target` instead. Filter it to find daemons running unconfined, for example `systemd.units.where(user == "" && noNewPrivileges == false)`.

packages.name: packages
packages.title: Terraform dependency inventory (SBOM cataloger)
packages.desc:
The providers and modules a Terraform workspace depends on. Three sources are read and merged: `.terraform.lock.hcl` for the provider versions `terraform init` resolved, the `*.tf` files for the modules the configuration calls and the providers it requires, and `.terraform/modules/modules.json` for what init actually installed. A dependency stated in more than one of them is reported once, at the most precise version available.

Note: the terraform.* namespace is also used by the dedicated Terraform provider for IaC resource scanning. These SBOM resources inventory dependencies; they do not analyze Terraform configuration.

tomcat.title: Apache Tomcat
tomcat.desc:
Locates a Tomcat installation through CATALINA_HOME / CATALINA_BASE and exposes its on-disk configuration: server.xml, the global web.xml and context.xml, catalina.properties, logging.properties, tomcat-users.xml, and the applications deployed under each Host's appBase. Nothing here needs a running JVM, so it also works against container images and filesystem snapshots.

Every nested collection (services, connectors, engines, hosts, valves, realms, listeners, contexts, users, webapps) is a list whenever the element is present — including when the XML holds exactly one — and an empty list when it is absent. It is never null and never a bare map, so a check written against a single-Connector server keeps working when a second Connector is added.

Pass `init(home: "...", base: "...")` to point at a non-default layout.
