sha256.desc: Hex-encoded SHA-256 digest of content, for detecting drift or pinning a known-good skill definition against a baseline.

source.name: source
source.title: Filesystem path to the SKILL.md file that defines the skill

trae.skill.title: Trae skill
trae.skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for the Trae agent. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

ufw.name: ufw

application.name: application
application.title: UFW application profile from /etc/ufw/applications.d/
application.desc: Named application profile that maps a service to the ports it needs, so UFW rules can reference it by name instead of listing ports. Each profile carries a `name` (for example "Nginx Full"), a human-readable `title` and `description`, and the `ports` specification it opens.

defaultRouted.name: defaultRouted
defaultRouted.title: Default policy for routed (forwarded) traffic
defaultRouted.desc: Read from DEFAULT_FORWARD_POLICY in /etc/default/ufw and reported with UFW policy names: "deny" for DROP, "allow" for ACCEPT, or "reject". This is the configured policy, so it never returns "disabled" or the raw iptables name "drop", even though `ufw status verbose` prints `disabled (routed)` while IP forwarding is off in the kernel. Compare against "deny" for a hardened stance, and read `kernel.parameters["net.ipv4.ip_forward"]` to check forwarding itself.

logging.name: logging
logging.title: Logging level (off, low, medium, high, full)

rule.name: rule
rule.title: Individual UFW rule
rule.desc: Single UFW rule as reported by `ufw status`, covering the action taken, the traffic direction, and the addresses, ports, protocol, and interface it matches. The `action` (ALLOW, DENY, REJECT, LIMIT), `direction`, and `port`/`from`/`to` fields together describe what the rule permits or blocks; `ipv6` flags IPv6 rules, and `raw` preserves the original text.

rules.name: rules
rules.title: All UFW rules
rules.desc: Read from user.rules and user6.rules in /etc/ufw on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/lib/ufw on Fedora and EPEL.

status.name: status
status.title: Whether UFW is active ("active", "inactive", "not installed")
status.desc: "not installed" when neither the ufw command nor ufw-init is present, including a package that was removed but not purged and left /etc/ufw/ufw.conf behind. The command is looked up in /usr/sbin, /sbin, and /usr/local/sbin, where the upstream tarball installs it. Where commands can run, "active" means the ufw rules are loaded, as `ufw status` reports, not only that ufw.conf sets ENABLED=yes. Fedora and EPEL ship ENABLED=yes on a firewall that was never enabled. Asking ufw needs root. Image scans read ENABLED from ufw.conf.

ufw.title: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) state and rules
ufw.desc: Uncomplicated Firewall status, default policies, configured rules, and application profiles on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and EPEL systems. Check `status` to confirm the firewall is active, and the `defaultIncoming` / `defaultOutgoing` / `defaultRouted` policies for the baseline stance (a hardened host typically denies incoming by default). Enumerate `rules` to audit the explicit allow/deny entries and `applications` for the service profiles UFW can reference by name.

ufw.application.name: ufw.application
ufw.application.title: UFW application profile from /etc/ufw/applications.d/
ufw.application.desc: Named application profile that maps a service to the ports it needs, so UFW rules can reference it by name instead of listing ports. Each profile carries a `name` (for example "Nginx Full"), a human-readable `title` and `description`, and the `ports` specification it opens.

ufw.rule.name: ufw.rule

interface.name: interface
interface.title: Network interface (e.g., "eth0"), empty if not specified
interface.desc: For a routed (FWD) rule that names both interfaces, such as `ufw route allow in on eth0 out on eth1`, the incoming interface.

ipv6.name: ipv6
ipv6.title: Whether this is an IPv6 rule

number.name: number
number.title: Rule number (sequential across IPv4 and IPv6 rules; may differ from `ufw status numbered`)

port.name: port
port.title: Port or port range (e.g., "22", "6000:6007", "any")

raw.name: raw
raw.title: Raw rule text as reported by ufw

ufw.rule.title: Individual UFW rule
ufw.rule.desc: Single UFW rule as reported by `ufw status`, covering the action taken, the traffic direction, and the addresses, ports, protocol, and interface it matches. The `action` (ALLOW, DENY, REJECT, LIMIT), `direction`, and `port`/`from`/`to` fields together describe what the rule permits or blocks; `ipv6` flags IPv6 rules, and `raw` preserves the original text.

usb.name: usb

device.name: device
device.title: Experimental: USB device
device.desc: Single attached USB device. `vendorId` and `productId` identify the hardware model, `class`/`className` give its function (e.g. mass storage, HID, hub), `serial` uniquely identifies the unit where the device reports one, and `isRemovable` distinguishes hot-pluggable peripherals from fixed internal devices.

usb.title: USB device inventory (experimental)
usb.desc: USB devices attached to the host, each with its vendor and product IDs, manufacturer, serial number, device class, and connection speed. The `devices` list inventories connected peripherals so you can flag removable storage or unexpected hardware.

usb.device.name: usb.device

class.name: class
class.title: USB device class code (e.g., "08" for mass storage, "03" for HID)

protocol.name: protocol
protocol.title: USB protocol code within the device class

usb.device.title: Experimental: USB device
usb.device.desc: Single attached USB device. `vendorId` and `productId` identify the hardware model, `class`/`className` give its function (e.g. mass storage, HID, hub), `serial` uniquely identifies the unit where the device reports one, and `isRemovable` distinguishes hot-pluggable peripherals from fixed internal devices.

user.name: user

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether the account is enabled (not locked or disabled)

hasLoginShell.name: hasLoginShell
hasLoginShell.title: Whether the account's shell starts an interactive session
hasLoginShell.desc: False when shell is `nologin`, `false`, or `true` in /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, or /usr/sbin (so both /sbin/nologin and /usr/sbin/nologin, and both /bin/false and /usr/bin/false, count). True for every other shell, including an empty one, which means /bin/sh. /etc/shells is not consulted: login and sshd do not read it, and some distributions list /bin/false in it. Null on Windows.

loggedIn.name: loggedIn
loggedIn.title: Whether the user currently has an active login session

ntuserDat.name: ntuserDat
ntuserDat.title: Path to this user's NTUSER.DAT registry hive file (Windows)
ntuserDat.desc: The per-user registry hive on disk, located at `<home>\NTUSER.DAT`. Pass it together with `sid` to `registrykey`/`registrykey.property` to read a user's HKCU settings even when their hive is not loaded, for example a SYSTEM scan running with no interactive session. Empty on non-Windows platforms or when the home directory is unknown.

shell.name: shell
shell.title: Login shell configured for the user (e.g., /bin/bash, /usr/sbin/nologin)

sshkeys.name: sshkeys
sshkeys.title: Private SSH keys discovered in the user's home directory

system.name: system
system.title: Whether this is a system account rather than an interactive user
system.desc: On Linux, true when uid is below UID_MIN, or above UID_MAX and at most 65535 outside the systemd-homed range 60001 to 60513. The upper band holds `nobody` (65534), Debian's static allocations (60000 to 64999) and systemd dynamic service users; uids above 65535 are container and directory-service ranges and count as regular users. UID_MIN and UID_MAX come from /etc/login.defs (or /usr/etc/login.defs when /etc has none), defaulting to 1000 and 60000 when the file is absent or a value is unset or unparsable. Root (uid 0) counts as a system account. On macOS, true when uid is below 500, which covers root, the `_`-prefixed service accounts, and `nobody` (-2). On FreeBSD, true when uid is below minuid, or above maxuid and at most 65535, which covers root, the service accounts and `nobody` (65534). minuid and maxuid come from /etc/pw.conf, defaulting to 1000 and 32000 like pw(8) when the file is absent or a value is unset or unparsable. Null on Windows and on other Unix platforms, which have no common convention. Combine with hasLoginShell to find service accounts that can log in, for example `users.where(system && name != "root").none(hasLoginShell)`.

user.title: User account on the system
user.desc: Single local user account: numeric UID and primary GID (Windows SID where applicable), name, home directory, configured login shell, and an `enabled` flag. Surfaces the primary `group` reference, the `authorizedkeys` resource that parses the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, the SSH private keys discovered in the user's home, and a `loggedIn` predicate that reflects whether the user currently has an active session. Used for identity audits, dormant-account hygiene, and SSH-key inventories.

users.name: users
users.title: All user accounts configured on the system
users.desc: Collection of every local `user` on the asset. The entry point for fleet-wide identity audits, e.g. asserting that every account with UID < 1000 is enabled, that no account shares another's home directory, or that no human user has the shell set to `/bin/bash` outside an approved list.

extensions.name: extensions

paths.name: paths

vscode.title: Visual Studio Code (and forks)
vscode.desc: Installed editor extensions discovered across all users for VS Code and compatible forks (Cursor, Windsurf, and similar). Iterate `extensions` to inventory what is installed per editor, review publishers and versions, and identify untrusted or outdated extensions. `paths` lists the extension directories that were searched.

vulnmgmt.title: Asset vulnerability assessment
vulnmgmt.desc: Vulnerability data Mondoo derives for an asset by joining its installed-package inventory and platform identity against the curated CVE and advisory feed. Exposes every CVE affecting the asset, every vendor advisory that mentions one of those CVEs, the affected packages with their currently-installed and patched-available versions, the timestamp of the last assessment run, and the rolled-up CVSS statistics: the surface used to score asset risk and to drive patch-status policies.

warp.name: warp

configPath.name: configPath
configPath.title: Path to the Warp configuration directory

package.name: package
package.title: Package that installed this tool
package.desc: Resolves to the system-package-manager entry that installed the tool when one can be identified; otherwise an abstract package (origin "unknown", empty format, absent from `packages`) that records the tool's presence and, where determinable, an inferred version. Read `.installed` for the install signal, or any package field (`version`, `purl`, `vendor`) for detail.

runtime.name: runtime
runtime.title: Host the agent runs in
runtime.desc: The environment the agent runs inside: the operating system for a standalone agent, the IDE/editor for an editor plugin, or the browser for a browser extension. The runtime's `package` carries the host's software identity (version and purl where known) so its own version and vulnerabilities can be looked up like any other software. Optional; null when the host cannot be determined.

skill.name: skill
skill.title: Warp skill
skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for Warp under the shared .agents/skills directory. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

skills.name: skills
skills.title: Skills installed for the agent, one resource per discovered SKILL.md file

warp.title: Warp AI terminal instance
warp.desc: Warp, an AI-powered terminal, installed on the target. Reports its presence and version via package, the host it runs in via runtime, and the SKILL.md definitions installed for it via skills. Warp reads skills from the shared .agents/skills directory in each user's home rather than its own .warp config directory; pass configPath to target a non-default install. Auditing this resource shows whether the agent is present and what skills extend it. URL: https://www.warp.dev/

warp.skill.name: warp.skill

allowedTools.name: allowedTools
allowedTools.title: Tools the skill is allowed to use
allowedTools.desc: Tool identifiers parsed from the frontmatter `allowed-tools` field (a comma-separated list), naming the capabilities the skill may invoke such as file edits, shell commands, or web access. Empty when the skill declares no restriction. The key field for reviewing what an installed skill is permitted to do.

argumentHint.name: argumentHint
argumentHint.title: Hint for expected arguments
argumentHint.desc: Usage hint from the frontmatter `argument-hint` field, shown when the skill is invoked. Empty when unset.

content.name: content
content.title: Full raw content of the SKILL.md file
content.desc: Complete Markdown body of the skill, including the YAML frontmatter and the prose instructions the agent follows. Inspect it to review exactly what an installed skill tells the agent to do.

description.name: description
description.title: Skill description
description.desc: Free-text summary from the frontmatter `description` field, stating what the skill does and when the agent should invoke it.

name.name: name
name.title: Skill name
name.desc: Name from the SKILL.md YAML frontmatter `name` field, falling back to the skill's directory name when the frontmatter omits it.

purl.name: purl
purl.title: Package URL identifying the skill's git origin

sha256.title: SHA-256 hash of the skill content
sha256.desc: Hex-encoded SHA-256 digest of content, for detecting drift or pinning a known-good skill definition against a baseline.

source.title: Filesystem path to the SKILL.md file that defines the skill

warp.skill.title: Warp skill
warp.skill.desc: A single SKILL.md definition discovered for Warp under the shared .agents/skills directory. Each skill is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter that adds instructions and tool access to the assistant; auditing them surfaces the capabilities granted.

windows.name: windows

acl.name: acl
acl.title: Windows access control list
acl.desc:
Discretionary access control list of a filesystem object, selected by `path`, for example `windows.acl("C:\\inetpub")` or `windows.acl(path: "C:\\Windows\\System32\\dns")`. Exposes the object's owner and primary group, whether it still inherits permissions from its parent, the security descriptor in SDDL form, and every access control entry with the principal it applies to and the rights it grants or denies.

This is the Windows counterpart of `file.permissions`, which models a POSIX mode and cannot express an access control entry, an inherited permission, or the difference between an owner and a principal. Also reachable as `file.acl` so it composes with `files.find`.

Each entry carries both the raw `rightsMask` and named predicates derived from it (`allowsWrite`, `allowsFullControl`, and so on). Prefer the predicates: the `rights` label is unreliable, since .NET renders a mask containing generic bits as a bare number rather than a name, and a principal granted Modify is a writer whose label does not contain the word Write.

auditPolicy.name: auditPolicy
auditPolicy.title: Windows advanced audit policy
auditPolicy.desc: Effective Windows advanced audit policy: every audit subcategory together with whether success and failure events are audited. Subcategory names and categories are reported in English regardless of the OS display language, so the same audit works unchanged on localized systems. Iterate the subcategories to assert audit coverage, for example `windows.auditPolicy.where(category == "Account Logon").all(success)`, or select a single subcategory with windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.

bitlocker.name: bitlocker
bitlocker.title: Windows BitLocker drive encryption
bitlocker.desc: BitLocker Drive Encryption state across volumes: the encryption, lock, and protection status of each `volume`, plus the BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings under `policy`. Use it to verify that OS and data drives are encrypted and protected.

certificate.name: certificate
certificate.title: Certificate in a Windows certificate store
certificate.desc: Single certificate as it sits in one store: the `store` holding it, the `location` that scopes it to the machine or to one account, its `thumbprint`, and whether the store also holds the matching private key. `store` carries the trust decision rather than the certificate itself. A certificate in Root is trusted as a certification authority, one in Disallowed is explicitly distrusted, and one in TrustedPublisher lets code it signed run without prompting, so the same certificate means different things in different stores. Read `certificate` for the subject, issuer, validity dates and extensions.

certificates.name: certificates
certificates.title: Certificates held in the Windows certificate stores

computerInfo.name: computerInfo
computerInfo.title: A consolidated object of system and operating system properties

defender.name: defender
defender.title: Microsoft Defender Antivirus
defender.desc: Complete runtime status and configuration of Microsoft Defender Antivirus, so policies can assert on every Defender security control. The `status` field exposes the live engine, signature, and protection state reported by Get-MpComputerStatus (real-time protection, behavior monitoring, network inspection, tamper protection, scan ages, and signature freshness). The `preferences` field exposes the configurable policy reported by Get-MpPreference, grouped into scan, real-time, cloud-delivered protection, signature-update, threat-action, controlled-folder-access, network-protection, and remediation settings, plus exclusions and Attack Surface Reduction rules. The `threats` and `threatDetections` fields expose the recorded threat history. On systems without Defender (for example servers running a third-party antivirus) these fields resolve to null rather than failing the query.

deviceGuard.name: deviceGuard
deviceGuard.title: Device Guard policy (Virtualization-Based Security, HVCI, and Credential Guard)

disk.name: disk
disk.title: Disk attached to a Windows computer
disk.desc: A physical or virtual disk as Windows Storage Management reports it through the MSFT_Disk class. Covers identity (`number`, `friendlyName`, `serialNumber`, `uniqueId`), capacity (`size` in bytes), how the disk is attached (`busType`), how it is laid out (`partitionStyle`), whether it holds the boot or system partition, and its offline, read-only, operational, and health state. For example, `windows.disks.where(isBoot).all(size >= 64 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)` checks the capacity of the disk Windows runs from.

disks.name: disks
disks.title: Disks attached to this computer, as reported by Windows Storage Management
disks.desc: Physical and virtual disks from the MSFT_Disk class, the same set that Get-Disk lists: size, bus type, partition style, and whether the disk holds the boot or system partition. `windows.disks.where(isBoot)` selects the disk that holds the running Windows installation.

dnsServer.name: dnsServer
dnsServer.title: Windows DNS Server
dnsServer.desc: Configuration of the Windows DNS Server role: global server settings, recursion, resolver cache hardening, forwarders, root hints, response rate limiting, stale record scavenging, event and debug logging, and every zone the server hosts together with its zone transfer, dynamic update and DNSSEC signing configuration. Backed by the DnsServer PowerShell module, which is read once per scan in a single batched call rather than one call per field. Every field requires the DNS Server role to be installed; gate an audit on `windows.serverFeature(name: "DNS").installed` so the checks do not run on hosts that are not name servers. That gate narrows an audit but does not close it: a host where the role was added and the restart has not happened yet reports the feature as installed while the management module is still absent, and every field here reports an error on such a host rather than a configuration. Complements the client-side `dns` resource in the network provider, which resolves names through the public DNS system and cannot see a server's own configuration.

driver.name: driver
driver.title: Windows kernel or file system driver
driver.desc: Single driver registered with the service control manager: the service `name` it loads under, the on-disk `path` of its image, the `startMode` that decides when it loads, and whether it is currently `running`. `signed` and `signer` carry the Authenticode verdict on the image, which is what a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver audit reads, and `purl` identifies the driver for vulnerability matching in the same pkg:windows-driver namespace as windows.printerDriver.

drivers.name: drivers
drivers.title: Kernel and file system drivers registered on the machine

eventlog.name: eventlog
eventlog.title: Windows Event Log channel configuration
eventlog.desc: Size, retention policy and collection state of a single Windows Event Log channel. The `name` field selects the channel by its log name, for example `windows.eventlog(name: "Security")`, `windows.eventlog(name: "Application")` or a modern provider channel such as `windows.eventlog(name: "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational")`. `maxSizeKB` reports the maximum log file size in KB and `retention` decodes how the channel behaves when that size is reached. `retention` reads the registry alone, so it works on a connection that cannot run commands. `enabled`, `logFilePath`, `isClassicLog` and `recordCount` report the live channel state and need a connection that can run commands.

firewall.name: firewall
firewall.title: Windows Firewall (Advanced Security)
firewall.desc: Windows Firewall with Advanced Security posture: the global settings, the per-profile defaults (Domain, Private, Public), and every configured firewall rule. Use `profiles` to assert that the firewall is enabled and blocks inbound traffic by default on each profile, and `rules` to audit which allow/block rules are active. Backed by the `Get-NetFirewallProfile` and `Get-NetFirewallRule` PowerShell cmdlets, read from the ActiveStore: the effective policy, local configuration merged with Group Policy.

hotfix.name: hotfix
hotfix.title: Windows hotfix
hotfix.desc: Single installed Windows hotfix (a Quick Fix Engineering update): its `hotfixId` (for example "KB5034441"), the `description` type of the fix, the knowledge-base `caption` URL, the `installedOn` date, and the account that installed it. Audit patch compliance across `windows.hotfixes`, for example `windows.hotfixes.where(installedOn > time.now - 30*time.day)`.

logonSession.name: logonSession
logonSession.title: Windows logon session
logonSession.desc: Single active logon session as the Local Security Authority reports it: the `logonType` that created it, the `authenticationPackage` that authenticated it, the account it runs as, and when it started. `logonType` and its readable form `logonTypeName` carry most of the audit value, since a session's type says how it was established: 10 is an incoming Remote Desktop logon, 3 is a network logon, and 9 is a session created with alternate credentials. `authenticationPackage` reports whether the session was authenticated with Kerberos or fell back to NTLM.

lsa.name: lsa
lsa.title: Windows Local Security Authority (LSA) security policy
lsa.desc: Local Security Authority configuration that backs the "Network access", "Network security", and related security options under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. These values control anonymous access restrictions, blank-password use, LAN Manager authentication level, NTLM hashing, LSA protection (RunAsPPL), and audit behavior, including whether the system halts when it cannot write security audits. On/off settings are exposed as booleans and graded settings (such as the LAN Manager authentication level) as integers. NTLM (MSV1_0 and WDigest) settings are grouped under `ntlm` and the Netlogon secure-channel settings under `secureChannel`. The FIPS algorithm policy, the Kerberos supported encryption types, the LDAP signing and channel-binding requirements, and the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) minimum password length limit are read from their own keys and exposed directly on this resource. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, letting checks assert on configured-vs-default precisely.

optionalFeature.name: optionalFeature
optionalFeature.title: Windows optional feature (desktop-only)
optionalFeature.desc: Windows optional feature reported by `Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online`, the desktop equivalent of server roles. Select one by its feature name, for example `windows.optionalFeature(name: "SMB1Protocol")`, to check whether a legacy or risky feature (such as SMBv1, Telnet client, or PowerShell v2) is turned on. `enabled` is the simple boolean; `state` carries the underlying DISM feature state for more granular checks.

optionalFeatures.name: optionalFeatures
optionalFeatures.title: Information about optional features in a Windows image.

powershell.name: powershell
powershell.title: Windows PowerShell logging policy
powershell.desc: PowerShell logging settings configured via Group Policy under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell: Script Block Logging, Module Logging, Transcription, and the machine execution policy, together with the system lockdown state that decides the session language mode. The policy settings are GPO-only values with no effective fallback, so when a value is absent the corresponding field is null, which is distinguishable from an explicit 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

printerDrivers.name: printerDrivers
printerDrivers.title: Print drivers registered with the Windows spooler
printerDrivers.desc: Print drivers as the spooler reports them, with the vendor version, the manufacturer, the print environment each is registered under, and the INF the package was installed from. Use it to assert which drivers are present and at which version. Drivers are read from the spooler rather than from installed software, because a driver delivered as an INF/CAB package lands in the driver store and creates no Add/Remove Programs entry, so a software inventory cannot see it while the spooler is still loading it.

rdp.name: rdp
rdp.title: Windows Remote Desktop / Terminal Services configuration
rdp.desc: Effective Remote Desktop (Terminal Services) policy posture: whether Network Level Authentication is required, the negotiated security layer and minimum client encryption level, device and resource redirection toggles, credential handling, and session idle / disconnection time limits. Each field resolves the Group Policy value (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft \Windows NT\Terminal Services) first, then the per-listener configuration (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp), and finally the documented Windows default when neither is set, so audits can assert the effective state without handling missing registry values.

schannel.name: schannel
schannel.title: Windows Schannel TLS configuration
schannel.desc:
Schannel (Secure Channel) TLS cipher-suite, supported-group, and signature-algorithm configuration that backs the Microsoft TLS/SSL stack, read from the effective local Schannel store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Cryptography\Configuration\Local\SSL. The 00010002 subkey holds the ordered cipher-suite list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value and the ordered elliptic-curve / supported-group list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `EccCurves` value, the same list `Get-TlsEccCurve` reports. The 00010003 subkey holds the ordered signature-algorithm list in its REG_MULTI_SZ `Functions` value. On Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 the supported-group list is where post-quantum ML-KEM key-exchange groups (for example secp256r1_mlkem768) appear once enabled.

When a key or value is absent (the common case on older Windows, on systems using the default order, and on non-Windows platforms) the list accessors resolve to an empty list and pqcKeyExchangeEnabled resolves to false rather than failing.

The protocols, ciphers, hashes, and keyExchangeAlgorithms lists come from the separate per-algorithm override store under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL. Windows applies a built-in default to every algorithm that has no override there, and that default differs between Windows releases, so an absent registry value does not mean the algorithm is off. Each list therefore always contains the well-known algorithm names, whether or not the registry mentions them, and reports configured as false with a null enablement for the ones it does not. Write audits against configured and the enablement fields together, for example `windows.schannel.protocols.where(name == "TLS 1.0").all(clientConfigured && clientEnabled == false)`, so a host that never set the value fails instead of passing on a null.

scheduledTask.name: scheduledTask
scheduledTask.title: Windows Task Scheduler task
scheduledTask.desc: Registered task from the Windows Task Scheduler: its identity (`name`, `path`, `uri`), run `state`, whether it is `enabled`, descriptive metadata (`description`, `author`), and the security context it runs under via `principal`. The `actions` it executes, the `triggers` that launch it, and its full `settings` are exposed as nested resources, while `lastRunTime`, `nextRunTime`, `lastTaskResult`, and `missedRuns` report the most recent run-time information. Audit which tasks run, as whom, and on what schedule, for example `windows.scheduledTasks.where(enabled).where(principal.runLevel == "Highest")` surfaces enabled tasks running with the highest available privileges.

security.name: security
security.title: Windows registered security products
security.desc: Antivirus, anti-spyware, and firewall providers registered with the Windows Security Center. Use `products` to verify that an up-to-date, enabled security product is present, for example `windows.security.products.where(type == "antivirus").any(productState == "on")`.

serverFeature.name: serverFeature
serverFeature.title: Windows Server role, role service, or feature
serverFeature.desc: Installable Windows Server component reported by `Get-WindowsFeature`. Select one by its command name, for example `windows.serverFeature(name: "Web-Server")`, to check whether a role such as IIS, DNS, or Hyper-V is present. `installed` is the simple boolean check, while `installState` distinguishes fully installed from removed or available-for-install states.

serverFeatures.name: serverFeatures
serverFeatures.title: Information about Windows Server roles, role services, and features that are available for installation and installed on a specified server.

smb.name: smb
smb.title: Windows SMB (Server Message Block) server
smb.desc: SMB shares published by the host, active inbound client sessions, and outbound connections to other SMB servers, along with the server and client registry hardening configuration and whether the deprecated SMBv1 driver is still enabled. Backed by the `Get-SmbShare`, `Get-SmbSession`, and `Get-SmbConnection` PowerShell cmdlets plus registry reads.

spooler.name: spooler
spooler.title: Windows Print Spooler security configuration
spooler.desc:
Hardening-relevant state of the Windows Print Spooler and printing subsystem. The fields are sourced from the Group Policy printer keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers (and its PointAndPrint, RPC, IPP, and WPP subkeys), the machine-wide HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print key, and the spooler service start configuration under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Spooler. These controls address the PrintNightmare and related spooler vulnerabilities: whether the service is disabled, whether remote RPC is accepted, and how Point-and-Print driver installation is restricted.

Integer settings that are not present in the registry resolve to null so "not configured" is distinguishable from an explicit value of 0 (important because several controls, for example registerRemoteRpcEndpoint == 0, are compliant precisely when set to 0). Boolean settings resolve to their documented Windows default when the value is absent.

telemetry.name: telemetry
telemetry.title: Windows diagnostic data (telemetry) and consumer cloud-content policy
telemetry.desc: Effective Windows privacy and telemetry posture read from the Group Policy keys HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DataCollection and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CloudContent. These are GPO-only DWORD values. The diagnostic data level is a graded integer; the remaining settings are on/off booleans. Every field is nullable so that an absent value (the policy is not configured) is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0. Read from the registry, so it is available even on connections that cannot run commands.

tpm.name: tpm
tpm.title: Windows Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
tpm.desc: Trusted Platform Module state: whether a TPM is present, ready for use, enabled, and activated, along with its manufacturer, its major specification version, its dictionary-attack lockout state, and whether Windows provisions it automatically. Presence and a 2.0 specification version are prerequisites for Windows 11 readiness and several BitLocker and device-health controls, and a locked out or unprovisioned TPM is present without being usable. On a system without a TPM the fields resolve cleanly (present is false) rather than erroring.

uac.name: uac
uac.title: Windows User Account Control (UAC) policy
uac.desc: User Account Control settings that back the "User Account Control" security options, read from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, together with the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy value in the same key that governs UAC remote restrictions for local accounts. These control whether Admin Approval Mode is on, how administrators and standard users are prompted for elevation, whether prompts use the secure desktop, installer detection, UIAccess restrictions, file and registry virtualization, and whether remote connections by local administrators receive a filtered token. On/off settings are exposed as booleans, with any non-zero DWORD reading true, and the two prompt behaviors as integers. Values are nullable: an absent value resolves to null so it is distinguishable from an explicit false or 0, and each field names the Windows default that applies when it is absent. Checks on a setting whose secure state is the default should therefore accept null, for example `windows.uac.localAccountTokenFilterPolicy != true`.

update.name: update
update.title: Windows Update Agent
update.desc: How a Windows host receives updates and what it has applied or has pending. The `config` field surfaces Windows Update Agent configuration and freshness (the effective catalog source, WSUS settings, the last successful detection / download / install times, and whether a reboot is pending). `installed` lists the updates the agent has applied (the installed-KB history), and `available` lists updates the agent has found but not yet installed, answered from the cache of its last detection rather than a live scan. Configuration is read from the registry and works even on connections that cannot run commands; the installed and available collections fall back to the Windows Update Agent COM API when commands are available.

winrm.name: winrm
winrm.title: Windows Remote Management (WinRM)
winrm.desc: Effective WinRM (Windows Remote Management) policy posture for both the WinRM client and service, plus the WinRS remote shell setting and the WinRM service start mode. The client and service settings are read from the Group Policy key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WinRM; these are GPO-only values with no per-listener effective fallback, so when a value is absent the documented Windows default applies. `serviceStartMode` reflects HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinRM\Start. Those fields are read from the registry, so they are available even on connections that cannot run commands. `listeners`, `client.trustedHosts`, `service.ipv4Filter` and `service.ipv6Filter` report the live WS-Management configuration instead and need a connection that can run commands.

windows.title: Windows-specific operating system surfaces
windows.desc: Windows host settings not covered by the cross-platform resources: consolidated `computerInfo`, installed `hotfixes`, Server roles and features, image `optionalFeatures`, attached `disks`, scheduled tasks, and hardening controls (Device Guard, Exploit Protection, SmartScreen). A starting point for Windows-specific audits.

windows.acl.name: windows.acl

allowedWritePrincipals.name: allowedWritePrincipals
allowedWritePrincipals.title: Principals granted write access by an allow entry
allowedWritePrincipals.desc:
The account names of every allow entry whose rights include any form of write, in the order the entries appear. Answers "who can change this object" directly, for example `windows.acl("C:\\inetpub").allowedWritePrincipals.all(_ in ["BUILTIN\\Administrators", "NT AUTHORITY\\SYSTEM"])`.

Deny entries are not subtracted. A deny entry only removes access, so this list is a superset of the principals that can really write, and an audit built on it reports a principal that a deny entry had already stopped rather than missing one that can write. Read `entries` when the deny entries matter.

auditEntries.name: auditEntries
auditEntries.title: System access control entries, the rules that decide what is audited
auditEntries.desc:
What the object records to the Security event log, rather than what it permits: each entry names a principal, the rights involved, and whether successful attempts, failed attempts, or both are audited. An object with no audit rule reports an empty list, and audits nothing.

Reading a system access control list requires the SeSecurityPrivilege right, which an unelevated session does not hold. Without it this field is an error rather than an empty list, so "nothing is audited here" can never be the answer to "the audit could not be read".

auditEntry.name: auditEntry
auditEntry.title: Windows audit control entry
auditEntry.desc:
Single entry of a system access control list: the principal whose attempts are recorded, the rights the rule covers, and whether success, failure, or both are written to the Security event log. Iterated from `windows.acl.auditEntries`.

An audit rule only takes effect while the matching advanced audit policy subcategory is enabled, which `windows.auditPolicy` reports. A rule present here with "Object Access / File System" auditing switched off records nothing.

entries.name: entries
entries.title: Access control entries

entry.name: entry
entry.title: Windows access control entry
entry.desc: Single entry of a discretionary access control list: the principal it applies to, whether it allows or denies, the rights involved, and whether it was inherited from a parent object. Iterated from `windows.acl.entries`.

inheritanceEnabled.name: inheritanceEnabled
inheritanceEnabled.title: Whether the object still inherits access control entries from its parent
inheritanceEnabled.desc: False when inheritance has been broken, in which case the entries on the object are the whole story and changes to the parent no longer reach it.

owner.name: owner
owner.title: Account that owns the object
owner.desc: In DOMAIN\name form, for example BUILTIN\Administrators. The owner can always rewrite the access control list regardless of the entries in it, so an unexpected owner defeats every other restriction on the object.

ownerSid.name: ownerSid
ownerSid.title: Security identifier of the owning account, empty when it cannot be resolved

sddl.name: sddl
sddl.title: Security descriptor in Security Descriptor Definition Language form

windows.acl.title: Windows access control list
windows.acl.desc:
Discretionary access control list of a filesystem object, selected by `path`, for example `windows.acl("C:\\inetpub")` or `windows.acl(path: "C:\\Windows\\System32\\dns")`. Exposes the object's owner and primary group, whether it still inherits permissions from its parent, the security descriptor in SDDL form, and every access control entry with the principal it applies to and the rights it grants or denies.

This is the Windows counterpart of `file.permissions`, which models a POSIX mode and cannot express an access control entry, an inherited permission, or the difference between an owner and a principal. Also reachable as `file.acl` so it composes with `files.find`.

Each entry carries both the raw `rightsMask` and named predicates derived from it (`allowsWrite`, `allowsFullControl`, and so on). Prefer the predicates: the `rights` label is unreliable, since .NET renders a mask containing generic bits as a bare number rather than a name, and a principal granted Modify is a writer whose label does not contain the word Write.

windows.acl.auditEntry.name: windows.acl.auditEntry

auditFlags.name: auditFlags
auditFlags.title: Which outcomes are audited, as Windows labels them
auditFlags.desc: One of None, Success, Failure, or "Success, Failure". Read `auditsSuccess` and `auditsFailure` for assertions rather than matching this string.

identity.name: identity
identity.title: Account whose attempts the entry records, in DOMAIN\name form

inheritanceFlags.name: inheritanceFlags
inheritanceFlags.title: How the entry propagates to child objects
inheritanceFlags.desc: For example "ContainerInherit, ObjectInherit", or None when the entry applies only to this object.

isInherited.name: isInherited
isInherited.title: Whether the entry was inherited from a parent object rather than set on this one

propagationFlags.name: propagationFlags
propagationFlags.title: How inheritance is applied to children, for example InheritOnly or None

rights.name: rights
rights.title: Rights the entry audits, as Windows labels them
rights.desc: For example FullControl, or "Modify, Synchronize". Unreliable for assertions: a mask containing generic bits has no label and renders as a bare signed number. Read `rightsMask` when the exact rights matter.

rightsMask.name: rightsMask
rightsMask.title: Raw access mask the entry audits
rightsMask.desc: The 32 bit access mask widened to a signed 64 bit value, so masks with the high generic bits set stay positive rather than appearing negative.

sid.name: sid
sid.title: Security identifier of the account, empty when it cannot be resolved
sid.desc: An entry whose identity cannot be translated is still reported, with the raw identity kept, rather than being dropped from the list.

windows.acl.auditEntry.title: Windows audit control entry
windows.acl.auditEntry.desc:
Single entry of a system access control list: the principal whose attempts are recorded, the rights the rule covers, and whether success, failure, or both are written to the Security event log. Iterated from `windows.acl.auditEntries`.

An audit rule only takes effect while the matching advanced audit policy subcategory is enabled, which `windows.auditPolicy` reports. A rule present here with "Object Access / File System" auditing switched off records nothing.

windows.acl.entry.name: windows.acl.entry

allowsDelete.name: allowsDelete
allowsDelete.title: Whether the entry grants delete on the object or its children

allowsExecute.name: allowsExecute
allowsExecute.title: Whether the entry grants execute or directory traverse

allowsFullControl.name: allowsFullControl
allowsFullControl.title: Whether the entry grants full control

allowsPermissionChange.name: allowsPermissionChange
allowsPermissionChange.title: Whether the entry grants the right to change permissions or take ownership
allowsPermissionChange.desc: A principal with either can grant itself everything else, so it is equivalent to full control even when the mask does not say so.

allowsRead.name: allowsRead
allowsRead.title: Whether the entry grants any form of read

allowsWrite.name: allowsWrite
allowsWrite.title: Whether the entry grants any form of write
allowsWrite.desc: True for writing data, appending, changing attributes or extended attributes, deleting, and for the Modify, FullControl and generic write or all masks that contain those. This is the predicate behind "who can change this object".

identity.name: identity
identity.title: Account the entry applies to, in DOMAIN\name form

inheritanceFlags.name: inheritanceFlags
inheritanceFlags.title: How the entry propagates to child objects
inheritanceFlags.desc: For example "ContainerInherit, ObjectInherit", or None when the entry applies only to this object.

isInherited.name: isInherited
isInherited.title: Whether the entry was inherited from a parent object rather than set on this one

propagationFlags.name: propagationFlags
propagationFlags.title: How inheritance is applied to children, for example InheritOnly or None

rights.name: rights
rights.title: Rights as Windows labels them
rights.desc: For example FullControl, or "Modify, Synchronize". Unreliable for assertions: a mask containing generic bits has no label and renders as a bare signed number, and Modify grants write without saying so. Use the allows* predicates instead.

rightsMask.name: rightsMask
rightsMask.title: Raw access mask
rightsMask.desc: The 32 bit access mask widened to a signed 64 bit value, so masks with the high generic bits set stay positive rather than appearing negative.

sid.name: sid
sid.title: Security identifier of the account, empty when it cannot be resolved
sid.desc: An entry whose identity cannot be translated is still reported, with the raw identity kept, rather than being dropped from the list.

type.name: type
type.title: Whether the entry grants or denies the rights
type.desc: Either Allow or Deny. A deny entry takes precedence over an allow entry for the same principal.

windows.acl.entry.title: Windows access control entry
windows.acl.entry.desc: Single entry of a discretionary access control list: the principal it applies to, whether it allows or denies, the rights involved, and whether it was inherited from a parent object. Iterated from `windows.acl.entries`.

windows.auditPolicy.name: windows.auditPolicy

subcategory.name: subcategory
subcategory.title: Windows audit policy subcategory
subcategory.desc: Audit settings of a single advanced audit policy subcategory. The `name` field selects the subcategory by its English name, for example `windows.auditPolicy.subcategory(name: "Logon")`, and also accepts a subcategory GUID or the localized name the system reports. `success` and `failure` indicate whether the subcategory audits success and failure events, and `setting` names the setting in English; all three are read from the audit policy's numeric setting, so they are the same in every OS display language. A subcategory that is not present on the system audits nothing (`success` and `failure` are false and the reported fields are null) so checks against it fail rather than error.

windows.auditPolicy.title: Windows advanced audit policy
windows.auditPolicy.desc: Effective Windows advanced audit policy: every audit subcategory together with whether success and failure events are audited. Subcategory names and categories are reported in English regardless of the OS display language, so the same audit works unchanged on localized systems. Iterate the subcategories to assert audit coverage, for example `windows.auditPolicy.where(category == "Account Logon").all(success)`, or select a single subcategory with windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.

windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.name: windows.auditPolicy.subcategory

category.name: category
category.title: Audit category the subcategory belongs to (e.g. `Logon/Logoff`)
category.desc: Null when the subcategory GUID is not one this provider knows, which is also the state of a subcategory that is not present on the system at all.

exclusionSetting.name: exclusionSetting
exclusionSetting.title: Per-user audit exclusion setting as reported by the system

failure.name: failure
failure.title: Whether failure events are audited
failure.desc: Null when the setting could not be read.

guid.name: guid
guid.title: GUID that identifies the subcategory across Windows versions and languages

inclusionSetting.name: inclusionSetting
inclusionSetting.title: Audit setting as reported by the system in its display language
inclusionSetting.desc: Deprecated in favor of `setting`, `success`, and `failure`, which don't depend on the display language. One of `Success`, `Failure`, `Success and Failure`, or `No Auditing`, localized to the OS display language.

localizedName.name: localizedName
localizedName.title: Subcategory name as reported by the system in its display language

name.name: name
name.title: Subcategory name in English (e.g. `Logon`), stable across OS display languages

setting.name: setting
setting.title: Audit setting in English, whatever the OS display language
setting.desc: One of `Success and Failure`, `Success`, `Failure`, or `No Auditing`. Null when the setting could not be read, and for a subcategory that is not present on the system.

success.name: success
success.title: Whether success events are audited
success.desc: Null when the setting could not be read.

windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.title: Windows audit policy subcategory
windows.auditPolicy.subcategory.desc: Audit settings of a single advanced audit policy subcategory. The `name` field selects the subcategory by its English name, for example `windows.auditPolicy.subcategory(name: "Logon")`, and also accepts a subcategory GUID or the localized name the system reports. `success` and `failure` indicate whether the subcategory audits success and failure events, and `setting` names the setting in English; all three are read from the audit policy's numeric setting, so they are the same in every OS display language. A subcategory that is not present on the system audits nothing (`success` and `failure` are false and the reported fields are null) so checks against it fail rather than error.

windows.bitlocker.name: windows.bitlocker

available.name: available
available.title: Whether the BitLocker WMI provider can be read on this target
available.desc: The Win32_EncryptableVolume class that backs `volumes` is registered by the BitLocker feature, so on a host where the feature is not installed the namespace does not exist and no volume encryption state can be read at all. This field reports that without failing, so a policy can skip such a host deliberately instead of treating an unreadable host as an encrypted one. It is false when the provider cannot be read and true when it can, and it never reports an error or a null.

policy.name: policy
policy.title: BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings configured for this system

volume.name: volume
volume.title: Windows BitLocker volume
volume.desc: Single BitLocker-managed volume: the `deviceID`, `driveLetter`, `conversionStatus` (encryption/decryption progress), `encryptionMethod` (algorithm and key size), `lockStatus` (0 = accessible, 1 = locked), `persistentVolumeID`, `protectionStatus` (0 = off, 1 = on, 2 = unknown), and BitLocker `version`. Iterated from `windows.bitlocker.volumes`.

windows.bitlocker.title: Windows BitLocker drive encryption
windows.bitlocker.desc: BitLocker Drive Encryption state across volumes: the encryption, lock, and protection status of each `volume`, plus the BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings under `policy`. Use it to verify that OS and data drives are encrypted and protected.

windows.bitlocker.policy.name: windows.bitlocker.policy

disableExternalDmaUnderLock.name: disableExternalDmaUnderLock
disableExternalDmaUnderLock.title: Whether new DMA devices are disabled when this computer is locked (DisableExternalDMAUnderLock)

driveSettings.name: driveSettings
driveSettings.title: Windows BitLocker per-drive-type Group Policy (FVE) settings
driveSettings.desc: BitLocker policy values that apply to a single drive type (operating system, fixed data, or removable data). Fields that the drive type does not define, or that are not configured, are null. For example, operating system drives have no `allowUserCert`, and only removable data drives define `denyCrossOrg` and `denyWriteAccess`.

enableBdeWithNoTpm.name: enableBdeWithNoTpm
enableBdeWithNoTpm.title: Whether BitLocker is allowed without a compatible TPM (EnableBDEWithNoTPM)

fixedDataDrives.name: fixedDataDrives
fixedDataDrives.title: BitLocker policy settings for fixed data drives (FDV* values)

operatingSystemDrives.name: operatingSystemDrives
operatingSystemDrives.title: BitLocker policy settings for operating system drives (OS* values)

osAllowSecureBootForIntegrity.name: osAllowSecureBootForIntegrity
osAllowSecureBootForIntegrity.title: Whether Secure Boot is allowed for integrity validation on operating system drives (OSAllowSecureBootForIntegrity)

removableDataDrives.name: removableDataDrives
removableDataDrives.title: BitLocker policy settings for removable data drives (RDV* values)

useAdvancedStartup.name: useAdvancedStartup
useAdvancedStartup.title: Whether additional authentication is required at startup (UseAdvancedStartup)

useEnhancedPin.name: useEnhancedPin
useEnhancedPin.title: Whether enhanced PINs for startup are allowed (UseEnhancedPin)

windows.bitlocker.policy.title: Windows BitLocker Group Policy (FVE) settings
windows.bitlocker.policy.desc: BitLocker Drive Encryption Group Policy settings stored under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\FVE`. Global settings are exposed directly; per-drive-type settings are grouped under `operatingSystemDrives`, `fixedDataDrives`, and `removableDataDrives`. A field is null when the corresponding policy value is not configured.

windows.bitlocker.policy.driveSettings.name: windows.bitlocker.policy.driveSettings

activeDirectoryBackup.name: activeDirectoryBackup
activeDirectoryBackup.title: Whether BitLocker recovery information is saved to Active Directory Domain Services (*ActiveDirectoryBackup)

activeDirectoryInfoToStore.name: activeDirectoryInfoToStore
activeDirectoryInfoToStore.title: Configure what BitLocker recovery information is stored in AD DS (*ActiveDirectoryInfoToStore)
activeDirectoryInfoToStore.desc: 1 = store recovery passwords and key packages, 2 = store recovery passwords only. Null when not configured.

allowUserCert.name: allowUserCert
allowUserCert.title: Whether a certificate-based data recovery agent / smart card is allowed (*AllowUserCert)

denyCrossOrg.name: denyCrossOrg
denyCrossOrg.title: Whether write access is denied to devices configured in another organization (RDVDenyCrossOrg)

denyWriteAccess.name: denyWriteAccess
denyWriteAccess.title: Whether write access is denied to removable drives not protected by BitLocker (RDVDenyWriteAccess)

discoveryVolumeType.name: discoveryVolumeType
discoveryVolumeType.title: Configure the format used when a drive is auto-unlocked / discovery volume type (*DiscoveryVolumeType)

driveType.name: driveType
driveType.title: Drive type these settings apply to: operatingSystem, fixedData, or removableData

enforceUserCert.name: enforceUserCert
enforceUserCert.title: Whether a certificate-based data recovery agent / smart card is enforced (*EnforceUserCert)

hideRecoveryPage.name: hideRecoveryPage
hideRecoveryPage.title: Whether recovery options are omitted from the BitLocker setup wizard (*HideRecoveryPage)

manageDRA.name: manageDRA
manageDRA.title: Whether a data recovery agent is allowed (*ManageDRA)

recovery.name: recovery
recovery.title: Choose how BitLocker-protected drives can be recovered (*Recovery)

recoveryKey.name: recoveryKey
recoveryKey.title: Allow 256-bit recovery key (*RecoveryKey)
recoveryKey.desc: 0 = disallow, 1 = require, 2 = allow. Null when not configured.

recoveryPassword.name: recoveryPassword
recoveryPassword.title: Allow 48-digit recovery password (*RecoveryPassword)
recoveryPassword.desc: 0 = disallow, 1 = require, 2 = allow. Null when not configured.

requireActiveDirectoryBackup.name: requireActiveDirectoryBackup
requireActiveDirectoryBackup.title: Whether BitLocker is blocked until recovery information is stored in AD DS (*RequireActiveDirectoryBackup)

windows.bitlocker.policy.driveSettings.title: Windows BitLocker per-drive-type Group Policy (FVE) settings
windows.bitlocker.policy.driveSettings.desc: BitLocker policy values that apply to a single drive type (operating system, fixed data, or removable data). Fields that the drive type does not define, or that are not configured, are null. For example, operating system drives have no `allowUserCert`, and only removable data drives define `denyCrossOrg` and `denyWriteAccess`.

windows.bitlocker.volume.name: windows.bitlocker.volume

conversionStatus.name: conversionStatus
conversionStatus.title: Status of the encryption or decryption on the volume

encryptionMethod.name: encryptionMethod
encryptionMethod.title: Encryption algorithm and key size used on the volume

keyProtector.name: keyProtector
keyProtector.title: Windows BitLocker volume key protector
keyProtector.desc: Single protector of a BitLocker volume encryption key: what has to be presented before the volume can be unlocked. `keyProtectorType` is the readable name of the protector and `keyProtectorTypeCode` the raw Win32_EncryptableVolume code behind it, which together answer whether a volume is bound to the TPM alone, additionally requires a PIN or a startup key, or carries a recovery password an operator can escrow. No key material is exposed: `keyProtectorId` names a protector, it does not unlock one.

keyProtectors.name: keyProtectors
keyProtectors.title: Key protectors that unlock the volume encryption key
keyProtectors.desc: One entry per protector configured on the volume, for example a TPM binding alongside a 48-digit recovery password. An empty list means the volume has no key protectors at all, which is what a volume that has never had BitLocker enabled reports. Reading the protectors needs an elevated session; when they cannot be read the field reports that failure rather than an empty list, so "no recovery password" is never inferred from a permission problem.

lockStatus.name: lockStatus
lockStatus.title: Whether the contents of the volume are accessible from Windows
lockStatus.desc: 0 = Full contents of the volume are accessible 1 = All or a portion of the contents of the volume are not accessible

persistentVolumeID.name: persistentVolumeID
persistentVolumeID.title: Persistent identifier for the volume on this system

protectionStatus.name: protectionStatus
protectionStatus.title: Status of the volume, whether or not BitLocker is protecting the volume
protectionStatus.desc: 0 = Protection off 1 = Protection on 2 = Protection unknown

version.name: version
version.title: BitLocker Full Volume Encryption metadata version of the volume

windows.bitlocker.volume.title: Windows BitLocker volume
windows.bitlocker.volume.desc: Single BitLocker-managed volume: the `deviceID`, `driveLetter`, `conversionStatus` (encryption/decryption progress), `encryptionMethod` (algorithm and key size), `lockStatus` (0 = accessible, 1 = locked), `persistentVolumeID`, `protectionStatus` (0 = off, 1 = on, 2 = unknown), and BitLocker `version`. Iterated from `windows.bitlocker.volumes`.

windows.bitlocker.volume.keyProtector.name: windows.bitlocker.volume.keyProtector

keyProtectorId.name: keyProtectorId
keyProtectorId.title: Identifier of this key protector on the volume

keyProtectorType.name: keyProtectorType
keyProtectorType.title: Name of the key protector type
keyProtectorType.desc: One of Tpm, TpmPin, TpmStartupKey, TpmPinStartupKey, ExternalKey, RecoveryPassword, PublicKey, Password, TpmCertificate, Sid, or Unknown. A type outside that set reads as Unrecognized, with the raw value available in keyProtectorTypeCode.

keyProtectorTypeCode.name: keyProtectorTypeCode
keyProtectorTypeCode.title: Raw Win32_EncryptableVolume key protector type code
keyProtectorTypeCode.desc: 0 = unknown or other protector type, 1 = TPM, 2 = external key, 3 = numerical password, 4 = TPM and PIN, 5 = TPM and startup key, 6 = TPM and PIN and startup key, 7 = public key, 8 = passphrase, 9 = TPM certificate, 10 = security identifier.

windows.bitlocker.volume.keyProtector.title: Windows BitLocker volume key protector
windows.bitlocker.volume.keyProtector.desc: Single protector of a BitLocker volume encryption key: what has to be presented before the volume can be unlocked. `keyProtectorType` is the readable name of the protector and `keyProtectorTypeCode` the raw Win32_EncryptableVolume code behind it, which together answer whether a volume is bound to the TPM alone, additionally requires a PIN or a startup key, or carries a recovery password an operator can escrow. No key material is exposed: `keyProtectorId` names a protector, it does not unlock one.

windows.certificate.name: windows.certificate

certificate.name: certificate
certificate.title: Parsed certificate
certificate.desc: Subject, issuer, validity dates, extensions and public key. Null when the stored bytes could not be parsed, which leaves the store entry reportable rather than dropping it from the list.

hasPrivateKey.name: hasPrivateKey
hasPrivateKey.title: Whether the store also holds the certificate's private key
hasPrivateKey.desc: True for a certificate the host can authenticate or sign with, rather than one it merely trusts. The private key itself is never read.

location.name: location
location.title: Store location the certificate was found in
location.desc: Either "LocalMachine", the machine-wide store every account on the host sees, or "CurrentUser", the store belonging to the account the scan runs as. CurrentUser is not the store of any other user on the machine, so an audit of machine trust reads LocalMachine.

store.name: store
store.title: Name of the store the certificate was found in
store.desc: For example "Root" for trusted root certification authorities, "CA" for intermediates, "My" for certificates the host holds an identity for, "TrustedPublisher" for publishers whose signed code runs without prompting, and "Disallowed" for certificates that are explicitly distrusted.

thumbprint.name: thumbprint
thumbprint.title: SHA-1 hash the store keys the certificate by
thumbprint.desc: Uppercase hex with no separators. Windows keys certificates by this value throughout its own tooling, so it is what matches a certificate against a vendor advisory or a removal instruction.

windows.certificate.title: Certificate in a Windows certificate store
windows.certificate.desc: Single certificate as it sits in one store: the `store` holding it, the `location` that scopes it to the machine or to one account, its `thumbprint`, and whether the store also holds the matching private key. `store` carries the trust decision rather than the certificate itself. A certificate in Root is trusted as a certification authority, one in Disallowed is explicitly distrusted, and one in TrustedPublisher lets code it signed run without prompting, so the same certificate means different things in different stores. Read `certificate` for the subject, issuer, validity dates and extensions.

windows.certificates.name: windows.certificates
windows.certificates.title: Certificates held in the Windows certificate stores

windows.defender.name: windows.defender

asrRule.name: asrRule
asrRule.title: Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction rule
asrRule.desc: Single Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule: its `id` (the rule GUID), the friendly `name` when the GUID is recognized, and the configured `action`. The `id` selects the rule, for example `windows.defender.preferences.attackSurfaceReductionRules.where(id == "...")`.

behavioralNetworkBlockSettings.name: behavioralNetworkBlockSettings
behavioralNetworkBlockSettings.title: Microsoft Defender behavioral network block settings
behavioralNetworkBlockSettings.desc: Behavioral network protection preferences that block attacks observed from the network: brute-force protection (against password-guessing attacks) and remote-encryption protection (against remote ransomware encryption). Each exposes its configured state, aggressiveness, and maximum block time.

cloudSettings.name: cloudSettings
cloudSettings.title: Microsoft Defender cloud-delivered protection settings
cloudSettings.desc: Microsoft Active Protection Service (MAPS) and cloud-delivered protection preferences: the reporting membership level, the sample-submission consent, the cloud block level and extended timeout, and the block-at-first-seen toggle. Together these control how much Defender relies on the cloud for rapid detection of new threats.

controlledFolderAccess.name: controlledFolderAccess
controlledFolderAccess.title: Microsoft Defender controlled folder access settings
controlledFolderAccess.desc: Controlled-folder-access (ransomware protection) configuration: whether it is enabled or in audit mode, the applications allowed to write to protected folders, and the list of additional protected folders beyond the system defaults.

enabled.name: enabled
enabled.title: Whether the Defender antimalware service and real-time antivirus and antispyware protection are all active

exclusions.name: exclusions
exclusions.title: Microsoft Defender scan exclusions
exclusions.desc: Every configured scan exclusion: file and folder `paths`, file `extensions`, `processes`, and `ipAddresses`. Empty lists mean no exclusions of that kind are configured. Exclusions are a common misconfiguration and malware-persistence vector, so audits often verify that these lists are empty or tightly scoped.

localSettingOverrides.name: localSettingOverrides
localSettingOverrides.title: Microsoft Defender local setting overrides
localSettingOverrides.desc:
Whether a locally configured preference is allowed to override the corresponding Group Policy setting. When an override is disabled (false) the policy value is enforced and users cannot change it locally, which is the hardened configuration.

Every field here is null on a host whose Defender platform does not report the preference. Recent platform releases dropped the LocalSettingOverride properties from Get-MpPreference, so on those hosts nothing about the overrides is known and a null must not be read as "no override allowed".

networkProtectionSettings.name: networkProtectionSettings
networkProtectionSettings.title: Microsoft Defender network protection settings
networkProtectionSettings.desc: Network-protection configuration: the enforcement mode and the toggles that extend protection to Windows Server, down-level clients, and datagram processing, plus DNS sinkhole enforcement. Network protection blocks outbound connections to malicious domains and IP addresses.

realTimeSettings.name: realTimeSettings
realTimeSettings.title: Microsoft Defender real-time protection settings
realTimeSettings.desc: Real-time protection preferences: the master real-time monitoring toggle, behavior monitoring, downloaded-file (IOAV) scanning, script scanning, on-access protection, the intrusion-prevention system, the scan direction, and file-hash computation. The toggles are phrased as "disable" flags, so false generally means the protection is on.

remediationSettings.name: remediationSettings
remediationSettings.title: Microsoft Defender remediation settings
remediationSettings.desc: Threat-remediation preferences: the scheduled remediation day and time, how long quarantined items are retained before purging, and whether system restore points are created before remediation.

scanSettings.name: scanSettings
scanSettings.title: Microsoft Defender scan settings
scanSettings.desc: Scheduled-scan and scan-behavior preferences: the schedule day and time, the quick-scan time, CPU load factor, and the toggles that disable scanning of archives, email, removable drives, mapped network drives, and network files. Useful for auditing whether periodic scans are scheduled and whether scanning coverage has been narrowed.

signatureSettings.name: signatureSettings
signatureSettings.title: Microsoft Defender signature and platform update settings
signatureSettings.desc: Definition, engine, and platform update preferences: the update schedule and interval, the catch-up interval, the fallback source order, file-share sources, and the release channels for definitions, engine, and platform. Useful for confirming signatures update frequently enough and from trusted sources.

status.name: status
status.title: Live engine, signature, and protection status (Get-MpComputerStatus)

threat.name: threat
threat.title: Microsoft Defender recorded threat
threat.desc: Single threat recorded in the Defender threat history: its `threatId`, `name`, `severityID`, `categoryID`, whether it `isActive` and whether it executed, and the affected `resources`. Useful for reviewing what Defender has detected on the host over time.

threatActionSettings.name: threatActionSettings
threatActionSettings.title: Microsoft Defender default threat actions
threatActionSettings.desc: Default remediation action applied to threats of each severity (severe, high, moderate, low, and unknown) plus any per-threat-ID action overrides. Audits use this to confirm that severe and high threats are quarantined or removed rather than allowed or left to user choice.

threatDetection.name: threatDetection
threatDetection.title: Microsoft Defender threat detection
threatDetection.desc: Single detection event recorded by Defender: the `detectionId`, the associated `threatId`, the `processName` and `domainUser` involved, the detection source and status, the action taken and whether it succeeded, and the detection and remediation timestamps.

threatDetections.name: threatDetections
threatDetections.title: Malware detections recorded by Defender
threatDetections.desc: An empty list means Defender has recorded no detections. Null means the history could not be read because Defender is not installed.

threatIdAction.name: threatIdAction
threatIdAction.title: Microsoft Defender per-threat-ID action override
threatIdAction.desc: Single override that pins the remediation action for a specific threat ID, pairing the `threatId` with the configured `action`. Overrides let an administrator handle one known threat differently from its severity default.

threats.name: threats
threats.title: Threats recorded in the Defender threat history
threats.desc: An empty list means Defender has recorded no threats. Null means the history could not be read because Defender is not installed, and must not be read as "no threats found".

windows.defender.title: Microsoft Defender Antivirus
windows.defender.desc: Complete runtime status and configuration of Microsoft Defender Antivirus, so policies can assert on every Defender security control. The `status` field exposes the live engine, signature, and protection state reported by Get-MpComputerStatus (real-time protection, behavior monitoring, network inspection, tamper protection, scan ages, and signature freshness). The `preferences` field exposes the configurable policy reported by Get-MpPreference, grouped into scan, real-time, cloud-delivered protection, signature-update, threat-action, controlled-folder-access, network-protection, and remediation settings, plus exclusions and Attack Surface Reduction rules. The `threats` and `threatDetections` fields expose the recorded threat history. On systems without Defender (for example servers running a third-party antivirus) these fields resolve to null rather than failing the query.

windows.defender.status.desc: Live state reported by Get-MpComputerStatus: whether the antimalware service and each protection component (real-time, behavior monitoring, IOAV, on-access, network inspection) are enabled, the engine and signature versions and their ages, the most recent quick and full scan times and whether they are overdue, tamper-protection state and source, and whether a reboot or signature update is pending. windows.defender.threat.name: windows.defender.threat

didThreatExecute.name: didThreatExecute
didThreatExecute.title: Whether the threat executed on the system

isActive.name: isActive
isActive.title: Whether the threat is currently active

name.name: name
name.title: Threat name as reported by Defender

resources.name: resources
resources.title: Resources (files, registry keys, processes) affected by the threat

rollupStatus.name: rollupStatus
rollupStatus.title: Aggregate rollup status of the threat

windows.defender.threat.title: Microsoft Defender recorded threat
windows.defender.threat.desc: Single threat recorded in the Defender threat history: its `threatId`, `name`, `severityID`, `categoryID`, whether it `isActive` and whether it executed, and the affected `resources`. Useful for reviewing what Defender has detected on the host over time.

windows.defender.threatActionSettings.name: windows.defender.threatActionSettings

highThreatDefaultAction.name: highThreatDefaultAction
highThreatDefaultAction.title: Default action for high-severity threats (see severeThreatDefaultAction for values)

lowThreatDefaultAction.name: lowThreatDefaultAction
lowThreatDefaultAction.title: Default action for low-severity threats (see severeThreatDefaultAction for values)

moderateThreatDefaultAction.name: moderateThreatDefaultAction
moderateThreatDefaultAction.title: Default action for moderate-severity threats (see severeThreatDefaultAction for values)

severeThreatDefaultAction.name: severeThreatDefaultAction
severeThreatDefaultAction.title: Default action for severe-severity threats
severeThreatDefaultAction.desc: 1 = clean, 2 = quarantine, 3 = remove, 6 = allow, 8 = user defined, 9 = no action, 10 = block.

unknownThreatDefaultAction.name: unknownThreatDefaultAction
unknownThreatDefaultAction.title: Default action for unknown-severity threats (see severeThreatDefaultAction for values)

windows.defender.threatActionSettings.title: Microsoft Defender default threat actions
windows.defender.threatActionSettings.desc: Default remediation action applied to threats of each severity (severe, high, moderate, low, and unknown) plus any per-threat-ID action overrides. Audits use this to confirm that severe and high threats are quarantined or removed rather than allowed or left to user choice.

windows.defender.threatDetection.name: windows.defender.threatDetection

cleaningActionID.name: cleaningActionID
cleaningActionID.title: Identifier of the cleaning action applied

currentThreatExecutionStatusID.name: currentThreatExecutionStatusID
currentThreatExecutionStatusID.title: Current execution status of the detected threat

domainUser.name: domainUser
domainUser.title: Domain user in whose context the detection occurred

initialDetectionTime.name: initialDetectionTime
initialDetectionTime.title: Time the threat was first detected

lastThreatStatusChangeTime.name: lastThreatStatusChangeTime
lastThreatStatusChangeTime.title: Time the threat status last changed

processName.name: processName
processName.title: Name of the process involved in the detection

resources.name: resources
resources.title: Resources (files, registry keys, processes) affected by the detection

threatId.name: threatId
threatId.title: Numeric threat identifier associated with the detection

windows.defender.threatDetection.title: Microsoft Defender threat detection
windows.defender.threatDetection.desc: Single detection event recorded by Defender: the `detectionId`, the associated `threatId`, the `processName` and `domainUser` involved, the detection source and status, the action taken and whether it succeeded, and the detection and remediation timestamps.

windows.defender.threatIdAction.name: windows.defender.threatIdAction

action.name: action
action.title: Action applied to the threat
action.desc: 1 = clean, 2 = quarantine, 3 = remove, 6 = allow, 8 = user defined, 9 = no action, 10 = block.

threatId.name: threatId
threatId.title: Threat ID the override applies to

windows.defender.threatIdAction.title: Microsoft Defender per-threat-ID action override
windows.defender.threatIdAction.desc: Single override that pins the remediation action for a specific threat ID, pairing the `threatId` with the configured `action`. Overrides let an administrator handle one known threat differently from its severity default.

windows.deviceGuard.name: windows.deviceGuard

availableSecurityProperties.name: availableSecurityProperties
availableSecurityProperties.title: Security properties the platform offers to Virtualization-Based Security (Win32_DeviceGuard AvailableSecurityProperties)
availableSecurityProperties.desc: One entry per available property: 0=no relevant properties, 1=hypervisor support, 2=Secure Boot, 3=DMA protection, 4=Secure Memory Overwrite, 5=NX protections, 6=SMM mitigations, 7=MBEC/GMET, 8=APIC virtualization. A service that will not start is usually missing one of these.

codeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus.name: codeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus
codeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus.title: Kernel-mode code integrity policy enforcement status (Win32_DeviceGuard CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus)

credentialGuardConfig.name: credentialGuardConfig
credentialGuardConfig.title: Credential Guard configuration (LsaCfgFlags)
credentialGuardConfig.desc: 0=off, 1=enabled with UEFI lock, 2=enabled without lock. Null when not configured.

hvciMatRequired.name: hvciMatRequired
hvciMatRequired.title: Whether HVCI requires a Memory Access Table (HVCIMATRequired)

hypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity.name: hypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity
hypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity.title: Hypervisor-Enforced Code Integrity / Memory Integrity (HypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity)
hypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity.desc: 0=disabled, 1=enabled with UEFI lock, 2=enabled without lock. Null when not configured.

kernelShadowStacksLaunch.name: kernelShadowStacksLaunch
kernelShadowStacksLaunch.title: Kernel-mode hardware-enforced stack protection (ConfigureKernelShadowStacksLaunch)
kernelShadowStacksLaunch.desc: 1=enabled in enforcement mode, 2=enabled in audit mode, 0=disabled. Null when not configured.

requirePlatformSecurityFeatures.name: requirePlatformSecurityFeatures
requirePlatformSecurityFeatures.title: Required platform security features for VBS (RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures)
requirePlatformSecurityFeatures.desc: 1=Secure Boot, 3=Secure Boot and DMA Protection. Null when not configured.

securityServicesConfigured.name: securityServicesConfigured
securityServicesConfigured.title: Security services configured for Virtualization-Based Security (Win32_DeviceGuard SecurityServicesConfigured)
securityServicesConfigured.desc: One entry per configured service: 0=no services configured, 1=Credential Guard, 2=memory integrity (HVCI), 3=System Guard Secure Launch, 4=SMM firmware measurement, 5=kernel-mode hardware-enforced stack protection, 6=kernel-mode hardware-enforced stack protection in audit mode, 7=hypervisor-enforced paging translation. Read alongside securityServicesRunning to find a service that is configured but is not running.

securityServicesRunning.name: securityServicesRunning
